- Apply semantic versioning correctly to libraries, services and APIs, and know when it does not apply. - Produce releases with changelogs, tags and artifacts that can be traced from a running system back to source. - Design a deprecation policy for APIs consumed by clients. - Coordinate releases of interdependent components without breaking consumers. ::: Chapters 9 and 10. :::

Version numbers are a communication protocol between producers and consumers of software. If 2.3.1 to 2.4.0 might break my integration, I must read every changelog and test every upgrade; if the convention guarantees it will not, I can upgrade with confidence. Release management is the discipline that makes the guarantee true, and that lets anyone answer "what exactly is running, and what changed since last week?"

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH , with optional pre-release ( 2.0.0-rc.1 ) and build metadata ( +build.42 ): - PATCH : backward-compatible bug fixes. Consumers upgrade freely. - MINOR : backward-compatible new functionality. Consumers upgrade freely; may adopt new features. - MAJOR : incompatible changes. Consumers must read the migration guide and change code. 0.y.z means "anything may change". Many projects stay there far too long; once anyone depends on you in production, release 1.0 and honour the contract. What counts as breaking? For a library: removing or renaming a public function, changing a signature or return type, tightening accepted inputs, changing default behaviour, raising the minimum runtime version. For an HTTP API: removing a field or endpoint, renaming a field, changing a type, making an optional parameter required, changing error codes clients depend on, changing authentication. Adding fields, endpoints, optional parameters and enum values is usually compatible if consumers were told to ignore unknown fields and handle unknown enum values; say so in your API documentation.

A deployed service has one version running at a time (or two, during rollout), chosen by you. Its consumers do not pick a version; they get whatever is deployed. So the service's build version (often just the Git SHA or a date-based tag like 2026.03.14.1 ) is for traceability, while its API version ( /v1/ , /v2/ ) is the contract consumers depend on. Part III chapter 2 covers API versioning in depth. Do not confuse the two: bumping the build version on every deploy is right; bumping the API version on every deploy is a disaster. Libraries, SDKs, CLI tools, Terraform modules, Helm charts and container base images that others consume follow semantic versioning strictly.

A release ties together: a Git tag, a changelog entry, built artifacts (container image, wheel, zip) with immutable identifiers, and a record of where and when it was deployed. Make the chain visible: # Tag and build git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release 2.4.0" git push origin v2.4.0 docker build -t registry/app:2.4.0 -t registry/app:sha-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \ --label org.opencontainers.image.revision=$(git rev-parse HEAD) \ --label org.opencontainers.image.version=2.4.0 . # /version endpoint: a production system should be able to say what it is @app.get("/version") def version(): return {"version": settings.app_version, "commit": settings.git_sha, "built_at": settings.build_time} The labels and the endpoint are populated at build time from the pipeline. During an incident, "which version is running?" should be answerable with one curl , not by asking around.

Keep CHANGELOG.md in the "Keep a Changelog" format: sections per version with Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. Write for the consumer: what they will notice and what they must do. Automation (Conventional Commits with tools like release-please or semantic-release ) can derive versions and changelog entries from commit messages like feat: , fix: , feat!: , which also forces thought about compatibility at commit time. Release notes for clients are a different document: fewer internals, more "what this means for you", written by a human.

When a client integrates against your API, removing anything becomes a negotiation. Publish a policy up front: 1. Mark deprecated elements in documentation and responses ( Deprecation and Sunset HTTP headers; @deprecated in SDKs). 2. Announce with a date and a migration path; log usage of deprecated features so you know who is still calling them. 3. Maintain the deprecated behaviour for a stated period (commonly 6–12 months for external APIs; shorter for internal ones). 4. Remove in a major version, after confirming usage is zero or stakeholders have signed off.

Frontend, backend and database rarely change in lockstep. Rules that keep rollouts safe: - Backend before frontend : the API must accept the new requests before any client sends them, and keep accepting old ones until all clients have moved. - Expand, then contract for databases: add columns and tables first (compatible with old code), deploy code that uses them, then remove old columns in a later release (Part X chapter 8). - Tolerant readers : consumers ignore unknown fields; producers never remove fields without the deprecation process. - Feature flags decouple deploy from release: ship the code dark, enable when all parts are in place.

Frequent small releases are safer than rare large ones: each carries less change, is easier to review, and if it fails, the suspect set is small. Teams deploying many times a day have lower change-failure rates than teams deploying monthly, not despite the frequency but because of what frequency forces: automation, small batches, good rollback. For clients who require scheduled releases, keep the internal cadence high (staging continuously) and batch only the production promotion.

Every release needs an answer to "how do we undo this?" Rolling back the application means deploying the previous artifact, which must still exist and still be compatible with the current database schema (this is why migrations are expand-first). Rolling forward means fixing quickly and releasing a new version; sensible when the fix is obvious and rollback is risky. Decide which applies before deploying, and write it in the deployment ticket.

- Breaking changes in minor versions, training consumers to distrust your versions. - Mutable tags ( latest , or re-tagging v1.2.0 to a new commit). - Services with no /version endpoint, so incidents begin with archaeology. - Removing API fields without a deprecation window because "nobody uses it" (someone does). - Frontend released before backend; users see errors for the duration of the gap. - Huge quarterly releases with dozens of changes and no idea which one broke things. questions A library changes a function's default timeout from 30 s to 10 s. Which version component should change? options PATCH MINOR MAJOR None; defaults are not part of the API answer explain Changing default behaviour can break consumers who relied on it. It is a breaking change. What should a deployed HTTP service's build version be used for? options Signalling API compatibility to consumers Traceability: linking the running instance to a commit, artifact and changelog Database schema versioning Nothing; services do not need versions answer explain API compatibility is communicated through the API version in the contract; the build version is for operations. Which deploy order is safe for a change that adds a field to an API response and displays it in the frontend? options Frontend first Backend first, then frontend Both simultaneously Order does not matter answer explain The frontend must not depend on something the backend does not yet provide. Backends must also tolerate old frontends. Why is

- Define the three architectural styles precisely and describe the operational cost of each. - Recognise when microservices solve a real problem and when they create one. - Design a modular monolith that can be split later without a rewrite. - Advise a client honestly on which style fits their team and constraints. ::: Chapters 1 and 11. :::

How you divide a system into deployable units determines how you build, test, deploy, scale, secure and debug it for years. The industry oscillated from monoliths to microservices and partly back, leaving many teams with distributed systems they did not need and cannot operate. Architecture should follow the problem and the team, not the conference circuit.

One codebase, one deployable, one process (or identical replicas of it), typically one database. Internal calls are function calls. A FastAPI application with routers for users, orders and billing, deployed as one container, is a monolith. Strengths: simplest to develop, test, deploy and debug; transactions across features are trivial; refactoring across boundaries is an IDE operation; one set of infrastructure to secure and monitor. Weaknesses: everything scales together (the PDF generator and the login endpoint share CPU); one bad deploy affects everything; large teams step on each other; the codebase can degrade into a tangle if modules are not enforced; a single runtime and language.

Still one deployable, but internally divided into modules with explicit boundaries: each module owns its tables, exposes a small interface, and is forbidden (by convention and by tooling) from reaching into another module's internals. Communication between modules goes through those interfaces, sometimes through in-process events. This captures most of the organisational benefits claimed for microservices (clear ownership, independent evolution, enforced contracts) with none of the distributed-systems cost. It is also the best preparation for extracting a service later, because the seams already exist.

Many independently deployable services, each owning its data, communicating over the network (HTTP, gRPC, messages). Each can use its own language, scale independently and be deployed by its own team on its own schedule. What you pay for that: every call across a boundary can fail, time out or be slow; data consistency across services needs sagas or eventual consistency instead of a transaction; debugging requires distributed tracing; each service needs its own pipeline, monitoring, secrets, scaling policy and on-call ownership; local development needs a way to run or mock a dozen services; versioning of inter-service contracts becomes a permanent concern; and the network itself must be secured service-to-service. Netflix-scale organisations absorb this with platform teams. A five-person team cannot. title The same features, three ways intro Click components to see what changes. Note where the network (and therefore failure) appears. nodes label Monolith users + orders + billing One process. A request to create an order calls billing.charge() as a function and writes users, orders and billing tables in one transaction. label One database Shared schema. Joins across features are easy. Enforcing that modules do not read each other's tables is a discipline problem. label Modular monolith users | orders | billing modules One process, but orders calls billing only through billing's public interface. Lint rules or import boundaries forbid cross-module internals. Each module owns it

Real reasons, in rough order of frequency: 1. Organisational scale : many teams need to deploy independently without coordinating releases. Below roughly 30–50 engineers this rarely applies. 2. Radically different scaling or runtime needs : a GPU inference component, a high-throughput ingestion path, a legacy system in another language. 3. Isolation requirements : a component handling card data (PCI scope) or a tenant that requires physical separation. 4. Independent failure domains where part of the product must stay up when another part is down, and the team can build the resilience patterns that make that true. A system is production-ready when it can be operated by people other than its authors, under real load and hostile input, with its failures detected, contained and recovered within agreed limits, without exposing data it should not, at a cost its owners accept. Every clause is load-bearing: - operated by people other than its authors : documented, automated, ownership assigned. - real load : capacity known, tested, scalable. - hostile input : validated, authenticated, authorised, hardened. - failures detected : observability and alerting. - contained : isolation, limits, graceful degradation. - recovered within agreed limits : backups, rollback, DR, SLOs. - without exposing data : confidentiality controls, privacy obligations. - at a cost its owners accept : budgeted, monitored, right-sized. "The feature works" is necessary and nowhere near sufficient.

No real system passes every item on day one. Prioritise by risk = likelihood × impact , then by cost to fix : 1. Fix before launch : anything that can leak client data or lose it irrecoverably (public database, no backups, secrets in Git, missing authorization checks), and anything that prevents you from knowing about failures (no alerting at all). 2. Fix within the first weeks : rollback automation, load test, runbooks for the two or three most likely incidents, cost alerts. 3. Schedule : tracing, chaos testing, DR drills, advanced security tooling. Write the gaps and the plan down. A readiness review that produces a list of accepted risks with owners and dates is a success; one that produces a "pass" with hidden gaps is a failure deferred.

A lightweight format that works for client deployments: 1. Two weeks before launch , the delivering engineer completes the checklist with evidence (links, screenshots, commands run) and lists known gaps. 2. In the 1960s and 70s, networks were built by vendors and each spoke its own language: an IBM network could not talk to a DEC network. The research that became the Internet asked a different question: how do you connect networks of networks owned by different organisations, running different hardware, with no central operator, so that any machine can reach any other, and so that the system keeps working when parts of it fail? The answers shaped everything you deploy today: 1. Packet switching. Data is chopped into small, independently routed packets rather than reserving a circuit. Links are shared; failures reroute. 2. Layering. Each layer provides a service to the one above and relies on the one below, so a web application does not care whether the bytes cross fibre, Wi-Fi or a satellite. 3. The end-to-end principle. The network core does one thing (deliver packets, best effort). Reliability, ordering, encryption and application semantics live at the endpoints. This is why your server implements TCP and TLS logic, and a router does not. 4. Decentralised addressing and routing. Addresses are allocated hierarchically; routes are exchanged between independent networks by a protocol that assumes no one is in charge.

A packet is a bounded chunk of bytes with headers describing where it is going, where it came from, and what it contains. The maximum size a link can carry is its mtu, typically 1,500 bytes on Ethernet. A 100 KB JSON response therefore travels as roughly 70 packets, each of which may take a different path and arrive out of order, duplicated, delayed or not at all. TCP (chapter 6) hides this from your application by numbering and re-sending; UDP does not. Every packet carries nested headers, one per layer: title One packet carrying part of an HTTPS response, outermost layer first layers Ethernet frame Layer 2 summary Source and destination MAC addresses for this hop only. Rewritten by every router. examples dst 3c:22:fb:.. src 00:1a:2b:.. type IPv4 MAC addresses identify a network interface on the local segment. They never leave the local network; a router strips this header and adds a new one for the next hop. Chapter 4. IP header Layer 3 summary Source and destination IP addresses: end-to-end, unchanged across the whole path (unless NAT rewrites them). examples src 52.95.110.1 dst 203.0.113.7 TTL 54 proto TCP The TTL (time to live) counts down at each router; when it hits zero the packet is discarded and an ICMP message is sent back. traceroute exploits this. Chapter 3 and 4. TCP header Layer 4 summary Source and destination ports, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags, window size. examples src port 443 dst port 51844 seq 1048577 ACK win 65535 Ports identify the appli

- A host is any endpoint: your laptop, a server, a phone, a load balancer. Hosts have IP addresses and run applications. - A switch connects hosts on the same local network (Layer 2). It learns which MAC address is on which port and forwards frames accordingly. It does not understand IP. - A router connects different networks (Layer 3). It looks at the destination IP, consults its routing table, and forwards the packet toward the next hop, rewriting the Layer 2 header. Your home router, your VPC's implicit router, and the core routers of an ISP all do this at different scales. - A gateway is simply the router a host sends to when the destination is not on its own network. In AWS these appear as abstractions: subnets are Layer 2 domains, the VPC router is implicit, an Internet Gateway is a router with NAT for public IPs, and security groups are firewalls attached to each host's virtual interface. Part VII chapter 5 maps them precisely.

The Internet is roughly 75,000 independently operated networks called autonomous systems (ASes), each with a number: AWS is AS16509 among others, Google AS15169, Cloudflare AS13335, your ISP has one too. ASes connect to each other through peering (exchanging traffic for free, usually at Internet exchange points) and transit (paying a larger provider to carry traffic to everyone else). Routes between ASes are exchanged with bgp, the Border Gateway Protocol. Each AS announces "I can reach 203.0.113.0/24" to its neighbours, who propagate it with their own AS prepended, building paths. Routers choose among paths by policy and length. BGP has no built-in authentication, which is why route leaks and hijacks occur (someone announces a prefix they do not own and traffic flows to them); RPKI is the slow fix being deployed. For an application engineer the practical lessons are: - Your users' path to you crosses networks you do not control, with latency and loss you do not control. Design for it (chapter 18). - Major outages are sometimes BGP incidents at a provider, not anything you did. Know how to check ( bgp.tools , provider status pages) before paging your whole team. - anycast lets CDNs and DNS providers announce the same prefix from dozens of locations; BGP routes each user to the nearest. This is how 1.1.1.1 is fast everywhere.

h: Why the network is "unreliable" by design
x: Packets can be lost (buffers overflow on a congested link, radio interference), delayed (queued behind other traffic), reordered (different paths), duplicated (retransmission races), or corrupted (bit errors, usually caught by checksums and discarded). The Internet's core does not fix any of this; it keeps the routers simple and fast and leaves recovery to the endpoints. Consequences for engineers: - TCP makes a byte stream look reliable, but at the cost of latency (retransmission timeouts) and throughput (congestion control backs off on loss). A "reliable" connection can stall for seconds. - A request that timed out may have succeeded on the server. Every operation that can be retried must be idempotent (Part III chapter 3). - Connections die silently when a middlebox (NAT, firewall) forgets about them. Long-lived connections need keep-alives. - Partial failure is normal: 0.1% of requests failing somewhere between client and server is a Tuesday, not an incident. Observability must distinguish network noise from application errors.

- Name the layers of the OSI and TCP/IP models and what each is responsible for. - Use layering as a debugging tool: locate a failure at the right layer in minutes. - Explain encapsulation and why Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancers behave differently. - Translate everyday networking vocabulary ("L7 firewall", "L4 proxy", "SNI") into the model. ::: Chapter 1. :::

Networking is too complex to reason about all at once. Models divide it into layers with defined responsibilities and interfaces, so you can change one (swap Wi-Fi for Ethernet, HTTP/1.1 for HTTP/2) without touching the others. For an engineer the real value is diagnostic: a problem lives at one layer, and the tools and fixes differ completely per layer. "It does not work" becomes "DNS resolves, TCP connects, TLS fails with certificate error", which is a two-minute fix instead of a two-hour hunt.

Seven layers, defined by the ISO in the 1980s. Nobody implements it literally, but everyone uses its numbering. title OSI layers, with what you actually encounter at each layers 7 Application summary Protocols your code speaks: HTTP, gRPC, SMTP, DNS, SSH. examples HTTP request/response · DNS query · WebSocket frame **Debug with:** curl, browser dev tools, application logs. **Failures look like:** 4xx/5xx, malformed payloads, auth errors. **L7 devices:** ALB, Nginx, API gateways, WAFs: they read the HTTP request and route on host/path/headers. 6 Presentation summary Data representation and encryption: TLS, serialisation (JSON, protobuf), compression. examples TLS 1.3 · gzip · UTF-8 TLS is often placed here (sometimes at 5 or 4). **Failures look like:** certificate errors, handshake failures, cipher mismatches, garbled encoding. **Debug with:** openssl s_client, curl -v. 5 Session summary Managing dialogues: establishing, maintaining and tearing down sessions. examples TLS session resumption · RPC sessions Rarely discussed separately on the Internet; TLS and the application handle it. Login sessions and cookies are an application-level concept, not Layer 5. 4 Transport summary End-to-end delivery between processes: TCP (reliable stream), UDP (datagrams), QUIC. examples TCP port 443 · UDP port 53 · three-way handshake **Debug with:** ss, nc, telnet to a port, tcpdump. **Failures look like:** connection refused, connection timed out, connection reset. **L4 devices:** NLB, HAProxy

The Internet's actual architecture uses four layers: Link (OSI 1–2), Internet (OSI 3), Transport (OSI 4), Application (OSI 5–7). When engineers say "Layer 4" or "Layer 7" they are using OSI numbers to talk about TCP/IP layers; the mixing is universal and harmless. TCP/IP layer OSI layers Unit of data Addressing Devices --- --- --- --- --- Application 5–7 message URL, hostname proxies, ALB, WAF Transport 4 segment (TCP) / datagram (UDP) port NLB, firewalls (ports) Internet 3 packet IP address routers, NACLs Link 1–2 frame MAC address switches, NICs

Sending: the application hands a message to the transport layer, which adds a TCP header (making a segment); IP adds its header (packet); the link layer adds a frame header and trailer. Receiving reverses it. Each layer only reads its own header and passes the payload up. This is why: - A router can forward your HTTPS traffic without any ability to read it: it stops at Layer 3. - A security group can allow "TCP 443" without knowing whether the content is HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2: it stops at Layer 4. - An ALB can route /api/ to one target group and /static/ to another: it decapsulates all the way to Layer 7, which requires terminating TLS (it must decrypt to read the path). - An NLB cannot route by path; it forwards TCP connections and is therefore faster, simpler and can pass TLS through untouched. That last contrast is the single most practically important consequence of layering for deployments, and chapter 13 builds on it.

- L4 load balancer / proxy : forwards TCP/UDP connections by IP and port. Fast, protocol-agnostic, preserves end-to-end TLS. AWS NLB, HAProxy TCP mode, IPVS. - L7 load balancer / proxy : understands HTTP. Routes by host, path, header; terminates TLS; can add headers, retry, rate limit, authenticate. AWS ALB, Nginx, Envoy, Traefik, Caddy. - L3/L4 firewall : filters by IP and port (security groups, NACLs, iptables). L7 firewall / WAF : inspects HTTP for attack patterns (AWS WAF, ModSecurity). - SNI (Server Name Indication): the hostname sent in clear text during the TLS handshake so one IP can host many certificates. Sits at Layer 6 but is visible to Layer 4 devices, which is how an NLB with TLS passthrough can still route by hostname. - MTU / fragmentation : a Layer 3 concern. VPNs and tunnels reduce the effective MTU; symptoms are connections that open but hang when transferring data. - Keep-alive : exists at two layers. TCP keep-alive (L4) probes an idle connection; HTTP keep-alive (L7) reuses one TCP connection for several requests. They are unrelated and both matter.

Real systems blur the layers. TLS sits awkwardly between 4 and 7. QUIC merges transport and encryption into one UDP-based protocol. Middleboxes inspect layers they "should not" (deep packet inspection, TLS interception on corporate networks). Service meshes do Layer 7 routing on behalf of Layer 4-unaware applications. Do not treat the model as law; treat it as a vocabulary and a diagnostic ladder.

Every host needs an address that routers can use to deliver packets. Addresses must be unique within the network they are routed in, allocated hierarchically so routing tables stay small, and divided into subnets that match physical or administrative boundaries. Getting the address plan wrong is one of the few infrastructure mistakes that is genuinely expensive to fix later: renumbering a VPC that peers with a client's network, or two merged companies both using 10.0.0.0/16 , costs weeks.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal octets: 203.0.113.7 . In binary: 203 .0 .113 .7 11001011 .00000000 .01110001 .00000111 There are 2^32 ≈ 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out around 2011. The Internet still runs mostly on IPv4 thanks to nat and careful allocation.

10.0.1.0/24 means: the first 24 bits are the network prefix (fixed for every address in the block); the remaining 8 bits are the host part (vary within the block). The block therefore contains 2^8 = 256 addresses from 10.0.1.0 to 10.0.1.255 . The subnet mask is the same information as 32 bits with 1s for the prefix: /24 is 255.255.255.0 , /16 is 255.255.0.0 , /20 is 255.255.240.0 . CIDR replaced the older class A/B/C system (where /8, /16 and /24 were the only sizes) so that blocks can be any size. value 10.0.1.0/24 Rules of thumb: - Each step down in prefix length (/24 → /23) doubles the addresses; each step up halves them. - /32 is a single address (used for "this one host" in firewall rules). /0 is everything ( 0.0.0.0/0 means "any address", used for default routes and, dangerously, open security groups). - The first address of a block is the network address ; the last is the broadcast address ; neither is assignable to a host in classic networking. AWS additionally reserves the first three usable addresses (router, DNS, future use) so a VPC subnet has 2^n − 5 usable addresses: a /24 gives 251, a /28 gives 11.

Split 10.0.0.0/16 (65,536 addresses) into /20 subnets (4,096 each): there are 2^(20−16) = 16 of them. The /20 boundary falls on multiples of 16 in the third octet: 10.0.0.0/20 , 10.0.16.0/20 , 10.0.32.0/20 , …, 10.0.240.0/20 . Which /20 contains 10.0.37.200 ? 37 ÷ 16 = 2 remainder 5, so it is in the third block: 10.0.32.0/20 (range 10.0.32.0 to 10.0.47.255). Does 10.0.1.37/27 describe the network address? /27 blocks are 32 addresses, boundaries at 0, 32, 64, … in the last octet. 37 is inside 10.0.1.32/27 (32–63); so 10.0.1.37 is a host, not the network address, and the network is 10.0.1.32/27 . Common sizes: Prefix Addresses Usable (classic) Usable (AWS) Typical use --- --- --- --- --- /16 65,536 65,534 65,531 A whole VPC /20 4,096 4,094 4,091 A large subnet (AWS default VPC subnets) /24 256 254 251 A typical subnet /26 64 62 59 Small subnet, e.g. for load balancers /28 16 14 11 Smallest AWS subnet; endpoints, NAT gateways /32 1 1 — A single host in a rule

Range Name Meaning --- --- --- 10.0.0.0/8 RFC 1918 private ~16.7 M addresses for internal networks 172.16.0.0/12 RFC 1918 private 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255; AWS default VPC uses 172.31.0.0/16 192.168.0.0/16 RFC 1918 private Home and small office networks 127.0.0.0/8 Loopback 127.0.0.1 is "this machine"; never leaves the host 169.254.0.0/16 Link-local Self-assigned when DHCP fails; AWS metadata service at 169.254.169.254 100.64.0.0/10 Carrier-grade NAT ISPs' internal space; also Tailscale 0.0.0.0/0 Default "Any" or "all addresses" 224.0.0.0/4 Multicast Rarely used in clouds Private addresses are not routed on the public Internet; a packet from 10.0.1.5 sent to the Internet must be translated to a public address (chapter 4). That is the entire reason your VPC can use 10.0.0.0/16 and so can every other customer's. 169.254.169.254 is the EC2 instance metadata service, which returns IAM role credentials to anything on the instance that can make an HTTP request to it. Server-side request forgery attacks (Part IV chapter 12) target this address specifically. IMDSv2 (session tokens, hop limit 1) is the mitigation; enforce it on every instance. :::

IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits, with leading zeros dropped and one run of zero groups collapsed to :: : 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 2001:db8::1 There are 2^128 addresses (340 undecillion); the design assumption is that every network gets a /64 (18 quintillion addresses) and every site a /56 or /48. Subnetting below /64 is unusual. Key ranges: ::1 loopback, fe80::/10 link-local, fc00::/7 unique local (the private analogue), 2000::/3 global unicast. Practical realities in late 2026: most clouds support dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6 on the same resources); some AWS services and many client corporate networks are still IPv4-only; IPv6-only VPC subnets exist and remove the NAT gateway cost for IPv6 egress. Public-facing endpoints should be dual-stack (an ALB with dualstack IP type) because a meaningful share of mobile users are on IPv6-first networks. Internally, IPv4 private addressing remains the default for most client environments. Design so you can enable IPv6 (choose dual-stack load balancers, do not hard-code 0.0.0.0/0 as the only "anywhere" in security policies; add ::/0 ).

t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
x: IP addresses say where a packet should go. Something must decide how it gets there at each step, and physical networks deliver frames to hardware addresses, not IP addresses. Meanwhile, the world has far more devices than public IPv4 addresses, so most hosts use private addresses that cannot be routed on the Internet. Three mechanisms resolve this: routing tables choose the next hop, ARP finds its hardware address, and NAT bridges private and public address spaces.

t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
h: MAC addresses and the local segment
x: A MAC address ( 3c:22:fb:ab:cd:ef , 48 bits) identifies a network interface on its local segment: the set of hosts that can exchange Ethernet frames directly through switches without crossing a router. A subnet normally corresponds to one segment. MAC addresses are only meaningful locally; routers replace them at every hop. Switches build a table of which MAC address is reachable through which port by watching source addresses on incoming frames, and forward frames only to the right port. A frame to an unknown MAC is flooded to all ports; a frame to the broadcast MAC ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff reaches every host on the segment.

t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
x: A host that wants to send to 10.0.1.1 on its own subnet needs that host's MAC address. It broadcasts an ARP request ("who has 10.0.1.1?"), the owner replies ("10.0.1.1 is at 3c:22:…"), and the mapping is cached for a few minutes. ip neigh show # the ARP cache (Linux); 'arp -a' on older systems # 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 lladdr 0a:58:0a:00:01:01 REACHABLE ARP has no authentication: any host can claim any IP (ARP spoofing), which lets an attacker on the same segment intercept traffic. This is one reason switched, segmented networks and encrypted protocols matter even internally, and why cloud providers implement their own secured equivalents rather than real ARP. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery (NDP) for the same purpose.

t: Private Networks, MAC Addresses, ARP, Routing and NAT
x: Every host has a routing table. For each outgoing packet, the kernel finds the most specific matching route (longest prefix match) and uses it: ip route # default via 10.0.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100 # 10.0.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.1.57 # 172.17.0.0/16 dev docker0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.1 Reading it: packets to 10.0.1.0/24 go directly out eth0 (the destination is on-link; ARP for its MAC); packets to Docker's 172.17.0.0/16 go to the docker0 bridge; everything else ( default , i.e. 0.0.0.0/0 ) is sent to the gateway 10.0.1.1 , whose MAC is found by ARP. A packet to 8.8.8.8 therefore gets an Ethernet header addressed to the gateway and an IP header addressed to 8.8.8.8. Routers do the same with bigger tables. Core Internet routers hold about a million prefixes learned via BGP; your VPC router holds a handful of routes you define.

x: AWS exposes this directly. Each subnet is associated with one route table: Destination Target Meaning --- --- --- 10.20.0.0/16 local Everything in the VPC is reachable directly (always present) 0.0.0.0/0 igw-… Public subnet: Internet via the Internet Gateway 0.0.0.0/0 nat-… Private subnet: outbound Internet via a NAT Gateway 192.168.0.0/16 vgw-… / tgw-… Client office network via VPN or Transit Gateway pl-… (S3 prefix list) vpce-… S3 traffic via a Gateway Endpoint, never leaving AWS A "public subnet" is nothing more than a subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway and whose instances have public IPs. A "private subnet" has no such route. An "isolated subnet" has no default route at all. The names are conventions; the route table is the reality.

This is a security feature (private subnets are unreachable by default) and a complication (webhooks to a service in a private subnet require a public entry point such as a load balancer). 2. - Explain what a socket is, how a connection is identified, and why a server can serve thousands of clients on one port. - Distinguish listening, established, and time-wait states and know what each means operationally. - Diagnose "address already in use", ephemeral port exhaustion, and file descriptor limits. - Configure bind addresses correctly inside containers and on servers. ::: Chapters 3 and 4; Part I chapters 3 and 6. :::

An IP address identifies a host; a host runs many programs. Ports are the kernel's way of delivering a segment to the right one. Sockets are the programming interface over all of this. Nearly every "my service does not respond" or "connection refused" conversation is really about ports, bind addresses and socket states, so precision here pays off daily.

A port is a 16-bit number (0–65535) in the TCP or UDP header. By convention: - 0–1023 : well-known ports, require root or CAP NET BIND SERVICE to bind on Linux. 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 25/587 SMTP. - 1024–49151 : registered ports. 3306 MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL, 6379 Redis, 8080 alternative HTTP, 9090 Prometheus, 27017 MongoDB. - 49152–65535 (Linux default 32768–60999 ): ephemeral ports, assigned by the kernel to the client side of outgoing connections. TCP and UDP port spaces are independent: TCP 53 and UDP 53 are different endpoints (DNS uses both).

A socket is a kernel object a program creates to communicate, referenced by a file descriptor. Servers follow the sequence socket() → bind(address, port) → listen(backlog) → accept() in a loop; clients do socket() → connect(address, port) . Each accept() returns a new socket for that one client; the listening socket keeps listening. A TCP connection is uniquely identified by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). This is why one server port can hold thousands of simultaneous connections: each has a different client IP or client port. It also bounds the number of connections between one client IP and one server port to the number of ephemeral ports (about 28,000 on default Linux), which matters for proxies and load generators.

bind() takes an address as well as a port. The address decides which interfaces accept connections: - 127.0.0.1:8000 : only connections from the same host. Right for a database that only a local app uses, or a dev server. Wrong inside a container that must be reached from outside it , because the container's loopback is not the host's. - 0.0.0.0:8000 : all IPv4 interfaces. Standard for a service inside a container (the container's network namespace is already the isolation boundary) and for servers behind a firewall. - 10.0.1.57:8000 : one specific interface. Used on multi-homed hosts to listen only on the internal network. - [::]:8000 : all IPv6 interfaces (and usually IPv4 too, via dual-stack). The most common "it works locally but the container returns connection refused" bug is a server bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the container. Docker's port mapping reaches the container's eth0 , not its loopback. Bind to 0.0.0.0 in containers. ::: Conversely, on a bare server with a public IP, binding a database or admin interface to 0.0.0.0 without a firewall exposes it to the Internet. Many breaches (exposed Redis, MongoDB, Elasticsearch instances) were simply default binds on public hosts.

ss -tan shows every TCP socket with its state. The ones that matter: State Meaning Operational note --- --- --- LISTEN Waiting for connections ss -ltnp lists them with the process SYN-SENT / SYN-RECV Handshake in progress Many SYN-RECV = backlog filling or SYN flood ESTABLISHED Open connection Count them per service for capacity FIN-WAIT / CLOSE-WAIT Closing Many CLOSE-WAIT = your application is not closing sockets after the peer did (leak) TIME-WAIT Closed, waiting ~60 s to ensure stray packets die Normal; thousands are fine; the side that closes first holds it ss -ltnp # listening sockets with process ss -tan state established | wc -l # open connections ss -tan | awk 'NR>1{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c # count by state ss -tn state established '( dport = :5432 )' # connections to PostgreSQL ss -s # summary

Connections that have completed the handshake but not yet been accept() ed queue in the backlog . Its size is the smaller of the application's listen() argument and the kernel's net.core.somaxconn (default 4096 on modern kernels, 128 on old ones). When it overflows, new connections are dropped (clients see slow connects or timeouts, not refusals). Signs: ss -ltn showing Recv-Q near Send-Q on a listening socket, and nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows increasing. Causes: the application is too slow to accept (event loop blocked, workers saturated). Raise the backlog as a stopgap; fix the saturation as the cure.

bind() fails if another socket already holds that address:port. Causes, in order of frequency: 1. The previous instance is still running. ss -ltnp grep :8000 shows the owner; stop it properly. 2. A connection in TIME-WAIT on that port after a restart. Servers set SO REUSEADDR so the listening socket can be rebound anyway; most frameworks do this for you. 3. A port mapping conflict in Docker : -p 8000:8000 when the host's 8000 is taken. Change the host side. 4. Two services configured with the same port by a copy-paste error in the unit file.

A process making many short-lived outbound connections to the same destination (a proxy without keep-alive, a load test, an app that opens a new database connection per request) runs out of ephemeral ports when the old ones sit in TIME-WAIT. Symptoms: connect(): Cannot assign requested address (EADDRNOTAVAIL) , latency spikes, intermittent failures. Fixes: reuse connections (HTTP keep-alive, connection pools), widen the range ( net.ipv4.ip local port range = 1024 65535 ), or enable net.ipv4.tcp tw reuse = 1 for outgoing connections. Through a NAT Gateway the same limit applies per destination at the gateway (chapter 4).

Every socket is a file descriptor. The per-process limit ( ulimit -n , often 1024 by default) caps connections; a busy proxy or WebSocket server needs tens of thousands. Set LimitNOFILE=65536 in the systemd unit, or ulimits in the container spec. Symptom: Too many open files , EMFILE , accept failures under load. If raising the limit only delays the error, you have a leak: connections not closed (see CLOSE-WAIT above).

Inside a container the process binds 0.0.0.0:8000 in its own network namespace. docker run -p 8080:8000 creates a DNAT rule from the host's 8080 to the container's 8000. In ECS with the awsvpc network mode, each task gets its own elastic network interface and IP, so the container port is reached directly on the task IP with no mapping; the ALB target group points at task-ip:8000 . In Kubernetes, a Service maps a stable virtual IP and port to pod IPs and container ports. Health checks follow the same rules: an ALB health check targets the task IP and the container port; it must hit a path the application serves on the interface it bound to.

# Is anything listening on 8000, and who? ss -ltnp 'sport = :8000' # Can I connect? (from the same host, then from another host) nc -vz localhost 8000; nc -vz 10.0.1.57 8000 # Who is connected to my service right now, by client IP? ss -tn state established '( sport = :8000 )' | awk 'NR>1{split($4,a,":"); print a[1]}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head # Which process owns a connection? sudo ss -tnp | grep 5432 # Current limits for a running process cat /proc/$(pgrep -o myapp)/limits | grep 'open files'

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: - Explain the guarantees TCP provides and the costs of providing them. - Walk through the three-way handshake, data transfer with acknowledgements, flow and congestion control, and the four-way close. - Choose between TCP and UDP (and QUIC) for a given application. - Diagnose resets, timeouts, retransmissions and half-open connections. ::: Chapter 5. :::

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: IP delivers packets unreliably and out of order. Applications want a reliable, ordered byte stream (a file transfer, an HTTP response) or, sometimes, fast delivery of small independent messages where a lost one should simply be forgotten (a voice packet, a DNS query). TCP and UDP are the two answers, and nearly everything else is built on one of them.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: UDP adds only ports and a checksum to IP. Each sendto() becomes one datagram; it may arrive, or not, in any order. No connection, no retransmission, no congestion control. Costs: none beyond IP. Used by DNS (small query, small answer; retry at the application), real-time media (a late packet is useless, so why retransmit), NTP, game state, and as the substrate for quic. For most backend engineers the operational facts about UDP are: it is stateless, so firewalls track it with timeouts (chapter 15); it is trivially spoofable, which is why it is used in amplification attacks and why your UDP services should never respond with more data than they receive to unauthenticated clients; and large UDP datagrams get fragmented at the IP layer, which is fragile across the Internet, so protocols keep them under ~1,200–1,400 bytes.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: Each byte has a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects; the sender keeps unacknowledged data until acked and retransmits on a timeout or on receiving duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit). Selective acknowledgements (SACK) let the receiver report exactly which ranges arrived. A retransmission timeout stalls the stream; on a lossy link this is the "reliable connection that sometimes freezes for a second" you see on hotel Wi-Fi.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: The receiver advertises a window : how many more bytes it can buffer. The sender never has more than that in flight. A slow consumer (an application that does not read from the socket) shrinks the window to zero and the sender stops. This is backpressure at the transport layer, and it is why a slow client downloading a large response ties up a server worker in blocking servers.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: The sender also maintains a congestion window estimating how much the network can take. It starts small (slow start: roughly 10 segments, ~14 KB) and grows per round trip until loss or delay signals congestion, then shrinks. Algorithms differ (CUBIC is the Linux default; BBR models bandwidth and delay and is often better on lossy or long paths). Two practical results: - Small transfers are dominated by round trips, not bandwidth. The first 14 KB go in one RTT; a 100 KB response needs several RTTs of window growth. Keeping initial HTML and critical API responses small has outsized effect on perceived latency. - Loss on a long path collapses throughput. The bandwidth-delay product and loss rate set a ceiling; a 1% loss on a 100 ms path can limit a single TCP stream to a few Mbps regardless of link speed. Chapter 18.

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: Either side sends FIN; the other acks and, when done, sends its own FIN, which is acked. The side that closed first waits in TIME-WAIT (2 × maximum segment lifetime, 60 s on Linux) so delayed packets from this connection cannot be mistaken for a new one using the same ports. A RST (reset) aborts a connection abruptly: sent when a segment arrives for a non-existent connection, when a process exits with unread data, or by firewalls and load balancers that want to drop you immediately. Clients see ECONNRESET / "connection reset by peer".

t: TCP versus UDP and the TCP Connection Lifecycle
x: If a host crashes or a NAT entry expires, the other side may believe the connection is still established indefinitely; nothing in TCP detects an idle dead peer. TCP keep-alive sends probes after an idle period (Linux default 2 hours, far too long; set net.ipv4.tcp keepalive time=60 or enable at the socket level with shorter intervals). Databases, message brokers and load balancers each have their own idle timeouts; a connection pool must either keep connections warmer than the shortest timeout in the path or validate connections before use. This is the root cause behind a large share of "first request after idle fails" bugs.

- Trace a DNS query from a browser through recursive resolvers to authoritative servers and back. - Use the major record types correctly: A, AAAA, CNAME, ALIAS, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, SRV, CAA. - Design records and TTLs for deployments, migrations and failover, and understand why "DNS propagation" is mostly a myth about caching. - Diagnose DNS failures with dig and avoid the outages DNS causes. ::: Chapters 3 and 6. :::

Humans and configuration files use names; packets use addresses. Addresses change: load balancers scale, servers are replaced, providers migrate. DNS is the indirection layer that lets api.client.com keep working while everything behind it changes. It is also a globally distributed, heavily cached database with eventual consistency, and when it is wrong, everything is down while every server reports healthy. "It's always DNS" is a joke because it is so often true.

DNS names are read right to left: api.client.com. is the api label inside client inside com inside the root (the trailing dot, usually implicit). Each level is a zone served by authoritative name servers that hold the records for that zone and delegate sub-zones via NS records. - Root servers (13 named letters, hundreds of anycast instances) know the authoritative servers for every top-level domain. - TLD servers ( .com , .io , .de ) know the authoritative servers for each registered domain. - Your zone's authoritative servers (Route 53, Cloudflare, your registrar) hold the actual records.

A TTL is the number of seconds a resolver may cache a record. When you change a record, no message is sent to the world's resolvers; each one simply keeps the old answer until its copy expires. "Waiting for propagation" is waiting for caches to expire, and the wait is bounded by the old TTL, not the new one. Strategy for a planned change (migrating a load balancer, moving providers): 1. Days before: lower the TTL from 3600 to 60. Wait for the old TTL to expire everywhere (an hour). 2. Make the change. Within ~60 s, nearly all resolvers see it. Some misbehaving resolvers ignore TTLs; keep the old endpoint serving (or redirecting) for a day. 3. Afterwards: raise the TTL back if the record is stable, to reduce query volume and resolver dependence. Typical TTLs: 60–300 s for records that participate in failover or point at things that change (load balancers, blue/green switches); 3600–86400 s for stable records (MX, TXT, NS). Route 53 Alias records to AWS resources inherit the resource's TTL (60 s for ALBs) automatically. Negative caching: an NXDOMAIN ("does not exist") answer is cached too, for the SOA minimum TTL. Creating a record and testing it before it exists can poison your own resolver's cache for minutes; test with dig @authoritative-server first.

- Point names at load balancers via ALIAS/CNAME , never at instance IPs. ALB and NLB IPs change (NLBs can have static EIPs if you need them for allow-lists). - Apex domains ( client.com ) cannot use CNAME; use the provider's ALIAS feature or redirect the apex to www with a small static redirector. - Health-checked failover : Route 53 can return a secondary record when a health check fails (failover routing), route users to the nearest healthy region (latency routing), or split traffic by percentage (weighted routing) for gradual migrations. These all depend on TTLs; a 60 s TTL means up to 60 s of users still going to the dead endpoint, plus resolver misbehaviour. - Certificate validation : ACM and Let's Encrypt DNS-01 challenges work by asking you to publish a TXT or CNAME record; automation (Route 53 integration, cert-manager) makes this hands-free. - Internal DNS : inside a VPC, Route 53 private hosted zones let you name internal services ( db.internal.client.com ) without exposing records publicly; ECS Service Connect and Kubernetes CoreDNS provide service discovery names ( orders.svc.cluster.local ). The VPC resolver lives at the base of the VPC CIDR plus two ( 10.20.0.2 ).

- DNS is unauthenticated by default; a resolver can be fed forged answers (cache poisoning) and queries are visible to anyone on the path. DNSSEC signs zones so resolvers can verify answers (Route 53 supports signing; adoption is partial). DNS over HTTPS/TLS encrypts the client-to-resolver leg. - Dangling records are a common takeover vector: a CNAME pointing at a deprovisioned S3 bucket, Heroku app or Elastic Beanstalk environment can be claimed by an attacker who registers that resource name, giving them a page on your domain (subdomain takeover). Delete records when you delete resources; audit periodically. - CAA records limit which certificate authorities can issue for your domain. - Registrar security : the registrar account controls the NS records, and therefore everything. MFA, registry lock, and a shared ownership model (not a departed contractor's personal account) are essential. Domains expire; set auto-renew and calendar reminders, and make sure the payment card is not an individual's. - Email authentication records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) are DNS-based; without them your domain can be spoofed for phishing against your own client.

- Read and write raw HTTP: request line, headers, body, status codes, and the semantics of each method. - Explain persistent connections, pipelining, HTTP/2 multiplexing and HTTP/3 over QUIC, and what each means for performance and infrastructure. - Use caching headers, conditional requests, content negotiation and ranges correctly. - Recognise the HTTP behaviours of load balancers and proxies that cause production surprises. ::: Chapters 5 and 6. :::

HTTP began as a way to fetch hypertext documents and became the universal application protocol: APIs, mobile backends, microservice calls, webhooks, streaming. Frameworks hide most of it, which is fine until a load balancer returns 502, a proxy strips a header, a client caches a response it should not have, or performance collapses because every request opens a new connection. The engineers who can read HTTP on the wire fix those in minutes.

A request is text: POST /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1 Host: api.client.com Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: 58 Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi... Accept: application/json User-Agent: client-app/2.4.0 {"customer_id":"c_123","items":[{"sku":"A1","qty":2}]} The request line gives the method, the path (plus query string) and the version. Headers are case-insensitive name-value pairs ending at a blank line. The body follows, with its length declared by Content-Length or sent in chunks with Transfer-Encoding: chunked . Host is mandatory in HTTP/1.1 and is how one IP serves many sites (virtual hosting) and how a load balancer picks a target group. A response mirrors it: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 142 Location: /api/v1/orders/o_789 Cache-Control: no-store X-Request-Id: 7f3a9c2e-... Date: Tue, 14 Mar 2026 10:21:07 GMT {"id":"o_789","status":"pending", ...}

Method Semantics Safe Idempotent Body --- --- --- --- --- GET Retrieve yes yes no HEAD GET without body yes yes no OPTIONS Capabilities; CORS preflight yes yes no POST Create or process; non-idempotent action no no yes PUT Replace the resource at this URL no yes yes PATCH Partial update no not by definition yes DELETE Remove no yes rarely "Safe" means no side effects (browsers and crawlers prefetch GETs; a GET that deletes something will be triggered by a link preview). "Idempotent" means repeating has the same result; proxies and clients may retry idempotent requests automatically after a network failure but must not retry POST. Part III chapters 2 and 3 build on this.

- 1xx informational: 100 Continue , 101 Switching Protocols (WebSocket upgrade). - 2xx success: 200 OK , 201 Created , 202 Accepted (queued for async processing), 204 No Content , 206 Partial Content . - 3xx redirection: 301 permanent (cached, method may change to GET), 302 / 303 temporary (use 303 See Other after POST), 304 Not Modified (conditional request hit), 307 / 308 temporary/permanent preserving method and body. - 4xx client errors: 400 Bad Request , 401 Unauthorized (actually "unauthenticated": missing or invalid credentials), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found , 405 Method Not Allowed , 409 Conflict , 410 Gone , 412 Precondition Failed , 413 Payload Too Large , 415 Unsupported Media Type , 422 Unprocessable Content (valid JSON, invalid semantics), 429 Too Many Requests . - 5xx server errors: 500 Internal Server Error , 501 Not Implemented , 502 Bad Gateway (proxy got an invalid response or connection failure from upstream), 503 Service Unavailable (overloaded or down; include Retry-After ), 504 Gateway Timeout (upstream too slow). The 502/503/504 distinction is diagnostic gold when a load balancer is involved: 502 means the backend connection failed or returned garbage (crashed process, wrong port, backend closed idle connection); 503 from an ALB means no healthy targets; 504 means the backend accepted but did not respond within the idle timeout (slow query, deadlock).

HTTP/1.0 opened a TCP connection per request. HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent by default ( Connection: keep-alive ), so many requests share one connection, amortising the handshake costs from chapter 6. But requests on one connection are sequential: the second cannot start until the first response completes (head-of-line blocking). Browsers open six parallel connections per host to compensate, and web performance folklore (domain sharding, sprite sheets, bundling) grew around that limit.

HTTP/2 (2015) keeps HTTP semantics (same methods, status codes, headers) and changes the wire format: - Binary framing instead of text. - Multiplexing : many concurrent streams over one TCP connection, interleaved; no application-level head-of-line blocking. One connection per origin. - Header compression (HPACK) : repeated headers (cookies, user agent) cost a few bytes. - Stream prioritisation and server push (push is now effectively dead; browsers removed it). - Browsers require TLS for HTTP/2 ( h2 ); the ALPN extension negotiates it during the TLS handshake. What it means for infrastructure: a client makes one TCP+TLS connection and sends everything over it. Load balancers typically terminate HTTP/2 from clients and speak HTTP/1.1 to backends (ALB does this by default; it can also use HTTP/2 or gRPC to targets). One remaining weakness: a single lost TCP segment stalls all streams until retransmitted, because TCP delivers in order.

HTTP/3 runs over quic instead of TCP: UDP-based, TLS 1.3 built in, independent streams so one loss does not block others, faster connection setup (1 RTT, 0 for resumption), and connection migration (your phone switches from Wi-Fi to cellular without dropping the connection). Browsers discover it via the Alt-Svc header or DNS HTTPS records and try it on UDP 443. For most backends, HTTP/3 is something the CDN or edge handles: CloudFront, Cloudflare and others terminate HTTP/3 from users and talk HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 to your origin. You get most of the benefit (faster, more resilient last mile) without changing your servers. Enabling it at the edge is usually a checkbox. Some corporate networks block UDP 443; clients fall back to HTTP/2 automatically. title HTTP versions in practice columns HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3 Transport TCP (+TLS in practice) QUIC over UDP (TLS 1.3 mandatory) Connections per origin 6 in browsers Concurrency sequential per connection multiplexed streams multiplexed, independent loss recovery Header compression HPACK QPACK Handshake cost TCP + TLS (2–3 RTT) 1 RTT, 0-RTT resume Where you enable it default ALB/CDN/Nginx listener; backends often stay 1.1 CDN/edge; ALB does not serve h3 to clients as of writing, CloudFront does Debugging readable with tcpdump needs decryption + h2 dissector needs QUIC key logging

Forwarding and identity behind proxies : X-Forwarded-For (client IP chain), X-Forwarded-Proto ( https when TLS was terminated upstream), X-Forwarded-Host , and the standard Forwarded header. Your application must trust these only from your own proxy (chapter 12), and use them for logging, rate limiting and generating absolute URLs. Getting X-Forwarded-Proto wrong produces redirect loops (the app thinks it is on HTTP and redirects to HTTPS, forever). Correlation : X-Request-Id or traceparent (W3C Trace Context). Generate at the edge if absent; log on every hop. Part XI. Content : Content-Type with charset; Accept for negotiation; Content-Encoding: gzip / br for compression (compress text, never already-compressed images; never compress responses containing secrets alongside attacker-controlled input over TLS without care, the BREACH attack). Size and safety : Content-Length limits enforced by the proxy ( client max body size in Nginx) protect against memory exhaustion; 413 is the right answer for oversize uploads. Caching : Cache-Control is the master switch. Transfer-Encoding: chunked lets a server send a response of unknown length piece by piece, which is how streaming responses (server-sent events, long generated reports, LLM token streams) work over HTTP/1.1. Proxies may buffer the whole response before forwarding unless told not to ( proxy buffering off in Nginx; ALB streams by default but has idle timeouts). Accept-Ranges / Range: bytes=0-1023 enable resumable downloads and video seeking; S3 and CloudFront support them natively.

Every packet between a user and your server crosses networks owned by strangers: coffee shop Wi-Fi, ISPs, exchange points, transit providers. Without protection, anyone on the path can read the traffic (passwords, tokens, personal data), modify it (inject scripts, change a payment amount) or impersonate the server. TLS solves all three for any TCP-based protocol: HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS, and the same layer protects SMTP, PostgreSQL connections, gRPC and more.

1. Confidentiality : the application data is encrypted with keys only the two endpoints know. 2. Integrity : any modification in transit is detected and the connection fails. 3. Server authentication : the client verifies it is talking to the holder of a private key that a trusted certificate authority has bound to the hostname. Optionally, client authentication (mTLS) verifies the client too. What it does not do: hide that you are connecting, or to whom (IP addresses and, usually, the hostname via SNI are visible); protect data once decrypted at a load balancer or server; prevent attacks on the application itself; or help if the client is tricked into trusting a bad CA (corporate TLS interception, malware-installed roots).

title TLS 1.3 handshake (1 round trip) intro TLS 1.3 (2018) halved the handshake to one round trip and removed every weak cipher. Nearly all traffic today is 1.3 or 1.2. actors label Client label Server steps label ClientHello title ClientHello detail The client sends: supported TLS versions; a list of cipher suites it accepts (e.g. TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256); its **key share**: an ephemeral public key for a Diffie-Hellman exchange (usually X25519); the **SNI** extension naming the hostname it wants (in clear text, unless Encrypted Client Hello is used); **ALPN** listing application protocols (h2, http/1.1); and a random value. Because the client speculatively sends its key share, the server can compute the shared secret immediately, saving a round trip compared to TLS 1.2. label ServerHello + key share title ServerHello detail The server picks the version and cipher suite and returns its own ephemeral key share and random. Both sides now compute the same shared secret via Diffie-Hellman. Everything after this point is encrypted with keys derived from that secret. label {EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished} title Server proves its identity detail Encrypted: the chosen ALPN protocol; the server's **certificate chain** (its leaf certificate for the hostname plus intermediate CA certificates); **CertificateVerify**: a signature over the handshake transcript made with the certificate's private key, proving the server holds it;

- Latency : one RTT on top of TCP's one (or one total with QUIC). For a user 100 ms away, each new HTTPS connection costs ~200 ms before the request. Connection reuse and session resumption are not optimisations; they are the difference between a snappy and a sluggish API. - CPU : the asymmetric operations (key exchange, signature) cost real CPU per handshake. A server handling many short connections spends more on TLS than on HTTP. Terminating at a load balancer offloads this; keep-alive reduces it. - Failures are loud and specific : a handshake error has a reason code. Learn to read it.

TLS 1.2 (2008) is still widely supported and acceptable with modern cipher suites (ECDHE key exchange, AES-GCM or ChaCha20). It costs two round trips and allows weak configurations if you are careless (RSA key exchange without forward secrecy, CBC ciphers vulnerable to padding oracles). TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated, broken, disabled in browsers and forbidden by PCI DSS. SSLv3 and SSLv2 are ancient history. Configure servers for TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only; use 1.3-only where every client is modern (service-to-service).

Where TLS ends is an architectural decision: title Where TLS terminates intro Click each path. The trade is operational simplicity versus how far plaintext travels. legend nodes label client label ALB terminates TLS ACM certificate The most common setup. The load balancer holds the certificate (free via ACM, auto-renewed), decrypts, and can read HTTP for routing, WAF and logging. Traffic to targets is HTTP on the private network, or re-encrypted. label Backend (HTTP :8000) Receives plaintext HTTP inside the VPC with X-Forwarded-Proto: https. Simple; acceptable for many workloads because the VPC is a private network, but compliance regimes (PCI, HIPAA, some client policies) require encryption in transit everywhere, including here. label ALB terminates + re-encrypts The ALB decrypts (for L7 features) then opens its own TLS connection to the backend. The ALB does not validate the backend certificate's name or CA, so a self-signed cert on the backend works; the value is encryption, not backend authentication. Satisfies most 'encryption in transit' requirements. label Backend (HTTPS :8443) Runs TLS itself with an internal certificate (private CA via ACM Private CA, or self-signed). Slightly more CPU and certificate management, but no plaintext anywhere. label NLB passthrough TCP 443, no decryption The NLB forwards encrypted bytes untouched. End-to-end TLS between user and backend; the backend must hold the public certificate and renew it. Required when the backend needs the client

In mTLS the client also presents a certificate, and the server validates it against a CA it trusts. It authenticates machines strongly without passwords or tokens: service-to-service inside a mesh (Istio, Linkerd, App Mesh do this automatically), client systems calling your API from a known fleet, or devices. Costs: a private CA, certificate distribution and rotation for every client, and load balancer support (ALB supports mTLS with a trust store; NLB passthrough lets the backend do it). For human users, mTLS is rare; passkeys and SSO cover that.

A server configuration that passes modern scanners (Mozilla's "intermediate" profile is the usual reference): ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305; ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off; # let modern clients pick; TLS 1.3 suites are not configurable here ssl_session_timeout 1d; ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m; # resumption: ~40k sessions ssl_session_tickets off; # or rotate ticket keys; static keys weaken forward secrecy ssl_stapling on; ssl_stapling_verify on; # OCSP stapling ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.client.com/fullchain.pem; # leaf + intermediates ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.client.com/privkey.pem; add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload" always; On an ALB, the equivalent is choosing a security policy : ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 (TLS 1.2 + 1.3, strong ciphers) is a good default; avoid policies allowing TLS 1.0/1.1 unless a specific legacy client forces it, and document that exception. Caddy does all of this automatically with sane defaults (chapter 12). HSTS ( Strict-Transport-Security ) tells browsers to never use plain HTTP for the domain again for max-age seconds, defeating downgrade attacks and the one unencrypted first request. The server's certificate binds its public key to one or more hostnames (SANs), is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA trusted by clients. The server must send the full chain (leaf plus intermediates, not the root); a missing intermediate is the most common cause of "works in Chrome, fails in curl/Python" (browsers fetch missing intermediates; libraries do not). Certificates expire (publicly trusted ones are limited to 398 days and the industry is moving toward much shorter lifetimes, which makes automation mandatory). Chapter 10 covers issuance, renewal and revocation.

- Explain what an X.509 certificate contains and how a chain of trust is verified. - Obtain and automatically renew certificates with ACME (Let's Encrypt) and AWS Certificate Manager, including wildcard and internal certificates. - Design for expiry: monitoring, automation, and the outages that certificates have caused. - Decide when a private CA is appropriate and how to operate one. ::: Chapter 9. :::

TLS encryption is easy; the hard part is knowing you are encrypting to the right party. A certificate is a third party's signed statement: "the holder of this public key controls api.client.com". The system of certificate authorities, trust stores, validation and revocation exists to make that statement trustworthy at Internet scale. Operationally, certificates are also time bombs: they expire, and expired certificates have taken down airlines, payment systems, cloud services and more.

An X.509 certificate contains: the subject (historically the Common Name; today the Subject Alternative Names extension lists the hostnames, and CN is ignored by browsers); the subject's public key ; the issuer (which CA signed it); validity dates (notBefore, notAfter); a serial number ; key usage and extended key usage (server auth, client auth); and the issuer's signature over all of it. openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text | head -40 # everything openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

title From your server's certificate to the browser's trust store layers Leaf certificate api.client.com summary Your server's certificate. Valid ≤ 398 days (publicly trusted). Lists SANs; signed by an intermediate. The server must present this and the intermediates. Private key stays on the server (or in ACM, never exported). Intermediate CA e.g. Let's Encrypt R11, Amazon RSA 2048 M02 summary Signs leaf certificates on behalf of a root. Valid for years. Kept online. Intermediates exist so the root's key can stay offline. If an intermediate is compromised, only it is revoked, not every certificate under the root. Servers must send intermediates; clients usually do not have them. Root CA e.g. ISRG Root X1, Amazon Root CA 1 summary Self-signed; valid for decades; private key in an offline HSM. Trusted because it is *distributed with* browsers and operating systems, not because of any signature. Servers should not send it; clients already have it. Trust store OS / browser / language runtime summary The list of root certificates the client trusts. Different clients have different stores. Mozilla, Apple, Microsoft and Google each run root programmes with strict audit requirements. Linux: /etc/ssl/certs; Python: certifi; Java: cacerts; Node: bundled. Corporate devices often have an extra internal root for TLS inspection. Validation walks the chain: the leaf's signature is checked with the intermediate's public key, the intermediate's with the root's, and the root must be in the tru

- Domain Validated (DV) : the CA checks you control the domain (via HTTP file, DNS record or email). Automated, free (Let's Encrypt, ZeroSSL, ACM), issued in seconds. What nearly everyone uses. - Organisation Validated (OV) and Extended Validation (EV) : the CA also verifies the legal entity. Browsers stopped showing EV indicators; practical value is minimal for most services, though some enterprise clients or procurement checklists still ask for OV. - Wildcard ( .client.com ): covers one level of subdomains; requires DNS validation. Convenient; wider blast radius if the key leaks.

acme is the protocol Let's Encrypt created to automate issuance. The client proves control of the domain and receives a certificate valid for 90 days, renewing automatically at 60. Short validity is a feature: it forces automation and limits the damage of a leaked key. HTTP-01 challenge : the CA fetches http://domain/.well-known/acme-challenge/ on port 80. Requires the host to be reachable from the Internet on port 80; cannot issue wildcards. DNS-01 challenge : you publish a TXT record acme-challenge.domain . Works for internal hosts and wildcards; requires API access to your DNS provider (Route 53, Cloudflare), which the client automates. TLS-ALPN-01 : validation over port 443 using a special TLS handshake; useful when port 80 is blocked. # Caddy: zero configuration. This Caddyfile obtains and renews automatically. api.client.com { reverse_proxy localhost:8000 } # certbot with Nginx plugin (HTTP-01) sudo certbot --nginx -d api.client.com -d www.client.com --agree-tos -m ops@client.com # certbot with Route 53 (DNS-01, wildcard) sudo certbot certonly --dns-route53 -d 'client.com' -d '*.client.com' # Renewal is installed as a systemd timer; verify: systemctl list-timers | grep certbot; sudo certbot renew --dry-run

ACM issues free public certificates for use on ALBs, NLBs, CloudFront, API Gateway and App Runner. Validation is by DNS (a CNAME ACM gives you; with Route 53 it is one click) or email. ACM renews automatically as long as the validation record stays in place and the certificate is attached to a resource. The private key never leaves AWS and cannot be exported, so ACM public certificates cannot be installed on an EC2 instance's Nginx; for that, use ACME on the instance or ACM Private CA with an exportable cert. CloudFront requires its certificate in us-east-1 regardless of where your origin is.

h: Expiry: the outage you can schedule
x: Certificates expire at a known second. Yet expiry outages remain common because renewal depended on a person, or the automation broke silently (DNS credentials rotated, port 80 firewalled, a renewal cron removed during a server rebuild), or a certificate lived somewhere nobody remembered (an internal service, a webhook endpoint, a client-provided cert for mTLS). Defences, all of them: 1. Automate issuance and renewal everywhere; no manually installed public certificates. 2. Monitor expiry from the outside : a synthetic check that connects to every public endpoint and alerts at 21, 14 and 7 days remaining. Blackbox exporter (Prometheus), Route 53 health checks do not do this, so use a dedicated check or CloudWatch Synthetics canary. ACM emits DaysToExpiry metrics; alarm on them. 3. Monitor the renewal job , not just the certificate: a failed certbot renew should page before the certificate runs out. 4. Inventory : a list of every certificate, where it is installed, how it renews, who owns it. Include client-provided certificates and internal ones. 5. Test renewal when you build the system ( --dry-run ) and after any change to DNS, firewall or hosting. Public certificate maximum lifetimes are shrinking by industry decision (398 days today, with a published schedule toward 47 days by 2029). Manual renewal is becoming impossible by design; treat automation as mandatory now.

If a private key leaks, the certificate must be revoked. Mechanisms: CRLs (lists downloaded by clients, often stale), OCSP (clients ask the CA per certificate; privacy and availability problems), and OCSP stapling (the server fetches the OCSP response and includes it in the handshake; enable this). Browsers increasingly rely on their own aggregated revocation lists and short lifetimes rather than live checks. Practical conclusion: revocation is unreliable; short-lived certificates and prompt key rotation are the real control. If a key leaks, revoke and reissue and deploy immediately.

Inside a VPC or a client's network you may want TLS between services (ALB to backend, service to database, mTLS between services) with certificates for names that are not public ( orders.internal , 10.20.64.12 ). Options: - Self-signed per service : fine for ALB-to-backend re-encryption because the ALB does not validate; fragile anywhere a client does validate. - Private CA : a root (and intermediates) you control; clients trust it by installing the root. AWS Private CA (ACM PCA) does this as a managed service (notable monthly cost per CA); step-ca , HashiCorp Vault PKI, or cert-manager with a CA issuer in Kubernetes are common alternatives. Service meshes run their own. - Public certificates for internal names : possible if the names are under a public domain you control ( orders.internal.client.com ) and you use DNS-01; the certificates appear in public Certificate Transparency logs, revealing hostnames, which may or may not be acceptable. Operating a private CA means owning: root key protection (HSM or at least offline), intermediate rotation, distribution of the root to every client trust store (base images, config management, mobile devices), and revocation. Do not start one casually; do start one if you need mTLS between many services or encryption to backends that validate.

Every publicly trusted certificate is logged in public CT logs; browsers require proof of logging. Monitor CT for your domains (free services exist) to detect certificates issued without your knowledge, which indicates DNS compromise or a rogue CA. Set a caa DNS record so only your chosen CAs may issue.

- Private keys are the crown jewels: mode 600, owned by root or the service user, never in Git, never emailed. ACM and KMS-backed HSMs remove the key from your hands entirely. - Key type: ECDSA P-256 keys are smaller and faster than RSA 2048 and universally supported now; RSA remains common for compatibility. Let's Encrypt and ACM offer both. - A wildcard key on a compromised host lets the attacker impersonate every subdomain; prefer per-service certificates where automation makes it cheap. - Pinning (hard-coding expected certificates in clients) causes outages on rotation; use CAA and CT monitoring instead, and reserve pinning for high-security mobile apps with a careful rotation plan.
