HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone. Yet applications need to know that this request comes from the same user who logged in five minutes ago. Cookies are the browser-side mechanism for carrying a small piece of state, and sessions are the server-side pattern built on top. Because cookies are attached automatically by the browser, they are also the mechanism behind cross-site request forgery and a prime target for theft via XSS. Part IV chapters 4 and 9 cover the attacks in depth; this chapter establishes how the mechanism works.

A server sets a cookie with a response header; the browser stores it and attaches it to subsequent requests that match its scope. HTTP/1.1 200 OK Set-Cookie: __Host-session=8f3c1d...; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=86400 GET /api/me HTTP/1.1 Host: app.client.com Cookie: __Host-session=8f3c1d... The browser decides whether to send a cookie based on the request's host (matching Domain), path , scheme (Secure), cross-site context (SameSite), and expiry . The server cannot see cookies that were not sent and cannot read cookies set by other sites.

Attribute Effect Recommendation --- --- --- Domain=client.com Sent to client.com and all subdomains Omit it. Without Domain, the cookie is host-only (sent only to the exact host that set it). Setting it widens exposure to every subdomain, including ones hosting user content or third-party tools. Path=/api Sent only for URLs under the path Use / . Path is not a security boundary (pages on the same origin can read each other's cookies via script). Expires / Max-Age Persistent cookie; otherwise a session cookie deleted when the browser closes (often not, with session restore) Set Max-Age explicitly for login sessions (hours to days) and rely on server-side expiry too. Secure Only sent over HTTPS Always. HttpOnly Not accessible to JavaScript ( document.cookie ) Always for session cookies. Blocks the most direct XSS theft path. SameSite=Strict Never sent on cross-site requests, even top-level navigation Strongest CSRF protection; breaks "arrive from an email link and be logged in". SameSite=Lax Sent on top-level GET navigations from other sites; not on cross-site POSTs, iframes, fetches Default choice. Good CSRF protection with normal UX. Modern browsers default to Lax when unspecified. SameSite=None Sent cross-site; requires Secure Only for cookies that must work in third-party contexts (embedded widgets, some SSO flows). Host- prefix Browser enforces: Secure, Path=/, no Domain Use it for session cookies. Prevents subdomain cookie injection. Secure- prefix Browser enforces Secure

Browsers cap cookies around 4 KB each and a few dozen per domain, and every cookie is sent with every request to matching hosts, including static assets. A 3 KB cookie on a page with 50 asset requests costs 150 KB of upload per page view. Keep cookies small (an opaque ID), and serve static assets from a cookieless domain or a CDN path that the cookie's scope does not cover.

The session pattern: the cookie holds an opaque, random session ID ; the server looks it up in a store (Redis, database, in-memory for a single process) to find the user and any state. # FastAPI sketch with Redis-backed sessions import secrets, json from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Response, HTTPException SESSION_TTL = 60 * 60 * 12 async def create_session(redis, user_id: str) -> str: sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32) # 256 bits of randomness await redis.set(f"sess:{sid}", json.dumps({"uid": user_id, "created": now()}), ex=SESSION_TTL) return sid def set_session_cookie(resp: Response, sid: str): resp.set_cookie("__Host-sid", sid, max_age=SESSION_TTL, path="/", secure=True, httponly=True, samesite="lax") async def current_user(request: Request, redis): sid = request.cookies.get("__Host-sid") data = sid and await redis.get(f"sess:{sid}") if not data: raise HTTPException(401) await redis.expire(f"sess:{sid}", SESSION_TTL) # sliding expiry return json.loads(data)["uid"] Properties: revocable (delete the key and the user is logged out everywhere); small cookie ; server holds the state , so it needs a shared store once you have more than one server (sticky sessions are a fragile alternative). Requirements: IDs with at least 128 bits of entropy from a cryptographic RNG; rotate the ID on login (and on privilege change) to defeat session fixation; absolute and idle expiry; delete on logout; store minimal data.

The alternative is to put signed state in the cookie or in an Authorization: Bearer header: a jwt or an encrypted, signed cookie (Rails, Django's signed cookies). The server verifies the signature and trusts the contents without a lookup. Benefits: no shared store, easy horizontal scaling, usable across services. Costs: cannot be revoked before expiry without reintroducing a store (a denylist), tokens grow with claims, and any bug in signature verification is catastrophic. Part IV chapter 5 covers the pitfalls. title Sessions versus stateless tokens columns Server-side session Stateless signed token Revocation / logout everywhere immediate only at expiry (or with a denylist) Infrastructure shared store (Redis) none beyond key management Cookie size hundreds of bytes to KBs Cross-service auth needs shared store or gateway any service with the public key can verify Failure mode of a bug lookup fails: user logged out forged token: full compromise Typical fit web apps with a browser frontend APIs consumed by many services, mobile clients, short-lived access tokens A common, sound hybrid: short-lived access tokens (minutes) for API calls plus a server-side session or refresh token (revocable) to mint new ones.

h: Cookies versus Authorization headers for SPAs
x: Single-page apps calling an API can store a token in JavaScript memory or localStorage and send it in the Authorization header, or rely on an HttpOnly cookie set by the API. Cookies are immune to theft via XSS (HttpOnly) but exposed to CSRF (mitigated by SameSite and tokens); header tokens are immune to CSRF but any XSS can steal them from storage. For a browser frontend on the same site as its API, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookies are the safer default. For third-party or mobile clients, bearer tokens in headers. Never store long-lived tokens in localStorage.

- app.client.com and api.client.com are different origins (for the same-origin policy) but the same site (for SameSite). A SameSite=Lax cookie set by api.client.com without a Domain attribute is host-only: sent to api.client.com from fetches made by the page at app.client.com (same site, so SameSite permits it; credentials: 'include' and CORS with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials are required). Part IV chapter 14. - A cookie set with Domain=client.com is sent to every subdomain. If any subdomain is less trusted (user-generated content, a vendor's tool, a forgotten staging host), it can read and set cookies for the whole domain (cookie tossing). The Host- prefix defends against injected cookies. - Public suffixes ( github.io , amazonaws.com , elb.amazonaws.com ) are on the Public Suffix List; browsers refuse Domain cookies at that level, so apps on raw load balancer hostnames cannot share cookies. Use your own domain.

With server-side sessions in a shared store, any instance can serve any request: the stateless-service goal. If the store is unavailable, every user is logged out; make Redis highly available (Multi-AZ ElastiCache) or fall back gracefully. Sticky sessions (ALB stickiness cookies AWSALB / AWSALBAPP ) route a user to the same target, which lets you keep sessions in process memory, but a deploy or scale-in logs users out and load distributes unevenly. Use stickiness as a temporary bridge for legacy apps, not a design.

- Session store sizing: sessions × size × TTL. Set TTLs; sessions without expiry fill Redis. - Logging: never log Cookie or Set-Cookie headers in full. Redact at the proxy and in application loggers. - Clock skew affects expiry checks on tokens; sessions in a store are immune. - GDPR-style consent applies to non-essential cookies (analytics), not to strictly necessary session cookies, but document what you set and why. - Rotation: when a user changes password or you detect compromise, invalidate all their sessions (store a per-user session generation number, or index sessions by user ID).

- Session cookie without HttpOnly or Secure . - Setting Domain=client.com out of habit, exposing the cookie to every subdomain. - Predictable or short session IDs; or using a database auto-increment ID. - Not rotating the session ID at login (session fixation). - Sessions in process memory behind a round-robin load balancer, "fixed" with stickiness. - Huge cookies carrying serialized user objects. - SameSite=None on the session cookie to make an embedded iframe work, removing CSRF protection everywhere. - Logging cookies. questions Which attribute prevents JavaScript from reading a cookie? options Secure SameSite=Strict HttpOnly Path=/ answer explain HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, blocking direct theft via XSS. Why is omitting the Domain attribute generally safer? options It makes the cookie larger The cookie becomes host-only and is not sent to (or settable by) other subdomains Browsers reject Domain It enables HttpOnly answer explain Host-only cookies limit exposure to the exact host. Domain=client.com shares with every subdomain. What is the main drawback of stateless signed tokens compared with server-side sessions? options They need Redis They cannot be revoked before expiry without adding server-side state They are smaller They do not work with load balancers answer explain Revocation requires a denylist or short lifetimes plus a revocable refresh mechanism. A `SameSite=Lax` session cookie is set by api.client.com. A page on evil.com submits a POST form

t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
x: Application servers are good at running your code and bad at everything else: terminating TLS efficiently, serving static files, absorbing slow clients, enforcing request size limits, compressing responses, routing several applications on one host, and presenting a stable public surface while backends change. A reverse proxy does all of that in front of your application. Nearly every production web deployment has at least one, whether it is Nginx on a VM, an ALB, a Kubernetes ingress controller, or a CDN.

t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
x: A forward proxy acts for clients : the client is configured to send requests to the proxy, which fetches from the Internet on its behalf. Uses: corporate egress control and filtering, caching, anonymity, giving private-subnet servers a controlled path out (Squid, or an explicit proxy with an allow-list of destinations). You meet forward proxies in client environments where all outbound traffic must pass through one, and HTTPS PROXY environment variables suddenly matter. A reverse proxy acts for servers : clients connect to it believing it is the server; it forwards to one or more backends. Everything in this chapter is about reverse proxies. title A reverse proxy in front of an application intro Click components. The proxy owns the public surface; the application owns business logic. nodes label Clients client Browsers, mobile apps, API consumers. They see one hostname and one certificate. Some are slow (mobile networks), some hostile. label Reverse proxy Nginx / Caddy :443 Terminates TLS; serves static files directly; buffers slow clients so backend workers are not tied up; enforces body size and rate limits; compresses; adds security headers; routes /api to the app and / to static files; logs every request with timing. label Static files /srv/app/static Served by the proxy from disk with long cache headers; the application never sees these requests. label Application gunicorn :8000, localhost only Bound to 127.0.0.1 or a Unix socket so it is reachable only via the proxy. t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
x: - Buffering ( proxy buffering on ): Nginx reads the whole response from the app quickly and dribbles it out to a slow client, freeing the application worker. Without it, a few slow mobile clients can hold all your Gunicorn workers. The exception is streaming, where buffering breaks the feature. - client max body size : a 2 GB upload to an endpoint expecting 1 MB JSON would otherwise be read into the application's memory. - Timeouts : proxy read timeout is where 504s come from; set it with your slowest legitimate operation in mind, and move anything slower to a background job. - Upstream keepalive ( keepalive 32 plus Connection "" ): avoids a TCP handshake per request to the backend. - proxy next upstream : retries on another backend when one fails; only safe for idempotent requests, and Nginx by default does not retry non-idempotent methods after a partial send ( non idempotent flag changes that; leave it off).

t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
h: Caddy: the same thing in ten lines
x: Caddy obtains and renews certificates automatically, defaults to modern TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and redirects HTTP to HTTPS without configuration. @file: /etc/caddy/Caddyfile api.client.com { encode zstd gzip header { Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains" X-Content-Type-Options nosniff Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin } request_body { max_size 10MB } handle_path /static/* { root * /srv/app/static file_server header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" } handle /ws* { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8001 } handle { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8000 { header_up X-Request-ID {http.request.uuid} transport http { dial_timeout 5s; response_header_timeout 30s } # Caddy sets X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host automatically flush_interval -1 # disable buffering for streaming (per-route if needed) } } log { output file /var/log/caddy/api.log; format json } } For a single VM or small client deployment, Caddy removes an entire class of operational risk (certificate expiry) and configuration error (weak TLS). Nginx remains the choice when you need its ecosystem, fine-grained tuning, or it is already the client's standard. Both are excellent; pick one and know it well.

t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
x: The application sees the proxy's address as the TCP peer. The real client IP, scheme and host arrive in headers set by the proxy. Two rules: 1. The application trusts these headers only from its own proxies. If an attacker can reach the application directly (or if the proxy forwards client-supplied X-Forwarded-For unchanged), they can forge any IP, bypassing rate limits and poisoning audit logs. Bind the application to localhost or a private network; configure the framework's trusted-proxy list ( ProxyHeadersMiddleware / --forwarded-allow-ips in uvicorn, app.set('trust proxy', ...) in Express, SECURE PROXY SSL HEADER in Django) to the proxy's address only. 2. X-Forwarded-For is a list. client, proxy1, proxy2 . The rightmost entries were added by proxies you control; the leftmost is client-supplied and unverifiable unless your edge overwrites it. Take the entry just before your own proxies. For TCP proxies (NLB, HAProxy TCP mode) that cannot add HTTP headers, the PROXY protocol prepends a line with the original addresses to the connection; both sides must enable it.

t: Proxies and Reverse Proxies with Nginx and Caddy
x: Often there are two proxies: an ALB in front, then Nginx or the application. The ALB terminates TLS and sets X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Port ; Nginx should append to those headers ( $proxy add x forwarded for ) and pass X-Forwarded-Proto through rather than overwriting it with $scheme (which would be http on the ALB-to-Nginx hop). Health checks from the ALB arrive at Nginx; route /health to the application and exclude it from access logs if it is noisy.

h: The problem: one server is not enough
x: A single server has three limits. Capacity : CPU, memory, connections and bandwidth are finite; past a point, latency climbs and requests fail. Availability : when it reboots for a kernel patch, crashes, or its Availability Zone has a bad day, the service is down. Deployability : replacing the running process means downtime unless something else is serving meanwhile. You can buy a bigger server (vertical scaling): simple, no code changes, but it has a ceiling, gets expensive quickly, and still leaves one point of failure. Or you can run several identical servers (horizontal scaling) and put something in front that spreads traffic across them and avoids the broken ones. That something is a load balancer, and it quietly solves all three problems: capacity (add servers), availability (route around failures and AZ outages), and deployability (rolling updates behind a stable endpoint). Horizontal scaling requires the servers to be stateless (or share state through a database, cache or session store), which is why Part I chapter 14 and this part's cookie chapter insisted on it.

A Layer 4 load balancer works on TCP/UDP connections. It sees IP addresses and ports, picks a backend, and forwards packets (or proxies the connection) without reading the payload. Fast, protocol-agnostic, preserves end-to-end TLS. It cannot route by URL, inspect headers, or retry a failed HTTP request. A Layer 7 load balancer terminates the connection, parses HTTP, and makes decisions per request : route /api to one pool and / to another, by hostname, by header; add forwarding headers; terminate TLS; redirect HTTP to HTTPS; return fixed responses; integrate with a WAF; authenticate users (ALB can do OIDC); and multiplex many client connections into fewer backend connections. title AWS Network Load Balancer versus Application Load Balancer columns NLB (Layer 4) ALB (Layer 7) Protocols TCP, UDP, TLS HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets Routing by listener port only host, path, header, query, method, source IP passthrough, or terminate (TLS listener) without L7 features terminates; ACM certs; SNI with many certs per listener; optional re-encrypt to targets Client IP preservation yes, natively (source IP seen by target) or PROXY protocol via X-Forwarded-For Static IP / Elastic IP yes, one per AZ no (use DNS alias; or put an NLB in front via ALB-type target group) Performance millions of connections, ultra-low latency, handles spikes instantly high but warms up; very sudden spikes can see brief 5xx while scaling Health checks TCP, HTTP, HTTPS HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC with path and status co

The ALB lives in public subnets across AZs; targets live in private subnets. nodes label Route 53 api.client.com ALIAS An alias record points at the ALB's DNS name (something like app-prod-123456.eu-west-1.elb.amazonaws.com). The ALB's IPs change; the alias follows them. Never hard-code ALB IPs. label Listener :443 ACM cert, TLS policy Checks for connections on 443, terminates TLS using an ACM certificate (free, auto-renewed) and a security policy (TLS 1.2+1.3). A second listener on :80 does nothing but redirect to HTTPS. rules label Rules host/path → target group Evaluated in priority order: `/api/*` → api target group; `/ws/*` → websocket group; host `admin.client.com` → admin group with OIDC auth; default → fixed 404. The load balancer's health check is the single most important configuration you will set. It decides when a target gets traffic and when it is removed. Design the endpoint well: - Readiness, not liveness : /health/ready should return 200 only when the instance can serve real requests: configuration loaded, database reachable (a cheap SELECT 1 with a short timeout, or a cached dependency status), caches warm enough, not shutting down. Part XI chapter 5 discusses the tradeoff of including dependencies. - Cheap and fast : it runs every 10–30 seconds per target per load balancer node. Do not run heavy queries. - Fail during shutdown : return 503 as soon as SIGTERM arrives (Part I chapter 6). - Return 200 explicitly ; ALB defaults to expecting 200 but you can set 200-299 . Tune the parameters: interval 10 s, healthy threshold 2, unhealthy threshold 2 gives roughly 20 s to detect a dead target and 20 s to readmit a recovered one. The default 30 s interval with threshold 5 means 2.5 minutes of sending traffic to a dead target. Deregistration delay: 10–30 s for APIs (as long as your longest request), longer only for long-polling or uploads.

- Round robin : each new request to the next target. Fine when requests are similar. - Least outstanding requests (ALB option): send to the target with the fewest in-flight requests. Better when request costs vary or targets differ in capacity; the usual recommendation for APIs. - Weighted (target groups with weights): canary deployments, blue-green traffic shifting. - Flow hash (NLB): 5-tuple hash so a connection always goes to the same target; inherent to L4. - Least connections / IP hash / consistent hashing : common in Nginx and HAProxy; consistent hashing matters for cache tiers where you want the same key on the same node.

Stickiness routes the same client to the same target, via a load-balancer cookie (ALB AWSALB ) or an application cookie. It exists for applications that keep session state in process memory. Costs: uneven load, loss of sessions on deploy or scale-in, and complexity. Prefer shared session stores (chapter 11) and leave stickiness off; enable it only as a bridge for legacy applications you cannot change, and document it as debt.

The ALB terminates TLS with ACM certificates: one per listener plus additional certificates served by SNI, or a wildcard. Enable HTTP→HTTPS redirect on the :80 listener as a redirect action. Choose a modern security policy. To targets, speak HTTP on the private network, or HTTPS if policy demands (the ALB will not validate the target's certificate name, so self-signed works). Chapter 9's diagram covers the options.

The ALB keeps connections to targets alive and reuses them. Two timeouts matter: the ALB idle timeout (default 60 s) applies to client and target connections; your target's keep-alive timeout must be longer (e.g. 120 s) or you get intermittent 502s. For long-running requests (large uploads, slow reports) raise the idle timeout, but anything over a minute should become asynchronous. The ALB generates X-Forwarded-For , X-Forwarded-Proto , X-Forwarded-Port , and X-Amzn-Trace-Id (a request ID you should log). Enable access logs to S3; they include target processing time and the status code the target returned versus what the ALB returned, which separates "app is slow" from "ALB is slow".

An ALB costs an hourly rate (≈$0.0225/h, about $16/month in us-east-1) plus Load Balancer Capacity Units based on new connections, active connections, processed bytes and rule evaluations; small APIs land around $18–25/month. An NLB is similar. The cost that surprises people is running one ALB per service : ten microservices with ten ALBs cost $200/month before any traffic. Share one ALB across services with host- and path-based rules, or use an ingress controller behind a single ALB. Verify current prices in the AWS Pricing Calculator.

Nginx and HAProxy as software load balancers on your own hosts (chapter 12 plus upstream blocks with several servers and max fails / fail timeout ); Kubernetes Services (L4, kube-proxy) and Ingress/Gateway controllers (L7); client-side load balancing in gRPC and service meshes (the client knows all endpoints and picks one); DNS round robin and Route 53 weighted/latency routing (coarse, TTL-bound, no health awareness unless health checks are configured); and global load balancing across regions via Route 53 or AWS Global Accelerator (anycast IPs in front of regional ALBs/NLBs).

- Choose between polling, long polling, server-sent events, WebSockets and gRPC streaming for a given real-time requirement. - Understand how each works at the protocol level and what it demands of proxies, load balancers and infrastructure. - Scale persistent connections across many instances and handle reconnection, backpressure and idle timeouts. - Use gRPC for service-to-service communication with awareness of its HTTP/2 requirements. ::: Chapters 6, 8 and 13. :::

HTTP's request-response model does not fit everything. A chat app needs the server to push messages the instant they arrive; a dashboard wants live metrics; a long-running job needs to report progress; services calling each other thousands of times a second want less overhead than JSON over HTTP/1.1. Several protocols extend or replace plain HTTP for these cases, and each one has infrastructure consequences: connection counts, proxy configuration, load balancer timeouts and stateful servers.

title Real-time and RPC options columns Short polling Long polling Server-Sent Events WebSockets gRPC (streaming) Direction client → server, repeat client → server, server holds server → client only bidirectional bidirectional (over HTTP/2) Transport plain HTTP plain HTTP HTTP, text/event-stream TCP after HTTP Upgrade HTTP/2 frames, protobuf Latency poll interval near real-time real-time real-time real-time Overhead high (empty responses) moderate lowest per message low, binary Proxies/LB trivial needs long timeouts disable buffering, long timeouts Upgrade support, long timeouts HTTP/2 end-to-end (ALB gRPC target type) Browser support all (EventSource; no custom headers) needs grpc-web proxy Auto-reconnect manual built in, with Last-Event-ID manual library-dependent Best for rarely; simple low-frequency checks legacy fallbacks notifications, feeds, progress, LLM token streams chat, collaboration, games, bidirectional control internal service-to-service APIs, streaming RPC A useful rule: if the server only needs to push, use SSE ; it is plain HTTP, works through everything, and reconnects itself. Use WebSockets only when the client must also send a high volume of messages with low latency. Use gRPC between services you control, not to browsers.

A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket and Connection: Upgrade ; the server replies 101 Switching Protocols , and from then on the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames in both directions until either side closes. Messages are framed (text or binary) with no HTTP semantics; you design the message protocol. // Server (Node, ws library) with heartbeat to detect dead clients import { WebSocketServer } from 'ws'; const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server, path: '/ws' }); wss.on('connection', (ws, req) => { const user = authenticate(req); // cookie or token in query/first message; reject early if (!user) return ws.close(4401, 'unauthorized'); ws.isAlive = true; ws.on('pong', () => { ws.isAlive = true; }); ws.on('message', (buf) => handle(user, JSON.parse(buf))); }); setInterval(() => wss.clients.forEach((ws) => { // every 30 s: terminate silent clients, ping the rest if (!ws.isAlive) return ws.terminate(); ws.isAlive = false; ws.ping(); }), 30_000); Infrastructure requirements: the proxy must forward the Upgrade headers ( proxy set header Upgrade $http upgrade; Connection "upgrade" in Nginx; ALB supports WebSockets natively on HTTP/HTTPS listeners); idle timeouts must exceed your ping interval; and each connection consumes a file descriptor and some memory on a specific server for its lifetime.

Persistent connections make servers stateful: user A is connected to server 1; a message for A arriving at server 2 must be routed to server 1. The standard solution is a pub/sub backplane : every server subscribes to a channel (Redis Pub/Sub, Redis Streams, SNS/SQS, Kafka); a message for A is published; the server holding A's connection delivers it. Connection counts per server are bounded by memory and file descriptors (tens of thousands per modest instance), so capacity planning is "connections per instance × instances", and deployments must handle mass reconnection (clients reconnect with randomised backoff, or storms follow). Managed alternatives: API Gateway WebSocket APIs, AppSync, Pusher, Ably. Authentication: browsers cannot set custom headers on WebSocket handshakes, so authenticate via the session cookie (SameSite rules apply), a short-lived token in the first message, or a one-time ticket in the URL (never a long-lived token in the URL; it lands in logs). Check Origin on the handshake to prevent cross-site WebSocket hijacking.

gRPC is an RPC framework: you define services and messages in Protocol Buffers, generate typed clients and servers for many languages, and calls travel as HTTP/2 streams with binary payloads. It supports unary calls and client-, server- and bidirectional streaming, deadlines propagated across hops, and rich status codes. syntax = "proto3"; service Orders { rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order); rpc WatchOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (stream OrderEvent); // server streaming } message GetOrderRequest { string id = 1; } message Order { string id = 1; string status = 2; repeated LineItem items = 3; } Why teams use it internally: strict contracts with generated code, small fast messages, streaming, deadlines and cancellation built in. Why not to browsers: browsers cannot speak raw gRPC (no control over HTTP/2 framing); grpc-web requires a proxy (Envoy) and loses some streaming modes. Why not for public APIs: tooling and debuggability ( curl cannot easily call it; use grpcurl ), and partners expect REST/JSON. Infrastructure: gRPC needs HTTP/2 end to end . An ALB supports gRPC target groups (protocol version gRPC) with gRPC-aware health checks and routing on service/method paths; Nginx proxies gRPC with grpc pass ; a plain L7 proxy that downgrades to HTTP/1.1 breaks it. Because one HTTP/2 connection carries many calls, L4 load balancing (NLB, Kubernetes Service) pins all of a client's calls to one backend; use an L7 balancer or client-side load balancing for even distribu

- Reconnection : clients must reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter, and resume from a cursor ( Last-Event-ID , a sequence number) so no events are lost or duplicated. Servers must tolerate reconnect storms after a deploy. - Backpressure : a slow consumer must not make the server buffer unboundedly. Bound per-connection queues; drop or coalesce low-value updates (the latest metric value supersedes old ones); close abusive connections. - Idle and dead connections : TCP will not tell you a client vanished. Use protocol-level pings and close on missed pongs. - Observability : track active connections per instance, messages per second, send-queue depth, reconnect rate. These are your capacity and health signals. - Deploys : a rolling deploy disconnects every client on the old instances. Drain gracefully (send a "reconnect" message, close with a code), and stagger instance replacement so reconnects spread out. - Authorization per message , not just per connection: a connection opened by user A must not be able to subscribe to user B's channel because the server forgot to check on subscribe.

- WebSockets where SSE would do, inheriting bidirectional complexity for a one-way feed. - Proxy buffering left on for SSE; streams arrive in 8 KB bursts or at the end. - Load balancer idle timeout at 60 s with no heartbeat; connections drop silently every minute. - Long-lived tokens in WebSocket URLs. - Pub/sub backplane missing; works perfectly with one instance, breaks at two. - gRPC behind an HTTP/1.1-only proxy, or L4-balanced so one backend takes all traffic. - No deadlines on gRPC calls; no reconnect backoff on clients. questions A dashboard needs live metric updates pushed from the server; the browser never sends data back except on page load. Which is the simplest robust choice? options WebSockets Server-Sent Events Short polling every second gRPC bidirectional streaming answer explain One-way push with built-in reconnection over plain HTTP. WebSockets add complexity without benefit here. Why do WebSocket servers need a pub/sub backplane when running more than one instance? options For TLS Because a client is connected to one specific instance, so messages arriving elsewhere must be relayed to it To store messages permanently Browsers require it answer explain Persistent connections make servers stateful; the backplane routes messages across instances. Which load balancer property breaks gRPC if ignored? options gRPC requires HTTP/2 end to end, so a proxy that downgrades to HTTP/1.1 breaks it gRPC cannot use TLS gRPC needs UDP gRPC requires sticky sessions answer exp

- Explain stateful versus stateless packet filtering and why "default deny" is the only sane posture. - Design layered network controls: security groups, network ACLs, host firewalls and WAFs, each doing what it is best at. - Write and read firewall rules in AWS, ufw and nftables without opening more than intended. - Debug "it times out" problems caused by filters, and spot dangerous rules in a client's environment. ::: Chapters 3, 4 and 5. :::

A server offers services on ports. Every open port reachable from an untrusted network is an attack surface: a database with a weak password, an admin interface, a debug endpoint, SSH exposed to password guessing. Firewalls restrict which sources can reach which ports, turning "everything is reachable unless the application defends itself" into "nothing is reachable unless explicitly allowed". They are the first and cheapest layer of defense in depth, and most of the catastrophic breaches of exposed databases needed only a firewall rule to prevent.

A stateless filter evaluates each packet alone against rules on source/destination address, protocol and port. To allow a TCP connection it needs two rules: inbound to the server port, and outbound from the server port back to the client's ephemeral ports (1024–65535), because it does not know the reply belongs to an existing connection. AWS Network ACLs are stateless. A stateful filter tracks connections. When an inbound packet is allowed and a connection is established, the return traffic is allowed automatically. One rule ("allow inbound 443 from anywhere") suffices; replies just work. AWS security groups, Linux nftables / iptables with conntrack, ufw , and nearly all modern firewalls are stateful. Stateful filters hold a connection table with timeouts (minutes for established TCP, seconds for UDP). Idle connections dropped from the table die silently, the same phenomenon as NAT in chapter 4; keep-alives are the cure.

The correct posture: deny everything, then allow the minimum . Inbound: only the ports the public needs (443, maybe 80 for redirects) from everywhere; administrative access (SSH) from specific addresses or via a bastion/VPN; internal services only from the components that use them. Outbound: ideally restricted too (a compromised server that cannot reach the Internet cannot download tools or exfiltrate data), though outbound allow-lists are operationally demanding and most teams start with outbound open and tighten for sensitive tiers.

Operates after TLS termination on the ALB. A WAF is not a substitute for secure code; it is a noisy, useful shield. label Network ACL subnet, stateless Ordered allow/deny rules on each subnet. Hard to debug; most teams keep NACLs permissive and rely on security groups. sgalb label SG: alb in: 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 Stateful. Allows HTTPS from the Internet to the load balancer. - Reference other security groups as sources instead of IP ranges wherever possible. "Allow 5432 from sg-app" stays correct as the app tier scales. - One security group per role (alb, app, db, bastion), not one per instance and not one giant shared group. - Inbound rules only for what the role serves. No SSH on application or database groups; use SSM Session Manager (chapter 16) or a bastion group. - Security groups allow only; there are no deny rules. Everything not allowed is denied. Rules are evaluated as a union across all groups attached to an interface. - Default outbound is "allow all". Restrict outbound on database and sensitive tiers (e.g., allow only to the VPC and to AWS service endpoints) when you can manage it. - Audit regularly: 0.0.0.0/0 on anything other than 80/443 on a load balancer is a finding. AWS Config rules and Security Hub flag these automatically.

Use them for coarse, subnet-level intent: data subnets accept traffic only from app subnet CIDRs; deny a known-malicious range; comply with a policy requiring subnet-level controls. Remember ephemeral ports (allow 1024–65535 inbound for return traffic from outbound connections, and outbound for replies to inbound connections) or you will spend an afternoon on a mystery timeout. Rules are numbered and the first match wins; leave gaps for insertion.

Even behind security groups, a host firewall adds defence against misconfigured cloud rules and documents intent on the machine itself. ufw (Ubuntu) is a friendly front end; nftables is the modern kernel interface ( iptables is its legacy predecessor, still everywhere). # ufw: default deny inbound, allow outbound, open what we serve sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw default allow outgoing sudo ufw allow from 203.0.113.0/29 to any port 22 proto tcp comment 'SSH from office' sudo ufw allow 80/tcp comment 'HTTP redirect' sudo ufw allow 443/tcp comment 'HTTPS' sudo ufw limit 22/tcp # rate-limit SSH connection attempts sudo ufw enable sudo ufw status numbered # nftables equivalent (/etc/nftables.conf), stateful with conntrack table inet filter { chain input { type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; ct state established,related accept iif lo accept ip protocol icmp accept ip6 nexthdr icmpv6 accept tcp dport 22 ip saddr 203.0.113.0/29 accept tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept log prefix "nft-drop " limit rate 5/minute } chain forward { type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop; } chain output { type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept; } } Docker manipulates iptables directly and bypasses ufw for published ports: -p 5432:5432 exposes the container to the world even if ufw denies 5432. Either bind published ports to localhost ( -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 ), rely on cloud security groups, or configure Docker's DOCKER-USER chain. This is a frequent, nasty surprise o

Outbound filtering is where mature environments differentiate themselves. Options in increasing strictness: security group outbound rules (by port/destination SG), route tables that keep private subnets off the Internet entirely (with VPC endpoints for AWS services), a NAT instance or AWS Network Firewall with domain allow-lists, or an explicit forward proxy that only permits known hosts. For client systems handling sensitive data, "the database tier cannot reach the Internet" is both a strong control and a simple one to implement with route tables and security groups.

A waf inspects HTTP requests after TLS termination and blocks patterns: SQL injection and XSS signatures, known bad bots, request floods (rate-based rules), geographic restrictions, and custom rules (block requests without a required header, or to admin paths from outside an IP set). AWS WAF attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway and AppSync; managed rule groups cover the common cases. Treat WAF as a shield that buys time and reduces noise, not as security: it can be bypassed by encoding tricks, it produces false positives (legitimate payloads containing SQL keywords), and it never fixes the underlying vulnerability. Start in count mode, review what would be blocked, then enforce.

The signature of a firewall is a timeout : packets dropped silently. (Some firewalls reject with RST or ICMP, giving "connection refused" or "unreachable" quickly, which is kinder to debuggers.) # From the client side nc -vz -w 3 10.20.128.10 5432 # times out → filtered somewhere; refused → reachable, nothing listening # AWS: Reachability Analyzer traces a path and names the blocking SG/NACL/route aws ec2 create-network-insights-path --source eni-app --destination eni-db --destination-port 5432 --protocol tcp # VPC Flow Logs show REJECT records with the interface and ports # On the host: are packets arriving at all? (if yes, the host firewall or the app is the problem) sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp port 5432 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' sudo nft list ruleset | grep -n 5432; sudo ufw status sudo journalctl -k | grep 'nft-drop' # logged drops Method: confirm the destination is listening ( ss -ltn on the target); confirm packets reach the target ( tcpdump there); if not, walk outward: host firewall, security group of the target, NACL of the target subnet, route tables, security group outbound of the source, NACL of the source subnet. Reachability Analyzer does this walk for you in AWS.

h: Red flags in a client environment
x: - Security group rules with 0.0.0.0/0 on 22, 3389, 3306, 5432, 6379, 27017, 9200. - A single "default" security group used by everything, allowing all traffic within itself. - Databases with public IPs or in public subnets "temporarily". - Firewall exceptions documented in nobody's head but a departed contractor's. - Docker-published ports on a public VM with only ufw for protection. - WAF in count mode for two years. Part XIII chapter 4 shows how to assess these without touching anything.

- Opening SSH to the world "to make deployment easier". - Stateless NACLs without ephemeral port rules; hours lost to a one-way connection. - Security groups by CIDR for internal tiers, breaking when IPs change. - Allowing all traffic within the VPC CIDR, which makes lateral movement trivial after one compromise. - Assuming ufw protects Docker-published ports. - Treating the WAF as the security strategy. - Not logging drops, so attacks and misconfigurations are both invisible. questions Why does a stateless firewall need an explicit rule allowing inbound traffic on ports 1024–65535 for a server that only makes outbound HTTPS calls? options For DNS Because reply packets arrive on the server's ephemeral source port and the filter does not track connections It does not; that is a misconfiguration For ICMP answer explain Stateless filters evaluate each packet alone. Return traffic to ephemeral ports must be allowed explicitly. What is the best source for a database security group's inbound 5432 rule? options 0.0.0.0/0 The VPC CIDR The application tier's security group ID The office IP range answer explain Referencing the app SG grants exactly the components that should connect, regardless of their IPs. You run `docker run -p 6379:6379 redis` on a public VM with ufw denying 6379. Is Redis exposed? options No, ufw blocks it Yes; Docker inserts iptables rules that bypass ufw's INPUT chain Only to the VPC Only over IPv6 answer explain Bind to 127.0.0.1, use cloud security groups, or

- Explain what a VPN provides and the difference between site-to-site, client and mesh VPNs. - Choose between a bastion host, SSM Session Manager, a client VPN and a zero-trust access proxy for administrative access. - Connect a VPC privately to a client's network or to other VPCs: VPN, Direct Connect, peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink. - Avoid the mistakes that make private connectivity either insecure or unmaintainable. ::: Chapters 4, 9 and 15. :::

Your database lives in a private subnet with no public address, as it should. Now a developer needs to run a query, a client's on-premises system needs to call your API without exposing it to the Internet, two VPCs need to talk, and an auditor asks how administrators reach production. "Private connectivity" is the set of mechanisms for reaching things that are deliberately unreachable from the public Internet, and each mechanism trades security, cost and convenience differently.

A Virtual Private Network creates an encrypted tunnel between two endpoints over an untrusted network, and makes remote networks appear local by routing traffic for their address ranges through the tunnel. Packets to 10.20.128.10 on your laptop are encrypted, sent to the VPN gateway's public address, decrypted there and forwarded into the VPC. Authentication is by certificates, pre-shared keys or an identity provider. Protocols: IPsec (the standard for site-to-site between routers and cloud gateways; complex but universal), WireGuard (modern, minimal, fast, in the Linux kernel; the basis of Tailscale and many self-hosted setups), OpenVPN (older, flexible, widely supported including AWS Client VPN), and TLS-based vendor VPNs.

Connects two networks: a client's office or data centre to your VPC. AWS Site-to-Site VPN pairs a Virtual Private Gateway (or Transit Gateway) with the client's firewall as a "customer gateway" over two IPsec tunnels for redundancy. Routing is static or via BGP. Throughput per tunnel is limited (1.25 Gbps). Address ranges must not overlap, which is why chapter 3 insisted on planning CIDRs.

Connects individual users' devices. AWS Client VPN (OpenVPN-based, authenticates with certificates, Active Directory or SAML) or self-hosted WireGuard/OpenVPN on a small instance. Users get a tunnel into the VPC for administrative access. Costs: per-endpoint-hour plus per-connection-hour for AWS Client VPN; a self-hosted WireGuard instance costs a few dollars a month but is yours to patch.

Tailscale, ZeroTier, Cloudflare WARP/Access and similar build an identity-based mesh where every device authenticates to a control plane and connects peer-to-peer over WireGuard, with access control lists per user and service. They remove the "once inside, everything is reachable" weakness of classic VPNs and are quick to set up; the trade is dependency on a third party's control plane for your access path.

title Ways to reach a private instance or database columns Option How it works Bastion (jump) host Hardened instance in a public subnet with SSH; you SSH through it (`ssh -J bastion target`) or port-forward to the DB Simple, universal, works for any TCP A public SSH endpoint to defend; key management; one more host to patch; audit logging needs setup SSM Session Manager The SSM agent on the instance opens an outbound channel to AWS; you get a shell or port forward via IAM-authenticated API calls. No inbound ports, no SSH keys No open ports, IAM auth + MFA, every session logged to CloudWatch/S3, works for RDS via port forwarding through an instance Needs the agent and an instance role; not for Fargate (use ECS Exec); slightly clunkier for file transfer Client VPN Tunnel into the VPC; then connect directly Natural for teams needing many internal services; IdP integration Cost; broad network access once connected unless ACLs are tight; split-tunnel decisions Zero-trust access proxy Identity-aware proxy (Cloudflare Access, Tailscale, Teleport, AWS Verified Access) brokers per-app access Per-user, per-app policy; strong audit; no VPN client sprawl Third-party dependency or new infrastructure; learning curve Public IP + security group Open the port to your office IP Nothing to build Office IPs change; mobile work breaks; a leaked credential plus a guessed IP equals breach. Not acceptable for databases For most AWS deployments the recommended default is SSM Session Manager for shell

A direct, non-transitive connection between two VPCs (same or different accounts/regions). Traffic stays on the AWS network. Each VPC adds routes for the other's CIDR; security groups can reference peered groups in the same region. Non-transitive means A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C. Fine for a handful of VPCs; a mess beyond that.

A regional hub that VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect attach to, with route tables controlling who can reach whom. Transitive, scalable, auditable; hourly cost per attachment plus per-GB. The standard for organisations with many VPCs or a hybrid network.

A dedicated physical link from a client's data centre to AWS via a partner location. Consistent latency and bandwidth (1–100 Gbps), traffic off the public Internet, lower data-transfer prices for heavy volumes; weeks to provision and significant fixed cost. Usually paired with a VPN as backup. Relevant when a client has serious on-premises systems; an FDE rarely provisions it but often works within it.

privatelink exposes a service (yours, behind an NLB, or an AWS service) as an elastic network interface inside the consumer's VPC. The consumer connects to a private IP; traffic never leaves AWS; no CIDR overlap concerns, no peering, no routing changes. This is how you offer a client's VPC private access to your SaaS API, and how your VPC reaches Secrets Manager, ECR or CloudWatch without a NAT gateway. Each interface endpoint has an hourly cost per AZ plus per-GB; gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free. title Private connectivity options between a client network and your VPC intro Click each link type to compare. legend nodes onprem label Client data centre 192.168.0.0/16 The client's existing network with its own firewalls, routing and address plan. Address overlap with your VPC must be ruled out before anything else. label Site-to-Site VPN IPsec, 2 tunnels Days to set up; ~$0.05/hour per connection plus data; 1.25 Gbps per tunnel; runs over the Internet so latency varies. Good enough for most integrations and as a Direct Connect backup. label Direct Connect dedicated fibre Weeks to months; fixed monthly port cost; predictable performance; needed for large data volumes or strict latency. Usually the client already has one if they are a serious AWS user. label PrivateLink endpoint service exposed via NLB No network merge at all: the client's VPC gets an interface for your specific service. Nothing else in your VPC is reachable. The cleanest way to expose an API to a

- A private network is not a trusted network. Encrypt in transit (TLS) over VPNs and peering too; authenticate every request. Private links reduce exposure; they do not replace application security. This is the core of zero trust. - Least privilege at the network layer still applies : a VPN user should reach the tools they need, not the whole VPC. Use security groups referencing the VPN's address pool narrowly, and client VPN authorization rules. - Audit every administrative session : SSM logs by default; bastions and VPNs need deliberate logging. - Avoid split-brain address plans : overlapping CIDRs force NAT hacks that nobody understands a year later. - Rotate and revoke : VPN certificates and WireGuard keys for people who leave; SSM access via IAM groups tied to the identity provider so offboarding is automatic. - Do not expose internal admin tools publicly behind "only we know the URL". Put them behind the VPN or an identity-aware proxy.

- SSH open to the Internet on production instances because "the bastion was too much work" (SSM is less work). - Agent forwarding to shared bastions. - A single VPN pre-shared key shared on a chat channel. - Client VPN users landing in a network where every security group allows the VPC CIDR. - Overlapping CIDRs discovered at VPN setup time, after infrastructure is deployed. - Relying on peering for a dozen VPCs, producing an unreadable mesh. - NAT gateway bills for traffic to AWS services that interface endpoints would carry privately (cost and security both improved). questions Which administrative access method requires no inbound ports and logs every session by default on AWS? options Bastion host with SSH AWS Client VPN SSM Session Manager Public IP with a security group answer explain The SSM agent connects outbound; access is IAM-authenticated and recorded. A client on AWS wants to call your API without traffic traversing the Internet, and does not want to peer networks. What fits best? options Site-to-Site VPN VPC peering PrivateLink (interface endpoint to your NLB-fronted service) Direct Connect answer explain PrivateLink exposes just the service, with no CIDR coordination or routing changes. Why is VPC peering unsuitable as the primary connectivity model for many VPCs? options It is expensive It is non-transitive, so every pair needs its own connection and routing It does not support security groups It only works in one region answer explain Peering scales as O(n²).

- Explain how a CDN serves content from the edge and what it can and cannot cache. - Design cache keys, TTLs, invalidation and origin configuration so that users get fast responses and never someone else's data. - Use CloudFront (or an equivalent) in front of static sites, APIs and media correctly. - Recognise when a CDN is unnecessary and when it is essential. ::: Chapters 1, 8 and 18 (latency) are closely related; read chapter 8 first. :::

Physics sets a floor on latency: a user in Sydney fetching from a server in Virginia waits 200 ms per round trip, and a page needs several. Meanwhile your origin serves the same static files millions of times, and a traffic spike or attack hits it directly. A Content Delivery Network places servers in hundreds of cities, answers users from the nearest one, caches what can be cached, absorbs floods, and terminates TLS close to the user so even uncacheable API calls get faster handshakes. In exchange you take on a new class of bugs: cache poisoning, stale content, and the infamous "user A sees user B's account page".

title A request through a CDN actors label User (Sydney) label label Edge PoP (Sydney) shield label Regional cache origin label Origin (Virginia) steps label resolve cdn.client.com title Steered to the nearest edge detail The CDN's authoritative DNS returns the address of a nearby point of presence (PoP), using anycast or latency-based DNS. The user's TCP and TLS handshakes complete in a few milliseconds with the Sydney PoP instead of 200 ms with Virginia. label GET /app.3f9a.js title Edge lookup detail The edge computes a **cache key** from the request (path, query string, selected headers and cookies as configured) and checks its cache. Hit: served immediately. Miss: forward toward the origin. shield label miss → regional tier title Origin shield / regional cache detail Many CDNs add a second tier (CloudFront Origin Shield, regional edge caches) so that hundreds of PoPs missing at once do not each hit the origin. Only the shield fetches from origin; the others get it from the shield. shield origin label GET /app.3f9a.js title Origin fetch detail The origin (S3, an ALB, any HTTP server) returns the object with caching headers. `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` tells every cache layer it can be kept for a year. origin label response, cached along the way title Stored and served detail Each tier stores the object for its TTL and serves it. Subsequent users in Sydney get it from the edge in milliseconds; users elsewhere get it from their own edge after their

- Fingerprinted static assets ( app.3f9a1c.js , logo.8bd2.png ): cache forever ( max-age=31536000, immutable ). The filename changes when content changes, so invalidation is never needed. Every modern bundler does this. - HTML shells and unfingerprinted files ( /index.html ): short TTL (seconds to minutes) or no-cache with ETag revalidation, so deploys take effect quickly. - Public API responses (product catalogue, public feeds): short s-maxage with stale-while-revalidate , keyed carefully on query parameters. - Media and downloads : long TTLs; range requests supported. - Personal or authenticated responses : never at a shared cache. Cache-Control: private, no-store , and configure the CDN behaviour for those paths to bypass caching entirely regardless of headers.

h: Cache keys and the "wrong user's data" disaster
x: The cache key decides which requests share a cached response. Too narrow (every header included) and nothing is ever a hit; too broad and responses leak between users. The classic incident: a CDN configured to cache based on URL only, an API endpoint /api/account that varies by session cookie, and a missing no-store . User A's account JSON is cached and served to users B through Z for the TTL. Defences, all of them: 1. Mark personal responses Cache-Control: private, no-store at the application. 2. Configure CDN behaviours per path: /api/ with caching disabled (CloudFront "CachingDisabled" policy) and all headers, cookies and query strings forwarded. 3. Include the relevant varying inputs in the cache key for anything that is cached and varies ( Vary: Accept-Encoding ; for per-language content, the Accept-Language header or a path prefix). Never include cookies in the cache key for public content (it destroys the hit rate); never cache content that depends on cookies. 4. Test it: fetch an authenticated endpoint as user A, then as user B, through the CDN, and compare; check the X-Cache / Age response headers to confirm misses.

Caches expire by TTL. To change content before expiry you invalidate (CloudFront: create an invalidation for paths; first 1,000 paths per month free, then per path) or purge (Cloudflare, Fastly: fast and cheap, often tag-based). Invalidation is slow (seconds to minutes) and blunt; design to need it rarely: - Fingerprint assets so they never need invalidation. - Give HTML a short TTL and invalidate only /index.html on deploy (one path). - For APIs, prefer short TTLs plus stale-while-revalidate over invalidation storms. - Version public API responses in the URL ( /v2/catalogue ) when their shape changes. Deploy order for a static site: upload new fingerprinted assets, then upload the new index.html referencing them, then invalidate /index.html (and / ). Never delete old assets immediately; users with the old HTML cached still need them.

- Origins : S3 (use Origin Access Control so the bucket is private and only CloudFront can read it), ALB, any custom HTTP origin, Lambda/API Gateway. Multiple origins with path-based behaviours: /api/ → ALB, / → S3. - Behaviours : per path pattern, with cache policy (what is in the key, TTLs), origin request policy (what is forwarded to origin), response headers policy (security headers added at the edge), compression, viewer protocol policy (redirect HTTP to HTTPS), allowed methods (enable PUT/POST/DELETE for API behaviours). - Certificates must be in us-east-1 (ACM) for CloudFront, regardless of origin region. - Edge functions : CloudFront Functions (lightweight, viewer request/response: URL rewrites, header manipulation, redirects) and Lambda@Edge (heavier, can call origins: auth at the edge, A/B routing). Also the place to implement SPA routing (serve /index.html for unknown paths) and security headers. - WAF and Shield : attach AWS WAF to the distribution; Shield Standard is automatic. Rate-based rules at the edge stop floods before they reach the ALB. - Logging : standard logs to S3 or real-time logs to Kinesis; x-edge-result-type tells you hit/miss/error rates per request. - Cost : data transfer out from CloudFront is cheaper than from EC2/ALB in most regions, there is a permanent free tier (1 TB/month out), and requests are billed per 10,000. For most client sites CloudFront reduces the bill. Verify current prices. # Minimal CloudFront behaviour design for a SPA + API

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: "The API is slow" is the most common complaint and the least specific. Slowness has at least four distinct physical causes with different remedies, and most engineers reach for the wrong one: they optimise database queries when the user is 200 ms away, or buy bandwidth when the problem is round trips. This chapter gives you the vocabulary and the arithmetic to diagnose performance before touching code.

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: - Latency : time for a unit of data to travel from source to destination (one-way), or the time for a request to get a response (round-trip time, RTT). Measured in milliseconds. Set by distance, hops and queueing. - Bandwidth : the capacity of a link, in bits per second. A 1 Gbps link can carry a gigabit per second if the protocol can use it. - Throughput : what you actually achieve: bytes per second transferred, or requests per second served. Always at or below bandwidth; often far below, limited by latency, loss and protocol behaviour. - Jitter : variation in latency. Matters for real-time media; a buffer absorbs it at the cost of added latency. - Packet loss : fraction of packets that do not arrive. Even 0.1% has outsized effects on TCP throughput over long paths. The intuition: bandwidth is how wide the pipe is; latency is how long the pipe is; throughput is how much water you actually move, which depends on both and on how the protocol behaves.

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: Light in fibre travels about 200,000 km/s, two-thirds of its speed in vacuum. Round trip across: Path Distance Theoretical RTT Typical measured RTT --- --- --- --- Same data centre < 1 km ~0 0.1–0.5 ms Between AZs in a region tens of km < 1 ms 1–2 ms London ↔ Frankfurt 640 km 6 ms 10–15 ms New York ↔ London 5,600 km 56 ms 70–80 ms New York ↔ Sydney 16,000 km 160 ms 200–250 ms Geostationary satellite 72,000 km round trip 480 ms 550–650 ms Measured RTTs exceed the theoretical because fibre routes are longer than great circles, and each router adds queueing and processing. Nothing you do on a server reduces these numbers; only moving the endpoint closer (regions, CDNs, edge compute) does.

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
h: Why round trips dominate small requests
x: A new HTTPS request costs: DNS (0–1 RTT), TCP handshake (1 RTT), TLS 1.3 handshake (1 RTT), request and first byte (1 RTT), plus server processing. For a Sydney user hitting Virginia (200 ms RTT): 600–800 ms before the server has even done any work, for a response that takes 5 ms to compute. With a warm, reused connection it is 200 ms plus 5. This is why: - Connection reuse (HTTP keep-alive, HTTP/2, connection pools) is the first performance tool. - Fewer, larger requests beat many small ones over high-latency links (and HTTP/2 multiplexing mitigates the many-small-requests cost). - Sequential dependent calls are latency multipliers : a page that loads HTML, then JS, then calls an API that calls another service, each dependent on the last, pays an RTT per step. Parallelise what can be parallel. - Chatty service-to-service calls across regions are architectural errors; keep tightly coupled services in the same region (ideally same AZ for the hottest paths, accepting the availability trade).

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
h: Why throughput falls short of bandwidth
x: TCP's congestion window limits how much data is in flight per RTT. Maximum throughput of one connection ≈ window ÷ RTT. With a 64 KB window and 100 ms RTT: 640 KB/s ≈ 5 Mbps, regardless of a 10 Gbps link. Modern stacks scale windows into megabytes, but loss resets growth. The Mathis formula gives the loss-limited ceiling: throughput ≈ (MSS ÷ RTT) × (1.22 ÷ √loss). At 100 ms RTT, 1,460-byte segments and 1% loss, that is about 1.4 Mbps per connection. Hence: - Long-distance, lossy paths need parallel connections or BBR congestion control to fill a link; or, better, move the data closer (CDN, regional buckets, S3 Transfer Acceleration). - Inside a region, loss is near zero and RTT is ~1 ms, so throughput approaches the link rate; EC2 instance bandwidth limits (which scale with instance size and are burstable on small types) become the ceiling. - Bandwidth-delay product (bandwidth × RTT) is the buffer size needed to keep a link full: 1 Gbps × 100 ms = 12.5 MB. Kernel defaults handle this now; very fast long links may still need tuning ( net.ipv4.tcp rmem/wmem ).

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: Time to transmit a payload = size ÷ bandwidth, added to latency. On a 10 Mbps mobile link, a 2 MB JavaScript bundle costs 1.6 s of pure transmission; on 100 ms RTT with slow start it costs several more RTTs. Compression (gzip/Brotli for text), smaller payloads (pagination, field selection, binary formats), image optimisation and code splitting attack this term. For APIs, a 1 MB JSON response that the client discards 90% of is a design problem visible in every metric.

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: Once the request arrives: queueing for a worker (visible as time between accept and handler start), middleware, business logic, database round trips (each one ~0.5–2 ms within a region; an N+1 query loop of 200 queries is 200–400 ms), calls to external APIs (tens to hundreds of ms, highly variable), serialisation, and the response write. Measure these separately; traces (Part XI) do exactly this.

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: Latency is skewed: most requests are fast, a tail is slow. The average hides the tail; the tail is what users remember and what SLOs are set on. Report p50, p95, p99 (and p99.9 for high-traffic systems). A p99 of 2 s means 1% of requests, often the same unlucky users repeatedly , wait 2 s or more. Tail latency compounds: a page making 10 parallel API calls experiences the p99 of the slowest, so at the page level the "p99" becomes roughly the p90 of each call. This is why high-fan-out systems obsess over tails.

The fixes are architectural (call the external API asynchronously or cache its result; batch the loop into one query), not micro-optimisations.

t: Latency, Throughput, Bandwidth and Packet Loss
x: 1. Eliminate round trips : connection reuse, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, batching, avoiding sequential dependent calls, caching DNS and auth lookups. 2. Move closer : CDN for static and cacheable content; regional deployments for users in distant markets; edge compute for lightweight personalisation. 3. Bound the tail : timeouts, hedged requests for idempotent calls, load shedding, avoiding GC pauses and cold starts on the hot path.

Every network problem is diagnosed by the same ladder, bottom to top, stopping at the first rung that fails. Write down what each step proved before moving on; the most common debugging failure is skipping a step on assumption. 1. Am I on the network? ip addr , ip route , ping , ping 1.1.1.1 . 2. Does the name resolve, and to what? dig +short name , compare resolvers. 3. Can I reach the host at all? ping (if ICMP allowed), mtr . 4. Can I open a TCP connection to the port? nc -vz host port ; refused versus timeout. 5. Does TLS negotiate? openssl s client -servername . 6. Does the application respond correctly? curl -v , status, headers, body, timing. 7. Is the server side seeing it? ss , tcpdump , application and proxy logs on the target. 8. Where is the time going? curl -w phases, mtr , traces. title Worked example: 'the API is unreachable from the new ECS tasks' situation A new ECS service in private subnets must call a client's partner API at partner.example.net:443. Packet capture is the ground truth. Capture narrowly and read in Wireshark when possible. sudo tcpdump -ni any 'host 10.20.128.10 and port 5432' # live, numeric, all interfaces sudo tcpdump -ni eth0 -w /tmp/cap.pcap 'tcp port 443' -c 2000 # save 2000 packets for Wireshark sudo tcpdump -ni any 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-rst) != 0' # only handshakes and resets sudo tcpdump -ni any -A 'tcp port 8000' # ASCII payload (plain HTTP only) sudo tcpdump -ni any 'icmp' # unreachable messages tell you who blocked you sudo tcpdump -ni any 'udp port 53' # DNS traffic # In a Fargate task without tcpdump: run a sidecar with tools, or use VPC Flow Logs / Traffic Mirroring What capture answers: Did the SYN leave? Did a SYN-ACK come back? Did we get a RST (and from whom)? Are retransmissions happening? Is TLS failing before or after the certificate? - Explain the client-server model and why separating presentation, logic and data into tiers is the default shape of web systems. - Decide where state lives in a multi-tier system and why each tier scales independently. - Describe the standard architecture for a modern application (SPA or mobile client, API, database, cache, queue, object storage, third parties) and the trust boundary at each hop. - Recognise common architectural mistakes that lead to coupling, data leaks and scaling walls. ::: Part I chapter 1; Part II chapter 20. :::

A program that runs on one machine has no architecture problem: everything is a function call. The moment users are elsewhere and data must outlive any single process, you must decide which parts run where, who owns which state, and how parts talk. Those decisions determine what you can scale, what you can secure, and what breaks when something fails. Multi-tier architecture is the accumulated answer to those questions, and understanding why each tier exists stops you from either skipping one you need or adding one you do not.

A client initiates requests; a server waits for and answers them. The browser is a client of your API; your API is a client of PostgreSQL; PostgreSQL is a client of the operating system's filesystem. The asymmetry matters: - The server is shared and must handle many clients concurrently, fairly, and without one client's behaviour affecting another's. - The client is untrusted . It runs on hardware you do not control, in software the user can modify. Nothing it sends can be believed without verification, and nothing it is told to hide is hidden. Every security rule in Part IV follows from this. - The server is available at a known address; clients come and go. State that must persist lives on the server side.

title Three tiers and what each owns intro Click a tier. The rule: each tier talks only to the one next to it, and state lives as far right as possible. legend nodes label Presentation tier browser SPA, mobile app, server-rendered HTML client Renders UI and collects input. Holds only transient UI state and cached copies of server data. In an SPA this tier is static files on a CDN plus JavaScript running in the user's browser; with server-side rendering it is a web process that produces HTML. logic label Application tier API servers: FastAPI / Express Enforces business rules, authentication and authorization, validation, and orchestrates data access and external calls. Stateless: any instance can serve any request, so it scales horizontally behind a load balancer and can be replaced at will. label Data tier PostgreSQL, Redis, S3 The durable truth, plus caches and blobs. Scaled differently (vertically, read replicas, partitioning) and protected most strictly: private network, least-privilege credentials, encrypted, backed up. edges logic label HTTPS, JSON, authenticated logic label SQL / Redis / S3 API, private network Why not let the browser talk to the database directly? Because the client is untrusted: authorization, validation and rate limiting have to happen somewhere you control, before data is touched. (Products like Supabase and Firebase that appear to allow client-to-database access insert a policy layer, row-level security, that plays the role of the application tier.

Layers are logical (presentation, domain, persistence code within one process). Tiers are physical (separate processes or machines). A monolith has many layers and one tier beyond the browser and database. Confusing the two leads people to think "clean architecture" requires separate services; it does not.

State is the enemy of scaling and the friend of correctness; put each kind where it belongs. Kind of state Lives in Why --- --- --- Durable business data Primary database Transactions, constraints, backups Files and large blobs Object storage Cheap, durable, served directly; databases are bad at blobs Sessions, rate limits, locks, hot cache Redis Fast, shared across instances, acceptable to lose In-flight work Queue Durable handoff between tiers; retries UI state Client Transient; never trusted Configuration Environment / parameter store Per environment, versioned Secrets Secrets manager Audited, rotated Nothing Application server memory Instances are disposable The last row is the discipline that makes horizontal scaling, rolling deploys and auto-healing possible. In-process caches are fine as performance optimisations only if losing them is harmless.

- Presentation : a CDN scales it essentially infinitely for static assets; server-rendered HTML scales like the application tier. - Application : add instances behind the load balancer; autoscale on CPU or request count. The limit becomes the data tier's connection count, which is why connection pooling and proxies (Part VIII chapter 6) matter. - Workers : scale on queue depth; they are the natural place to absorb bursts. - Data : vertical scaling first (bigger RDS instance), then read replicas for read-heavy loads, then caching, then partitioning or a specialised store for the hot path. Each step is more work than the last; the application tier's statelessness buys time before you need them.

- Server-side rendering (SSR) and full-stack frameworks (Next.js, Django templates, Rails): the presentation tier is a server process. It still should not hold state, and the API and data tiers remain. Often the SSR layer and the API are the same process early on. - Backend-for-frontend (BFF) : a thin API tailored to one client (web, mobile) in front of shared services; useful when clients need very different shapes. - Serverless : Lambda functions as the application tier; the same rules (stateless, data in managed stores) apply even more strictly, because instances live for milliseconds. - Two-tier (fat client to database) : legacy desktop apps, and still sometimes proposed with "the database has security built in". Avoid for anything multi-user and Internet-facing.
