- Design resource-oriented HTTP APIs with consistent naming, methods, status codes and error shapes. - Implement pagination, filtering, sorting and field selection that perform well and do not leak data. - Validate input rigorously at the boundary and return actionable errors. - Version an API and evolve it without breaking clients. ::: Part II chapter 8; Part I chapter 13. :::

An API is a contract with people you cannot talk to: mobile apps you cannot force to update, a client's integration team, your own frontend six months from now. Inconsistency costs every consumer time; ambiguity causes bugs; a careless change breaks production for someone else. Good API design is mostly about being boringly predictable, and about doing the hard things (pagination, errors, versioning) the same way every time.

Model the domain as resources (nouns) with identifiers, and use HTTP methods as the verbs: GET /v1/orders list orders (filtered, paginated) POST /v1/orders create an order GET /v1/orders/{id} fetch one PATCH /v1/orders/{id} partial update PUT /v1/orders/{id} full replacement (less common) DELETE /v1/orders/{id} delete (or soft-delete) GET /v1/orders/{id}/items sub-resource collection POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel action that does not map to CRUD: a verb sub-resource, used sparingly Conventions that prevent arguments: plural nouns; lower-case, hyphenated path segments; identifiers that are opaque and non-sequential (UUIDv7 or prefixed IDs like ord 01HZX… ) so URLs do not reveal volume or invite enumeration; nesting at most two levels deep; no verbs in URLs except for genuine actions that would otherwise be awkward ( /cancel , /approve , /search with complex bodies). Use the methods by their semantics (Part II chapter 8): GET is safe and cacheable; PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is for creation and non-idempotent actions, and should support an idempotency key when it causes side effects (chapter 3).

Situation Code Body --- --- --- Fetched 200 the resource Created 201 + Location header the resource Accepted for async processing 202 a job resource with a status URL Deleted, nothing to return 204 empty Malformed request (bad JSON, wrong types) 400 error Unauthenticated 401 + WWW-Authenticate error Authenticated but forbidden 403 (or 404 to avoid confirming existence) error Not found 404 error State conflict (duplicate, version mismatch) 409 error with details Valid JSON, invalid semantics 422 error with field details Rate limited 429 + Retry-After error Server bug 500 generic error with request ID Dependency down 503 + Retry-After error Return a consistent error shape . RFC 9457 (Problem Details) is a good standard: { "type": "https://api.client.com/errors/validation", "title": "Validation failed", "status": 422, "detail": "One or more fields are invalid.", "instance": "/v1/orders", "request_id": "7f3a9c2e-...", "errors": [ {"field": "items[0].qty", "message": "must be at least 1", "code": "min"}, {"field": "customer_id", "message": "unknown customer", "code": "not_found"} ] } Never leak internals in errors: stack traces, SQL, file paths, library versions. Log them server-side with the request ID; return the ID to the user so support can correlate.

Every input (path, query, headers, body) is validated against a schema before any logic runs: types, required fields, lengths, ranges, formats, enums, and unknown fields rejected or ignored deliberately . With FastAPI and Pydantic this is the natural style; with Express use zod or similar. from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ConfigDict from typing import Literal class LineItemIn(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") sku: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=64, pattern=r"^[A-Z0-9-]+$") qty: int = Field(ge=1, le=10_000) class OrderCreate(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") # reject unexpected fields (mass assignment defence) customer_id: str = Field(pattern=r"^cus_[a-z0-9]{20}$") items: list[LineItemIn] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200) currency: Literal["EUR", "USD", "GBP"] notes: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=2000) @app.post("/v1/orders", status_code=201, response_model=OrderOut) async def create_order(body: OrderCreate, user: User = Depends(current_user)): ... Separate input models from output models from database models . The output model is an allow-list of what leaves the system; it is how you avoid returning password hash or another tenant's fields by accident when someone adds a column. Semantic validation (does the customer exist, is the SKU purchasable, does the user own the customer) happens after schema validation, inside the service layer, and yields 404/409/422 as appropriate.

Never return unbounded collections. Two schemes: Offset pagination ( ?page=3&page size=50 or ?offset=100&limit=50 ): simple, allows jumping to a page, but OFFSET in SQL gets slower as the offset grows (the database still reads and discards the skipped rows), and inserts or deletes between requests cause skipped or duplicated items. Cursor (keyset) pagination : the response includes an opaque cursor encoding the last item's sort key; the next request passes it. Constant time at any depth, stable under concurrent writes, cannot jump to arbitrary pages. The right default for APIs and infinite scroll. GET /v1/orders?limit=50&cursor=eyJjcmVhdGVkX2F0IjoiMjAyNi0wMy0wMVQxMDoyMTowN1oiLCJpZCI6Im9yZF8wMUhaWCJ9 { "data": [ ... 50 orders ... ], "next_cursor": "eyJjcmVhdGVk…", "has_more": true } -- keyset: sort by a unique, indexed combination; the cursor carries the last (created_at, id) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 51; -- fetch one extra to know has_more Enforce a maximum limit (100 is typical); clamp silently or reject above it. Always include the tenant or owner filter inside the query, never applied after fetching.

Filtering: ?status=shipped&created after=2026-01-01 . Allow-list filterable fields; map each to a parameterised predicate; never interpolate field names from input into SQL. Sorting: ?sort=-created at,total with an allow-list of sortable columns, each backed by an index. Field selection ( ?fields=id,status,total ) and embedding ( ?include=customer ) reduce payloads but complicate caching; add them when a real client needs them. Full-text or complex search: a POST /v1/orders/search with a structured body is acceptable when query strings become unwieldy.

Two clients updating the same resource overwrite each other unless you prevent it. Optimistic concurrency : include a version ( ETag or a version field) in responses; clients send If-Match: "v7" on updates; the server rejects with 412 or 409 if the version changed. Cheap and sufficient for most APIs. Pessimistic locking is for workflows that genuinely need exclusive editing.

Breaking changes (Part I chapter 13) require a version boundary. Options: - URL path ( /v1/ , /v2/ ): explicit, cacheable, easy to route and document. The common choice. - Header ( Accept: application/vnd.client.v2+json or a custom header): cleaner URLs, harder to test in a browser, easy to forget. - Date-based (Stripe style, Version: 2026-03-01 ): fine-grained, requires a translation layer per version. Whichever you pick: additive changes (new optional fields, new endpoints, new enum values with documented "ignore unknown" behaviour) do not bump the version; removals, renames, type changes and semantic changes do. Keep old versions running for a published deprecation period, measure their usage, and tell consumers with Deprecation and Sunset headers. Resist versioning per-endpoint; version the API.

Generate OpenAPI from the code (FastAPI does this; for Express use a schema-first tool) and publish it. Chapter 14 covers contract testing and client generation. A good API has: a quick-start, authentication instructions, the error format, pagination rules, rate limits, a changelog and a sandbox.
Return 429 with Retry-After and expose RateLimit-Limit / RateLimit-Remaining / RateLimit-Reset headers so clients can behave. Chapter 5 covers implementation.

- Authorization on every endpoint, at the resource level (does this user own this order?), not just "is logged in". Part IV chapter 7. - Do not expose internal IDs that reveal counts or enable enumeration; use random identifiers. - Reject unknown fields on input to block mass assignment (Part IV chapter 13). - Limit payload sizes and array lengths in schemas; a 50 MB JSON body is a denial of service. - Return the same 404 for "does not exist" and "exists but not yours" when existence itself is sensitive. - Treat all query parameters as untrusted; they are logged, so never accept secrets in them.

- 200 for everything with an error field in the body. - Unbounded list endpoints, or offset pagination on tables with millions of rows. - Sequential integer IDs in URLs with no ownership check. - Returning database rows directly (every column, including sensitive ones). - Inconsistent naming across endpoints ( customerId , customer id , CustomerID ). - Versioning on day one with /v1/ , then making breaking changes within v1 anyway. - Error messages that leak stack traces or SQL. - GET endpoints with side effects. questions Which status code fits a request with syntactically valid JSON whose `qty` field is negative? options answer explain 422 Unprocessable Content is for semantically invalid input; 400 is for malformed requests. Why is keyset (cursor) pagination preferred for large collections? options It allows jumping to any page It is constant-time at any depth and stable under concurrent inserts and deletes It is required by HTTP It compresses better answer explain OFFSET scans and discards skipped rows and shifts as data changes; keyset seeks directly via an index. Adding a new optional field to a response is: options A breaking change requiring v2 Non-breaking, provided clients were told to ignore unknown fields Only allowed with a header version Never allowed answer explain Additive changes are compatible; removals, renames and type changes are not. What does `extra=\"forbid\"` on an input model protect against? options SQL injection Mass assignment: clients setting fie

- Explain why retries are unavoidable in distributed systems and why they are dangerous without idempotency. - Implement idempotency keys for POST operations correctly, including storage, concurrency and response replay. - Design message consumers and webhooks to tolerate duplicate delivery. - Recognise operations that are naturally idempotent and those that must be made so. ::: Part II chapters 1 and 6; chapter 2 of this part. :::

A client sends POST /payments to charge €50. The server charges the card, writes the record, and the response is lost: the user's Wi-Fi blipped, a load balancer timed out, the mobile app went to background. The client sees a timeout. Did the charge happen? It cannot know. If it retries, the customer may be charged twice; if it does not, an order may go unpaid. Every system that spans a network faces this, because networks lose replies (Part II chapter 1), and every robust system resolves it the same way: make the operation safe to repeat. An idempotent operation produces the same result whether performed once or many times. DELETE /orders/123 is idempotent (the order is gone either way). PUT /profile {name: "Ana"} is idempotent. POST /payments is not, unless you make it so.

- Client retries after timeouts or 5xx responses (including automatic retries in HTTP libraries and SDKs). - Users double-clicking submit buttons. - Load balancers and proxies retrying idempotent methods (and sometimes misconfigured to retry POST). - Message queues with at-least-once delivery: SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ all redeliver on failure or visibility timeout expiry. - Webhook providers retrying when your endpoint did not return 2xx fast enough. - Replayed events during recovery or reprocessing. Design assumption: every message and request may arrive more than once . Exactly-once delivery is not something networks provide; exactly-once processing is something you build with idempotency.

The standard pattern, used by Stripe, Adyen and others: 1. The client generates a unique key (UUIDv4) per logical operation and sends it in a header: Idempotency-Key: 5c8f… . 2. On first sight, the server records the key (scoped to the authenticated caller), processes the request, and stores the response alongside the key. 3. On a repeat with the same key and the same request body, the server returns the stored response without re-executing. 4. Same key with a different body is an error (422/409): the client is misusing the key. 5. Keys expire after a window (24 hours is common) to bound storage. title Idempotent POST with a retry actors label Client label store label Idempotency store (Redis/DB) label Payment provider steps label POST /payments, Idempotency-Key: K1 title First attempt detail The client generated K1 before sending and persisted it locally so that a retry after a crash uses the same key. store label SET K1 → in_progress NX title Claim the key atomically detail An atomic insert-if-absent (Redis SET NX, or a unique-constraint INSERT) claims the key. Queues deliver at least once. A consumer that sends an email per message will send duplicates unless it remembers what it has processed: async def handle(msg): event_id = msg.attributes["event_id"] # producer-assigned, stable across redeliveries async with db.transaction(): inserted = await db.fetchval( "INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING true", event_id) if not inserted: return # duplicate: already processed, ack and move on await apply_business_change(msg) # same transaction: all or nothing await send_email(msg) # side effect outside the transaction: still at-least-once! That last line shows the limit: external side effects cannot be rolled back. Options: make the external call idempotent too (email providers accept idempotency keys or message IDs), record the intent in the transaction and let a separate step perform it with its own dedup, or accept rare duplicates for low-stakes actions. The outbox pattern (Part IX chapter 6) formalises this. Also handle ordering : duplicates may arrive out of order relative to newer events. Carry a version or timestamp and ignore events older than the current state.

Prefer operations that are idempotent by construction: - PUT with full state instead of POST with deltas: "set balance to 120" versus "add 20". (Though "set" has its own concurrency hazards; pair with If-Match .) - Upserts keyed by a natural identifier : INSERT … ON CONFLICT (external id) DO UPDATE . - Absolute instructions in jobs : "ensure user X has role Y" rather than "grant role Y to X", so re-running is harmless. - Infrastructure as code is idempotent by design: declare the desired state, apply repeatedly. - Conditional writes in DynamoDB and S3 ( If-None-Match: ) to create-once.

Idempotency makes retries safe; retries still need discipline: a bounded number, exponential backoff with jitter, retrying only on retryable errors (timeouts, 429, 502/503/504, connection resets; never on 400/401/403/422), honouring Retry-After , and a total deadline. Part IX chapter 8 covers this fully. Retrying non-idempotent operations without keys is how you get duplicate orders.

- Treating POST as safe to retry "because the server probably didn't get it". - Idempotency keys generated server-side (useless: the retry gets a new one) or derived from the request body (two legitimate identical requests collide). - Keys not scoped per caller. - Checking for the key, then inserting it, non-atomically; two concurrent requests both proceed. - Storing only "key seen" without the response, so the replay returns a different answer. - Consumers that dedupe in memory (lost on restart) or not at all. - Forgetting that the downstream provider also needs an idempotency key. questions A client's POST /orders times out. Without idempotency, what is the correct inference about the order? options It was not created It was created Unknown: the request may or may not have been processed It will be created later answer explain A lost reply is indistinguishable from a lost request. Idempotency keys resolve the ambiguity safely. Why must the idempotency key be generated by the client? options Servers cannot generate UUIDs Only the client knows that two sends are the same logical operation; a server-generated key would differ per attempt For caching To reduce server load answer explain The key ties retries together. The client creates it once and reuses it on every attempt. Two identical requests with the same key arrive at the same instant. What prevents double processing? options HTTP/2 An atomic claim (unique constraint or SET NX) so only one can proceed while the other see

- Trace a request from the socket through the server, framework, middleware stack and handler, and back out. - Order middleware correctly and know what belongs in middleware versus handlers. - Implement the production middleware set: request IDs, proxy headers, security headers, CORS, authentication, rate limiting, timeouts, error handling, logging and metrics. - Debug problems that live between the network and your code. ::: Part II chapters 8 and 12; chapter 2 of this part. :::

Between "bytes arrived on a socket" and "my handler function ran" sits a stack of machinery you did not write and probably have not read. When a request is slow, mis-authenticated, missing a header, or logged without context, the cause is usually in that stack. Owning it is what separates "I write endpoints" from "I run a service".

title A request through a FastAPI service behind Gunicorn intro The same shape applies to Express, Django, Spring and Rails with different names. actors label Kernel label Server (uvicorn worker) label Middleware stack label Dependencies / guards label Handler label Database steps label accept(); read bytes title Socket to HTTP detail The kernel completed the TCP handshake and queued the connection in the listen backlog. The worker's event loop accepts it and reads bytes. The HTTP parser (h11 or httptools) turns them into method, path, headers and a body stream, enforcing limits on header size and count. Malformed requests die here with 400, before any of your code. label ASGI scope + receive/send title Framework entry detail The server calls the application with a standardised representation (ASGI in Python, the req/res objects in Node). The framework wraps it and begins the middleware chain, outermost first. label request ID · proxy headers · timing title Outer middleware: context detail Generate or adopt a request ID (from X-Request-ID / X-Amzn-Trace-Id / traceparent) and bind it to the logging context; interpret X-Forwarded-* from trusted proxies to set the real client IP and scheme; start the timer. These must run first so everything later, including error handlers, has context. If the proxy-headers middleware is missing or trusts the wrong source, every later decision (rate limits, audit logs, HTTPS redirects) is wrong. label security headers · CORS · body limits title

Middleware wraps like layers of an onion: the first registered is the outermost, running first on the way in and last on the way out. Getting the order wrong is a classic source of subtle bugs. A sound production order (outermost first): 1. Request ID and logging context : everything downstream, including error handlers and access logs, needs it. 2. Proxy headers (trusted proxies only): client IP and scheme must be correct before rate limiting, redirects and audit logs. 3. Timing and metrics : measures the whole stack. 4. Error handling : catches exceptions from everything inside and renders a consistent error. (In some frameworks the error handler is registered separately; conceptually it wraps the rest.) 5. Security headers : applied to every response, including errors. 6. CORS : preflights answered before authentication (an OPTIONS request carries no credentials). 7. Body size limits and request timeout . 8. Authentication (identify the principal). 9. Rate limiting (needs the principal). 10. Routing, validation, dependencies, handler . Frameworks differ in syntax but the principle holds: context first, protection next, identity, then quota, then your code. # FastAPI / Starlette: add_middleware order is reversed (last added = outermost), so register inner-most first. app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan) app.add_middleware(RateLimitMiddleware) # innermost of the custom set app.add_middleware(AuthMiddleware) app.add_middleware(BodySizeLimitMiddleware, max_bytes=10 * 1024 * 1024)

Concern Middleware Handler / service --- --- --- Request ID, logging context ✓ Client IP / scheme from proxies ✓ Security headers, CORS ✓ Body size, request timeout ✓ Authentication (who) ✓ Authorization (may they do this?) ✓ (needs the resource) Input validation (shape) framework Semantic validation (exists, owned, allowed state) ✓ Rate limiting ✓ ✓ for per-resource quotas Transactions per-request dependency ✓ boundaries Metrics, access logs ✓ business metrics in service Error rendering ✓ raise typed exceptions Authorization in middleware ("admins only on /admin/ ") is fine as a coarse gate but never a substitute for resource-level checks in handlers.

A request ID generated at the edge (CloudFront and ALB both provide one) and propagated through every log line and downstream call is the single highest-value observability feature you can add in an afternoon. Bind it to the logging context so handlers do not pass it around manually: import logging, contextvars, uuid request_id_var = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id", default="-") class RequestIDMiddleware: def __init__(self, app): self.app = app async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send): if scope["type"] != "http": return await self.app(scope, receive, send) headers = dict(scope["headers"]) rid = headers.get(b"x-request-id", b"").decode() or headers.get(b"x-amzn-trace-id", b"").decode() or str(uuid.uuid4()) token = request_id_var.set(rid) async def send_with_id(message): if message["type"] == "http.response.start": message["headers"].append((b"x-request-id", rid.encode())) await send(message) try: await self.app(scope, receive, send_with_id) finally: request_id_var.reset(token) class ContextFilter(logging.Filter): def filter(self, record): record.request_id = request_id_var.get(); return True Log as JSON with timestamp, level, logger, message, request id, user id, tenant id, route, status, duration ms . Part XI chapter 1.

A handler with no time bound is a liability: one slow dependency and the worker is gone. Set a request timeout (middleware or server level), per-call timeouts on every outbound request and query, and handle client disconnects (ASGI delivers http.disconnect ; Starlette's request.is disconnected() ). Keep the server's timeout above the proxy's so that the proxy, not the application, reports 504 consistently, or below it so the application can return a clean 503 with a message; pick one and document it.

Convert every exception into a consistent response. Known business errors (not found, conflict, forbidden) are raised as typed exceptions carrying a status; unknown exceptions become 500 with a request ID and are logged at ERROR with the stack trace. Never return exception messages from unknown errors to clients; they leak internals. Validate that error responses still carry security headers and CORS headers, or browsers will show a confusing CORS error instead of the real one.

- Request never reaches the handler : 404/405 from the router (path, trailing slash, method), 401 from auth middleware, 413 body limit, 422 validation. Enable debug logging for the middleware or add a temporary middleware that logs method, path and headers at entry. - Handler runs but the client sees something else : a later middleware altered the response (compression, caching, error handler swallowing). Compare curl output with handler logs. - Wrong client IP or http:// redirects : proxy headers middleware missing or untrusted hop count wrong. - CORS error in the browser but curl works : preflight not answered, credentials flag mismatch, error responses lacking CORS headers. - Slow with low CPU : blocked event loop or pool exhaustion; look at where time is spent per stage with timing middleware. - Streaming broken : a middleware that buffers the body (some gzip and logging middleware do).

- Logging middleware registered inside authentication, so failed auth attempts have no request ID. - Trusting proxy headers from everyone ( trust proxy: true in Express). - CORS middleware inside auth, so preflights get 401. - Security headers only on successful responses. - No request timeout; no outbound timeouts. - Catch-all exception handler that returns str(exc) to the client. - Doing authorization in middleware by URL pattern and forgetting resource ownership. - Heavy work (database lookups) in middleware that runs for static or health check routes. questions Why should the request-ID middleware be the outermost layer? options It is the fastest So that every later component, including error handlers and access logs, has the ID in context HTTP requires it To bypass authentication answer explain Anything that runs before the ID is set cannot be correlated. A browser shows a CORS error for a request that returns 500. The server's CORS configuration is correct for 200 responses. What is likely wrong? options The browser is broken The error handler produces responses without CORS headers because it runs outside the CORS middleware CORS does not apply to errors The request used the wrong method answer explain Error responses must pass through the same header-adding layers. Where does resource-level authorization belong? options In the load balancer In middleware by URL pattern In the handler or service, where the resource is known In the database only answer explain You canno

- Explain what an API gateway does, when it earns its place, and when a load balancer plus middleware is enough. - Implement rate limiting with token bucket and sliding window algorithms, in-process and distributed with Redis. - Choose limit keys, tiers and responses that protect the service without punishing legitimate users. - Understand AWS API Gateway's role and costs relative to an ALB. ::: Chapter 4; Part II chapter 13. :::

Every public API faces the same cross-cutting demands: authenticate callers, stop any one of them from consuming all capacity, shape and route traffic, and present a stable surface while backends change. Implementing these in every service is repetitive and inconsistent; implementing them at the edge, once, is the idea of an API gateway. Rate limiting in particular is both a fairness mechanism and a safety mechanism: it stops bugs, abuse and traffic spikes from becoming outages.

A gateway is a reverse proxy with API-specific features: routing by path and version; authentication and authorization offload (validating JWTs, API keys, OAuth scopes); rate limiting and quotas per consumer; request and response transformation; caching; schema validation; observability (per-route metrics, logging); and developer-facing features (keys, usage plans, documentation portals). Products: AWS API Gateway, Kong, Apigee, Tyk, Envoy-based gateways, Nginx with modules, and the ALB itself for a subset (routing, OIDC authentication, WAF). When it earns its place: many backend services exposed under one API; external developers needing keys and quotas; a need to authenticate at the edge consistently; serverless backends (API Gateway + Lambda is a natural pair). When it does not: a single service behind an ALB where the middleware chapter already covers the needs. A gateway is another hop (latency, cost, config) and another place for drift; add it for a reason.

Two flavours: HTTP APIs (cheaper, lower latency, JWT authorizers, Lambda and HTTP integrations) and REST APIs (more features: usage plans and API keys, request validation, caching, WAF, private endpoints, canary deployments; roughly three times the per-request price). Both bill per million requests plus data transfer, which is attractive at low volume and expensive at high volume compared with an ALB's hourly model: at tens of millions of requests per month, an ALB in front of ECS is usually cheaper; at a few million, API Gateway's zero-idle cost wins. Timeouts are capped (29 seconds default on REST APIs, with a quota-increase path), payloads are capped at 10 MB, and WebSocket APIs are a separate type. Treat the limits as design constraints: long operations become asynchronous jobs.

A rate limit bounds requests per time window per key (100 requests/minute per API key). A quota bounds a longer period (1 million requests/month per plan). A concurrency limit bounds in-flight requests (10 simultaneous per tenant), which protects against slow requests in a way rate limits do not. Choose the key carefully: per authenticated principal (user, API key, tenant) for fairness; per IP as a fallback for unauthenticated routes, knowing that NAT and mobile carriers make IPs unfair in both directions; per route for expensive endpoints (login, search, export). Apply multiple layers: a generous global per-IP limit at the edge (WAF rate rule) to absorb floods, a per-tenant limit in the gateway or application for fairness, and tight per-route limits where abuse hurts (5 login attempts per minute per account).

- Fixed window : count requests in each calendar minute; reset at the boundary. Simple; allows 2× bursts across a boundary (100 at 12:00:59 and 100 at 12:01:00). - Sliding window log : store each request's timestamp; count those within the last N seconds. Exact; memory grows with rate. - Sliding window counter : weight the previous window's count by its overlap with the current sliding window. Near-exact, constant memory. A common production choice. - token bucket : a bucket holds up to B tokens, refilled at R per second; each request takes one; empty bucket means reject. Allows controlled bursts (B) with a sustained rate (R). The most widely used algorithm (AWS, Stripe, Nginx limit req is a variant called leaky bucket). - Leaky bucket : requests queue and drain at a fixed rate; smooths output. Nginx's limit req with burst behaves this way. # Token bucket in Redis, atomic via Lua: returns [allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms] TOKEN_BUCKET = """ local key, capacity, refill_per_ms, now, cost = KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3]), tonumber(ARGV[4]) local data = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts') local tokens = tonumber(data[1]) or capacity local ts = tonumber(data[2]) or now tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) * refill_per_ms) local allowed = 0 local retry = 0 if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 else retry = math.ceil((cost - tokens) / refill_per_ms) end redis.call('HSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now) redi

Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and the standard RateLimit- headers so well-behaved clients back off. Log limited requests with the key, so you can distinguish abuse from a legitimate client that needs a higher tier. Never rate-limit health checks. For login and other sensitive routes, limit per account and per IP, and consider progressive delays rather than hard blocks to avoid letting attackers lock users out deliberately.

Rate limiting at the edge protects your API; your API also needs to protect what it calls. Per-tenant concurrency limits (semaphores) stop one tenant's bulk job from exhausting the database pool; client-side rate limiters toward third-party APIs keep you within their quotas; circuit breakers stop hammering a failing dependency; and load shedding (returning 503 quickly when overloaded, based on queue depth or latency) keeps the service responsive for the requests it can serve. Part IX chapters 8 and 9.

Commercial APIs often combine a burst rate limit with monthly quotas per plan. Implement quotas as counters with a period key ( quota:tenant:2026-03 ) incremented atomically, checked before processing, and surfaced in a usage endpoint and dashboard so clients are never surprised. Decide the behaviour at the limit (hard stop, soft overage billing, degrade features) with the business, not alone.

- Rate limiting only by IP, blocking a whole office or university while an attacker rotates IPs. - Non-atomic counters across instances, so limits leak under load. - Limits with no Retry-After and no headers; clients retry immediately in a tight loop. - Limiting health checks or internal service calls accidentally. - Fixed windows allowing double bursts on expensive endpoints. - Using API Gateway for a high-volume service without modelling the per-request cost. - No limits on login, password reset or OTP endpoints, enabling credential stuffing and SMS pumping. questions Why is a token bucket preferred over a fixed window for most APIs? options It is simpler It allows controlled bursts while enforcing a sustained rate, and avoids the double-burst at window boundaries It needs no storage It is required by HTTP answer explain Fixed windows permit 2× the limit across a boundary; token buckets smooth this with a capacity and refill rate. Why implement the distributed limiter as a Lua script in Redis? options Lua is faster than Python The read-modify-write becomes atomic across all application instances, preventing races Redis requires Lua To avoid network calls answer explain Separate GET and SET calls from many instances race and let extra requests through. Which key is most appropriate for fair rate limiting of an authenticated API? options Client IP User agent Authenticated principal (user, API key or tenant), with IP as fallback for anonymous routes Request path only answer ex

- Decide which work belongs on the request path and which should be deferred to background workers. - Build a job system that is reliable: durable queueing, retries with backoff, idempotent handlers, dead-letter handling and visibility. - Operate workers: scaling on queue depth, graceful shutdown, poison messages, scheduled jobs. - Avoid the classic failures: lost jobs, duplicate side effects, unbounded retries and silent backlogs. ::: Chapters 1 and 3; Part I chapter 6. :::

A user clicks "Export report". The export takes 40 seconds, calls a third-party API that is occasionally down, and emails the result. Doing all of that inside the HTTP request means the user stares at a spinner, the load balancer may time out, a worker is tied up, and a third-party hiccup fails the whole request. The request path must be fast and reliable; slow and unreliable work goes elsewhere. "Elsewhere" is a queue and a pool of worker processes, and getting the mechanics right is what separates a system that silently drops exports from one that always delivers.

Defer to a job Keep synchronous --- --- Sending email, SMS, push notifications Validating input Calling third-party APIs that are slow or flaky Reading and writing the primary record Generating files: PDFs, exports, thumbnails, video transcodes Returning the created resource Webhook delivery to customers Authorization decisions Bulk operations, imports, recalculations Anything the user needs in the response Scheduled work: reports, cleanups, reconciliations Reads that must be fresh The response tells the user what happened to their request (created, accepted) and, for long work, how to track it: 202 Accepted with a job resource and status endpoint, or a notification when done.

Redelivery after a fixed visibility timeout is a crude retry. Better: compute a delay per attempt with exponential backoff and jitter and re-enqueue with DelaySeconds (SQS supports up to 15 minutes; for longer, store run after in the job row and have a scheduler pick it up). Cap attempts (5–10). Make failure visible : a jobs dashboard of queued/running/failed counts and ages, an alert on dead-letter queue depth, and an alert on the oldest queued job's age (a backlog growing silently is the most common job-system incident).

Periodic work (nightly reports, hourly reconciliation, cleanup) uses a scheduler that enqueues a message: EventBridge Scheduler → SQS, or a cron process. Rules: the scheduler must run once (not on every API instance, or you get N copies), jobs must be idempotent and safe to re-run, and long schedules should be checked by an alert that fires if the job did not run (a missing nightly report is noticed by the client, not by your error logs). Avoid in-process setInterval schedulers in the API (Part I chapter 2 showed what happens) and cron on a single VM with no monitoring.

- Scale worker count on queue depth (SQS ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible ) or on backlog per worker . ECS and Kubernetes both support this (target tracking on a custom metric, or KEDA). - Concurrency per worker : CPU-bound work (PDF rendering) wants one job per core; I/O-bound work (API calls) can run many concurrently with asyncio, bounded by a semaphore to protect downstream services. - Graceful shutdown : on SIGTERM stop receiving, finish in-flight jobs (within the orchestrator's grace period), and exit. Jobs longer than the grace period must checkpoint or tolerate being retried. - Resource limits : a job that loads a 2 GB file into memory kills the worker; stream, chunk, and bound. - Priority : separate queues for urgent (user-facing) versus bulk work, with separate worker pools, so an import of a million rows does not delay password-reset emails. - Isolation : one bad job type must not take down all workers; separate queues or pools per job family.

Python: Celery (mature, complex), RQ (simple, Redis), Dramatiq, arq (asyncio), or hand-rolled SQS consumers as above. Node: BullMQ (Redis), bee-queue, SQS consumers. Managed: SQS + ECS/Lambda, Step Functions for multi-step workflows, EventBridge for scheduling, Temporal for durable workflows with complex orchestration. Choose the simplest thing that gives you durability, retries, visibility and a DLQ. Hand-rolled consumers on SQS are often the right answer on AWS; a full workflow engine is right when jobs have many steps and long waits.

At-least-once delivery requires ack-after-success and idempotent handlers. A 90-second job is consumed from a queue with a 30-second visibility timeout. What happens? options Nothing unusual Another worker receives the same message after 30 s and runs the job concurrently The job is cancelled The message goes to the DLQ answer explain Set the visibility timeout above the job's maximum duration or extend it while working. - Distinguish queues from streams, commands from events, and point-to-point from publish/subscribe. - Reason about delivery guarantees (at-most-once, at-least-once, effectively-once), ordering and dead-letter handling. - Choose among SQS, SNS, EventBridge, RabbitMQ, Kafka and Redis Streams for a given problem. - Design event-driven integrations that stay debuggable. ::: Chapters 3 and 6. :::

Synchronous calls couple services in time: the caller waits, and if the callee is slow or down the caller fails. As systems grow, more components need to react to the same fact ("an order was placed": billing, inventory, email, analytics), and wiring each one as a synchronous call makes the order endpoint slower and more fragile with every consumer. Messaging decouples producers from consumers in time and in knowledge: the producer records that something happened; consumers react when they can. The cost is a new set of concerns: delivery semantics, ordering, duplicates, schema evolution and observability across asynchronous hops.

- Message : a unit of data sent through a broker. A command asks a specific receiver to do something ("SendInvoiceEmail"). An event states that something happened ("OrderPlaced"); the producer does not know or care who listens. - Queue (point-to-point): each message is consumed by exactly one of possibly many competing consumers. Work distribution. SQS, RabbitMQ queues. - Topic (publish/subscribe): each message is delivered to every subscriber. Fan-out. SNS, RabbitMQ exchanges, Kafka topics with consumer groups. - Stream : an append-only, ordered log that consumers read at their own position and can replay. Kafka, Kinesis, Redis Streams. - Broker : the server that stores and routes messages. - Consumer group : a set of consumers sharing the work of a topic/stream, each partition read by one member.

Networks lose and duplicate messages (Part II chapter 1), so brokers offer a choice: - At-most-once : fire and forget; a crash loses the message. Acceptable for metrics and ephemeral signals. - At-least-once : the broker redelivers until acknowledged; duplicates are possible. The default for every durable system. Consumers must be idempotent (chapter 3). - Exactly-once : not achievable end to end across arbitrary systems. What exists is effectively once : at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, sometimes helped by broker features (SQS FIFO deduplication IDs, Kafka transactions within Kafka). Design for duplicates regardless. Ordering : standard SQS does not guarantee order; SQS FIFO orders within a message group; Kafka orders within a partition; RabbitMQ orders within a queue for a single consumer. Ordering is per-key at best, never global at scale. Design events to carry a version or timestamp so consumers can detect staleness, and partition by the entity whose order matters (order ID, tenant ID).

Chapter 6: producer enqueues, competing consumers process, DLQ catches failures.

Publish OrderPlaced once to an SNS topic or EventBridge bus; each interested service has its own SQS queue subscribed (SNS → SQS fan-out). Each consumer processes independently with its own retries and DLQ. Adding a consumer never touches the producer. title Event fan-out with SNS and SQS intro One event, several independent consumers, each with its own queue and failure handling. legend nodes label Orders service Writes the order and publishes OrderPlaced. Ideally via the outbox pattern so the publish cannot be lost if the process dies between commit and publish. label SNS topic: orders Durable fan-out. Message filtering lets subscribers receive only event types they care about. label SQS: billing label SQS: inventory label SQS: notifications label Billing workers Charges the card; idempotent by order ID. label Inventory workers Reserves stock; publishes StockReserved or StockUnavailable. label Notification workers Sends the confirmation email with an idempotency key. edges label publish

Writing to the database and publishing to the broker are two operations; if the process dies between them, the event is lost (or, in the other order, published for a transaction that rolled back). The outbox pattern writes the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change; a relay process publishes rows from the table and marks them sent. Exactly-once recording , at-least-once publishing . Part IX chapter 6.

Events can carry full state ( OrderPlaced with all items and amounts) so consumers need not call back, or just an ID ( OrderPlaced {order id} ) so consumers fetch current state. Full-state events decouple more but grow and version harder; thin events keep consumers coupled to the producer's API. Many teams send enough state for common consumers and include the ID for the rest.
Multi-step business processes across services (reserve stock → charge → confirm) coordinate through events with compensating actions on failure (release stock if the charge fails). Part IX chapter 6.

Messages outlive deployments: a consumer may read an event produced by last week's producer. Define schemas (JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf), version them, and make changes additive: add optional fields, never rename or remove without a migration period. Include event type , event version , event id , occurred at , producer and a trace id in an envelope around the payload. A schema registry (Confluent, EventBridge Schema Registry) formalises this at scale.

Tracing breaks when a request becomes a message. Propagate the trace context in message attributes and continue the trace in the consumer, so one trace shows the API call, the queue wait, and the worker's processing (Part XI chapter 2). Log event id everywhere. Measure per queue: depth, oldest message age, consumer errors, DLQ depth, and end-to-end latency from occurred at to processed.

- Poison messages : always configure a DLQ and alert on it; redrive after fixing. - Backpressure : consumers that cannot keep up should be scaled, and producers may need to slow or shed; unbounded queues hide problems until the backlog is hours long. - Message size : SQS caps at 256 KB (1 MB extended with an S3 pointer library); large payloads go to S3 with a reference in the message (the claim-check pattern). - Security : encrypt queues at rest (SQS SSE-KMS), restrict who can publish and consume with IAM, and validate message contents like any other input; a compromised producer can inject malicious messages. - Cost : SQS is cheap per message but polling costs; use long polling and batching. Kafka clusters have a high fixed cost. - Local development : LocalStack or ElasticMQ for SQS; Docker images for RabbitMQ, Redpanda (Kafka-compatible) and Redis.

If the caller needs the result now, a queue adds latency and complexity without benefit. If there is one producer and one consumer in the same codebase with no slow work, a function call is better. If the team cannot operate the broker, pick a managed one or stay synchronous. Event-driven architecture is a tool for decoupling across time and teams, not a default.

Which AWS combination implements fan-out of one event to several independent consumers? options SQS alone SNS topic with an SQS queue per consumer Lambda alone RDS triggers answer explain SNS fans out; each SQS queue gives its consumer independent retries and dead-lettering. Why does the outbox pattern exist? options To speed up publishing To make the database write and the event publish atomic, so a crash between them cannot lose or fabricate events To store messages forever To avoid queues answer explain Dual writes are not atomic; the outbox puts the event in the same transaction and relays it afterwards. When is Kafka a better choice than SQS? options Always on AWS For small job queues When consumers need to replay history or many independent consumers read th

- Identify where caching helps (and where it harms) across browser, CDN, application and database layers. - Implement cache-aside with Redis correctly: keys, TTLs, serialization, stampede protection and invalidation. - Reason about staleness, consistency and the failure modes caches introduce. - Measure cache effectiveness and know when to remove a cache. ::: Part II chapters 8 and 17; this part's chapter 1. :::

Some data is read far more often than it changes: a product catalogue, a user's permissions, an exchange rate, a rendered page fragment. Recomputing or re-fetching it on every request wastes the most expensive resources you have (database CPU, third-party API quotas, user latency). A cache keeps a copy closer and cheaper. The price is the second-hardest problem in computer science: knowing when the copy is wrong.

title Cache layers, from the user inward layers Browser cache summary Controlled by Cache-Control and ETag. Zero network cost on a hit. Best for fingerprinted assets (forever) and conditional revalidation of HTML/API data. Part II chapter 8. CDN / edge cache summary Shared across users near them. Public, cacheable responses only. Static assets, public API responses with s-maxage. Never personal data. Part II chapter 17. Reverse proxy cache summary Nginx proxy_cache or Varnish in front of the app. Useful for server-rendered public pages; largely superseded by CDNs for Internet-facing systems. Application cache (distributed) Redis / Memcached summary Shared by all app instances. Sessions, computed results, hot entities, rate limits. The main subject of this chapter. Sub-millisecond, explicit keys and TTLs, you control invalidation. In-process cache LRU dict, Caffeine, lru_cache summary Per instance, nanoseconds, no network. Inconsistent across instances. For tiny, slow-changing data (feature flags, config, permission maps) with short TTLs. Must be bounded in size. Part I chapter 7's leak example was an unbounded one. Database caches summary Buffer pool / page cache; query result caches; materialised views. Automatic and large; good indexes keep hot data in memory. Materialised views precompute expensive aggregates on a refresh schedule.

The dominant application pattern: the application checks the cache; on a miss it loads from the source, stores the result with a TTL, and returns it. import json, asyncio, random from redis.asyncio import Redis async def get_product(redis: Redis, db, product_id: str) -> dict | None: key = f"product:v2:{product_id}" # include a schema version so you can change the shape safely cached = await redis.get(key) if cached is not None: return None if cached == b"__none__" else json.loads(cached) # negative caching: remember misses briefly row = await db.fetchrow("SELECT ... FROM products WHERE id = $1", product_id) if row is None: await redis.set(key, "__none__", ex=30) return None data = serialise(row) ttl = 300 + random.randint(0, 60) # jitter so keys do not expire in lockstep await redis.set(key, json.dumps(data), ex=ttl) return data async def update_product(redis, db, product_id, patch): await db.execute("UPDATE products SET ... WHERE id = $1", product_id) await redis.delete(f"product:v2:{product_id}") # invalidate after the write commits; next read repopulates Design decisions in that snippet: - Keys are namespaced ( product: ), versioned ( v2 ), and built from stable identifiers. Include the tenant when data is tenant-scoped: tenant:{t}:product:{id} , or you will serve one tenant's data to another. - TTL always. Even data you invalidate explicitly gets a TTL as a safety net against missed invalidations. Jitter prevents mass expiry. - Negative caching stops repeated lookups of m

- Read-through / write-through : the cache library itself loads and writes to the source; the application only talks to the cache. Convenient; makes the cache a dependency on the write path. - Write-behind : writes go to the cache and are flushed to the database asynchronously. Fast writes; risk of data loss if the cache dies before flush. Rarely appropriate for business data. - Refresh-ahead : proactively refresh popular keys before expiry. Smooths latency for hot items.

When a popular key expires, hundreds of concurrent requests miss simultaneously and all hit the database: a cache stampede. Mitigations: - Lock or single-flight : the first miss acquires a short lock ( SET lock:key NX EX 5 ) and recomputes; others wait briefly or serve stale. Within one process, coalesce concurrent loads of the same key. - Stale-while-revalidate : store the value with a logical expiry earlier than the physical TTL; serve the stale value while one request refreshes. - Probabilistic early expiration : each request recomputes early with a probability that rises as expiry nears. - Jittered TTLs against synchronised expiry across many keys. Hot keys (one key read a million times a second) can overload a single Redis shard; replicate hot values into in-process caches with very short TTLs, or shard the key ( key:{rand(0..9)} ) and read any.

A cache is a copy; copies lag. Decide per data type how stale is acceptable: a product description can be a minute old; a user's permission revocation should take effect within seconds; an account balance must be read from the source for any financial decision. Use short TTLs plus explicit invalidation for sensitive data, and never cache anything where staleness causes harm you cannot tolerate: authorization decisions that must be immediate, inventory counts at checkout, idempotency records. When several things cache the same data (CDN plus Redis plus browser), the effective staleness is the sum. Invalidation is hard because the writer must know every key that depends on the changed data. Keep dependencies simple (cache entities, not arbitrary query results), or use tag-based invalidation (track which keys belong to an entity and delete them together), or accept TTL-based eventual freshness for derived data.

Treat Redis as ephemeral by default : the application must work (slower) if the cache is empty or unavailable. Wrap cache calls with short timeouts (50–100 ms) and fall through to the source on error; a cache outage must not become a service outage. For data that is not reconstructible (sessions, rate-limit counters you cannot lose), either accept the loss on failure or use Redis persistence (AOF) and Multi-AZ replication (ElastiCache with automatic failover). Set maxmemory and an eviction policy ( allkeys-lru for pure caches; volatile-lru when some keys must never be evicted). Monitor hit ratio, evictions, memory, latency and connected clients. Part VIII chapter 11 covers Redis itself.

Hit ratio alone misleads; measure what the cache saves: database QPS and p99 with and without, origin cost, end-to-end latency. A cache with a 40% hit ratio on cheap queries may be worth nothing; one with 20% hits on a 2-second report is gold. Track per-key-family metrics ( product , permissions ), not one global number, and review periodically whether each cache still earns its complexity. Removing a cache that no longer helps is a legitimate improvement.

Caches hold copies of data with none of the database's row-level controls. Scope keys by tenant and user; never cache a response that depends on the requester under a key that omits the requester; encrypt Redis in transit and at rest (ElastiCache supports both) and require AUTH; do not cache secrets or tokens longer than needed; keep Redis in private subnets with a security group allowing only the application tier. Cached authorization data needs a tight TTL and invalidation on permission change.

- Caching without TTLs; stale forever after a missed invalidation. - Tenant or user missing from the key; data leaks between customers. - Cache as a hard dependency; Redis blip equals full outage. - Unbounded in-process caches (memory leaks). - Caching mutable, correctness-critical data (balances, permissions) with long TTLs. - Stampedes on hot keys at expiry; no jitter. - Caching ORM objects or responses with user-specific fields under shared keys. - Measuring hit ratio and nothing else. questions In cache-aside, what should the application do after a successful database write? options Update the cache with the new value Delete the cache key so the next read repopulates it Nothing; the TTL handles it Flush the whole cache answer explain Delete-on-write avoids race conditions where a concurrent slow read writes stale data back. Keep a TTL as a safety net. A popular key expires and 500 concurrent requests hit the database at once. What is this and one fix? options A hot key; add more Redis nodes A cache stampede; use single-flight locking or stale-while-revalidate Normal operation Eviction; raise maxmemory answer explain Coalesce the refresh so only one request recomputes while others wait or serve stale. Why must Redis timeouts be short and errors swallowed in a pure cache layer? options Redis is unreliable So a cache outage degrades performance rather than causing a service outage To save money Redis does not support long timeouts answer explain A cache is an optimisation; t

1. Add cache-aside to one hot read path with versioned, tenant-scoped keys, jittered TTL and delete-on-write. Measure database QPS before and after under load. 2. Reproduce a stampede by expiring a hot key under concurrent load; then implement single-flight locking and compare database query counts. 3. Stop Redis while the application runs. Verify the application keeps serving (slower) and recovers when Redis returns. If it does not, fix the timeouts and error handling.

- Design upload flows that never stream large files through your API servers, using presigned URLs and object storage. - Validate, scan and process uploaded files safely. - Organise S3 buckets, keys, access control, lifecycle and encryption for user content. - Serve files securely to the right users and no one else. ::: Chapters 1 and 6; Part II chapter 17. :::

Files are large, slow to transfer, and dangerous: a 500 MB upload through your API ties up a worker for minutes and fills its memory; a file named report.pdf may be a web shell; a bucket misconfigured for convenience leaks every client document. Object storage (S3 and its equivalents) solves scale and durability; the engineering is in how your application hands files to it and controls who can read them.

S3 stores objects (bytes plus metadata) under keys in buckets . It is not a filesystem: keys are flat strings, "folders" are a display convention based on / , there is no rename (copy and delete), and listing is paginated and relatively slow. It is extremely durable (designed for eleven nines), highly available, effectively infinite, and cheap for storage with costs for requests and egress. Access is via authenticated HTTP API calls, or via presigned URLs that embed a time-limited signature so an unauthenticated client can perform exactly one operation on exactly one key. Strong read-after-write consistency applies to all operations; what you PUT is immediately readable.

title Direct-to-S3 upload with presigned URLs intro File bytes never touch the API. The API only authorises and records. actors label Browser / app label label S3 bucket (private) label Worker steps label POST /uploads {filename, size, type} title Request permission to upload detail The client declares what it wants to upload. The API authenticates, authorises (may this user upload to this project?), validates the declared size against limits and the declared content type against an allow-list, and creates an `uploads` row with status=pending and a generated key such as `tenant/t_7/uploads/01HZX…/original`. label 201 {upload_id, url, fields, expires_in: 300} title Presigned URL (or POST policy) detail The API generates a presigned PUT URL (or a presigned POST with a policy) valid for a few minutes, bound to the exact key, and with conditions: content-length-range to cap size, and the expected Content-Type. The client never receives AWS credentials. label PUT bytes (direct, over HTTPS) title Upload directly detail The browser uploads straight to S3. S3 enforces the signed conditions: wrong key, oversized body or expired signature are rejected. For files over ~100 MB, use multipart upload with presigned URLs per part, which also enables resume and parallelism. CORS on the bucket must allow the app's origin for PUT. label POST /uploads/{id}/complete title Confirm detail The client tells the API it finished. The API does a HEAD on the object to confirm it exists and check its act

Trust nothing about an uploaded file: - Size : enforced by the presigned policy and re-checked on complete. - Type : the Content-Type header is client-supplied. Detect the real type from content (magic bytes: python-magic , file-type in Node) and compare with an allow-list. Reject mismatches. - Name : never use the client's filename as a key or on disk; generate IDs and store the original name as metadata, sanitised for display. Path traversal via filenames (Part IV chapter 12) is a classic. - Content : parse images with a library that rejects malformed data (and re-encode them to strip payloads); treat SVGs as dangerous (they can contain scripts; serve with Content-Disposition: attachment or sanitise); treat HTML uploads as dangerous; scan documents for malware; limit archive extraction (zip bombs: cap total extracted size and file count). - Metadata : strip EXIF (GPS coordinates in photos are personal data). - Serving : serve user content from a different origin than the application (a separate domain or CloudFront distribution) so that any HTML or script that slips through cannot access your cookies. Set Content-Disposition: attachment for downloads and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff .

- One bucket per environment per purpose (uploads, exports, backups), not one bucket for everything and not one per tenant (you will hit account bucket limits; use key prefixes for tenants). - Key layout : {tenant id}/{entity}/{object id}/{variant} keeps tenant isolation visible and makes IAM policies with prefix conditions possible. High request rates are fine with any prefix layout today; the old advice about random prefixes is obsolete. - Block Public Access on at the account and bucket level. Always. Public distribution goes through CloudFront with Origin Access Control. - Encryption at rest : SSE-S3 by default (free) or SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key for sensitive client data and auditability (KMS request costs apply; use bucket keys to reduce them). - Versioning : on for buckets with irreplaceable content; protects against accidental deletes and overwrites. Pair with lifecycle rules to expire old versions. - Lifecycle rules : transition cold data to Infrequent Access or Glacier tiers; expire temporary uploads that never completed after a day; expire old versions; abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days (otherwise they silently accumulate charges). - Object Lock for compliance retention where regulations require immutability. - Access logging / CloudTrail data events for sensitive buckets. - Bucket policies : deny unencrypted uploads, deny non-TLS access ( aws:SecureTransport ), allow only the application role and the CloudFront OAC.

Options for letting users read their files: 1. Presigned GET URLs from the API after an authorization check; short expiry (minutes); the URL can be shared within that window, which is usually acceptable. 2. CloudFront signed URLs or signed cookies for media-heavy apps: the CDN caches and serves, signatures enforce access, and the origin stays private. 3. Streaming through the API : authorise, then proxy bytes. Simple and fully controlled, but every byte flows through your servers; acceptable for small, sensitive documents, wrong for video. Never grant read via public ACLs or by guessing that long random keys are unguessable; "security by obscure URL" fails the moment a URL is logged, cached or shared.

Storage is cheap (around $0.023/GB/month for Standard in us-east-1); requests cost per thousand; egress to the Internet costs per GB (through CloudFront it is cheaper and includes a free tier). Multipart uploads of incomplete objects, forgotten versions, and lifecycle rules that never ran are the typical waste. Use S3 Storage Lens or an inventory to see what you are paying for. For performance, use multipart for large objects, parallel part uploads, and Transfer Acceleration for distant users if measurement shows benefit.

GCS and Azure Blob are equivalent with similar presigned mechanisms. MinIO runs an S3-compatible server locally for development and tests; LocalStack also emulates S3. Keep the storage client behind a small interface so tests can use a local bucket.

- Streaming uploads through the API; workers blocked and memory exhausted. - Trusting the client's Content-Type and filename. - Public buckets, or presigned URLs with week-long expiry. - Serving user uploads from the application's origin (XSS via uploaded HTML/SVG). - One bucket for all environments; staging tests delete production files. - No lifecycle rule for incomplete multipart uploads or abandoned pending uploads. - Processing files inline in the request (virus scan, thumbnailing) instead of a worker. - Forgetting CORS on the bucket for browser uploads. - EXIF location data served back to the world. questions Why should uploads go directly from the browser to S3 rather than through the API? options S3 is faster at validation API workers are not tied up and do not buffer large files; S3 enforces size and type conditions from the signed policy Browsers cannot send files to APIs It is cheaper for S3 answer explain The API authorises and records; the bytes bypass it entirely. A user uploads `invoice.pdf` with Content-Type application/pdf. What must the worker still do? options Nothing; the type is declared Detect the real type from content, scan it, and parse it before marking it ready Rename it Make it public answer explain Client-declared metadata is untrusted. Verify by content. Why serve user-uploaded content from a different origin than the application? options For CDN caching So any HTML or SVG that slips through cannot run with access to the application's cookies and

Try to upload an oversize file and a wrong-type file; confirm both are rejected by the storage layer. 2. Write a worker that verifies magic bytes, strips EXIF from images, and generates a thumbnail; wire it to S3 event notifications. 3. - Receive webhooks from third parties securely: signature verification, replay protection, idempotency and fast acknowledgement. - Send webhooks to customers reliably: signing, retries with backoff, ordering, delivery logs and endpoint management. - Design the operational tooling (replay, inspection, dead-lettering) that webhooks always end up needing. ::: Chapters 3, 6 and 7. :::

Polling a provider every few seconds to ask "did the payment settle yet?" wastes both sides' resources and is slow. A webhook inverts the direction: the provider makes an HTTP request to a URL you register when something happens. Simple in concept, webhooks are a classic source of security holes (unauthenticated endpoints that do what any caller says), reliability bugs (lost or duplicated events) and operational pain (who delivered what, when, and why did it fail?). You will both receive them (Stripe, GitHub, identity providers) and send them (to your clients' systems).

A webhook endpoint is an unauthenticated, Internet-facing POST handler that triggers business logic. Treat it as hostile input until proven otherwise. title Handling an inbound webhook correctly actors label Provider label Webhook endpoint label Database label Queue / worker steps label POST /webhooks/stripe (raw body + signature header) title Delivery detail The provider POSTs a JSON body and a signature header (`Stripe-Signature`, `X-Hub-Signature-256`, etc.) computed with a shared secret over the body and usually a timestamp. label verify HMAC over the RAW body title Authenticate the sender detail Compute HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + '.' + raw_body) and compare with the header using a constant-time comparison. The body must be the exact bytes received: parsing and re-serialising JSON changes whitespace and key order and breaks the signature. Reject with 400 if invalid. Without this step, anyone who finds the URL can fake events. Frameworks that parse JSON before your handler runs are the most common reason signature verification 'does not work'. Read the raw body. label check timestamp freshness title Replay protection detail Reject signatures whose timestamp is older than a few minutes. Otherwise a captured valid request can be replayed indefinitely. label INSERT event_id ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING title Deduplicate detail Providers retry on any non-2xx or timeout, so the same event arrives more than once. Record the provider's event ID; if already seen, return 200 immedia
When your product notifies customers' systems, you become the provider, and your customers will judge your reliability and your documentation.

- Event model : event id (unique, stable), type ( order.completed ), created at , api version , data (the object, or a reference and the fields that changed). Document every type with sample payloads. - Endpoint management : customers register URLs (HTTPS only; validate the URL, and resolve and check the IP at send time to prevent SSRF against your own network: Part IV chapter 12), choose event types, and receive a signing secret they can rotate. Provide a test-send button. - Signing : X-Signature: t= ,v1= . Publish verification code in several languages. - Delivery : from workers, with a short timeout (5–10 s), treating any non-2xx or timeout as failure. Expect customers to be slow and down. - Retries : exponential backoff with jitter over hours or days (e.g., 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 12 h, 24 h, up to 72 h), then mark the endpoint failing and notify the customer. Do not retry forever; do disable endpoints that fail for days (with notification) to protect your workers. - Ordering : deliver per endpoint in order where feasible but document that consumers must tolerate out-of-order and duplicate delivery. Include a version or sequence per object so they can detect staleness. - Delivery log : every attempt with timestamp, response code, latency and truncated response body, visible to the customer in a dashboard and to you in support. Allow manual replay of an event. - Volume control : batch or coalesce high-frequency events if customers request it; rate-limit per endpoint to

Both sides eventually need: a searchable log of events and delivery attempts; the ability to replay an event (inbound: re-enqueue from the stored raw payload; outbound: resend); alerts on failing endpoints and on inbound processing backlog; and a status page or dashboard customers can see. Build the log table and the replay button on day one; you will use them during the first incident.

- Verifying the signature over a parsed-and-reserialised body (always fails, so someone disables verification). - No signature verification at all; anyone can mark orders as paid. - Running business logic inline; provider times out and retries; duplicates everywhere. - No idempotency on inbound events. - Trusting event payloads for state instead of re-fetching for critical decisions. - Sending to customer URLs without SSRF checks (a customer registers http://169.254.169.254/ and your worker reads your own cloud credentials). - Retrying forever, or giving up after one attempt. - No delivery log; support tickets become archaeology. - Secrets in the URL ( ?token=… ), which land in logs on both sides. questions Why must webhook signatures be verified over the raw request body? options Raw bodies are smaller Parsing and re-serialising JSON changes bytes (whitespace, key order), so the HMAC would not match Frameworks require it To avoid JSON injection answer explain The signature covers the exact bytes the provider sent. Read the body before any parsing middleware touches it. What should an inbound webhook handler do before returning 200? options Fully process the business logic Verify signature, check freshness, deduplicate, persist the event and enqueue processing Call the provider's API to confirm Nothing; just return 200 answer explain Acknowledge fast after durably recording; do the work asynchronously. A customer registers a webhook URL of http://10.0.0.5/admin. What is the r

Test with a provider CLI or by signing requests yourself; include a replayed request and a tampered body. 2. Build an outbound sender with retries, a delivery log table and a replay function. Point it at a local endpoint that randomly fails and watch the schedule. 3. Write the SSRF-safe URL validator for customer endpoints and test it against localhost , 169.254.169.254 , a private range, and a hostname that resolves to a private IP.

- Choose a real-time delivery mechanism and architecture appropriate to the product requirement. - Design presence, fan-out, ordering and reconnection for live features. - Scale connection-heavy services and keep them operable. - Avoid real-time features that are more fragile than the problem they solve. ::: Part II chapter 14; chapters 6 and 7 of this part. :::

"Real-time" covers a live dashboard that updates every few seconds, collaborative editing with sub-100 ms expectations, chat, notifications, and progress bars. Each has different tolerances for latency, ordering and loss, and the infrastructure that is right for one is wrong for another. The mistakes are usually in two directions: building WebSocket infrastructure for a feature that polling would serve, or bolting a real-time channel onto a stateless API without thinking about how messages find their recipient across many servers.

Question Why it matters --- --- How fresh must data be? Seconds, hundreds of ms, tens of ms? Decides polling vs push vs persistent connection Who sends? Server only, or client too, at what rate? SSE vs WebSocket How many concurrent users, and how many per "room"? Connection capacity; fan-out cost Must messages be ordered? Delivered exactly once? Persisted? Sequence numbers, acks, history store What happens offline? Catch-up on reconnect; push notifications Is presence (who is online) needed? Heartbeats, expiry, consistent state across servers A dashboard refreshed every 10 seconds by polling a cached endpoint is cheap, stateless and robust. Do not build more than the requirement demands.

Give every message a monotonically increasing sequence per channel (a database sequence, or a Redis Streams ID). Clients track the last sequence seen; on reconnect they request everything after it from the database (catch-up), then resume live. Servers deliver live messages with their sequence; a client that sees a gap requests the missing range. This turns the lossy live channel into effectively reliable delivery without needing the live channel itself to be reliable. Deduplicate on the client by sequence. Acknowledgements and read receipts are application messages stored in the database, not a transport feature.

"Who is online" is deceptively hard: connections drop without notice, a user has three tabs, and instances disagree. Standard approach: each connection server sets a key presence:{user} in Redis with a short TTL (30–60 s) and refreshes it on heartbeat; presence equals key exists; multiple connections are a count or a set with per-connection expiry. Publish presence changes on the backplane with debouncing so a flapping connection does not spam. Accept that presence is eventually consistent and approximate; design the UI accordingly ("last seen" rather than a hard online/offline binary).

A message to a room of 10 users is cheap. A message to a channel with 100,000 subscribers spread over 50 connection servers means each server receives it once from the backplane and writes it to its local sockets; the cost is sockets × message size on egress. Hot channels need: coalescing (send the latest state rather than every intermediate update), rate limiting of publishers, and sometimes sharding channels. For broadcast-heavy products, consider managed services (AWS API Gateway WebSocket, AppSync subscriptions, Ably, Pusher) that have solved fan-out at scale.

Concurrent edits to the same document need a merge strategy: Operational Transformation or CRDTs (Yjs, Automerge). These are well-trodden libraries; do not invent one. The server's job becomes relaying updates, persisting document state, and enforcing authorization per document.

- Scale connection servers on connection count and memory, not CPU. - Raise file descriptor limits; tune kernel socket buffers for many idle connections. - Heartbeats below every idle timeout on the path (ALB 60 s default, NAT, proxies). - Deployments: drain connections gradually (close a few percent at a time with a reconnect hint) to avoid reconnect storms that overload authentication. - Metrics: connections per instance, messages in/out per second, backplane lag, reconnect rate, per-socket send-queue depth (slow clients), authentication failures. - Backpressure: bound per-socket outgoing queues; disconnect clients that cannot keep up rather than growing memory. - Multi-region: real-time across regions needs a global backplane or regional isolation with routing by room; this is where complexity explodes, so avoid unless required.

Authenticate at connect (cookie or short-lived token), check Origin , and authorise every subscription against the resource (user may join room 42 only if a member). Re-validate long-lived connections periodically or on permission change (publish a "revoke" event that the connection tier acts on). Rate-limit client messages per socket. Validate message schemas; a WebSocket message is as untrusted as a POST body. Never trust client-supplied sender IDs: the server stamps the sender from the authenticated connection.

- WebSockets for a feed that SSE or polling would serve. - Business logic in the connection servers, coupling deploys to disconnections. - No sequence numbers; lost messages are undetectable. - Pub/Sub only, with no catch-up path from persistent storage. - Presence via "connection closed" events alone (never fire on network death). - Authorization only at connect, not per subscription. - Idle timeout mismatches silently dropping connections every minute. - Unbounded per-socket send buffers. questions What makes a lossy live channel effectively reliable? options TCP guarantees it Per-channel sequence numbers with client-side gap detection and catch-up from persistent storage Sending each message twice Using HTTP/2 answer explain The database is the source of truth; the live channel is an accelerator. Why separate the connection tier from the API tier? options Different programming languages Deploying API changes would otherwise disconnect every user, and the tiers scale on different resources Load balancers require it For TLS answer explain Sockets are long-lived state; APIs are stateless and deployed often. How is presence usually implemented across many servers? options Each server keeps a list in memory Short-TTL keys in Redis refreshed by heartbeats, so a silent disconnect expires automatically Database rows updated on connect/disconnect Clients broadcast to each other answer explain Connections die without notice; TTL expiry makes presence self-healing.
