- Structure application configuration so that every environment is explicit, validated and documented. - Design an error taxonomy that separates expected business outcomes from bugs and from dependency failures. - Decide what users see, what gets logged, what pages someone, and what is retried. - Make failures observable and safe: no leaked internals, no swallowed exceptions, no partial writes. ::: Part I chapter 8; chapter 4 of this part. :::

Two kinds of code decide whether a production system is pleasant or miserable to operate: the code that loads configuration, and the code that handles errors. Both are usually written last, in a hurry. Bad configuration code produces services that start in a broken state or behave differently per environment for reasons nobody can see. Bad error handling produces either users seeing stack traces, or silent failures that corrupt data while dashboards stay green.

Part I chapter 8 established the principles: config from the environment, typed and validated at start-up, secrets from a secrets manager. The application-level structure that makes this maintainable: # app/config.py — one object, sections per concern, documented, validated class DatabaseSettings(BaseModel): url: PostgresDsn pool_min: int = Field(2, ge=1) pool_max: int = Field(10, ge=1, le=200) statement_timeout_ms: int = Field(10_000, ge=100) class HttpClientSettings(BaseModel): connect_timeout_s: float = 2.0 read_timeout_s: float = 10.0 retries: int = Field(2, ge=0, le=5) class FeatureFlags(BaseModel): new_checkout: bool = False export_v2: bool = False class Settings(BaseSettings): model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter="__", extra="forbid") env: Literal["dev", "staging", "prod"] service_name: str = "orders-api" version: str = "dev" log_level: Literal["debug", "info", "warning", "error"] = "info" database: DatabaseSettings http: HttpClientSettings = HttpClientSettings() features: FeatureFlags = FeatureFlags() payments_api_key: SecretStr allowed_origins: list[AnyHttpUrl] @model_validator(mode="after") def prod_guards(self): if self.env == "prod" and self.log_level == "debug": raise ValueError("debug logging is not permitted in prod") return self DATABASE POOL MAX=20 maps to settings.database.pool max . Everything has a type, a default where safe, and no default where a wrong guess is dangerous (the database URL, the API key). The validator shows environment g

Not all errors are alike, and treating them alike is the root problem. Four categories: Category Examples HTTP Log level Alert? Retry? --- --- --- --- --- --- Expected client outcome Validation failure, not found, forbidden, conflict, rate limited 4xx INFO (or none) No (alert on rate anomalies) No Dependency failure Database timeout, payment API 503, Redis unavailable 503 / 502 / 504 WARNING or ERROR On rate/duration Yes, if idempotent Bug Unhandled exception, assertion, null dereference 500 ERROR with stack trace Yes, on any occurrence (or rate) No Invariant violation / data corruption Negative balance found, duplicate primary key where impossible 500 CRITICAL Immediately No; stop and investigate Design the code so the category is explicit: class AppError(Exception): status = 500; code = "internal_error"; expose_message = False class NotFound(AppError): status = 404; code = "not_found"; expose_message = True class Forbidden(AppError): status = 403; code = "forbidden"; expose_message = True class Conflict(AppError): status = 409; code = "conflict"; expose_message = True class ValidationFailed(AppError): status = 422; code = "validation_failed"; expose_message = True class DependencyUnavailable(AppError): status = 503; code = "dependency_unavailable"; expose_message = False; retryable = True @app.exception_handler(AppError) async def app_error_handler(request, exc: AppError): log = logger.bind(request_id=request_id_var.get(), code=exc.code) if exc.status >= 500: log.error("req

Users need: that something went wrong, whether it was their fault (and how to fix it), whether retrying will help, and a reference they can quote to support. They never need: stack traces, SQL, internal hostnames, library names, or the specific reason an authentication failed ("user not found" versus "wrong password" enables enumeration; say "invalid credentials"). For browser frontends, map error codes to friendly messages client-side; show the request ID in a small "reference" line; for 503s offer a retry; for 401s redirect to login once (not in a loop).

Every 5xx with full context (request ID, route, user and tenant IDs, the stack trace, sanitised request summary). 4xx at INFO or sampled; a spike in 401/403/422 is itself a signal (attack, broken client). Never log request bodies wholesale (PII, secrets); log specific safe fields. Never log credentials, tokens, cookies or full card numbers; implement redaction in the logging layer as a backstop. Part XI chapter 1 covers structure; Part IV chapter 22 covers audit logs, which are a separate stream from error logs.

Alert on symptoms , not on individual exceptions: 5xx rate above threshold, p99 latency above SLO, dependency error rate, queue age. Use error-tracking tools (Sentry and similar) to group unhandled exceptions by fingerprint and notify on new ones, which catches bugs introduced by a deploy without paging for every known noisy exception. Part XI chapter 5.

An error mid-operation must not leave half-written state. Within one database: wrap the operation in a transaction so an exception rolls everything back (chapter 13). Across systems (database plus external API): order operations so the irreversible external action happens last, or record intent first and reconcile (outbox, sagas), and make everything idempotent so retries complete the work. Never catch an exception, log it, and continue as if the operation succeeded; that is how silent corruption begins. # Anti-pattern: swallowing try: await charge_card(order) except Exception: logger.warning("charge failed") # order proceeds as 'paid'?! No. await mark_paid(order) # Correct: fail the operation, keep state consistent, let the caller decide try: await charge_card(order) # idempotent via key except PaymentDeclined as e: raise Conflict(f"payment declined: {e.reason}") except PaymentProviderError as e: raise DependencyUnavailable("payment provider") from e await mark_paid(order)

A timeout is an error whose cause you do not know (the operation may have succeeded). Treat it as a dependency failure, make the operation idempotent, and surface it honestly ("we could not confirm your payment; please check before retrying"). Client disconnects cancel handlers in async frameworks; ensure cleanup runs ( finally , context managers) so pool connections and locks are released.

h: Health and readiness as error reporting
x: The readiness endpoint is where the service reports whether it can work: configuration loaded, dependencies reachable within a short timeout, not draining. Keep it cheap and honest; a readiness check that always returns 200 hides a service that cannot reach its database, and a check that calls every dependency deeply turns a Redis blip into a full outage via the load balancer (Part XI chapter 5 discusses the balance).

- except Exception: pass . - Returning str(exc) from unknown exceptions to users. - Driver exceptions leaking to handlers; database timeouts rendered as 500 instead of 503. - Logging whole request bodies or headers. - Distinct messages for "user not found" and "wrong password". - Alerting on every exception instance; alert fatigue; then alerts ignored. - Config read from os.environ scattered through the codebase with different defaults in each place. - No request ID in error responses, so support cannot find the log. questions A database timeout occurs while handling a request. Which status and log level fit? options 500 and DEBUG 503 with Retry-After, logged at WARNING/ERROR with context 200 with an error field answer explain Dependency failures are not client errors and not bugs; they are retryable server-side conditions. Why should login failures return the same message for unknown user and wrong password? options Simplicity To prevent account enumeration Browsers require it It is faster answer explain Different messages let attackers discover valid accounts. What is wrong with catching an exception from a payment call, logging it, and continuing to mark the order paid? options Nothing if logged It leaves inconsistent state: the order appears paid without a successful charge Logging is expensive The exception should be re-raised as 200 answer explain Swallowed errors cause silent corruption. - Decide where a transaction begins and ends in a web request, a background job and a multi-step workflow. - Apply the unit-of-work pattern so that a request's writes succeed or fail together. - Avoid long transactions, lock contention and work-inside-transactions that cannot be rolled back. - Handle operations that span a database and external systems without partial writes. ::: Chapters 3, 6 and 12; Part VIII chapter 5 covers the database mechanics in depth. :::

Creating an order touches several tables: the order, its lines, an inventory reservation, an audit entry. If the process dies after the first insert, the database holds a headless order. Transactions exist to make a group of changes atomic. The engineering question is where to draw the box : too small and you get partial writes; too large and you hold locks while waiting on networks, serialise your throughput, and make the box impossible to roll back because it included an email.

The dominant pattern for request handling: one transaction per request (per logical operation), opened when the handler begins its writes and committed when it finishes successfully; any exception rolls it back. Frameworks support this as a dependency or middleware: # FastAPI dependency providing a transactional session per request async def get_uow(pool=Depends(get_pool)): async with pool.acquire() as conn: async with conn.transaction(): # BEGIN yield conn # handler runs here # COMMIT on normal exit; ROLLBACK if the handler raised @app.post("/v1/orders", status_code=201) async def create_order(body: OrderCreate, user=Depends(current_user), db=Depends(get_uow)): order_id = await orders.insert(db, body, user.tenant_id) await order_lines.insert_many(db, order_id, body.items) await inventory.reserve(db, body.items) # raises Conflict if insufficient → rollback everything await audit.record(db, user, "order.created", order_id) await outbox.add(db, "OrderPlaced", {"order_id": str(order_id)}) # event recorded atomically; relayed later return {"id": str(order_id)} Everything inside is all-or-nothing. The outbox.add line is how side effects that must eventually happen (publishing an event, sending an email) join the transaction without actually performing a non-rollbackable action inside it (Part IX chapter 6).

h: What must not be inside a transaction
x: - Network calls to other systems : payment APIs, email, S3 uploads, other services. They cannot be rolled back, they are slow (holding locks and a connection for hundreds of milliseconds), and they fail independently. Record intent in the transaction; perform the call after commit (or from a worker reading the outbox); reconcile on failure. - User interaction or long computation : a transaction open while rendering a PDF or awaiting a client is a transaction holding locks for seconds. - Unbounded loops : processing a million rows in one transaction creates a giant undo log, blocks vacuum, and if it fails at row 999,999 you lose everything. Batch (1,000–10,000 rows per transaction) with restartable progress. The rule of thumb: a transaction should contain database statements and pure computation only, and last milliseconds.

Read-only requests often need no explicit transaction (autocommit; each statement is its own), unless you need a consistent snapshot across several reads (a report summing several tables), in which case a read-only transaction at REPEATABLE READ gives one. Read-your-writes within a request is automatic inside the same transaction and connection; across requests, replica lag can break it (Part VIII chapter 8).

Transactions that touch the same rows wait for each other. Patterns that cause pain: - Hot rows : a single counters row incremented by every request serialises all requests. Use per-shard counters, Redis, or append-only tallies. - Lock ordering : transaction A updates row 1 then row 2; transaction B updates 2 then 1. Deadlock; the database kills one. Always touch rows in a consistent order (sort IDs before updating). - Check-then-act : SELECT stock; if ok: UPDATE stock lets two transactions both see enough stock. Use atomic conditional updates ( UPDATE ... SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty = 1 and check the row count) or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE , or serializable isolation with retry. - Long transactions block others and, in PostgreSQL, prevent vacuum from cleaning dead rows, degrading the whole database. Set idle in transaction session timeout and statement timeout . -- Atomic reservation: no race, no explicit lock UPDATE inventory SET reserved = reserved + $2 WHERE sku = $1 AND on_hand - reserved >= $2 RETURNING on_hand - reserved AS available; -- zero rows returned means insufficient stock

A job typically has several steps with external calls between them; one transaction cannot span them. Structure jobs as a sequence of small transactions with explicit state transitions recorded in the job row, so that a retry resumes from the last completed step rather than repeating the whole job: async def fulfil_order(job): order = await load(job.order_id) if order.state == "created": await capture_payment(order) # external, idempotent by key await transition(order, "created", "paid") # tiny transaction with WHERE state='created' guard if order.state == "paid": await reserve_shipping(order) # external await transition(order, "paid", "shipping_booked") if order.state == "shipping_booked": async with db.transaction(): # local work can be one transaction await write_invoice(order); await outbox.add("OrderFulfilled", ...) await transition_in(db, order, "shipping_booked", "fulfilled") The WHERE state = ... guard on each transition makes concurrent or duplicate executions safe: the second one updates zero rows and knows to stop.

When an operation spans two services with separate databases, there is no shared transaction. Options, in increasing complexity: make one side the source of truth and the other eventually consistent via events; sagas with compensating actions (Part IX chapter 6); two-phase commit (rare, fragile, avoid). Design boundaries so that the common operations live inside one service's transaction; cross-service consistency is expensive and should be rare.

ORMs (SQLAlchemy, Prisma, Django) have their own session/transaction semantics; know them. Common traps: the ORM auto-commits per statement unless you open a transaction explicitly; lazy loading issues queries after the transaction closed (or inside it, holding it open); "savepoints" (nested transactions) are not real nested transactions. Keep the unit of work explicit and the ORM's session lifetime bound to it.

Transactional tests (wrap each test in a transaction and roll back) are fast and isolate state, but they cannot test commit-dependent behaviour (outbox relays, triggers, read-after-commit). Keep a smaller set of integration tests that commit for real against a disposable database.

- An HTTP call to a payment provider inside the database transaction. - No transaction around multi-table writes; partial orders in production. - Transactions held open across await s on external I/O. - Million-row updates in one transaction. - Check-then-act races on stock, balances and unique names. - Inconsistent lock ordering producing deadlocks under load that never appear in tests. - Relying on the ORM's implicit behaviour without reading its documentation. - Treating an email send as rollbackable. questions Which should happen inside the request's database transaction? options Calling the payment provider Sending the confirmation email Inserting the order, its lines, the audit row and an outbox event Uploading the invoice PDF to S3 answer explain Database writes are atomic together; external effects are recorded as intent and performed after commit. Two requests both read stock=1, then both update stock to 0 and succeed. What is this? options Deadlock A check-then-act race; fix with an atomic conditional UPDATE or row locking Replication lag A phantom read answer explain Reading then writing separately lets both see the same state. Make the check part of the write. Why are long-running transactions harmful in PostgreSQL beyond holding locks? options They use more disk They prevent VACUUM from reclaiming dead rows, degrading the whole database They cause replication to stop They are not harmful answer explain Set statement and idle-in-transaction timeouts, and batch lar

- Describe an HTTP API precisely with OpenAPI and keep the description in sync with the implementation. - Generate clients, validate requests and responses, and publish documentation from one source. - Detect breaking changes before they ship and practise contract testing between producers and consumers. - Use contracts as the handshake between your team and a client's integration team. ::: Chapter 2. :::

An API's behaviour lives in code; its consumers live elsewhere and read documentation that drifts. Integration teams guess at field types, break on undocumented enum values, and discover changes in production. A machine-readable contract fixes this by making the description the thing everyone builds from: the server validates against it, clients are generated from it, documentation renders from it, and a diff of it tells you whether a change is breaking.

openapi (formerly Swagger) is a JSON/YAML format describing paths, operations, parameters, request and response schemas (JSON Schema), authentication schemes and metadata. Version 3.1 aligns fully with JSON Schema. openapi: 3.1.0 info: { title: Orders API, version: 1.4.0 } servers: [{ url: https://api.client.com/v1 }] security: [{ sessionCookie: [] }] paths: /orders/{orderId}: get: operationId: getOrder summary: Fetch one order parameters: - { name: orderId, in: path, required: true, schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/OrderId' } } responses: '200': { description: The order, content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/Order' } } } } '404': { $ref: '#/components/responses/NotFound' } components: securitySchemes: sessionCookie: { type: apiKey, in: cookie, name: __Host-sid } schemas: OrderId: { type: string, pattern: '^ord_[0-9a-z]{20}$', examples: [ord_01hzx3k9m2p7q8r9s0t1] } Order: type: object required: [id, status, currency, total, items, created_at] additionalProperties: false properties: id: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/OrderId' } status: { type: string, enum: [pending, paid, shipped, cancelled], description: "Clients must tolerate new values." } currency: { type: string, enum: [EUR, USD, GBP] } total: { type: string, pattern: '^-?\d+\.\d{2}$', description: "Decimal string to avoid float rounding." } items: { type: array, items: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/LineItem' }, maxItems: 200 } created_at: { type: string, format: date-time } responses:

Code-first (FastAPI, NestJS, Spring with annotations): the framework generates OpenAPI from typed handlers and models. Zero drift between code and spec; the spec is a build artifact you publish and diff. The right default when one team owns both. Schema-first : write the spec, generate server stubs and validation, implement handlers. Better when the contract is negotiated with another team or client before implementation, or when several implementations must match. Tooling: openapi-generator , oapi-codegen (Go), openapi-typescript , datamodel-code-generator (Python). Either way, the spec is checked into version control, produced in CI, and diffed on every pull request.

Validate requests against the schema (FastAPI and Pydantic do this inherently; for Express, express-openapi-validator ). Validate responses against the schema in non-production environments and in tests, so a handler that returns an undocumented field or a wrong type fails loudly before clients see it. Production response validation is a judgement call: it catches bugs but costs CPU and can turn a minor omission into an outage; many teams sample or enable it in staging only.

From the spec, generate typed clients for the frontend ( openapi-typescript plus a small fetch wrapper, or orval ), for mobile (Swift/Kotlin generators) and for client integration teams. Typed clients turn API misuse into compile errors and make breaking changes visible as build failures in consumers. Publish clients with the same version as the API, or let consumers generate from the published spec.

Diff the spec between the base branch and the pull request in CI with a tool that understands compatibility ( oasdiff , openapi-diff ). Breaking: removed paths or operations, removed or renamed properties, type changes, new required request fields, narrowed enums on input, widened enums on output (debatable; documented tolerance makes it non-breaking), changed authentication. Non-breaking: new optional fields, new endpoints, new optional parameters, relaxed input constraints. Fail the build on breaking changes unless the PR is explicitly labelled as a new major version. # GitHub Actions step - name: Check for breaking API changes run: | oasdiff breaking origin/main:openapi.yaml openapi.yaml --fail-on ERR

Schema validation proves the response matches the spec; it does not prove the spec matches what a consumer relies on . Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact and similar) has each consumer record the interactions it depends on; the provider's CI replays them against the real implementation. A provider change that breaks a specific consumer fails before deploy, and you learn which consumer. Valuable when many services or teams integrate; for a single frontend and API owned by one team, generated types plus response validation usually suffice.

Render the spec with Swagger UI, Redoc, Scalar or Stoplight. FastAPI serves Swagger UI at /docs automatically; lock it behind authentication or disable it in production if the API is not public. Good docs add what the spec cannot express: authentication walkthrough, error-handling guidance, pagination semantics, rate limits, idempotency keys, webhooks, a changelog, and copy-pasteable curl examples. Tie them to the version.

When a client's team will integrate with your API, the OpenAPI document is the agreement. Share it early (schema-first for the negotiated parts), version it, generate a client for them if they want one, provide a sandbox environment with test data, and publish a changelog with deprecation notices. In return, ask for their contract (the systems you must call) in the same form; if they cannot provide one, write it yourself from observation and have them confirm it. Most integration slippage traces back to an undocumented field or an assumed enum value. :::

GraphQL has its schema (SDL) and introspection; gRPC has Protocol Buffers; AsyncAPI describes event-driven interfaces (queues and webhooks) the way OpenAPI describes HTTP. The principles are identical: one source of truth, generated artefacts, diffed in CI.

- A hand-written spec that drifts from the code within a month. - Missing required and additionalProperties , so the schema validates anything. - Floats for money. - No breaking-change check in CI; discovering incompatibility from a client's bug report. - Swagger UI exposed publicly on an internal API, leaking its surface. - Enum values added without telling consumers to tolerate unknown values. - Treating the spec as documentation only, rather than as the validation and generation source. questions What is the main benefit of generating OpenAPI from typed code (code-first)? options Prettier docs The specification cannot drift from the implementation It is required by FastAPI It avoids versioning answer explain The spec becomes a build artifact of the real code. Which change is breaking for API consumers? options Adding an optional response field Adding a new endpoint Making a previously optional request field required Adding an example answer explain Existing clients that omit the field will start failing. Why represent money as a decimal string in JSON? options Strings are smaller JSON numbers are typically parsed as binary floats, which cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly It is required by OpenAPI For localisation answer explain 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 in floating point. Decimal strings or integer minor units avoid rounding errors. What does consumer-driven contract testing add over schema validation? options Nothing It verifies the provider still satisfies the specific

- Compare the isolation models (shared schema, schema-per-tenant, database-per-tenant, infrastructure-per-tenant) on security, cost, operations and flexibility. - Enforce tenant isolation at every layer: request context, queries, row-level security, caches, storage keys, background jobs and logs. - Recognise and test for the leaks that happen in practice. - Choose an isolation model for a client project and document the decision. ::: Chapters 1, 2, 8 and 13. :::

A SaaS product serves many customers (tenants) from shared infrastructure. The economics depend on sharing; the trust depends on perfect separation. A tenant must never see, modify or degrade another tenant's data or service. The failure mode is not hypothetical: a large share of SaaS data-leak incidents are tenant-isolation bugs, usually a query missing a WHERE tenant id = ? . Isolation therefore cannot rely on developers remembering; it must be structural.

title Tenant isolation models columns Shared schema (tenant_id column) Schema per tenant Database per tenant Stack per tenant Data separation logical: every query filtered; RLS as enforcement logical, stronger: separate namespaces physical: separate databases (possibly one server) physical: separate accounts/VPCs/clusters Blast radius of a missing filter cross-tenant leak limited: wrong schema in search_path none across tenants Noisy neighbour shared resources; needs quotas shared server shared server unless separate instances isolated Operations one schema to migrate, one backup N schemas to migrate (automate); backups per schema harder N databases to migrate, back up, monitor N environments; heavy automation required lowest moderate (connections, instances) highest Per-tenant customisation hard (feature flags) moderate easy (versions, extensions, regions) Compliance / data residency hard (one database, one region) feasible (place DB per region) natural Scale (tenants) millions thousands hundreds to low thousands Typical fit self-serve SaaS with many small tenants mid-size B2B enterprise B2B with strict contracts regulated or very large enterprise clients Hybrids are common: shared schema for the long tail of small tenants, database-per-tenant for enterprise tenants who pay for it ("cells" or "pods"), with the application supporting both via a tenant → connection routing layer.
The shared-schema model is the most common and the most dangerous, so its enforcement deserves detail.

h: 1. Tenant context from identity, never from input
x: The tenant is derived from the authenticated principal (session or token claims) at the start of the request and stored in request context. It is never taken from a URL parameter, header or body supplied by the client. A request to /tenants/t 99/orders by a user of t 7 is rejected at the authorization layer because the path tenant does not match the principal's tenant (or the principal's set of permitted tenants for multi-tenant users).

h: 2. Every table carries tenant_id; every query filters on it
x: Make it structural: a repository layer whose methods require the tenant ( orders.list(tenant id, ...) ), with no generic "find by id" that omits it. Composite primary keys (tenant id, id) or at minimum composite indexes with tenant id first, and foreign keys that include tenant id so a line item cannot reference another tenant's order.

h: 3. Database-enforced row-level security as the backstop
x: PostgreSQL row-level security makes the database refuse to return or modify rows outside the current tenant, regardless of what the application's SQL says: ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE orders FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; -- applies to the table owner too CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid) WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid); # per request/transaction: set the tenant on the connection, scoped to the transaction async with conn.transaction(): await conn.execute("SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', $1, true)", str(tenant_id)) # 'true' = local to txn rows = await conn.fetch("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'open'") # RLS adds tenant filter automatically The application connects as a role that is not the table owner and does not have BYPASSRLS . A forgotten WHERE now returns zero rows instead of everyone's rows. Use set config(..., true) so the setting is cleared at transaction end even with connection pooling; a leaked setting on a pooled connection is itself a cross-tenant bug. Test RLS explicitly: run a query with the wrong tenant set and assert it returns nothing.

- Caches : tenant:{id}:… in every key (chapter 8). Cache poisoning across tenants is a classic leak. - Object storage : tenant prefix in every key; presigned URLs generated only after tenant checks; IAM policies with prefix conditions for per-tenant credentials if ever issued. - Search indexes : a tenant field in every document and a mandatory filter in every query (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch document-level security or filtered aliases). - Background jobs : the job payload carries the tenant; the worker sets the tenant context before any query. Jobs that iterate "all tenants" do so explicitly, one tenant context at a time. - Logs and metrics : include tenant id for debugging; never include another tenant's data in error messages. - Exports and reports : generated within tenant context; file names and IDs unguessable. - Webhooks and emails : templates rendered with tenant-scoped data only; recipient lists from the tenant's own records. - Third-party integrations : per-tenant credentials stored encrypted and resolved by tenant.

A UNIQUE (email) across the whole users table means tenant A can discover that someone exists in tenant B (and blocks legitimate reuse). Use UNIQUE (tenant id, email) . Use random IDs (UUIDv7) so sequential IDs cannot be enumerated across tenants.

Shared resources need quotas: per-tenant rate limits (chapter 5), per-tenant concurrency limits on expensive operations, separate worker queues or weighted scheduling so one tenant's bulk import does not starve others, query timeouts, and storage quotas. Monitor resource usage per tenant so you can see who is expensive and move them to a dedicated cell if needed.

A tenant registry maps tenant → connection details (host, database, credentials in a secrets manager). The application resolves the tenant, obtains a connection from a per-tenant pool (bounded total pools; lazy creation; idle eviction), and runs. Migrations run across all tenant databases in a controlled loop with progress tracking and the ability to pause. Backups, monitoring and alerts are per database; automate them from the registry. Onboarding a tenant provisions a database via infrastructure code. Connection counts become the scaling constraint; PgBouncer or RDS Proxy per server helps.

- Unit tests for the repository layer asserting the tenant filter is present (or that RLS blocks). - Integration tests that create two tenants, write data for both, and assert every list/get/update/delete endpoint returns or affects only the caller's tenant, including with manipulated IDs and path parameters. - A periodic automated "cross-tenant probe" in staging that attempts access with mismatched tenants and alerts on any success. - Code review checklist item: "Is every new table tenant-scoped, indexed by tenant, covered by RLS, and every new query filtered?"

Ask: How many tenants, and how big? Do contracts or regulations require physical separation or data residency? Does any tenant need custom versions or schedules? What is the operations budget? Most B2B products start shared-schema with RLS and per-tenant quotas, keep a clean tenant abstraction, and add a database-per-tenant tier when an enterprise customer requires it. Write the decision down as an ADR, including the triggers for moving to a stronger model. Part XIII chapter 8 gives the full decision process. :::

- Tenant ID taken from the request instead of the identity. - A single generic get by id that bypasses tenant filtering. - RLS not forced for the owner role, or the app connecting as a superuser. - Tenant setting leaking across pooled connections (session-level instead of transaction-level). - Global unique constraints leaking existence. - Cache keys and S3 keys without tenant prefixes. - Background jobs running without tenant context, or iterating tenants and leaking context between iterations. - No per-tenant quotas; one customer takes down everyone. questions Where must the tenant identifier for a request come from? options A query parameter A custom header The authenticated principal's identity (session or token claims) The URL path, trusted as-is answer explain Client-supplied tenant identifiers are attacker-controlled. Path tenants must be checked against the principal. - State the CIA triad and apply it to classify what a system must protect. - Apply least privilege, defense in depth, secure by default, fail closed, minimise attack surface, and separation of duties to concrete engineering decisions. - Think like an attacker long enough to find the obvious paths, then like a defender to close them structurally rather than case by case. - Understand why security is a property of the whole system and its operation, not a feature or a tool. ::: Part I; Part II chapter 20. :::

Security failures are rarely exotic. They are an S3 bucket left public, a database with a default password reachable from the Internet, an API endpoint that forgot to check who owns the record, a dependency with a known vulnerability nobody updated, a secret in a Git repository, an admin account without MFA. Each is simple. Each happens constantly. They happen because security was treated as a layer to add rather than a set of principles applied to every decision, and because the people building the system never deliberately asked "how would I break this?" This part teaches the mechanisms. This chapter teaches the principles that make the mechanisms coherent.

h: What you are protecting: the CIA triad
x: - Confidentiality : data is readable only by those authorised. Breaches: data leaks, credential theft, exposed backups. - Integrity : data and systems are modified only by those authorised, in intended ways. Breaches: tampered orders, injected code, altered logs. - Availability : the system works when needed. Breaches: outages, denial of service, ransomware. Every control serves at least one. Encryption serves confidentiality; signatures and checksums serve integrity; redundancy and rate limiting serve availability. When you evaluate a design, ask of each asset: what is the impact if this is disclosed, altered, or unavailable? That question is the seed of a threat model (chapter 2) and of every prioritisation decision afterwards. Two more properties appear in regulated contexts: authenticity (we know who did it) and non-repudiation (they cannot deny it), both served by authentication and audit logging.

Every identity (human, service, process) gets exactly the permissions required for its function, for exactly as long as needed. A web application's database role can read and write its tables, not drop them, not read other schemas. An ECS task role can read one secret and write to one bucket prefix. A developer has read access to production logs, not to the production database. A CI pipeline can deploy to staging automatically and to production only after approval. Why it works: the damage from any compromise is bounded by the privileges of what was compromised. An SQL injection in an application whose database role cannot read users.password hash leaks far less than one whose role is the superuser. Where it is violated most: AdministratorAccess on everything "to get it working", shared root database accounts, wildcard IAM policies ( "Action": "s3: ", "Resource": " " ), containers running as root, long-lived credentials with broad scope.

Assume any single control will fail: the developer will forget the check, the firewall rule will be wrong, the library will have a bug. Layer independent controls so that a failure of one is caught by another. The database is in a private subnet and has a security group and requires TLS and uses least-privilege roles and has row-level security and is encrypted at rest and has audit logging. An attacker must defeat all of them; a mistake in one is not a breach. Depth does not mean redundancy of the same control; two firewalls with the same rule set add nothing. It means different kinds of controls at different layers: network, identity, application, data, monitoring.

The default configuration should be the safe one; enabling the dangerous option must be explicit and visible. New S3 buckets block public access. New endpoints require authentication unless marked public. Input models reject unknown fields. Cookies are Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax unless overridden. Debug modes are off. Frameworks that are secure by default (parameterised queries, auto-escaping templates) eliminate whole vulnerability classes; choosing them is a security decision. The corollary: make the secure path the easy path. If obtaining a secret safely takes an afternoon of IAM wrangling and pasting it into an environment variable takes a minute, people will paste. Platform work that makes the right thing easy is some of the highest-leverage security work there is.

When a security control cannot make a decision, it denies. The session store is unreachable: the request is rejected as unauthenticated, not admitted as anonymous. The authorization service times out: 503, not "allow". The signature cannot be verified because the key is missing: reject. Failing open for availability's sake turns every dependency outage into an authentication bypass. Availability-critical paths need availability engineering (redundancy, caching of allow decisions with short TTLs), not weakened security.

Every open port, endpoint, dependency, feature flag, admin page, installed package and user account is a potential entry point. Remove what is not needed: no SSH on application hosts, no debug endpoints in production, no unused dependencies, no dormant accounts, no sample applications on servers. Smaller systems are easier to secure and to audit.

h: Separation of duties and privilege boundaries
x: No single person or credential should be able to do everything. The engineer who writes code does not approve their own production deploy; the account that runs the application cannot alter audit logs; development and production are different AWS accounts. Boundaries limit both malice and accident.

Every access to every resource is checked, every time, in one place. Not "we checked at login" (privileges change); not "the UI hides the button" (the API is reachable directly); not "that endpoint is internal" (networks get crossed). Authorization lives in a layer every request passes through, and the check is at the resource level.

Reiterated because it is violated daily: anything that runs on the user's device is under the user's control. Prices, roles, tenant IDs, validation results, hidden fields and "disabled" buttons are suggestions. The server validates, authorises and computes everything that matters.

h: Keep it simple; use proven mechanisms
x: Security mechanisms are hard to get right; novel ones are almost always wrong. Do not write your own cryptography, session management, password hashing or token format. Use the framework's authentication, a maintained library's JWT verification, the cloud provider's KMS. Complexity hides bugs; the simplest design that meets the requirement is the most secure.

Perfect prevention does not exist. Design so that when (not if) something is compromised, you notice (audit logs, anomaly alerts, integrity checks), contain (least privilege, segmentation, short-lived credentials that expire), and recover (backups, rotation procedures, incident response plans). A system that can be breached silently and permanently is worse than one that can be breached briefly and visibly.

A short exercise for any design: trace the data flows, mark every trust boundary (Part I chapter 1), and at each one ask: 1. Who can send data across this boundary? Only who I expect? 2. What if the data is malformed, enormous, or malicious? 3. What if the sender lies about who they are? 4. What if the same request arrives twice, or out of order? 5. What does the receiving side have access to that the sender should not? 6. What would I see in the logs if this boundary were abused? Then, for the most valuable assets (credentials, personal data, money), ask the attacker's favourite question: what is the cheapest path to it? It is usually not a zero-day in TLS. It is a leaked key in a repository, a phished admin, a misconfigured bucket, an unauthenticated internal endpoint, or an employee's laptop. Chapter 24 catalogues the real patterns.

A system is not secure because it was built securely; it is secure because it is operated securely: patched, monitored, credentials rotated, access reviewed, incidents handled, backups tested. Part IV concentrates on building; Parts X, XI and XIII return to operating. For a Forward Deployed Engineer, the handover is where this becomes acute: a secure system handed to a client that cannot operate it decays into an insecure one within months. Design for the operator you are actually handing to.

h: Applying the principles: a worked example
x: A client wants an endpoint for support staff to look up any customer's order by email address. - Least privilege : a support role with read-only access to the order-lookup endpoint, not admin. - Complete mediation : the endpoint checks the role on every call and logs who looked up whom (audit). - Confidentiality : the response omits payment details the support flow does not need (data minimisation). - Defense in depth : rate-limited per user (a stolen support account cannot dump the customer list), behind the identity provider's MFA, reachable only from the corporate network or VPN. - Secure by default : the lookup requires an exact email match, not a wildcard search, unless explicitly expanded with approval. - Assume breach : an alert fires if any support user performs more than N lookups per hour. - Do not trust the client : the support UI's tenant selector is irrelevant; the server derives the tenant from the support user's assignment. None of this is exotic; all of it is just principles applied before writing the handler. questions An authorization service becomes unreachable. Following 'fail closed', the API should: options Allow requests so users are not blocked Deny or return 503 for requests needing authorization Allow read requests but deny writes Cache the last decision indefinitely answer explain A control that cannot decide must deny. Availability is solved with redundancy, not by bypassing security. Which is an example of defense in depth rather than redundancy?

1. For a system you operate, list its five most valuable assets and rate the impact of disclosure, alteration and unavailability for each. This is the first table of a threat model. 2. Audit one IAM policy, one database role and one container's user in your system against least privilege. Write down the excess privileges. 3. Find one place where your system fails open (a security decision that defaults to allow on error). Fix it or document the risk.

- Run a lightweight, repeatable threat modeling session for a feature or system in under two hours. - Draw a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries and use STRIDE to enumerate threats at each one. - Rate and prioritise threats, choose mitigations, and record them so they are tested and maintained. - Integrate threat modeling into design reviews and client discovery. ::: Chapter 1. :::

Security review at the end of a project finds the problems when they are most expensive to fix. Threat modeling moves the question "how could this be attacked?" to the design stage, where the answer changes the architecture rather than patching it. It is also the single most useful artefact for a client conversation about security, because it shows what you considered and why you chose each control, rather than a list of tools. The method here is deliberately lightweight. A two-hour session with a whiteboard beats a forty-page document nobody reads.

Adam Shostack's framing, used by most practical teams: 1. What are we working on? Draw it. 2. What can go wrong? Enumerate threats systematically. 3. What are we going to do about it? Mitigate, accept, transfer or eliminate. 4. Did we do a good job? Verify mitigations exist and work; revisit when the system changes.

h: Step 1: data-flow diagram with trust boundaries
x: Draw the system as processes (your services), data stores, external entities (users, third parties) and the data flows between them. Then draw trust boundaries : lines where the level of trust changes. For each element and especially each boundary-crossing flow, ask the six STRIDE questions: Threat Violates Question Example in the export feature --- --- --- --- S poofing Authentication Can someone pretend to be another user, service or system? A forged job message with another tenant's ID; a phished support account T ampering Integrity Can data be modified in transit or at rest without detection? Export CSV altered in S3; job payload modified in the queue R epudiation Non-repudiation Can an actor deny having done something? Support staff exports a customer's data and no record exists I nformation disclosure Confidentiality Can data be read by someone not authorised? Export includes other tenants' rows; presigned URL forwarded; link in email logs; CSV injection reveals data when opened D enial of service Availability Can someone exhaust resources or block legitimate use? A user requests 1,000 exports; a giant tenant export locks the database E levation of privilege Authorization Can someone do more than they are allowed? A regular user triggers a support-only export via the API; worker role can read all buckets Work through the flows methodically. Most threats will be familiar from the vulnerability chapters in this part; the value is in systematically asking , not in cleverness.

Rate each threat by likelihood (how easy, how motivated an attacker, how exposed) and impact (CIA damage, number of users, regulatory consequence). A simple High/Medium/Low grid is enough; numerical scoring (CVSS, DREAD) adds false precision without more insight for most teams. For each threat choose one of four: - Mitigate : add a control. "Worker derives tenant from the job's signed payload and sets RLS context; exports bucket has per-tenant prefixes; presigned URLs expire in 15 minutes; CSV fields are escaped against formula injection; per-user export rate limit of 5/hour; every export logged with requester, target, time." - Eliminate : remove the feature or the data. "Do not include payment card fields in exports at all." - Transfer : move the risk to a party better placed to handle it. "Use the email provider's link-tracking opt-out; rely on S3's encryption and durability." - Accept : consciously, with a named owner and a review date. "A customer who forwards their own export link within 15 minutes exposes their own data; accepted." Record every decision. The table of threats, ratings and decisions is the threat model.

Each mitigation becomes a requirement with a test or a check: an integration test that a user cannot export another tenant; a configuration check that the bucket is private; an alert on export volume anomalies. Link them from the model. Revisit the model when the design changes (new data flow, new integration, new role), when an incident reveals a missed threat, and at least annually.

- Browser ↔ API : everything crossing is untrusted; authenticate, validate, authorise, rate limit. - API ↔ internal services : often treated as trusted "because it is inside the VPC". It should not be: authenticate service-to-service (IAM, mTLS, signed tokens), validate inputs, and assume one compromised service tries to reach others. This is the zero trust posture. - Application ↔ queue ↔ worker : the queue is a boundary; a message is input. Sign or at least validate payloads; derive authority from the message's recorded requester, not from a field anyone can set. - Your system ↔ third parties : their webhooks are untrusted input (verify signatures); your calls to them carry your credentials (least privilege API keys, scoped per integration). - Build pipeline ↔ production : a boundary attackers love. Pipeline credentials, dependency sources and build scripts are all inputs to production. - Operators ↔ production : humans with access are a boundary; MFA, least privilege, audit.

- Separate identity, authentication, session management and authorization as distinct problems with distinct controls. - Choose an authentication architecture (sessions, tokens, federated identity) appropriate to the clients and risks of a system. - Design authorization so it is enforced centrally, at the resource level, and testable. - Avoid the conflations that produce the most common access-control bugs. ::: Chapters 1 and 2; Part II chapter 11. :::

"Auth" is one word for two different questions, and systems that blur them fail in predictable ways. Authentication answers "who is this?" Authorization answers "may they do this?" A system can authenticate perfectly and authorise nothing (every logged-in user sees every record: the classic idor). A system can authorise meticulously against an identity that was never verified (trusting a user id header). Most access-control vulnerabilities, which top the OWASP list, come from treating "logged in" as the end of the question.

title From a credential to an allowed action layers Identity summary A stable identifier for a principal: user u_42, service orders-worker, tenant admin role. Stored in your user directory or in an external identity provider. Everything downstream refers to it; never to a mutable attribute like email. Credential summary Proof of identity: password, passkey, TOTP code, client certificate, API key, cloud IAM signature. Chapter 8 covers passwords, MFA and passkeys; chapter 18 covers machine credentials. Credentials are secrets; their storage and transport define the first attack surface. Authentication summary Verifying the credential and establishing the principal for this interaction. Happens at login (or per request for API keys and signatures). Outcome: a verified principal, plus authentication context (method used, MFA done, time). Session / token summary Carrying the authenticated state across subsequent requests. Server-side sessions (chapter 4) or signed tokens (chapter 5). This layer has its own attacks: fixation, theft, replay, missing expiry. Authorization summary Deciding whether this principal may perform this action on this resource now. Roles, attributes, ownership, tenant, state, time. Enforced on every request at the resource level. Chapter 7. Audit summary Recording who did what. Chapter 22. Closes the loop: authentication and authorization decisions are evidence.

Login verifies the credential, creates a server-side session, sets an HttpOnly cookie with the session ID. Every request looks up the session. Revocable, simple, the right default for browser applications talking to their own backend.

Login (or a token endpoint) issues a signed token the client presents in an Authorization: Bearer header. Verifiable without a lookup, good for APIs consumed by many services and mobile clients, hard to revoke; mitigated with short lifetimes and refresh tokens.

Your application does not verify passwords at all. An identity provider (Okta, Entra ID, Google, Auth0, Cognito, the client's corporate IdP) authenticates the user, including MFA, and tells your application who they are via OpenID Connect or SAML. Your application then creates its own session. This is the right answer for anything enterprise: clients want their staff managed in their own directory, with their own MFA policy and offboarding.

Services authenticate to each other with cloud IAM (SigV4 signatures from roles), mTLS, or short-lived service tokens; API consumers use API keys or OAuth client credentials. Never with a shared human user's password. title Choosing an authentication architecture columns Situation Recommendation Browser SPA + your own API, consumer or small business users Session cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax); passwords with Argon2 + optional passkeys/TOTP; or social login via OIDC Enterprise client, staff users OIDC/SAML federation to the client's IdP; your own session afterwards; roles mapped from IdP groups Mobile app OIDC authorization code with PKCE against your IdP; short-lived access token + refresh token in secure storage Third-party developers calling your API API keys for simple cases; OAuth client credentials for machine access; OAuth authorization code for acting on behalf of users Service to service inside AWS IAM roles and SigV4; or mTLS via a mesh; never static API keys between your own services Internal admin tools SSO with MFA enforced, behind VPN or identity-aware proxy; never a separate password database

Authentication yields a principal. Authorization needs three more inputs: the action (read, update, approve), the resource (order 123, belonging to tenant 7, in state pending ), and sometimes context (time, IP, MFA freshness). Models: - Role-based (RBAC) : principals have roles; roles grant permissions. "Support agents can read orders." Simple, auditable, coarse. - Attribute-based (ABAC) : rules over attributes of principal, resource and context. "A user may read an order if order.tenant id == user.tenant id and (user.role == 'admin' or order.owner id == user.id)." - Relationship-based (ReBAC) : permissions follow relationships in a graph (Google Zanzibar, OpenFGA, SpiceDB). "Users who are editors of the folder containing this document may edit it." In practice most applications need RBAC for coarse roles plus resource-level ownership and tenant checks, which is a simple form of ABAC. Chapter 7 goes deep. The non-negotiable rule: every request that touches a resource verifies that this principal may perform this action on this specific resource , in a central layer, before the action, with deny as the default.

Confusing authenticated with authorised. @login required on an endpoint that then does Order.get(id) with no ownership check. Any logged-in user can read any order by changing the ID. This is IDOR, OWASP's number one category. Authorization by obscurity. "Nobody knows the admin URL." "The mobile app never calls that endpoint." Attackers read JavaScript and proxy mobile traffic. Trusting identity from the client. A X-User-Id header, a user id in the body, a role claim in a token that was never verified, a tenant ID in the URL used without checking it matches the session. Authorization in the wrong place. Checks in the UI only; checks in middleware by URL pattern that miss new endpoints or alternate paths ( /api/orders/123 protected, /api/v2/orders/123 not); checks scattered through handlers and forgotten in one. Privilege that outlives its grant. Role changes or offboarding not reflected until the token expires (hours later, or never); sessions not invalidated on password change; API keys of departed staff still valid. Vertical versus horizontal confusion. Testing that a user cannot become admin (vertical) while never testing that user A cannot see user B's data (horizontal).

1. Derive the principal from the verified credential or session only. Everything about identity comes from the server side. 2. Make authorization a function: authorize(principal, action, resource) - allow deny , called in one place (service layer or a policy layer), with default deny and tests. 3. Load the resource first, then check, then act. Checks that do not see the resource cannot check ownership. 4. Return 404 for "not yours" when existence is sensitive; otherwise 403. Be consistent. 5. Re-check on every request. Cache role lookups briefly if needed, with invalidation on change. 6. Separate authentication strength from authorization: sensitive actions can require recent authentication or MFA (step-up). 7. Log authentication events (success, failure, MFA, logout) and authorization denials. 8. - Implement server-side sessions that resist fixation, hijacking, replay and brute force. - Choose session storage, lifetimes, rotation and invalidation policies deliberately. - Build login, logout, "log out everywhere", remember-me and step-up authentication correctly. - Test the session layer against the attacks that actually occur. ::: Part II chapter 11; chapter 3 of this part. :::

After a user proves who they are once, every subsequent request must be tied to that proof without re-entering a password. The session is that tie, and because it is a bearer secret (whoever presents it is treated as the user), its generation, transport, storage, lifetime and termination are all security-critical. Session bugs are quiet: nothing crashes, the attacker simply becomes someone else.

# sessions.py — Redis-backed sessions with rotation, sliding + absolute expiry, generation-based invalidation import secrets, json, time IDLE_TTL = 60 * 60 * 2 # 2 hours idle ABSOLUTE_TTL = 60 * 60 * 12 # 12 hours max class SessionStore: def __init__(self, redis): self.r = redis async def create(self, user_id: str, generation: int, mfa: bool) -> str: sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32) now = int(time.time()) data = {"uid": user_id, "gen": generation, "created": now, "auth_time": now, "mfa": mfa} await self.r.set(f"sess:{sid}", json.dumps(data), ex=IDLE_TTL) await self.r.sadd(f"user_sessions:{user_id}", sid) # for listing/revoking per user return sid async def load(self, sid: str, current_generation_for) -> dict | None: raw = await self.r.get(f"sess:{sid}") if not raw: return None data = json.loads(raw) now = int(time.time()) if now - data["created"] > ABSOLUTE_TTL: await self.destroy(sid, data["uid"]); return None if data["gen"] != await current_generation_for(data["uid"]): await self.destroy(sid, data["uid"]); return None await self.r.expire(f"sess:{sid}", IDLE_TTL) # sliding idle window return data async def rotate(self, old_sid: str, data: dict) -> str: # at login and privilege change new_sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32) pipe = self.r.pipeline() pipe.set(f"sess:{new_sid}", json.dumps(data), ex=IDLE_TTL); pipe.delete(f"sess:{old_sid}") pipe.srem(f"user_sessions:{data['uid']}", old_sid); pipe.sadd(f"user_sessions:{data['uid']}", new_sid) await pipe.execute() return new_sid async

Session fixation : the attacker sets a known session ID in the victim's browser (via a link or subdomain cookie injection) before login; after login the attacker uses the same ID. Defence: issue a new ID at login (rotation), never accept session IDs from URLs, use the Host- prefix so subdomains cannot plant cookies. Session hijacking via theft : XSS reading the cookie (defeated by HttpOnly), network sniffing (Secure plus HSTS), malware on the device (not solvable by you; short lifetimes and anomaly detection limit damage). Binding sessions to IP addresses breaks mobile users; binding to a coarse fingerprint (user agent) with re-authentication on change is a reasonable soft signal. Brute force on session IDs : impossible with 256-bit random IDs; trivial with sequential or timestamp-based IDs. Use the CSPRNG. Brute force on login : rate limits per account and IP, progressive delays, lockout with care (attackers can lock out victims), CAPTCHA after failures, breached-password checks, MFA. CSRF : SameSite=Lax cookies block most; add a synchroniser token or double-submit cookie for state-changing requests when supporting older clients or SameSite=None (chapter 9). Session not invalidated : on logout (cookie cleared but server session alive: it can be replayed), password change, role change, account compromise. Invalidate server-side; implement "log out everywhere". Replay after expiry : absolute expiry caps a stolen session's lifetime; idle expiry ends abandoned sessions; both enf

Redis (ElastiCache Multi-AZ) is the standard: fast, TTL-native, shared across instances. Treat it as a hard dependency for authentication (fail closed if unreachable) and therefore make it highly available. A database table works at lower scale (index on session ID, periodic cleanup of expired rows). In-process memory only for single-instance prototypes. Store minimal data (IDs, timestamps, auth context); load user details from the user table per request or cache them briefly. Never store the password or raw tokens in the session.

Decide: unlimited (default for web), limited (banking often allows one), or visible (a "your active sessions" page listing device, location hint, last seen, with per-session revoke). The user sessions set above enables the page and the revocation.

Alert on failure spikes (credential stuffing), on logins from new countries for admins, and on impossible travel if you have geo data. These logs are also the audit trail chapter 22 requires.

- Explain what a JSON Web Token is, what it guarantees, and what it does not. - Verify tokens correctly: algorithm pinning, key selection, claim validation, clock skew. - Recognise the classic JWT vulnerabilities (alg=none, algorithm confusion, weak secrets, missing audience checks, unrevocable tokens) and their fixes. - Decide when a JWT is the right tool and when a session is better. ::: Chapters 3 and 4; Part II chapter 11. :::

JWTs became popular because they look simple: a self-contained, signed blob of claims that any service can verify without a database. That same property is their weakness: a token is valid until it expires regardless of what happened to the user, and every service that verifies tokens must do so perfectly, because a single accepting bug is a universal skeleton key. Many "JWT vulnerabilities" are really library misuse and design mistakes; this chapter shows how to avoid both.

A JWS compact token is base64url(header).base64url(payload).base64url(signature) . - Header : {"alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT", "kid": "2026-03-key-1"} . The algorithm and a key identifier. - Payload : claims. Registered ones: iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiry), nbf (not before), iat (issued at), jti (token ID). Plus custom claims ( tenant id , roles , scope ). - Signature : over header.payload with the algorithm and key. The payload is not encrypted ; anyone can read it. JWE (encrypted JWTs) exist but are rare; assume everything in a JWT is visible to the holder and to anyone who intercepts it. Never put secrets or sensitive personal data in a JWT.

- HS256/384/512 : HMAC with a shared secret. Whoever can verify can also forge. Appropriate only when issuer and verifier are the same service (or a tightly controlled pair) and the secret is long (≥ 256 bits) and random. - RS256 (RSA), ES256 (ECDSA P-256), EdDSA (Ed25519): asymmetric. The issuer signs with a private key; verifiers need only the public key, usually published at a JWKS URL ( /.well-known/jwks.json ). Correct for multi-service verification and for anything an identity provider issues. ES256 and EdDSA produce smaller tokens and are faster than RSA. - none : unsigned. Must never be accepted.

alg: none : early libraries honoured a header saying the token was unsigned. Fix: the verifier specifies the permitted algorithms; the header is never trusted to choose. Algorithm confusion (RS256 → HS256) : the verifier is configured with an RSA public key and a library that accepts whatever alg the token names. The attacker signs with HS256 using the public key (which is public) as the HMAC secret; the library "verifies" it with the same public key. Fix: same as above, pin algorithms; use library APIs that bind a key to a specific algorithm. Weak HMAC secrets : secret , the app name, a 12-character string. Offline brute force recovers it and the attacker mints tokens. Fix: 256+ random bits from a secrets manager; prefer asymmetric. kid injection : the key ID header used to look up a key from a path or SQL ( kid: "../../etc/passwd" ). Fix: kid selects from a known set only. Missing claim validation : not checking exp (tokens never expire), aud (a token for service A accepted by service B), iss (a token from any issuer accepted), nbf . Fix: validate all of them explicitly. JWKS fetched insecurely or cached forever : a jku header pointing at an attacker's key set; or key rotation breaking verification because the cache never refreshes. Fix: fetch JWKS only from the configured issuer's URL over TLS, cache with a TTL and refresh on unknown kid , never follow jku / x5u from the token. Tokens in URLs or localStorage : logged, leaked via referrers, stolen by XSS. Fix: Authorization

# PyJWT with explicit algorithm pinning, JWKS, and full claim validation import jwt from jwt import PyJWKClient jwks = PyJWKClient(f"{settings.issuer}/.well-known/jwks.json", cache_keys=True, lifespan=3600) def verify_access_token(token: str) -> dict: signing_key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token) # selects by kid from the trusted JWKS only return jwt.decode( token, signing_key.key, algorithms=["RS256", "ES256"], # pinned; header cannot choose 'none' or HS256 audience=settings.api_audience, # e.g. "https://api.client.com" issuer=settings.issuer, # e.g. "https://auth.client.com/" leeway=30, # seconds of clock skew tolerance options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "sub", "aud", "iss"]}, ) // jose (Node): same discipline import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose'; const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${ISSUER}/.well-known/jwks.json`)); export async function verifyAccessToken(token) { const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, { issuer: ISSUER, audience: AUDIENCE, algorithms: ['RS256', 'ES256'], clockTolerance: 30 }); return payload; } Then authorise using the sub (and tenant/scope claims) against the resource, as in chapter 3. Claims about roles are only as fresh as the token; for anything sensitive, look up current permissions.

If your service issues tokens (an auth service, or a backend minting tokens for its own API): - Use ES256 or RS256 with keys in a KMS or at least generated and stored in a secrets manager; publish the public keys at a JWKS endpoint with kid s. - Rotate keys: publish the new key, start signing with it, keep the old one in the JWKS until all tokens signed with it have expired, then remove it. - Set iss , aud (specific to the API), sub (stable user ID, not email), exp (short), iat , jti (unique, for denylisting if needed). - Minimal claims: identity and coarse scope. Not the user's full profile; not roles that change often unless lifetimes are very short. - Never issue tokens that grant more than the session that requested them.

1. Short lifetimes + refresh tokens : access tokens live 5–15 minutes; a long-lived, revocable, rotating refresh token (stored server-side, hashed) mints new ones. Revoke the refresh token and the user is out within minutes. The standard design. 2. Denylist by jti : store revoked token IDs until their exp ; check on each request. Reintroduces a lookup; fine at modest scale. 3. Per-user generation claim : include gen in the token; store the current generation per user in a cache; reject tokens with old generations. A cheap lookup that enables "log out everywhere". 4. Accept the window : for low-risk, read-only, short-lived tokens, accept that revocation takes effect at expiry. If you find yourself adding a database lookup on every request to make JWTs revocable, consider whether a plain session (chapter 4) was the simpler answer all along.

Good fits: access tokens issued by an identity provider (OIDC), consumed by APIs; service-to-service tokens with short lifetimes; signed one-time links (password reset, email verification) with exp and jti ; stateless API tokens for third-party consumers at scale where a central session store is impractical. Poor fits: browser sessions for a single application (a session cookie is simpler and revocable); long-lived tokens of any kind; tokens carrying permissions that must be revoked instantly; anything where "stateless" is the only argument.

- SPA : access token in memory (not localStorage), refreshed via a refresh-token flow using an HttpOnly cookie or the BFF pattern (the browser talks to a backend-for-frontend that holds tokens server-side and uses a session cookie). The BFF pattern is increasingly the recommended approach for browser apps. - Mobile : secure storage (Keychain, Keystore) for refresh tokens; access tokens in memory. - Servers : in memory, fetched from the token endpoint as needed; never on disk unencrypted.

- jwt.decode(token, verify=False) or decode() without the key "just to read the claims", then trusting them. - Accepting algorithms from the header. - HS256 with a short, guessable secret shared across environments. - No aud check; tokens from a mobile app accepted by the admin API. - Lifetimes of hours or days with no revocation. - Roles in the token, role revoked, token still valid. - Tokens in URLs or localStorage. - Trusting the email claim as the user key instead of sub . questions What is the correct defence against both `alg: none` and RS256→HS256 confusion? options Use longer secrets The verifier pins the permitted algorithms and never lets the token header choose Encrypt the token Use JWE answer explain Both attacks rely on the verifier honouring the attacker-controlled alg field. A service verifies signature and expiry but not `aud`. What can go wrong? options Nothing; signature is enough A valid token issued for a different API or client can be replayed against this service Clock skew errors Tokens become too large answer explain Audience binding prevents cross-service token reuse. What is the standard way to make JWT-based authentication revocable? options Longer tokens Short-lived access tokens plus revocable, rotating refresh tokens Storing the JWT in the database Signing with HS256 answer explain The access token's short life bounds exposure; revoking the refresh token ends the session within minutes. - Explain what OAuth 2.0 authorises, what OpenID Connect adds, and how the authorization code flow with PKCE works end to end. - Integrate an application with an identity provider (Cognito, Okta, Entra ID, Auth0, Keycloak) for single sign-on, including role mapping and offboarding. - Recognise the flows to avoid (implicit, resource owner password) and the validation steps that must never be skipped. - Understand SAML well enough to integrate with enterprise clients that require it. ::: Chapters 3, 4 and 5. :::

Two different needs share a toolbox. First: an application wants to access a user's data in another system (read their calendar, post on their behalf) without receiving their password for that system. That is delegated authorization , which oauth 2.0 solves. Second: an application wants to let users log in with an identity managed elsewhere (their company directory, Google) instead of a local password. That is federated authentication , which openid connect adds on top of OAuth. Enterprise clients call the second one SSO , and expect you to support it. Getting these wrong produces account takeover: a mis-validated ID token, a redirect URI that an attacker can control, a missing state parameter. The flows are well-specified; the failures are in skipped steps.

- Resource owner : the user. - Client : your application (the one asking for access or identity). Confidential clients can keep a secret (server-side apps); public clients cannot (SPAs, mobile apps). - Authorization server : the identity provider (IdP) that authenticates the user and issues tokens. - Resource server : the API that accepts access tokens. - Access token : a credential for calling the resource server. Opaque or JWT; the client should treat it as opaque. - ID token (OIDC): a JWT for the client stating who the user is and how they authenticated. - Refresh token : a long-lived credential to obtain new access tokens. - Scopes : strings naming the access requested ( openid profile email , orders:read ).
