Cryptography reduces the problem of protecting data to the problem of protecting keys. Secrets management is the same problem for credentials: database passwords, API keys, signing keys, certificates. The failure modes are mundane and devastating: a key in a Git history, a .env file on a laptop, an environment variable dumped by a debug endpoint, a secret never rotated after a contractor left, a backup of a backup containing everything. The solution is structural: secrets live in one audited place, are delivered to workloads through identity rather than copies, rotate on a schedule, and are never written down anywhere else.

A kms holds master keys (customer managed keys, CMKs) in hardware security modules. You never see the key material; you call the service to encrypt, decrypt, sign or generate keys, and every call is authorised by IAM and logged in CloudTrail. Encrypting every record by calling KMS would be slow and expensive. envelope encryption solves this: title Envelope encryption with AWS KMS actors label Application label KMS (master key) label Database steps label GenerateDataKey(KeyId=alias/app-data, KeySpec=AES_256, EncryptionContext={tenant: t_7}) title Request a data key detail KMS generates a random 256-bit key and returns it twice: in plaintext, and encrypted under the master key. The encryption context is bound to the ciphertext and logged; decrypting later requires the same context. label encrypt record with plaintext data key (AES-GCM) title Encrypt locally detail Fast, local, no further KMS calls for this record (or batch). The plaintext data key is held in memory only as long as needed, then discarded. label store ciphertext + encrypted data key + key version title Persist detail The small wrapped key travels with the data. The database holds nothing that decrypts without KMS. label Decrypt(encrypted data key, EncryptionContext={tenant: t_7}) title Read path detail To read, the application asks KMS to unwrap the data key (one small call, cacheable briefly with a data key cache), then decrypts the record locally. IAM decides who may call Decrypt on this key; CloudTrail records

A secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Parameter Store SecureString, HashiCorp Vault, cloud equivalents) stores secrets encrypted with KMS, controls access with IAM, versions them, audits every read, and can rotate them automatically. title Secret storage options on AWS columns Secrets Manager Parameter Store (SecureString) Vault $0.40/secret/month + $0.05 per 10k API calls Standard tier free; advanced tier per parameter Self-hosted or HCP; operational cost Rotation Built-in for RDS, Redshift, DocumentDB; Lambda-based custom rotation None built in Dynamic secrets: short-lived DB credentials generated on demand Cross-account Resource policies Limited Integration ECS/EKS secrets injection, RDS, Lambda extension ECS/EKS injection, cheap config storage Agents, sidecars, broad ecosystem Use for Credentials that rotate, cross-account secrets Config values and static secrets at low cost Multi-cloud, dynamic credentials, PKI, advanced policies For most client deployments on AWS: Parameter Store for configuration and low-churn secrets, Secrets Manager for database credentials with rotation and anything needing cross-account access. Vault when the client already runs it or needs dynamic credentials across clouds.

The hierarchy from worst to best (Part I chapter 8 introduced it): 1. In code or images: never. 2. In a file on the host, restricted permissions: acceptable for a single VM with no better option; weak audit, manual rotation. 3. Injected by the platform at start : ECS task definitions reference a Secrets Manager or Parameter Store ARN in secrets ; the agent fetches it with the task execution role and sets it as an environment variable in the container. Kubernetes: External Secrets Operator syncs into Secrets, or the Secrets Store CSI driver mounts them as files. Simple and standard. Downside: environment variables are visible to the whole process tree and in some debug outputs; rotation requires a restart. 4. Fetched by the application at runtime via SDK using its IAM role: GetSecretValue at start-up and on a refresh interval or on authentication failure. Enables rotation without redeploy, fine-grained audit, and keeps secrets out of the environment. Cache in memory with a TTL; handle the brief window during rotation where both old and new versions are valid (Secrets Manager's AWSCURRENT / AWSPREVIOUS staging labels exist for this). 5. No long-lived secret at all : IAM database authentication (RDS issues 15-minute tokens to the role), IAM roles for AWS services, workload identity federation to third parties (OIDC from GitHub Actions to AWS, Part X chapter 2), Vault dynamic secrets. Nothing to leak, nothing to rotate manually. # Runtime fetch with caching and rotation tolerance

Rotation limits the window a leaked secret is useful and proves the rotation procedure works before you need it in anger. - Database credentials : Secrets Manager rotation with the alternating-users strategy (two users; rotate the inactive one, then swap) avoids downtime; applications must re-read on failure. Or use IAM authentication and skip the problem. - API keys to third parties : most providers allow two active keys; create the new, deploy, delete the old. Schedule quarterly or per policy; immediately on suspicion. - Signing keys (JWT, webhooks) : publish the new public key (JWKS) or share the new secret, sign with the new, keep the old for verification until all tokens expire, then retire. Key IDs ( kid ) make this clean. - KMS keys : enable automatic annual rotation of the key material; old versions remain usable for decryption transparently. Re-encrypting existing data is unnecessary for KMS rotation; it is necessary if you suspect the data key leaked. - TLS certificates : Part II chapter 10; automated. - Human credentials : SSO with MFA; access keys for IAM users should not exist (chapter 18). Track every secret in an inventory: name, location, owner, consumers, rotation method, last rotated, rotation deadline. Alert when a deadline passes.

- One IAM role per workload with permission to read exactly its secrets (resource ARNs, not ); condition keys to restrict by tag or VPC endpoint. - Humans read production secrets rarely, via a break-glass path (a role requiring MFA, with alerting on assumption), never routinely. - CloudTrail logs every GetSecretValue , Decrypt and GenerateDataKey ; alert on reads from unexpected principals or volumes, and on key policy changes. - Separate KMS keys and secrets per environment; staging must not be able to read production secrets. - Encryption context on every KMS call (tenant, purpose) so misuse is both prevented and visible in logs.

1. Rotate immediately. Do not debate, do not first purge Git history; rotation is the only thing that ends the exposure. 2. Revoke the old credential at the provider (delete the key, disable the user, revoke the token). 3. Assess what the credential could access and look for use: CloudTrail, provider logs, database audit logs, since the earliest possible exposure. 4. Contain related exposure: anything the leaked secret could have unlocked (other secrets readable with it) is now suspect. 5. Clean up the leak location (purge from Git with git filter-repo , delete the paste, rotate anything else in the same file), and add scanning (Part X chapter 3) so it does not recur. 6. Record it as an incident with a postmortem; "a secret was in Git" is a process failure, not an individual one. Keys pushed to public repositories are found and abused by automated scanners within minutes; speed matters.

Developers use separate, low-privilege development secrets (or local stand-ins: a local database, a sandbox API key), never production values. CI gets secrets from the platform's secret store, scoped per environment, with production secrets only in protected environments requiring approval (Part X chapter 9). Prefer OIDC federation so CI holds no long-lived cloud credentials at all. Secret scanning runs on every push and on the whole history.

- Secrets in Git, Docker images, build args, CloudFormation templates or Terraform state in a public or shared bucket. - Production secrets in developers' .env files. - One secret for all environments. - Secrets logged at start-up ("Connecting with password=…") or in error messages. - Applications with secretsmanager: on . - No inventory; secrets of departed staff and old integrations still valid. - Rotation never tested until the night it is needed. - Treating a leaked secret as handled once it is deleted from the repository. questions In envelope encryption, what does the application store alongside each encrypted record? options The master key The plaintext data key The data key encrypted under the KMS master key (and a key version) Nothing; KMS stores everything answer explain The wrapped data key is useless without KMS, which enforces IAM and logs every unwrap. A production database password is pushed to a Git repository. What is the first action? options Purge the Git history Rotate the credential immediately and revoke the old one Make the repository private Add a .gitignore entry answer explain Only rotation ends the exposure. Clean-up and scanning follow. Which approach eliminates long-lived database credentials entirely? options Storing them in Secrets Manager IAM database authentication issuing short-lived tokens to the workload's role Environment variables Rotating yearly answer explain No static secret exists to leak or rotate; access follows the IAM role. Why us

1. Move a service's secrets from environment files into Secrets Manager or Parameter Store with a least-privilege role; inject via the platform; verify with CloudTrail that reads are logged. 2. Implement rotation for a database credential (Secrets Manager rotation or a manual two-user swap) and prove the application survives rotation without downtime by rotating under load. 3. Build the secrets inventory for a system: every secret, where it lives, who reads it, when it was last rotated. Rotate the oldest one.

- Issue, store, scope, rotate and revoke API keys for consumers of your API. - Handle credentials your services use to call other systems, and replace static keys with identity-based access wherever possible. - Apply IAM roles for AWS workloads correctly: instance profiles, task roles, execution roles, cross-account roles. - Detect and respond to credential misuse. ::: Chapters 3, 5 and 17. :::

Machines need to authenticate too: a partner's system calling your API, your worker calling a payment provider, your application reading from S3, your CI deploying to production. Machine credentials outnumber human ones, live longer, are copied more freely, and are rarely rotated. Leaked machine credentials are the entry point in a large share of cloud breaches, often harvested from public repositories, CI logs, container images and laptops. The two moves that matter: scope every credential narrowly, and replace static credentials with short-lived, identity-derived ones wherever the platform allows.

For consumers who call your API programmatically (partner systems, customer integrations, your own mobile apps in some designs), API keys are the simplest mechanism. Done well: - Generation : 256 bits from a CSPRNG, encoded ( base62 / base64url ), with a recognisable prefix ( ck live … , ck test … ) so keys are identifiable in logs and by secret scanners (GitHub's scanning partner programme recognises prefixed formats). Show the full key once at creation. - Storage : store only a hash (SHA-256 is adequate for high-entropy random keys; the slow hashes of chapter 8 are for low-entropy passwords). Store a short key ID or the prefix in plaintext for lookup and display ( ck live a8f3… ). Lookup: find by key ID, then compare hash in constant time. - Scope : each key carries the tenant it belongs to, a set of permissions (scopes), optional IP allow-list, optional expiry. The effective permission is key scope ∩ tenant entitlements. - Rotation : allow multiple active keys per tenant so consumers can create a new one, switch, then revoke the old. Record last used at so unused keys can be identified and pruned. - Revocation : immediate, server-side, by key ID. Keys are looked up per request, so revocation takes effect instantly (unlike JWTs). - Transport : Authorization: Bearer or a custom header; never in query strings (logged everywhere). - Rate limiting and audit per key (Part III chapter 5; chapter 22). - Environments : test-mode keys that only touch sandbox data, distinguished by p

Your services call databases, caches, queues, cloud APIs, payment providers, email services. For each, the question is: can this be identity-based instead of a stored secret? Target Static secret Identity-based alternative --- --- --- AWS services (S3, SQS, KMS, Secrets Manager…) IAM user access keys IAM role on the instance/task/function; SDK obtains temporary credentials automatically RDS PostgreSQL/MySQL Password in Secrets Manager IAM database authentication (15-minute tokens) Another AWS account Shared keys Cross-account role assumption via STS GitHub Actions → AWS Access keys in repo secrets OIDC federation: short-lived role credentials per job Kubernetes workload → AWS Node role shared by all pods IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) / Pod Identity Service → service inside your platform Shared API token mTLS via mesh, signed service tokens, IAM SigV4 for internal ALBs Third-party SaaS (Stripe, SendGrid) API key in Secrets Manager (unavoidable) Scope it minimally; rotate; some support OAuth or IP restrictions IAM roles are the central mechanism on AWS. A role is an identity with a permission policy and a trust policy saying who may assume it. Compute services assume roles automatically: an EC2 instance profile , an ECS task role (what your code can do) distinct from the task execution role (what the ECS agent needs: pull images, fetch secrets, write logs), a Lambda execution role, an EKS service account role. The SDK's default credential chain finds these without confi

IAM users with access keys should not exist for humans: use IAM Identity Center (SSO) with short-lived sessions (Part VII chapter 3). For the rare automation that cannot federate, an IAM user with one key, minimal policy, rotation every 90 days, and an alert on use from unexpected locations. Root account access keys: delete them; root has MFA (hardware) and is used only for the handful of tasks that require it.

When you deploy into a client's AWS account, you do not want their long-lived keys on your laptop or in your CI. Have the client create a role in their account with a trust policy allowing your account (or your CI's OIDC identity) to assume it, with an external ID to prevent the confused-deputy problem, MFA or session-duration conditions as agreed, and a permission policy scoped to what the deployment needs. You assume it for a session (one hour by default, up to twelve), do the work, and the session expires. The client sees every action in their CloudTrail under that role, can revoke access by deleting the role, and never shared a secret. Part XIII chapter 9 details the arrangement. :::

- CloudTrail: alert on credential use from new IP ranges or regions, on AssumeRole by unexpected principals, on IAM policy changes, on access key creation. - GuardDuty: detects credential exfiltration patterns (instance credentials used from outside AWS), unusual API activity, and known-bad IPs. - Provider dashboards: unusual spend or volume on third-party API keys (SMS pumping, compute abuse). - Your own API: per-key anomaly detection (sudden volume, new endpoints, geographic shift) and last used at reviews. - Secret scanning on repositories and CI logs; honeytokens (fake credentials that alert when used) in places attackers look.

Same drill as chapter 17: revoke/rotate first, then investigate usage, then contain, then clean up. For API keys you issued to a customer: revoke, notify them, help them rotate, and review what the key accessed. For cloud keys: disable the key or revoke the role's sessions ( aws iam put-role-policy with a deny on sessions issued before a timestamp, the "revoke sessions" button), then investigate CloudTrail for the exposure window.

- Storing API keys in plaintext in the database. - Keys in query strings; keys with no prefix; keys that cannot be rotated without downtime. - One key per customer with every permission, forever. - IAM users with access keys baked into AMIs, images, config files or CI. - Shared node roles in Kubernetes giving every pod every permission. - "Resource": " " on task roles. - Confusing task role with task execution role and granting both broad access. - No last used at ; thousands of orphaned keys. - Cross-account roles without external IDs or with "Principal": " " . questions How should an API key you issue be stored on your side? options Plaintext, so it can be shown again Encrypted with a reversible key As a hash (SHA-256 is fine for high-entropy keys) with a plaintext key ID for lookup In a cookie answer explain Random keys have enough entropy for a fast hash; store the ID for lookup and compare hashes in constant time. What is the preferred way for an ECS task to access S3? options Access keys in environment variables An IAM task role scoped to the bucket; the SDK picks up temporary credentials automatically A shared IAM user Public bucket answer explain Identity-based access: nothing to leak or rotate, every call attributed to the task role. What does an external ID in a cross-account role trust policy prevent? options Expired sessions The confused-deputy problem, where a third party is tricked into using its role access on behalf of the wrong customer Brute force MFA bypass

1. Implement API key issuance, hashed storage, scoped authentication, rotation (multiple active keys) and revocation; add last used at and a report of keys unused for 90 days. 2. Find every IAM user with access keys in an AWS account you control; replace each with a role or federation, or document why it must remain and set rotation. 3. Set up a cross-account role with an external ID between two accounts (or two sandbox accounts); assume it from the CLI and find the actions in the target account's CloudTrail.

- Map each OWASP Top 10 category to the concrete vulnerabilities, code patterns and controls covered in this book. - Use the list as a review checklist for your own applications and for client questionnaires. - Understand what the list is (awareness and prioritisation) and what it is not (a complete standard). ::: Chapters 1 to 18. :::

The owasp Top 10 is a periodically updated awareness document ranking the most impactful web application risk categories by prevalence and severity across large datasets of real applications. It is not a standard or a complete checklist (the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, ASVS, is the checklist); it is the shared vocabulary for "the things that actually go wrong" and the list every client security questionnaire references. The 2021 edition is the most widely cited; a 2025 edition has been published with similar categories and a reshuffled order, adding emphasis on supply chain and on mishandling of exceptional conditions. The categories below use the 2021 names with notes on later changes, because the underlying weaknesses are stable and all of them map to chapters in this book.

The most common category. Users act outside their intended permissions: IDOR, missing function-level checks, privilege escalation, tenant boundary violations, CORS misconfiguration, forced browsing to admin pages, JWT or cookie tampering. Controls: central authorization with default deny at the resource level (chapter 7), tenant-scoped loading and row-level security (Part III chapter 15), exact CORS allow-lists (chapter 14), verified sessions and tokens (chapters 4 and 5), tests for horizontal and vertical access. Checklist: Does every endpoint that touches a resource check ownership/tenant against the verified principal? Are list endpoints filtered by scope in the query? Are there tests as another user and another tenant?

Sensitive data exposed because of missing or weak cryptography: plaintext transport, weak algorithms, hard-coded keys, unsalted or fast password hashes, missing at-rest encryption, poor randomness, certificates not validated. Controls: TLS everywhere with validation (Part II chapters 9–10), Argon2id/bcrypt (chapter 8), AEAD and CSPRNG via maintained libraries (chapter 16), KMS and secrets management (chapter 17), data classification so you know what needs protecting (chapter 23). Checklist: Is every hop encrypted and validated? Are passwords hashed with a slow algorithm? Are keys outside code? Is randomness cryptographic? Which fields need application-level encryption?

SQL, NoSQL, OS command, LDAP, XPath, template and header injection; XSS is folded into this category in 2021. Controls: parameterised queries and allow-listed identifiers (chapter 11), argument arrays without shells and path canonicalisation (chapter 12), context-aware output encoding plus CSP (chapters 10 and 15), schema validation at the boundary (Part III chapter 2), safe deserialization and XML parsers (chapter 13). Checklist: Grep for string-built queries, shell=True , innerHTML / safe , unsafe loaders. Is SAST in CI? Are database roles least-privilege?

Flaws in the design rather than the implementation: missing threat modeling, business logic abuse (unlimited coupon reuse, race conditions in transfers, password reset by guessable questions), lack of rate limits on sensitive flows, trusting the client for business rules. Controls: threat modeling (chapter 2), explicit requirements for abuse cases, rate limiting and quotas (Part III chapter 5), idempotency and atomic operations against races (Part III chapters 3 and 13), secure defaults (chapter 1), design review (Part XII chapter 3). Checklist: Does a threat model exist? Are abuse cases written down? Which flows have no rate limit? Where does the client compute anything that matters?

Default credentials, unnecessary features and ports, verbose errors, missing headers, cloud storage open to the world, outdated or absent hardening, XML external entities (merged here in 2021). Controls: secure-by-default infrastructure as code with policy checks (Part X chapters 5–6), server and container hardening (Part V chapter 4, Part VI chapter 7), security headers (chapter 15), error handling that hides internals (Part III chapter 12), AWS Config and Security Hub baselines (Part VII chapter 12), disabling DTDs (chapter 13). Checklist: Any public buckets or 0.0.0.0/0 on non-web ports? Debug modes off? Headers present? Defaults changed? Config drift detected?

Known-vulnerable libraries, frameworks, base images and runtimes; unknown inventory; no patch process. Controls: lockfiles and reproducible builds (Part I chapter 9), dependency and image scanning with SBOMs (chapter 20), automated update PRs, base image refresh cadence, runtime patching (Part V chapter 12). Checklist: Is there an inventory (SBOM)? Does CI fail on critical CVEs? When was the base image last rebuilt? Who owns updates?

Credential stuffing, weak passwords, missing MFA, session fixation, sessions that never expire, tokens in URLs, insecure recovery. Controls: chapters 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 in full: rate limits, breached-password checks, MFA with phishing-resistant options, session rotation and expiry, federation for enterprise users, recovery flows designed as alternative logins. Checklist: Is MFA available and enforced for admins? Is login rate-limited per account and IP? Does the session rotate at login and die at logout? Is recovery as strong as login?

h: A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures
x: Trusting updates, plugins, CI pipelines and serialized data without integrity verification; insecure deserialization (merged here); compromised dependencies; unsigned artifacts; pipelines that can be modified by untrusted PRs. Controls: safe deserialization (chapter 13), signed and pinned dependencies and provenance (chapter 20), protected branches and reviewed pipeline changes (Part X chapters 2 and 9), signed container images and artifacts, integrity checks on downloaded resources (Subresource Integrity for CDN scripts). Checklist: What enters production without a signature or hash check? Can an unreviewed PR change the pipeline or deploy? Are serialized formats safe?

h: A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
x: Attacks that go unnoticed: no audit logs for logins and sensitive actions, logs without context, logs not centralised or not retained, no alerting, no incident response plan. Controls: audit logging (chapter 22), structured logs with correlation IDs (Part XI chapter 1), alerting on authentication anomalies and error spikes (Part XI chapter 5), CloudTrail and GuardDuty (Part VII chapter 12), incident response procedures (Part XI chapter 6, Part XV chapter 4). Checklist: Can you answer "who accessed record X last month"? Would you notice 10,000 failed logins? Are logs tamper-evident and retained? Has the incident process been exercised?

Fetching attacker-influenced URLs from the server, reaching internal services and cloud metadata. Controls: chapter 12 in full: scheme/port allow-lists, resolved-IP checks with pinning, no redirects, response bounds, network isolation of fetchers, IMDSv2, minimal instance roles; webhook destination validation (Part III chapter 10). Checklist: Where does the server fetch URLs from user input? Is IMDSv2 enforced? Can fetchers reach internal networks?

Things the list under-represents that this book covers because they cause client incidents: tenant isolation (Part III chapter 15), cloud IAM misconfiguration (Part VII chapter 2), secrets in repositories (chapters 17 and 20), backup exposure and recoverability (Part V chapter 11), and operational decay after handover (Part XIII). The 2025 edition's additions ("Software Supply Chain Failures" as its own category; "Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions") map to chapter 20 and to Part III chapter 12 respectively.

Client questionnaires ask "how do you address the OWASP Top 10?" The honest, useful answer is a table: category, the specific controls in your system, how each is verified (test, scan, review), and the evidence (links to CI checks, policies, logs). The chapter references above are that table's skeleton. Avoid "we follow OWASP best practices" without specifics; reviewers see through it. # OWASP Top 10 self-assessment (one line of evidence per item) ## A01 Broken Access Control - Central authorization with default deny; resource-level ownership and tenant checks on every endpoint. - Automated tests for horizontal (other user) and vertical (other role) access. ## A02 Cryptographic Failures - TLS with certificate validation on every hop; HSTS on public endpoints. - Argon2id/bcrypt for passwords; AEAD for application encryption; CSPRNG for tokens; keys in KMS/secrets manager. ## A03 Injection - Parameterised queries everywhere; identifiers allow-listed; no shell invocation with user input; path canonicalisation. - Output encoding by default; CSP enforced; SAST in CI. ## A04 Insecure Design - Threat model exists and is maintained; abuse cases documented; rate limits on sensitive flows; races closed with atomic operations. ## A05 Security Misconfiguration - Infrastructure as code with policy checks; no public storage; security headers; debug off; errors sanitised; config drift detection. ## A06 Vulnerable Components - Lockfiles; dependency and image scanning failing on critical CVEs

1. Complete the self-assessment above for a system you operate, with one piece of evidence per line. Lines without evidence are your backlog. 2. Take a client security questionnaire (or a public one such as the CAIQ) and map each question to a chapter and a control in your system. 3. Read the current OWASP Top 10 and ASVS Level 2 requirements for authentication; identify three ASVS requirements your system does not meet.

t: Secure Dependency Management and Supply Chain Security
x: - Explain the supply chain of a modern application and where it is attacked: registries, maintainers, build systems, base images, CI, and distribution. - Operate a dependency vulnerability programme: inventory (SBOM), scanning, triage, update cadence, and exceptions. - Harden the build pipeline: pinned actions, minimal permissions, provenance and signing. - Evaluate new dependencies before adopting them. ::: Part I chapter 9; chapters 17 and 18 of this part. :::

t: Secure Dependency Management and Supply Chain Security
x: Your application is a thin layer of your code over a thick layer of other people's code, built by tools you did not write, fetched from registries you do not control, assembled by a pipeline with credentials to production. An attacker who compromises any link runs code inside your system with your privileges, without ever touching your code. Supply chain attacks have hit widely used npm and PyPI packages, build tools, CI actions and container base images; the targets are everyone downstream.

t: Secure Dependency Management and Supply Chain Security
x: You cannot patch what you do not know you have. A sbom (CycloneDX or SPDX format) lists every component in an artifact with versions and hashes. Generate it in CI for every build ( syft , cyclonedx- tools, npm sbom , trivy sbom ), attach it to the artifact, and store it. When the next critical vulnerability is announced, the question "are we affected, where?" becomes a query over SBOMs rather than a week of archaeology. Clients in regulated sectors increasingly require SBOMs as a deliverable.

t: Secure Dependency Management and Supply Chain Security
x: - Software composition analysis (SCA) : compares your dependency tree against vulnerability databases. Tools: npm audit , pip-audit , osv-scanner , Trivy, Grype, Snyk, Dependabot alerts, GitHub's dependency review. Run in CI on every PR and on a schedule against main (new CVEs appear without code changes). - Image scanning : Trivy/Grype on built images; ECR's built-in scanning (basic or enhanced via Inspector) on push and continuously. - Policy : fail the build on critical/high findings with a fix available ; warn on the rest; require an explicit, time-boxed exception record for anything accepted. Without a policy, scanners become noise and get ignored. - Triage : not every CVE in a dependency is exploitable in your usage (the vulnerable function may never be called). Reachability analysis helps; so does VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) to record "not affected, because…". Prioritise by exploitability (known exploited vulnerabilities lists), exposure (Internet-facing?), and privilege. - Cadence : automated update PRs (Dependabot, Renovate) grouped weekly for minors/patches, immediate for security fixes, scheduled for majors; base images rebuilt monthly and on CVE; runtimes updated on their security releases. Measure mean time to remediate critical findings and keep it under days.

t: Secure Dependency Management and Supply Chain Security
x: Provenance is a signed statement of how an artifact was built: the source repository and commit, the builder, the build instructions. The SLSA framework defines levels; GitHub's artifact attestations and Sigstore's cosign attest produce them. Signing (cosign with keyless OIDC-based identities or KMS keys) lets deployers verify an image came from your pipeline and was not replaced. Verification happens at deploy time: a Kubernetes admission policy (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller) or a deploy script step refusing unsigned or unattested images. For client deliverables, a signed image plus SBOM plus provenance is the modern equivalent of a release with checksums.

x: Before adding a package, ask: Is it necessary, or is it twenty lines you can write? Who maintains it, how many maintainers, how active, how responsive to security reports? How many transitive dependencies does it pull in? Does it have install scripts or native code? Is it widely used (downloads, dependents)? Is there a security policy and a history of CVEs handled well? What licence (copyleft obligations matter for client deliverables)? Record the decision for anything significant. Removing dependencies is as valuable as updating them.

Why pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs rather than tags? options Tags are slower Tags are mutable; a compromised action can move its tag to malicious code, while a SHA is immutable SHAs are shorter GitHub requires it answer explain Use a bot to update pinned SHAs so you still receive fixes. What is an SBOM for? options Licensing only An inventory of every component in an artifact, so vulnerability impact can be determined quickly and provided to clients Faster builds Replacing scanning answer explain Inventory is the prerequisite for every other supply chain control. - Build a layered security testing programme: unit tests for security logic, SAST, SCA, secret scanning, DAST, and periodic penetration testing. - Write security-focused automated tests that prevent regressions in authentication, authorization, injection and tenant isolation. - Scope and commission a penetration test responsibly, and act on its results. - Test only what you are authorised to test. ::: Chapters 7, 10, 11, 14 and 20; Part XII chapter 5. :::

Security controls regress. A refactor drops a tenant filter; a new endpoint skips the authorization dependency; a framework upgrade changes a default; a CSP exception is added during a crunch and never removed. Without tests, each regression is found by an attacker or an auditor. Security testing is ordinary testing applied to the properties this part has described, plus specialised tools for the classes of bugs ordinary tests do not find. Test only systems you own or have explicit, written authorisation to test, within the agreed scope and time window. Scanning or probing a client's production system without a signed agreement is illegal in most jurisdictions and will end the engagement. For client systems, propose a test plan, get it approved in writing, test in staging or a dedicated window, and never use techniques that could disrupt service. Part XIII chapter 4 covers assessing a client's posture without testing. :::

The highest-value investment, because they run on every change. Patterns: # Authorization matrix: every endpoint × every role × own/other/other-tenant resource import pytest ENDPOINTS = [("GET", "/v1/orders/{id}"), ("PATCH", "/v1/orders/{id}"), ("DELETE", "/v1/orders/{id}"), ("GET", "/v1/orders/{id}/invoice")] ROLES = ["member", "support", "admin"] @pytest.mark.parametrize("method,path", ENDPOINTS) @pytest.mark.parametrize("role", ROLES) def test_cannot_access_other_tenant_resource(client, make_user, make_order, method, path, role): me = make_user(tenant="t_1", role=role) other = make_order(tenant="t_2") r = client.request(method, path.format(id=other.id), auth=me) assert r.status_code in (403, 404), f"{role} {method} {path} leaked cross-tenant" @pytest.mark.parametrize("method,path", ENDPOINTS) def test_member_cannot_access_other_users_resource_in_same_tenant(client, make_user, make_order, method, path): me = make_user(tenant="t_1", role="member") other = make_order(tenant="t_1", owner=make_user(tenant="t_1")) r = client.request(method, path.format(id=other.id), auth=me) assert r.status_code in (403, 404) def test_unauthenticated_rejected(client, all_routes): for method, path in all_routes: # introspect the router so new routes are covered automatically if path.startswith("/health"): continue r = client.request(method, path.replace("{id}", "x")) assert r.status_code == 401, f"{method} {path} is reachable without auth" # Mass assignment, injection canaries, headers, CSRF def

SAST tools pattern-match source for dangerous constructs. Semgrep (with community and OWASP rulesets, plus your own rules for project-specific sinks), Bandit (Python), ESLint security plugins, CodeQL (deep dataflow analysis; free for public repos, available via GitHub Advanced Security), gosec, Brakeman (Rails). Run on every PR; start with a small high-signal ruleset to avoid alert fatigue; write custom rules when you find a bug class ("never call render template string with a variable"; "every router must include the auth dependency").

DAST tools (OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite's scanner, Nuclei for known misconfigurations) crawl and attack a running application. Run nightly against staging with an authenticated session (ZAP supports scripted auth), import the OpenAPI spec so the scanner knows every endpoint, and triage results into tickets. Expect false positives; expect it to miss authorization logic. It excels at headers, reflected XSS, outdated software banners and forgotten debug endpoints.

Scan infrastructure code before apply (Checkov, tfsec/Trivy, cfn-nag, Prowler for live accounts) and watch live configuration continuously (AWS Config rules, Security Hub standards such as the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, GuardDuty). Part X chapter 6 and Part VII chapter 12. These catch the misconfigurations that dominate cloud breaches: public buckets, open security groups, unencrypted storage, IAM wildcards, missing logging.

A penetration test is a time-boxed, authorised, manual (tool-assisted) attack on a defined scope by people whose job is to think like attackers. It finds what automation cannot: chained weaknesses, business logic abuse, authorization gaps that require understanding the product. Commission one before a major launch, annually for anything handling sensitive data, and after significant architectural change; many clients and compliance regimes require it. Scoping well: define targets (URLs, APIs, accounts, excluding third-party services unless they permit it), environment (staging with production-like data shape, or production in a window with safeguards), rules of engagement (no denial of service, no social engineering unless agreed, hours, emergency contacts), what the testers get (credentials for each role, documentation, source code for a grey/white-box test, which is more efficient than black-box), and the deliverable (report with severity, reproduction steps, remediation advice; a retest of fixes). Acting on results: triage into the normal workflow with deadlines by severity (critical: days; high: weeks); fix the class, not the instance (one IDOR usually means a pattern); add regression tests; retest; share a summary with the client. A report that sits in a folder is a liability: it proves you knew. Notify the cloud provider if required by their policy (AWS permits testing of most services on your own resources without prior approval; some simulated attacks, like DDoS, requ

Publish a security.txt (RFC 9116) and a disclosure policy so researchers can reach you. A bounty programme (HackerOne, Bugcrowd, self-run) rewards findings; it suits mature products with a response process, not early-stage systems where the backlog would overwhelm you.

Track: security test coverage of endpoints (every route in the authorization matrix?), SAST/SCA findings open by severity and age, mean time to remediate, DAST findings trend, pentest findings by class over time, secret-scanning hits (should trend to zero). Present these to clients as evidence of a working programme, not as a one-time certificate.

- Running scanners and ignoring their output. - Security tests as a separate suite nobody runs; integrate into the main CI. - Testing production without authorisation or safeguards. - Pentest once, before launch, then never, while the system changes monthly. - Fixing the one IDOR the pentest found and leaving the pattern. - No security.txt , so a researcher who finds something cannot tell you. - Trusting a clean DAST run as proof of security. questions Which testing layer most reliably prevents authorization regressions? options Annual penetration test Automated tests covering every endpoint × role × foreign resource, run on every PR answer explain Logic regressions are caught by tests that encode the intended policy. What must exist before any security testing of a client's system? options A staging environment Written authorisation with defined scope, rules of engagement and timing A WAF A bug bounty answer explain Unauthorised testing is illegal and ends engagements. A penetration test reports one IDOR on the invoices endpoint. What is the correct response? options Fix that endpoint Fix that endpoint, audit every endpoint for the same pattern, add regression tests, and retest Add a WAF rule Ask for a retest only answer explain Findings are samples of patterns; fix the class. What does DAST typically miss? options Missing headers Reflected XSS Authorization logic and business-logic flaws Outdated server banners answer explain Scanners do not understand what each user should

- Distinguish audit logs from application and access logs, and know what each must record. - Design an audit event schema and emit events for every security-relevant action. - Store audit logs so they are tamper-evident, retained appropriately, searchable and free of secrets and excess personal data. - Use audit logs in investigations, compliance evidence and anomaly detection. ::: Chapters 3, 7 and 17; Part XI chapter 1. :::

When a client asks "who exported our customer list on March 3rd?", "did anyone view this patient's record?", or "when did this user gain admin rights?", application logs rarely answer. They record what the system did for debugging, at whatever level a developer chose, rotated after a week. An audit log answers who did what to which resource, when, from where, and with what outcome , for every action that matters, in a store that nobody can quietly edit. It is also what turns a suspected breach into a scoped incident instead of a worst-case assumption.

Log Purpose Content Retention Access --- --- --- --- --- Application logs Debugging, operations Errors, warnings, traces, timings Days to weeks Engineers Access logs Traffic analysis, security monitoring Every request: IP, path, status, latency, user agent Weeks to months Engineers, security Audit logs Accountability, compliance, forensics Security-relevant actions by identified actors Months to years (by regulation/contract) Restricted; append-only Audit events are emitted deliberately from code at the point of the action, not derived from debug logs. They can flow through the same pipeline as other logs but land in a separate, protected store.

Authentication: login success/failure (with method), MFA enrolment/removal, logout, password change/reset, session revocation, account lockout, recovery actions. Authorization and identity: role or permission changes, group membership changes, API key creation/revocation, SSO configuration changes, impersonation ("log in as user") start and end. Data access and change: create/update/delete of business records (at least for sensitive entities), reads of sensitive records (health, financial, PII) where regulation or the threat model demands, exports and bulk downloads, report generation, search over personal data. Administrative and configuration: changes to settings, feature flags, integrations, webhook endpoints, billing, retention policies; deployments and infrastructure changes (from CI/CD and CloudTrail). Security events: rate limit triggers, authorization denials, signature verification failures, suspicious patterns. The test: if this action appeared in a breach report, would you need to know who did it?

An audit log that administrators can edit is a story, not evidence. Properties to aim for: - Append-only : the application role can INSERT into audit events but not UPDATE or DELETE (database grants). Admins do not have write access to the audit store in normal operation. - Off-box copy : ship events to a store outside the application's blast radius: CloudWatch Logs with a retention policy, then S3 with Object Lock (WORM) for the long-term archive; or a dedicated logging account. An attacker who compromises the application should not be able to erase their tracks. - Integrity : hash chaining (each event includes the hash of the previous) or periodic signed digests (S3 Object Lock plus CloudTrail log file validation for AWS events) makes tampering detectable. - Retention : by regulation and contract: often 1 year hot, 6–7 years cold for financial and health contexts; GDPR requires you not to keep personal data longer than necessary, so define retention per event type and purge on schedule (chapter 23). - Access control : reading audit logs is itself a sensitive action; restrict and log it. - Clock discipline : NTP everywhere; UTC; consistent timestamps across services.

Your application's audit log covers business actions; the platform's covers infrastructure. On AWS: CloudTrail for every API call (enable in all regions, log to a dedicated account bucket with Object Lock and log file validation, include data events for sensitive S3 buckets); AWS Config for configuration history; VPC Flow Logs for network; RDS/pgAudit for database statements where required; SSM Session Manager logs for shell access; ALB access logs . Together they answer who changed the infrastructure and who touched the data store directly.

- Investigations : "show every action by actor X between T1 and T2", "every access to target Y", "every export in tenant Z". Index by actor, target, action and time; keep the hot window queryable (OpenSearch, CloudWatch Logs Insights, or the database table with indexes). - Detection : alerts on privilege changes outside change windows, on impersonation, on exports above a threshold, on bursts of denials, on logins from new geographies for admins, on audit pipeline failures (silence is an alert). - Compliance evidence : SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA and PCI all ask for audit trails of access and changes; export samples and retention proofs on request. - Customer-facing : enterprise tenants want their own audit log (who in their organisation did what); expose it per tenant via API and UI, read-only.

Audit logs are personal data too. Minimise: IDs rather than names and emails where possible (resolve at display time), coarse user agents, IP addresses only where justified (and consider truncation), no document contents. Define retention and honour deletion obligations where the law requires, balancing against legal-hold and integrity requirements (often: pseudonymise the actor rather than delete the event).

- Relying on debug logs rotated weekly as the audit trail. - Audit rows writable and deletable by the application role or by admins. - Logging secrets, tokens or full records into audit events. - No denials recorded, so probing is invisible. - No off-box copy; attacker deletes the evidence. - Timestamps in local time, or servers with drifted clocks. - Audit pipeline failures unnoticed for months. - Reads of sensitive data not audited because "it is just a read". questions What distinguishes an audit log from an application log? options Audit logs are JSON Audit logs deliberately record who did what to which resource with what outcome, in a protected, long-retained store Application logs are more detailed There is no difference answer explain Audit events are emitted on purpose for accountability; debug logs are incidental and transient. Why must the application's database role be unable to UPDATE or DELETE audit rows? options Performance Tamper-evidence: a compromised application or a rogue admin must not be able to erase evidence Storage cost Schema stability answer explain Append-only grants plus an off-box immutable copy make the log trustworthy. Which of these should be audited even though it changes nothing? options Health check requests A support agent viewing a customer's full record Static asset downloads Cache hits answer explain Reads of sensitive data are accountability events; many breaches are unauthorised reads. t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: - Classify data by sensitivity and apply proportionate controls to each class. - Apply privacy principles (minimisation, purpose limitation, retention, transparency) in system design. - Implement the mechanics regulations require: data inventories, deletion and export, consent records, breach notification readiness, processor agreements. - Handle personal data responsibly in logs, analytics, backups, non-production environments and third parties. ::: Chapters 1, 2, 16 and 22. :::

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: Every client system holds personal data: customers, employees, patients, end users. Laws (GDPR in the EU and UK, CCPA/CPRA in California, LGPD in Brazil, HIPAA for US health data, PCI DSS for card data by contract, and many others) impose obligations on how it is collected, used, protected, retained and deleted, with fines and mandatory breach disclosure. Beyond the law, a client's customers trust them with data, and a Forward Deployed Engineer who copies the production database to a laptop "to debug" has broken that trust regardless of outcome. Privacy is an engineering property: you design systems that can comply, or you build an incident. This chapter is engineering guidance, not legal advice; the client's legal or data protection function decides obligations, and you implement them.

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: - Personal data / pii : anything relating to an identifiable person: names, emails, IDs, IP addresses, device identifiers, location, behavioural data, and combinations that identify someone. - Special categories / sensitive data : health, biometrics, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, political opinions, criminal data; children's data. Higher protection, often explicit consent. - Controller : decides why and how data is processed (usually the client). Processor : processes on the controller's behalf (often you, and your cloud providers). Processors need a data processing agreement (DPA) and must follow instructions. - Data subject : the person. Has rights : access (a copy of their data), rectification, erasure ("right to be forgotten"), portability, restriction, objection. - Lawful basis : consent, contract, legal obligation, legitimate interest, etc. Determines what you may do. - Breach : unauthorised access, loss or disclosure; often notifiable to regulators within 72 hours (GDPR) and to individuals when risk is high.

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: Class Examples Controls --- --- --- Public Marketing content, public docs Integrity only Internal Architecture docs, non-sensitive config Access control Confidential Business data, customer lists, contracts Encryption at rest, least-privilege access, audit Personal (PII) Names, emails, addresses, IPs, behaviour All of the above, plus minimisation, retention limits, subject rights support, DPAs Sensitive personal / regulated Health, financial account data, government IDs, card data, children's data Field-level encryption, strict need-to-know, enhanced audit (reads), tokenisation, regulatory scope (HIPAA, PCI) Secrets Credentials, keys Chapter 17 Tag data at the schema level (a column comment or a data catalogue entry: pii , sensitive ) so that tooling, reviews and retention jobs can find it. A data inventory (what personal data, where it lives, why, for how long, who accesses it, which processors) is both a legal requirement (records of processing) and the map you need for every control below.

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: Minimisation : collect only what the purpose needs. Do you need date of birth, or just "over 18"? Full address, or country for tax? Every field you do not collect cannot leak. Purpose limitation : data collected for order fulfilment is not automatically available for marketing or model training. Enforce in design: separate stores or explicit flags, and access paths tied to purposes. Retention : define a retention period per data category (and per legal requirement) and implement deletion : scheduled jobs that delete or anonymise expired records, including in backups' lifecycle, logs, analytics and search indexes. "We keep everything forever" is a liability, not a feature. Pseudonymisation and anonymisation : replace identifiers with tokens (pseudonymisation: reversible with a key kept elsewhere; reduces exposure and enables analytics on less sensitive data) or remove identifiability irreversibly (anonymisation: aggregate, generalise, add noise; true anonymisation is hard, and re-identification from "anonymous" datasets is a well-documented risk). Transparency : the privacy notice must match what the system does. Engineers often add a data flow (a new analytics tool, a new third-party API) that nobody told legal about; make "new processor or new purpose" a design-review checkbox. Security proportionate to risk : the controls of this whole part, applied with intensity matching the classification.

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: - Access and portability : an export per user of all their personal data across systems, in a common format (JSON/CSV), delivered securely (authenticated download, short-lived link), within the legal window (one month under GDPR). Build it as a job over the data inventory, not an ad-hoc SQL session. - Erasure : delete or anonymise the subject's data across the primary database, caches, search indexes, object storage, analytics, logs (within retention), and notify processors to do the same. Keep what law requires (invoices for tax) with a documented basis, and pseudonymise instead where integrity matters (audit logs, chapter 22). Backups: most regulators accept deletion from backups on their normal rotation if restored backups are re-purged; document the approach. - Rectification : edit flows that propagate to derived data. - Consent management : record what was consented to, when, how, and the version of the notice; honour withdrawal immediately across systems (marketing flags, cookie consent for non-essential cookies and trackers). Design the identity graph first: all personal data must be findable by subject ID. Data keyed only by email in a third-party tool with no link to your user IDs will be missed.

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
h: Personal data in the places people forget
x: - Logs : request bodies, query strings with emails, IPs, user agents, stack traces containing record contents. Redact at the logging layer (allow-list fields; mask patterns for emails, card numbers, tokens); set retention; treat log stores as personal-data stores. - Analytics and error tracking : Sentry events with user context, product analytics with free-text fields, session replay tools recording form input. Configure scrubbing; disable replay on sensitive pages; sign DPAs. - Non-production environments : never raw production PII (Part I chapter 11); use synthetic data or verified masking. - Backups and exports : encrypted, access-controlled, retained per policy, included in deletion procedures. - Caches and queues : PII in Redis and SQS messages inherits none of the database's controls; minimise what is placed there and set TTLs. - Emails and notifications : content stored by the email provider; links containing IDs. - Third parties and AI tools : sending customer data to an LLM API or a SaaS tool is processing by a processor; it needs a DPA, a purpose, and often explicit client approval. Many clients forbid it without review. - Developer laptops and chat : CSV exports, screenshots, log snippets pasted into Slack or tickets. Policy, training and tooling (redaction, short-lived access) all matter. - Cross-border transfers : storing EU residents' data in a US region, or support staff in another country accessing it, triggers transfer rules. t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: You will handle a suspected breach eventually. Prepare: an incident process that includes legal and the client's DPO from the first hour (Part XI chapter 6); audit logs that let you scope what was accessed (chapter 22); a data inventory to determine which subjects and categories are involved; templates for regulator and subject notifications; a decision log. The 72-hour clock starts at awareness; the quality of your logs determines whether you can say "17 records of category X" or must say "possibly everything".

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: GDPR / UK GDPR : applies to personal data of people in the EU/UK regardless of where you are; lawful basis, rights, DPAs, records of processing, DPIAs for high-risk processing, breach notification in 72 hours, fines up to 4% of global turnover. CCPA/CPRA : California residents; disclosure, opt-out of sale/sharing, deletion, non-discrimination. HIPAA : US protected health information; covered entities and business associates (you sign a BAA), administrative/physical/technical safeguards, audit controls, breach notification. PCI DSS : contractual standard for card data; minimise scope by never touching card numbers (use a payment provider's hosted fields and tokens); if in scope, twelve requirement areas including network segmentation, encryption, access control, logging and testing. SOC 2 (not a privacy law but a client expectation): audit of controls including privacy criteria. Part XII chapter 7.

t: Data Privacy and Personally Identifiable Information
x: Ask early: what personal data will the system hold, where may it live (region), who are the processors, what retention applies, who handles subject requests, and who is the DPO or legal contact. Put the answers in the data inventory and the threat model. Refuse to copy production data into lower environments or onto laptops, and say why; clients respect it. When a client asks you to do something that looks unlawful (scrape and store data without a basis, retain forever, send PII to an unapproved tool), raise it in writing to their legal function. You are not their lawyer, but you are a professional who notices. :::

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: Public breach reports and incident post-mortems repeat the same dozen stories with different logos. Almost none involve novel attacks. They involve a default left in place, a check forgotten in one endpoint, a credential in the wrong file, a copy of data in a place with no controls, or a vendor nobody reviewed. This chapter is the catalogue, each entry with how it happens, how it is found (usually by someone else), and the structural fix. Treat it as the review you run on every system before launch and every quarter after.

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : an S3 bucket (or Azure blob, GCS bucket) created with public read for a quick demo, a static site, or a CDN origin; backups, exports or user uploads land in it later; a researcher or a scanner enumerates bucket names and lists it. Variants: a presigned URL with a one-year expiry shared in a support ticket; a bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject to on the whole bucket to fix a 403. Fix : Block Public Access at the account level; CloudFront with Origin Access Control for anything served publicly; presigned URLs with minutes of validity; AWS Config rule s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited alerting; periodic listing of every bucket's policy. Part III chapter 9, Part VII chapter 10.

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : an AWS access key, a database URL with password, a Stripe secret, or a private key committed in a config file, a notebook, a test fixture or a commit "removed later". The repository is public, or becomes public, or a contractor's laptop is stolen, or a former employee still has a clone. Automated scanners find keys on GitHub within minutes of a push and use them for crypto-mining or data theft. Fix : secret scanning on every push and across history (chapter 20); pre-commit hooks; secrets manager and IAM roles so keys do not exist (chapters 17–18); treat any committed secret as compromised and rotate immediately. Review access to repositories at offboarding.

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : GET /api/invoices/{id} checks login but not ownership; invoices are numbered sequentially; a user (or a scraper) iterates. Variants: the export endpoint, the PDF endpoint, the mobile API that was "internal", the GraphQL field resolver, the batch endpoint that checks only the first ID. Fix : central authorization at the resource level with default deny; tenant-scoped loading; RLS; random IDs; the authorization matrix test on every route (chapters 7 and 21).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
h: 4. The exposed database or admin tool
x: How : MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Redis or PostgreSQL bound to 0.0.0.0 with a default or no password on a VM with a public IP, or in a public subnet with a 0.0.0.0/0 security group rule "temporarily". Internet-wide scanners find it within hours. Variants: an admin dashboard (Grafana, pgAdmin, Kibana, a Django admin) on a public URL with default credentials; a Kubernetes dashboard; a Jenkins instance. Fix : private subnets for data stores; security groups referencing application groups only; no public IPs on anything but load balancers; admin tools behind SSO and VPN or identity-aware proxy; Docker port-binding discipline; Config rules on open security groups (Part II chapter 15, Part V chapter 7, Part VII chapter 6).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
h: 5. Logs and error trackers full of personal data
x: How : request bodies logged at INFO; exceptions carrying record contents sent to an error tracker; query strings with emails and tokens in access logs; logs shipped to a third-party tool with broad staff access and years of retention. The "leak" is often internal over-access, then an exposed logging dashboard or a vendor breach. Fix : structured logging with allow-listed fields; redaction middleware; no-store for tokens in URLs (never put them there); retention; DPAs and access control for log vendors; PII tagging (chapters 22–23, Part XI chapter 1).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
h: 6. The CDN or cache serving the wrong user's page
x: How : a caching layer configured by URL only, an authenticated endpoint without Cache-Control: no-store , a Vary header missing: user B receives user A's account page. Variants: a reverse proxy cache enabled broadly; an in-process cache keyed without the tenant. Fix : private, no-store on personal responses; CDN behaviours disabling cache for authenticated paths; cache keys including every varying dimension (Part II chapters 8 and 17, Part III chapter 8).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
h: 7. Backups and exports in the wrong place
x: How : nightly database dumps copied to a developer's laptop, a shared drive, an unencrypted bucket, or an FTP server set up years ago; a one-off CSV export for a client sent by email and forwarded; a staging environment seeded from production and left running with weak auth. Fix : backups encrypted, in a dedicated bucket with Object Lock and restricted access, deleted on schedule; exports via short-lived presigned URLs with audit; synthetic or masked data in lower environments (Part V chapter 11, Part I chapter 11, chapter 23).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : an analytics script loaded from a compromised CDN skims form input (Magecart-style); a vendor with API access to your customer data is breached; a dependency update exfiltrates environment variables from CI; a browser extension on a staff laptop. Fix : Subresource Integrity and CSP for third-party scripts; minimal, scoped vendor access with DPAs and reviews; pinned, scanned dependencies with release-age delays; OIDC instead of long-lived CI keys; inventory of every processor (chapters 15, 20, 23).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : an application role with AdministratorAccess ; a Lambda that can read every bucket; a CI user with ; instance metadata exposed via SSRF to a role that can read Secrets Manager wholesale. One foothold becomes the whole account. Fix : least-privilege roles per workload, resource-scoped; IMDSv2; permission boundaries and SCPs; IAM Access Analyzer; GuardDuty for credential misuse (chapters 12 and 18, Part VII chapters 2 and 12).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : an engineer's console password without MFA phished; a shared "admin" login on a sticky note; a departed contractor's account still active; SMS MFA defeated by SIM swap. Fix : SSO with phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/security keys) for everything administrative; no shared accounts; offboarding tied to the identity provider; access reviews (chapters 6 and 8, Part VII chapter 3).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : a stack trace with connection strings shown to users; a /debug or /metrics endpoint exposing environment variables; Spring Boot Actuator or Django debug mode in production; GraphQL introspection and verbose errors leaking schema and data. Fix : production error handling that returns IDs only; debug modes off by configuration validation; metrics and admin endpoints bound internally or behind auth; scanners for known debug paths (Part III chapter 12, chapter 15).

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
x: How : an old microservice, a demo environment, a client's previous vendor's VM, a marketing site on a legacy CMS, a dangling DNS record pointing at a released cloud resource (subdomain takeover). Nobody patches it, nobody monitors it, it still has access to something. Fix : asset inventory (every domain, account, host, service, with an owner); decommissioning procedures that delete DNS records, credentials and data; periodic external attack-surface scans of all your domains (Part II chapter 7, Part XIII chapter 12).

x: 1. Contain : close the exposure (make the bucket private, revoke the credential, disable the endpoint, take the system offline if needed). Minutes matter. 2. Preserve evidence : snapshot logs and configurations before changing more; note times. 3. Scope : what data, how many subjects, what period, who accessed it (audit logs, access logs, CloudTrail, provider logs). Be precise and honest; "we cannot tell" is a finding about logging. 4. Notify : the client's leadership and legal/DPO immediately; regulators and subjects per their decision and the legal timelines; affected third parties. 5. Rotate anything that might have been exposed alongside. 6. Remediate the pattern, not just the instance; add the automated check that would have caught it. 7. Postmortem blamelessly (Part XI chapter 7); update the audit checklist above with whatever was new.

t: How Client Data Leaks Actually Happen
h: The habit that prevents most of this
x: Before every launch and every quarter, run the afternoon audit with fresh eyes, preferably someone who did not build the system. Automate what can be automated (Config rules, secret scanning, the authorization test, header checks, bucket policy checks) so the audit becomes a review of alerts rather than a hunt. The patterns above are boring precisely because the fixes are known; the only question is whether anyone checked. questions Which single AWS setting prevents the most common storage leak pattern? options Versioning Block Public Access at the account level Lifecycle rules Transfer Acceleration answer explain It makes public bucket policies and ACLs impossible regardless of individual bucket configuration. A key was committed to a private repository and removed in the next commit. What is the correct assumption? options It is safe because the repo is private It is compromised: rotate it, then clean history and add scanning It is safe once history is purged Only public repos matter answer explain Clones, forks, CI logs and future exposure all keep the key alive; rotation is the only cure. t: Servers: Physical, Virtual, Containers and Serverless
x: Every application runs on a physical machine somewhere. Between that machine and your code are layers of abstraction, each trading control for convenience: virtual machines hide the hardware, containers hide the operating system, serverless hides the server. Picking the wrong layer costs money and operational pain; not understanding the layer you picked makes performance problems inexplicable ("why does my t3.micro get slow every afternoon?").

t: Servers: Physical, Virtual, Containers and Serverless

You patch the OS, configure the firewall, run the process supervisor. Part V is mostly about this level. You own node patching and capacity. t: Servers: Physical, Virtual, Containers and Serverless
x: A hypervisor (KVM, Xen, AWS Nitro, VMware ESXi) runs directly on hardware and presents each guest VM with virtual devices. Modern hardware virtualisation (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) runs guest code natively on the CPU with the hypervisor intervening only for privileged operations and I/O. AWS Nitro offloads networking and storage to dedicated cards, so EC2 instances get near-bare-metal performance. Consequences you will observe: - vCPU ≠ core : on most x86 instances a vCPU is one hyperthread; two vCPUs are one physical core's two threads, not two cores. Graviton (ARM) instances map one vCPU to one physical core. Compare benchmarks, not vCPU counts. - Steal time ( st in top ): the hypervisor scheduled another VM on your core. Significant on oversubscribed hosts and on burstable instances out of credits. - Network and disk performance are per-instance allowances that scale with size; small instances have "up to" bandwidth with burst credits, and EBS throughput is capped per volume and per instance.

t: Servers: Physical, Virtual, Containers and Serverless
x: t3 / t4g instances earn CPU credits while below a baseline utilisation (20% for a t3.medium) and spend them to burst to 100%. Out of credits, the CPU is throttled to the baseline (or you pay for unlimited mode). This is the cause of "the server is fine all morning and crawls after lunch": sustained load drained the credits. Burstable instances are excellent for dev/staging and low-traffic services, wrong for sustained CPU work. Monitor CPUCreditBalance .

t: Servers: Physical, Virtual, Containers and Serverless
x: Start from measurement, not guesses: 1. CPU : profile the application under a load test (Part XI chapter 8). Web APIs are usually I/O-bound and need fewer cores than people assume; serialisation, compression and TLS are the CPU costs. Target 50–60% utilisation at peak for headroom. 2. Memory : per-worker RSS × workers plus runtime baseline plus page cache for databases (Part I chapter 7). Memory is the resource that kills; oversize it relative to CPU. 3. Disk : capacity (data plus logs plus headroom), IOPS and throughput. gp3 EBS gives 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline regardless of size, configurable upward; databases often need more. Local NVMe (instance store) is fast but ephemeral. 4. Network : bandwidth allowances per instance; packets per second limits matter for chatty services; NAT gateway and cross-AZ transfer costs. Instance families: general purpose (m, t) for web servers; compute optimised (c) for CPU-heavy work; memory optimised (r, x) for databases and caches; storage optimised (i, d) for local disk I/O; accelerated (g, p, inf) for GPUs and ML. Graviton (ARM, g suffix like m7g) is typically 20–40% cheaper for the same performance when your software has ARM builds (most interpreted-language stacks and container images do; check native dependencies).

Choose EC2 when a dependency genuinely needs a VM, when the client already operates VMs well and wants consistency, or when sustained load makes reserved EC2 materially cheaper and someone will own patching. Always compute the three-year cost including people time, not just the instance price.

t: Servers: Physical, Virtual, Containers and Serverless
x: On-demand is the list price. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances discount 30–70% for one- or three-year commitments; commit only to the baseline you are certain of. Spot instances are spare capacity at up to 90% off that can be reclaimed with two minutes' notice; good for stateless workers and CI, wrong for databases. Right-sizing (turning off idle instances, downsizing underused ones, Graviton) usually saves more than any purchasing option. Part VII chapter 4.

t: Linux Server Architecture and the Boot Process
x: - Describe what happens from power-on to your service accepting connections: firmware, bootloader, kernel, init, services. - Navigate the pieces of a running server: kernel, systemd, udev, networking stack, logging, cron/timers, users. - Use cloud-init and user data to configure instances at first boot. - Diagnose a server that will not boot or will not start its services. ::: Part I chapters 3 and 6; chapter 1 of this part. :::

t: Linux Server Architecture and the Boot Process
x: A server that does not come up after a reboot is a worse incident than one that crashes, because the usual tools are gone. Knowing the boot sequence tells you where it stopped and what to look at (the serial console, the recovery volume, the cloud-init log). It also explains how your application becomes a service that starts automatically, in the right order, with the right environment, which is the subject of chapter 5.

t: Linux Server Architecture and the Boot Process
x: - Kernel : scheduler, memory, filesystems, networking, security modules (AppArmor/SELinux). Parameters via sysctl ( /etc/sysctl.d/ ); loaded modules via lsmod . Version via uname -r ; kernel updates require a reboot (or live patching). - systemd : PID 1 and a family of tools: systemctl (units), journalctl (logs), timedatectl , hostnamectl , networkctl / resolvectl (where systemd-networkd/resolved are used), systemd-analyze blame (boot timing). Unit types: services, sockets, timers (cron replacement), mounts, targets. Chapter 5. - udev : device management; creates /dev entries and applies rules (e.g., persistent names for NVMe volumes). - Networking : configured by netplan (Ubuntu), NetworkManager, or systemd-networkd; on cloud instances DHCP from the VPC. Chapter 7. - Time : chrony or systemd-timesyncd against the cloud time source. Essential (Part I chapter 3). - Logging : journald collects everything; rsyslog may forward to files or remote collectors; the CloudWatch agent or a log shipper sends logs off-box. Chapter 9. - Scheduled jobs : cron ( /etc/cron.d , user crontabs) or systemd timers (preferred: logging, dependencies, randomised delays). - Users and access : /etc/passwd , /etc/group , sudoers , sshd . Chapters 3 and 4. - Packages : apt/dnf with the distribution's repositories plus any you added; unattended upgrades for security patches. Chapter 12. - Filesystems and mounts : /etc/fstab , LVM, EBS volumes attached by device name. Chapter 6.

t: Linux Server Architecture and the Boot Process
x: Without SSH, your tools are: the serial console (EC2 Serial Console or "Get system log" screenshot) showing kernel and systemd messages; cloud-init logs once you can reach the disk; and the rescue procedure : stop the instance, detach its root volume, attach it to a healthy instance as a secondary volume, mount it, fix the problem (bad /etc/fstab entry, broken sshd config, full disk, wrong permissions on /etc/sudoers ), detach, reattach as root, start. Common causes: an fstab entry for a volume that no longer exists (boot hangs waiting; use nofail on non-root mounts), a kernel update that failed, disk full preventing services from starting, a typo in sshd config (always sshd -t before restart), or a security group/NACL change that merely looks like a boot failure. systemd-analyze blame | head # what took long at boot systemctl --failed # units that failed journalctl -b -p err # errors since this boot journalctl -b -1 -e # end of the previous boot's log (why did it go down?) sudo cat /var/log/cloud-init-output.log | tail -50

x: Kernel and some library updates require reboots. Plan them: behind a load balancer with at least two instances, drain one (deregister or set unhealthy), reboot, verify, re-register, repeat. Single-instance systems need a maintenance window and a communicated downtime. Test that services come back without manual steps ( systemctl is-enabled ); a service that someone started by hand and never enabled is a classic post-reboot outage.
