- Explain how SSH authenticates servers and users, and why key-based authentication is mandatory. - Generate, protect and distribute keys; configure clients and servers securely; use jump hosts and port forwarding. - Harden sshd and manage access for a team, including rotation and offboarding. - Know when to replace SSH with SSM Session Manager or certificate-based access. ::: Part I chapter 5; Part II chapter 16. :::

SSH is the administrative door to every Linux server. Password authentication on a public SSH port is attacked within minutes of a server coming online, continuously, by automated credential-guessing. Keys fix that, but introduce their own management problem: who has which key on which server, how keys are protected, and how access ends when people leave. Most organisations' SSH key sprawl is unknowable, which is why the modern direction is to remove the door entirely (SSM) or to issue short-lived certificates.

1. Transport : the client connects (TCP 22), negotiates algorithms, and performs a key exchange to establish an encrypted channel. 2. Server authentication : the server presents its host key ; the client checks it against ~/.ssh/known hosts . The first connection shows a fingerprint prompt (trust on first use); a changed host key later produces the loud "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED" warning, which means either the server was rebuilt or you are being intercepted. Do not blindly delete the line; verify. 3. User authentication : public key (the server has your public key in ~/.ssh/authorized keys ; it sends a challenge your private key signs), or password, or certificate, optionally plus a second factor. 4. Session : a shell, a command, or forwarded ports/sockets.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 64 -C "ana@laptop-2026" # Ed25519: small, fast, modern; -a adds KDF rounds protecting the passphrase # → ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private, mode 600) and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public) ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 # macOS: load into the agent; Linux: ssh-add ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub deploy@server # append the public key to the server's authorized_keys (or do it via cloud-init/config management) Rules: one key per person per device , with a passphrase, stored only on that device (ideally in a hardware token: YubiKey via FIDO2 ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk , or the macOS Secure Enclave). Never share private keys; never copy them to servers; never commit them. The public key is not secret and can be published freely. Use the SSH agent to avoid typing passphrases, but do not forward the agent to untrusted hosts ( ForwardAgent yes lets root on that host use your key; use ProxyJump instead). Rotate keys yearly or when a device is lost. Client configuration keeps things sane: @file: ~/.ssh/config Host * AddKeysToAgent yes IdentitiesOnly yes # only offer the configured key, avoiding "too many authentication failures" ServerAliveInterval 30 HashKnownHosts yes Host bastion HostName bastion.client.com User ana IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_client Host prod-app-* User deploy ProxyJump bastion # transparent jump; your key never leaves the laptop IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_client ssh prod-app-1 # via bastion automatically ssh -L 15432:prod-db

@file: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf Port 22 # changing the port reduces log noise, not risk; keep 22 unless policy says otherwise PasswordAuthentication no # keys only KbdInteractiveAuthentication no PermitRootLogin no # log in as a user, then sudo PubkeyAuthentication yes AuthenticationMethods publickey # or "publickey,keyboard-interactive" with a PAM MFA module for a second factor MaxAuthTries 3 LoginGraceTime 20 AllowGroups ssh-users # only members of this group may log in X11Forwarding no AllowAgentForwarding no AllowTcpForwarding yes # needed for port forwarding; set no on application servers if unused ClientAliveInterval 300 ClientAliveCountMax 2 LogLevel VERBOSE # logs key fingerprints used: you can tell *which* key logged in # Modern algorithms only (Mozilla modern profile); drop legacy ciphers/MACs/KEX KexAlgorithms sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com,curve25519-sha256 Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-gcm@openssh.com MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh # ALWAYS test the config before reloading; keep your current session open until a new login works Plus: a firewall rule limiting port 22 to known ranges or the bastion (Part II chapter 15); fail2ban or sshguard to ban brute-forcers; unattended security updates for OpenSSH; no SSH at all on servers that do not need it (containers, Fargate).

The simple approach (authorized keys managed by configuration management or cloud-init, one AllowGroups group, keys listed in a repository) works for small teams and single-client deployments if you are disciplined: keys are added and removed by a reviewed change, never by hand on the server; every key has an owner and a comment; a quarterly audit lists keys per server against current staff; offboarding removes keys everywhere the same day. It breaks down as servers and people multiply. Better options: - SSH certificates : a certificate authority (your own ssh-keygen CA, HashiCorp Vault's SSH secrets engine, Teleport, Smallstep) signs short-lived user certificates (hours) after SSO authentication; servers trust the CA ( TrustedUserCAKeys ) instead of individual keys. No authorized keys to manage; offboarding is automatic when SSO access ends; certificates carry principals and can be audited. Host certificates likewise eliminate known hosts prompts. - SSM Session Manager (Part II chapter 16): no SSH daemon exposed, IAM-based, logged. For AWS fleets this is the recommended default; keep sshd for emergencies behind the bastion or disable it entirely. - Identity-aware access tools (Teleport, Boundary, Tailscale SSH): SSO, short-lived credentials, session recording.

journalctl -u ssh shows logins with the key fingerprint at LogLevel VERBOSE , so "who logged in" is answerable even with shared accounts (do not have shared accounts). Ship auth logs off-box. Alert on logins from unexpected sources, root login attempts, and bursts of failures. Session recording (SSM, Teleport, or script /auditd on the host) is needed for regulated environments.

Immutable infrastructure rebuilds servers often, generating new host keys and triggering client warnings. Options: publish host keys via DNS SSHFP records, use host certificates signed by your CA, or pre-seed known host keys from a secure source. Do not train people to ignore the warning by making it routine.

- Password authentication left on; root login allowed. - One shared key pair for the whole team, copied to every laptop and CI. - Private keys on servers "for convenience" (jump host with keys to everything else). - Agent forwarding to shared hosts. - Editing sshd config and restarting without sshd -t ; locked out. - SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0 . - Keys of departed staff still in authorized keys on servers nobody remembers. - Treating a host key change warning as noise. questions Why is ProxyJump preferred over agent forwarding when reaching servers via a bastion? options It is faster Your private key and agent never become usable from the bastion; a compromised bastion cannot borrow your identity Agent forwarding is deprecated It avoids known_hosts answer explain ProxyJump tunnels the connection; authentication to the target still happens from your laptop. What does a 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED' warning mean? options Your key expired The server's host key differs from the one recorded: either the server was rebuilt or the connection is being intercepted; verify before proceeding The server is down DNS changed answer explain Confirm through an independent channel (console, published fingerprint) before updating known_hosts. - Reduce a server's attack surface systematically: packages, services, ports, users, privileges, kernel settings. - Configure sudo, user accounts and groups for accountability and least privilege. - Apply automatic security updates, intrusion prevention and host auditing. - Use benchmarks (CIS) and scanners to verify and to produce evidence for clients. ::: Chapters 2 and 3; Part I chapter 5; Part II chapter 15. :::

A freshly installed server is configured for convenience and compatibility, not security: more packages than needed, services listening on all interfaces, permissive defaults, a user who can do everything. Hardening is the process of removing what is not needed and constraining what remains, so that a vulnerability in one component does not become control of the machine. It is mostly a checklist, best applied by building hardened images and configuring with code rather than by hand on each server.

- Minimise : install only what the service needs; remove compilers, docs, unused daemons from production images. - Least privilege : services run as dedicated users; humans use personal accounts and sudo ; nothing runs as root that does not need to. - Default deny : host firewall, sshd restrictions, mandatory access control where available. - Patch : automatic security updates for the OS; a schedule for kernel reboots. - Observe : auth logs, auditd for sensitive operations, file integrity monitoring where required, logs shipped off-box. - Immutable where possible : rebuild from a hardened image rather than patching in place; treat a compromised host as disposable.

# Linux server hardening baseline (Ubuntu/Debian flavour; adapt for RHEL-family) ## Accounts and privileges - Personal accounts for every human; no shared logins; root login disabled; root password locked. - sudo via group membership with logging; NOPASSWD only for automation accounts with narrowly scoped commands. - Service accounts are system users with nologin shells and no home directories unless required. - Password policy irrelevant where keys/SSO are used; lock password auth for all human accounts (`passwd -l`). - Remove or disable unused default accounts; audit `/etc/passwd` for UID 0 entries other than root. ## SSH - Keys only; root login off; AllowGroups; modern algorithms; fail2ban; firewall limited to bastion/VPN (chapter 3). ## Packages and services - Minimal install; `apt list --installed` reviewed; remove compilers, build tools and unused daemons on production hosts. - `ss -ltnup`: every listening socket is intended, bound to the narrowest interface (127.0.0.1 for local-only services). - Unattended security updates enabled with automatic reboot in a window (or a managed patching process). ## Network - Host firewall default-deny inbound (ufw/nftables), allow only required ports; outbound restricted on sensitive tiers. - IPv6 configured or disabled deliberately, not ignored. - sysctl hardening: ignore ICMP redirects and source routing, enable reverse path filtering, log martians, disable IP forwarding unless a router. ## Filesystem - Separate volume for data and

# Human user, in the ssh-users and sudo groups, key-based only sudo adduser --disabled-password --gecos "Ana Lopez" ana sudo usermod -aG ssh-users,sudo ana sudo install -d -m 700 -o ana -g ana /home/ana/.ssh echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... ana@laptop' | sudo tee /home/ana/.ssh/authorized_keys >/dev/null sudo chmod 600 /home/ana/.ssh/authorized_keys && sudo chown ana:ana /home/ana/.ssh/authorized_keys # Service account sudo useradd --system --home /srv/app --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --no-create-home app # Offboarding: lock, expire, remove keys, kill sessions; keep the UID reserved so file ownership stays attributable sudo usermod -L -e 1 ana && sudo gpasswd -d ana sudo && sudo gpasswd -d ana ssh-users sudo pkill -KILL -u ana Sudo configuration lives in /etc/sudoers.d/ (edit with visudo -f to validate): @file: /etc/sudoers.d/10-ops Defaults logfile=/var/log/sudo.log, log_input, log_output # record commands (and optionally sessions) Defaults timestamp_timeout=5, passwd_tries=3 %sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL # humans: full sudo with password/MFA deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart app, /bin/systemctl reload nginx, /usr/bin/journalctl -u app * The deploy line shows least-privilege automation: the CI user may restart exactly two services and read one log, nothing else, without a password. Avoid NOPASSWD: ALL for anything that is not a tightly controlled automation identity; avoid wildcards that allow argument injection ( /bin/systemctl would allow systemctl start evil ).

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades # /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades: security origin enabled; set # Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true"; Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-Time "03:30"; # Unattended-Upgrade::Mail "ops@client.com"; sudo systemctl status unattended-upgrades Security patches apply daily; kernel updates take effect at the scheduled reboot. Behind a load balancer, stagger reboot times across instances. For RHEL-family, dnf-automatic with apply updates = yes . In managed fleets, AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager schedules and reports patching (Part VII chapter 13). For immutable fleets, rebuild the AMI weekly and roll the Auto Scaling Group instead (chapter 12).

- fail2ban : watches logs and bans IPs after repeated failures (SSH, Nginx auth, custom apps). Reduces noise and slows brute force; not a substitute for keys and firewalls. - auditd : kernel-level audit of system calls and file access by rule. Minimal useful rule set: changes to /etc/passwd , /etc/shadow , /etc/sudoers , /etc/ssh/sshd config , use of sudo , loading kernel modules, and access to your secrets directory. - AIDE / Wazuh / OSSEC : file integrity monitoring: a baseline of file hashes, alerts on change. Mandatory in PCI scope; valuable anywhere a host is long-lived. - GuardDuty and cloud-level detection see credential misuse and network anomalies that host tools miss; use both. - Log shipping : everything above is useless if the attacker can delete local logs; ship to CloudWatch or a logging account in near real time.

AppArmor and SELinux confine processes to profiles regardless of Unix permissions: a confined Nginx cannot read /home even as root. Ubuntu ships AppArmor enforcing with profiles for common daemons; RHEL ships SELinux enforcing with targeted policy. Keep them on; when something is denied, read the audit log and adjust the policy or file contexts rather than disabling the system ( setenforce 0 "to make it work" is how MAC dies). Container runtimes apply default AppArmor/seccomp profiles too (Part VI chapter 7).

The CIS Benchmarks for each distribution enumerate hundreds of settings with rationale; Level 1 is the practical baseline, Level 2 for high-security environments. Scanners (OpenSCAP with the CIS or DISA STIG profiles, Lynis, cloud marketplace scanners, AWS Inspector for CVEs) produce reports you can hand to a client as evidence. Hardened base images (CIS-hardened AMIs, your own Packer-built AMI applying the benchmark via Ansible) make compliance a property of the image rather than per-server effort.

On Fargate or Kubernetes, most host hardening is the platform's job (Fargate) or applies to node images (EKS-optimised or Bottlerocket AMIs, which are minimal and immutable by design). Your hardening moves to the image and the pod specification: non-root, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, seccomp, no privileged containers (Part VI chapter 7 and chapter 13). The principles are identical; the surface shifts.

- Shared accounts; NOPASSWD: ALL for everyone. - Disabling AppArmor/SELinux at the first denial. - Services bound to 0.0.0.0 that only need localhost. - No automatic security updates; kernels years old. - Logs only on the host; wiped by the intruder. - Hardening by hand on each server; drift within weeks. - Compilers and package development tools on production hosts. - World-writable directories under the web root. questions Which sudo rule follows least privilege for a deployment account? options deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart app, /bin/systemctl reload nginx deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl * %sudo ALL=(ALL) ALL answer explain Exact commands, no wildcards; the account can do its job and nothing else. A web server's AppArmor profile denies reading a new config path. The correct action is: options Set AppArmor to complain or disable it Read the audit log and add the path to the profile Run the server as root Move the config to /tmp answer explain MAC only works if it stays enforcing; adjust the policy for legitimate needs. Why ship logs off the host in near real time? options To save disk So an intruder who gains root cannot erase the evidence of how they got in For faster grep Compliance only answer explain Local logs are under the attacker's control after compromise. What is the most sustainable way to keep a fleet hardened? options Weekly manual audits Build hardened images with configuration applied by code and

- Write production-quality systemd unit files: dependencies, restarts, environment, resource limits, sandboxing. - Operate services with systemctl and journalctl, and understand targets, timers and socket activation. - Apply systemd's security hardening options so a compromised service is contained. - Diagnose services that fail to start, restart in loops, or hang on shutdown. ::: Part I chapter 6; chapters 2 and 4 of this part. :::

A process started from a shell dies with the shell. A production service must start at boot in the right order, run as the right user with the right environment, be restarted when it crashes, stop gracefully when asked, have its output captured, and be constrained so that a bug or a compromise cannot take the machine with it. That is process supervision, and on Linux the supervisor is systemd.

@file: /etc/systemd/system/app.service [Unit] Description=Client App API (gunicorn) Documentation=https://wiki.client.com/runbooks/app After=network-online.target postgresql.service Wants=network-online.target StartLimitIntervalSec=300 StartLimitBurst=5 [Service] Type=notify # gunicorn/uvicorn support sd_notify; use 'simple' or 'exec' otherwise User=app Group=app WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/current EnvironmentFile=/etc/app/app.env # KEY=value lines, 640 root:app; no secrets if a secrets manager is used at runtime Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 ExecStartPre=/srv/app/current/.venv/bin/python -m app.preflight # validate config, check migrations applied; fail fast ExecStart=/srv/app/current/.venv/bin/gunicorn app.main:app -c /srv/app/current/gunicorn.conf.py ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID KillSignal=SIGTERM KillMode=mixed # SIGTERM to main, then SIGKILL to the whole group after the timeout TimeoutStopSec=30 # must exceed the app's graceful drain timeout Restart=always RestartSec=2 LimitNOFILE=65536 # Resource limits (cgroups) MemoryMax=1536M MemoryHigh=1280M CPUQuota=200% # two cores TasksMax=4096 # Sandboxing NoNewPrivileges=yes ProtectSystem=strict # whole filesystem read-only except... ReadWritePaths=/srv/app/shared/uploads /var/lib/app ProtectHome=yes PrivateTmp=yes PrivateDevices=yes ProtectKernelTunables=yes ProtectKernelModules=yes ProtectControlGroups=yes RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX RestrictNamespaces=yes LockPersonality=yes MemoryDenyWriteExecute=y

EnvironmentFile is the standard way to pass configuration (Part I chapter 8). For secrets, prefer fetching from a secrets manager at start-up using the instance role; if a file is unavoidable, 640 root:app, and consider LoadCredential= / SetCredentialEncrypted= (systemd's credentials mechanism, which exposes secrets to the service via $CREDENTIALS DIRECTORY without putting them in the environment). Never put secrets in the unit file itself; it is world-readable.

@file: /etc/systemd/system/app-cleanup.service [Unit] Description=Nightly cleanup of expired uploads [Service] Type=oneshot User=app EnvironmentFile=/etc/app/app.env ExecStart=/srv/app/current/.venv/bin/python -m app.jobs.cleanup @file: /etc/systemd/system/app-cleanup.timer [Unit] Description=Run app-cleanup nightly [Timer] OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:15:00 RandomizedDelaySec=600 # spread load across a fleet Persistent=true # run at boot if the last schedule was missed [Install] WantedBy=timers.target Timers give you logging in the journal, dependency ordering, resource limits and sandboxing identical to services, systemctl list-timers to see what runs when, and Persistent catch-up. Cron is fine for simple cases; timers are better for anything important.

Socket activation ( app.socket listening, app.service started on first connection) enables zero-downtime restarts (systemd holds the socket; connections queue while the service restarts) and on-demand start. Template units ( worker@.service , instantiated as worker@1 , worker@2 ) run N copies with %i substitution. Drop-ins ( /etc/systemd/system/app.service.d/override.conf , created with systemctl edit app ) override parts of a vendor unit without copying it.

A typical single-server deployment: postgresql.service , redis-server.service , app.service (After both), app-worker.service (After app), nginx.service (After app, so health checks pass quickly), app-cleanup.timer . Draw the graph; systemd-analyze critical-chain app.service shows it.

- Explain block devices, partitions, filesystems, mounts and LVM, and how cloud volumes map onto them. - Add, grow, mount and persist a data volume on a Linux server safely. - Diagnose "no space left on device" in all its forms, and understand I/O performance metrics. - Choose filesystem and volume types for databases, logs and application data. ::: Part I chapters 3 and 4; chapter 2 of this part. :::

Storage problems are slow-motion outages. A disk fills over weeks and then everything fails at once; a volume is attached but not mounted at boot; a database sits on a volume with too few IOPS; a filesystem runs out of inodes with gigabytes free. The vocabulary (block device, partition, filesystem, mount point) is old and the tools are stable; an hour learning them prevents a class of 3 a.m. incidents.

title From a cloud volume to a file your application writes layers Block device /dev/nvme1n1, EBS volume summary A raw array of blocks presented by the hypervisor. No structure until you add one. On Nitro instances EBS volumes appear as NVMe devices; the device name in the console (/dev/sdf) differs from the OS name (/dev/nvme1n1). Use `lsblk -o NAME,SERIAL` to map by volume ID, and label filesystems so mounts do not depend on device names. Partition table (optional) summary Divides a device into partitions. Data volumes often skip this and format the whole device. Root volumes have partitions (EFI, root). For a dedicated data volume, formatting the raw device is simpler and avoids partition-resizing steps when growing. LVM (optional) physical volume → volume group → logical volume summary Pools devices and carves flexible logical volumes that can be grown, snapshotted and moved. Valuable on physical servers; on cloud VMs, EBS volumes already resize online, so LVM is often unnecessary. Use it when you need to span volumes or snapshot at the OS level. Filesystem ext4, XFS summary Organises blocks into files, directories, permissions and metadata (inodes). ext4 is the safe default; XFS excels with large files and parallel I/O and is the RHEL default. Both grow online; neither shrinks easily (ext4 can, offline; XFS cannot). Choose at creation. Mount point /var/lib/postgresql summary Where the filesystem appears in the directory tree; configured in /etc/fstab for persistence. Mou

# 1. Attach the volume in the console/CLI (e.g. 100 GB gp3) as /dev/sdf; find it in the OS lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,SERIAL # nvme1n1 100G disk vol0abc123... # 2. Format (ONCE; this destroys data) with a label sudo mkfs.ext4 -L appdata /dev/nvme1n1 # or: sudo mkfs.xfs -L appdata /dev/nvme1n1 # 3. Mount point, fstab by label, mount sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/app echo 'LABEL=appdata /var/lib/app ext4 defaults,noatime,nodev,nosuid,nofail,x-systemd.device-timeout=10 0 2' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo mount -a df -h /var/lib/app sudo chown app:app /var/lib/app && sudo chmod 750 /var/lib/app # 4. Grow later: resize the EBS volume in AWS (online), then sudo growpart /dev/nvme0n1 1 # only if partitioned (root volumes) sudo resize2fs /dev/nvme1n1 # ext4, online; XFS: sudo xfs_growfs /var/lib/app Always mount by LABEL= or UUID= (from blkid ), never by device name; NVMe names can change between boots. Always nofail for anything that is not the root filesystem.

Use Filesystem EBS type Notes --- --- --- --- Root / OS ext4 (distro default) gp3 Small (20–50 GB); keep data off it PostgreSQL / MySQL data ext4 or XFS gp3 with provisioned IOPS/throughput, or io2 for heavy loads noatime ; separate volume; size for WAL and growth; snapshots for backup Logs ext4 gp3 Separate volume or at least a quota so logs cannot fill root; rotation Uploads / shared files prefer S3; else EFS for multi-instance — Local disks do not scale across instances Scratch / temp tmpfs (RAM) or instance store — Ephemeral by nature gp3 baseline is 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of size (configurable up to 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s for extra cost); gp2 scales IOPS with size and bursts, which is why small gp2 database volumes mysteriously slow down after sustained load (burst balance exhausted). io2 provides consistent high IOPS with higher cost. Instance store (local NVMe) is extremely fast and vanishes on stop; suitable for caches and scratch, not for data you cannot lose.

Four different problems share one message: 1. Blocks exhausted : df -h shows 100%. Find the consumers: du -xh --max-depth=2 / sort -rh head ; typical: logs, Docker images, old releases, core dumps, journal ( journalctl --disk-usage ), database bloat, temp files. 2. Inodes exhausted : df -i shows 100% with blocks free. Millions of tiny files (sessions on disk, cache files, mail queues). Find with find / -xdev -printf '%h\n' sort uniq -c sort -rn head . Fix the source; ext4 inode count is fixed at format time. 3. Deleted-but-open files : df full, du small. lsof +L1 lists them; restart or signal the holding process (log rotation without reopening is the usual cause; use copytruncate or SIGHUP). 4. Reserved blocks : ext4 reserves 5% for root by default; non-root processes hit "full" at 95%. tune2fs -m 1 reduces the reserve on data volumes. Prevention: data, logs and Docker on their own volumes with alerts at 80% (CloudWatch agent disk used percent ), log rotation and journald limits (chapter 9), image pruning, and a documented growth procedure.

iostat -xz 1 5 # per device: r/s w/s, rkB/s wkB/s, await (ms latency), %util # await > 10 ms on an SSD-backed volume under load = saturated or throttled; %util near 100 = busy iotop -oPa # which processes are doing I/O (install iotop) pidstat -d 1 # per-process I/O rates cat /sys/block/nvme1n1/queue/scheduler Symptoms of storage trouble: high await , high wa CPU, database queries slow with low CPU, EBS VolumeQueueLength and BurstBalance (gp2) metrics in CloudWatch. Fixes in order: cut the I/O (indexes, caching, batching), increase IOPS/throughput on gp3, move to io2, add memory so the page cache absorbs reads.

EBS snapshots are block-level, incremental and taken while the volume is in use; they are crash-consistent (like a power loss), not application-consistent. Databases recover from crash-consistent snapshots via their journal, but for guaranteed consistency: freeze writes ( fsfreeze -f ), snapshot, unfreeze; or use the database's own backup tooling; or use RDS, which handles this. Snapshot data volumes on a schedule (AWS Backup or Data Lifecycle Manager) with retention, and test restores (chapter 11).

Enable EBS encryption by default at the account level (KMS-backed, transparent, no performance penalty worth mentioning). Snapshots of encrypted volumes are encrypted; AMIs too. For on-premises or extra assurance, LUKS encrypts at the OS level with keys from a KMS or TPM; it complicates boot and recovery, so use cloud-native encryption where available.

NFS (and EFS, AWS's managed NFS) lets several instances share a filesystem. Use it for legacy applications that need a shared directory; prefer S3 for new designs. EFS performance modes and throughput modes need matching to the workload; latency per operation is higher than local disk, which hurts applications doing many small file operations. Never put a database on NFS.

- Mounting by device name; volume not mounted after reboot or mounted in the wrong place. - Missing nofail ; boot hangs when a volume is absent. - Everything on the root volume; one log flood takes down the server. - gp2 for databases; burst exhaustion. - No disk usage alerts. - Formatting the wrong device (always check lsblk and the serial). - Treating EBS snapshots as application-consistent database backups. - Logs rotated by renaming while the process keeps the old file open. questions Why mount data volumes by LABEL or UUID rather than by device name? options It is faster Device names like /dev/nvme1n1 can change between boots or attachments, mounting the wrong volume or failing Labels are encrypted fstab requires it answer explain Labels and UUIDs identify the filesystem itself. `df -h` shows the volume 100% full but `du` finds far less data. What should you check? options Inode usage Deleted-but-open files with lsof +L1 Reserved blocks Filesystem corruption answer explain Deleted files held open by a process keep their blocks allocated. A small gp2 database volume performs well at first and degrades under sustained load. Why? options The filesystem fragments gp2 IOPS burst balance is exhausted; baseline IOPS scale with volume size ext4 is slow Snapshots are running answer explain Move to gp3 with provisioned IOPS, or io2. What consistency does an EBS snapshot of a running database volume provide? options Application-consistent Crash-consistent: like a power loss, recove

1. Attach, format, label, mount and persist a data volume on a test instance; reboot and verify. Then grow it online. 2. Fill a small test filesystem with millions of empty files until inodes run out; diagnose with df -i and locate the directory. 3. Set up CloudWatch agent disk metrics with an alarm at 80% and verify the alarm fires by filling a volume with fallocate .

- Inspect and configure a server's interfaces, addresses, routes and DNS settings, and understand how cloud networking supplies them. - Lock down a host with nftables or ufw, default deny, with rules you can read and test. - Reconcile host firewalls with Docker, cloud security groups and IPv6. - Diagnose host-level connectivity problems in minutes. ::: Part II chapters 3, 4, 5 and 15. :::

A server's network configuration is mostly supplied by the cloud (DHCP for addresses, VPC routing, security groups for filtering), which is why engineers rarely look at it until something breaks: a second interface that does not route, DNS pointing at the wrong resolver after a change, IPv6 silently enabled, Docker publishing a port through the firewall. Host-level knowledge is also what you need on client-owned VMs and on-premises servers where there is no VPC doing the work.

ip -br addr # interfaces and addresses, brief ip -br link # link state (UP/DOWN), MACs ip route; ip -6 route # routing tables; "default via" is the gateway ip route get 8.8.8.8 # which interface/gateway a destination uses resolvectl status # DNS servers per interface (systemd-resolved); else cat /etc/resolv.conf ss -ltnup # what is listening, on which address ping -c 3 <gateway>; ping -c 3 1.1.1.1; dig +short example.com # L3, Internet, DNS in order networkctl status # systemd-networkd summary (where used) Cloud specifics: the primary interface gets its private IP from the VPC via DHCP, and DNS points at the VPC resolver ( .2 of the VPC CIDR) through systemd-resolved 's stub ( 127.0.0.53 ) on Ubuntu; the public IP is never visible on the interface (it is NAT at the Internet Gateway); the MTU is 9001 inside a VPC (jumbo frames) but 1500 toward the Internet, handled by path MTU discovery, which breaks if ICMP is blocked.

Ubuntu uses netplan (YAML in /etc/netplan/ , rendering to systemd-networkd or NetworkManager); RHEL-family uses NetworkManager ( nmcli ). On cloud images the primary interface is DHCP and you should leave it alone. Configuration you might actually do: @file: /etc/netplan/60-secondary.yaml (a second ENI with a static route for a private network) network: version: 2 ethernets: ens6: dhcp4: true dhcp4-overrides: { use-routes: false } # do not install a second default route routes: - to: 192.168.50.0/24 via: 10.20.65.1 sudo netplan try # applies with automatic rollback in 120 s if you lose connectivity; then `netplan apply` Multiple interfaces need policy routing so replies leave via the interface they arrived on (asymmetric routing is dropped by reverse-path filtering and by cloud security groups). The amazon-ec2-net-utils package handles this automatically for secondary ENIs on Amazon Linux and Ubuntu AWS images; on other systems you configure ip rule / ip route table entries. DNS: on servers, point at the VPC resolver or your corporate resolvers; set search domains for internal names; avoid hard-coding public resolvers inside a VPC (you lose private hosted zones). resolvectl flush-caches after record changes. Hostnames: hostnamectl set-hostname app-1.prod.client.internal ; keep /etc/hosts resolving the hostname to a local address so tools that resolve the local hostname do not hang.

@file: /etc/sysctl.d/90-network.conf net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0 # 1 only on routers/NAT instances/Docker hosts (Docker sets it) net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1 # drop spoofed/asymmetric packets (set 2 = loose on multi-homed hosts) net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0 net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0 net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0 net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1 net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1 # SYN flood resistance net.core.somaxconn = 4096 # listen backlog ceiling (Part II chapter 5) net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 1024 65535 # more ephemeral ports for busy clients/proxies net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1 net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_time = 300 # detect dead peers sooner (default 7200) net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_intvl = 30 net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_probes = 5 net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6 = 0 # keep IPv6 if the network provides it; disable deliberately (1) if not managed Apply with sudo sysctl --system . Containers inherit the host's network namespace settings for some parameters and have their own for others; Kubernetes exposes safe sysctls per pod.

Cloud security groups filter before packets reach the instance, but a host firewall adds defence in depth, protects against misconfigured groups, documents intent locally, and is the only control on non-cloud servers. nftables is the current Linux framework ( iptables commands are now a compatibility layer over it). @file: /etc/nftables.conf #!/usr/sbin/nft -f flush ruleset define ADMIN_NETS = { 203.0.113.0/29, 10.20.0.0/16 } # office + VPC (bastion lives there) table inet filter { set ratelimit_ssh { type ipv4_addr; flags dynamic, timeout; timeout 10m; } chain input { type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop; ct state invalid drop ct state established,related accept iif "lo" accept # ICMP/ICMPv6 needed for PMTU, neighbour discovery, diagnostics (rate-limited) ip protocol icmp icmp type { echo-request, destination-unreachable, time-exceeded, parameter-problem } limit rate 10/second accept ip6 nexthdr icmpv6 icmpv6 type { echo-request, destination-unreachable, packet-too-big, time-exceeded, parameter-problem, nd-neighbor-solicit, nd-neighbor-advert, nd-router-advert } accept # SSH only from admin networks, with per-source rate limiting tcp dport 22 ip saddr $ADMIN_NETS ct state new add @ratelimit_ssh { ip saddr limit rate 6/minute } accept # Web (if this host terminates TLS itself; otherwise only the app port from the LB subnet) tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept # Application port from the load balancer subnets only tcp dport 8000 ip saddr { 10.20.0.0/20, 10.20.16.0/20,

Docker programs iptables/nftables directly: published ports ( -p 8080:80 ) are DNAT'd in the nat table and accepted in the DOCKER chain before your input rules. ufw does not see them; your nftables input chain is bypassed because the packets are forwarded to the container, not delivered to the host. Options: bind publications to localhost ( -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 ) and front with a proxy; add rules in the DOCKER-USER chain (iptables) which Docker guarantees to evaluate first; set "iptables": false in the daemon config and manage everything yourself (expert mode); or rely on cloud security groups as the authoritative filter and treat the host firewall as secondary on Docker hosts. Document whichever you choose; this surprise has exposed many databases.

If the VPC assigns IPv6 addresses, the host has a globally routable address with no NAT between it and the Internet; only security groups and the host firewall protect it. Either filter IPv6 identically (the inet family table above covers both) or disable IPv6 on hosts that should not have it. Services bound to :: listen on IPv4 too (dual-stack) by default on Linux.

Order: link up ( ip -br link ) → address present ( ip -br addr ) → route exists ( ip route get ) → gateway reachable ( ping ) → DNS ( resolvectl , dig ) → firewall (is the drop logged? nft list ruleset , journalctl -k ) → service listening on the right address ( ss -ltnp ) → security group / NACL (cloud side) → remote end. For "works from the host, not from outside": bind address, host firewall, Docker forwarding, security group, in that order. Part II chapter 19 has the full toolkit.

- Two default routes after adding an ENI; traffic leaves the wrong interface and is dropped. - Hard-coded public DNS inside a VPC; private zones stop resolving. - IPv6 enabled with no filtering. - Host firewall bypassed by Docker-published ports. - Applying firewall rules without a connectivity test, locking out SSH. - Blocking all ICMP, breaking path MTU discovery; large transfers hang. - rp filter=1 on multi-homed hosts without policy routing, dropping legitimate replies. - Forgetting to persist nftables at boot. questions What does `netplan try` give you that `netplan apply` does not? options Faster application Automatic rollback if you do not confirm within a timeout, protecting against lockout IPv6 support Validation of DNS answer explain Always use a rollback mechanism when changing network config remotely. Why must ICMP 'packet too big' / 'destination unreachable' be allowed through a host firewall? options For ping Path MTU discovery depends on them; blocking them causes connections to open but hang on larger transfers They carry DNS They are required for TCP handshakes answer explain Allow diagnostic and control ICMP types with rate limits; block nothing you do not understand. A port published by Docker is reachable from the Internet despite an nftables input policy of drop. Why? options nftables is broken Docker DNATs and forwards the traffic, so it never traverses the host's input chain; use DOCKER-USER rules, localhost binds or security groups The port is below 10

1. Apply the nftables ruleset on a test VM (adjusting networks) from a session you keep open; verify SSH from an allowed and a disallowed source, and find the drop in the kernel log. 2. Publish a container port with Docker and demonstrate it bypasses the input chain; fix with a DOCKER-USER rule or a localhost bind. 3. Attach a secondary ENI to a test instance, observe the routing table, and configure it so that only the intended traffic uses it.

t: TLS Certificates and Reverse Proxy Configuration
x: Part II explained TLS and reverse proxies conceptually. On a server you have to make it real: a certificate that renews itself, a proxy that terminates TLS with a modern configuration, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, forwards to the application with the right headers, serves static files, and keeps working at 3 a.m. when the certificate would otherwise have expired. This chapter is the hands-on configuration for the two common choices.

t: TLS Certificates and Reverse Proxy Configuration
x: Caddy obtains certificates from Let's Encrypt (or ZeroSSL) via ACME, renews them, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, enables HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and applies a modern TLS configuration, all by default. For a single server or small deployment it removes the most common operational failure (expired certificates) entirely. # Install (Debian/Ubuntu, official repo) sudo apt install -y debian-keyring debian-archive-keyring apt-transport-https curl curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/gpg.key' | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/caddy-stable-archive-keyring.gpg curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/debian.deb.txt' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/caddy-stable.list sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y caddy @file: /etc/caddyfile (/etc/caddy/Caddyfile) { email ops@client.com # ACME account contact (expiry notices if renewal fails) # acme_dns route53 # for wildcard/internal certs via DNS-01 (needs the DNS plugin build and IAM permissions) } api.client.com { encode zstd gzip header { Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains" X-Content-Type-Options nosniff Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin -Server } request_body { max_size 10MB } log { output file /var/log/caddy/api.access.log { roll_size 100mb roll_keep 10 } format json } handle_path /static/* { root * /srv/app/current/static file_server header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" } handle { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8000 { header_up X-Request-ID {ht

t: TLS Certificates and Reverse Proxy Configuration
x: If an ALB terminates TLS in front of these hosts, the host proxy serves plain HTTP on the application port to the ALB (or HTTPS with a self-signed or private certificate for re-encryption), does not redirect (the ALB does), passes through the ALB's X-Forwarded- headers instead of overwriting them, and the certificate lives in ACM, not on the host. The host proxy remains useful for static files, buffering and local health checks; some teams drop it and let the ALB talk to the application directly.

t: TLS Certificates and Reverse Proxy Configuration
x: Name-based virtual hosts: one server block (Nginx) or site block (Caddy) per hostname, each with its own certificate (SNI selects it), each proxying to a different local port. Caddy handles the certificates for all of them automatically; certbot issues one certificate per hostname or a SAN certificate covering several ( -d a.client.com -d b.client.com ).

x: - Maintenance page : the error page 502 503 504 block above serves a static page with Retry-After when the app is down or deploying; Caddy equivalent via handle errors . - Large uploads : raise client max body size / max size deliberately per location, not globally. - WebSockets and SSE : Part II chapter 12 settings; Caddy handles upgrades automatically. - Rate limiting : limit req zones (Nginx) or the rate limit module (Caddy) per route for login and expensive endpoints. - Log rotation : logrotate for Nginx (default config rotates daily, postrotate reloads), Caddy rolls its own. - Certificate for an internal-only host : DNS-01 with a public domain ( internal.client.com ), or a private CA (Part II chapter 10); do not disable verification in clients. - Renewal failing : common causes are port 80 closed after a security group change, DNS credentials rotated, or the domain's A record moved. - Know where every kind of log lives on a Linux server and how to read it quickly under pressure. - Configure journald persistence and limits, log rotation, and shipping to a central store. - Emit application logs that are structured, bounded and free of secrets. - Correlate proxy, application and system logs during an incident. ::: Part I chapter 4; chapter 5 of this part; Part XI chapter 1 covers log design across services. :::

When something breaks, logs are the primary evidence, and they are useless if you cannot find them, if they were rotated away, if the disk they filled took the server down, or if the intruder deleted them. Logging on a server is a small set of decisions: where logs go, how long they stay, how they leave the machine, and what they contain.

Source Location Read with --- --- --- systemd services (stdout/stderr) and kernel the journal ( /var/log/journal if persistent, else /run/log/journal ) journalctl Traditional syslog consumers /var/log/syslog (Debian/Ubuntu), /var/log/messages (RHEL) via rsyslog tail , less , grep Authentication journal ( SYSTEMD UNIT=ssh.service , sudo ) and /var/log/auth.log / /var/log/secure journalctl -u ssh , last , lastb Nginx / Caddy /var/log/nginx/ .log , /var/log/caddy/ .log tail -f , jq PostgreSQL /var/log/postgresql/ or the journal tail , pgBadger Package manager /var/log/apt/history.log , /var/log/dpkg.log , /var/log/dnf.log what changed and when cloud-init /var/log/cloud-init.log , /var/log/cloud-init-output.log first-boot problems Kernel ring buffer dmesg (also in the journal) OOM kills, disk errors, firewall drops Audit /var/log/audit/audit.log ausearch , aureport

journalctl -u app -f # follow one service journalctl -u app -n 200 --no-pager # last 200 lines journalctl -u app --since "2026-03-14 09:00" --until "09:30" journalctl -u app -p err # priority err and worse (emerg..debug) journalctl -b # this boot; -b -1 previous boot journalctl -k # kernel messages (OOM: journalctl -k | grep -i 'killed process') journalctl _PID=12345 # by PID; _UID=1001 by user journalctl -o json-pretty -u app -n 1 # every field journald stores journalctl -u app -o cat # message only (handy for JSON logs → pipe to jq) journalctl --disk-usage; sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=1G journalctl -g 'request_id=7f3a' # grep across everything Make the journal persistent (survive reboots) and bounded : @file: /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/10-server.conf [Journal] Storage=persistent Compress=yes SystemMaxUse=2G SystemKeepFree=1G MaxRetentionSec=1month RateLimitIntervalSec=30s RateLimitBurst=20000 # a chatty app should not be silently dropped; raise and alert instead ForwardToSyslog=no # unless rsyslog is your shipper sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal && sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal && sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald

logrotate runs daily ( /etc/logrotate.d/ ): @file: /etc/logrotate.d/app /var/log/app/*.log { daily rotate 14 missingok notifempty compress delaycompress dateext create 0640 app app sharedscripts postrotate systemctl kill -s HUP app.service >/dev/null 2>&1 || true # app reopens log files on SIGHUP endscript } The postrotate step matters: a process that keeps the old file open after rotation fills the disk invisibly (Part I chapter 3). Prefer logging to stdout under systemd (the journal handles rotation) or to a shipper; file logs are for software that insists.

Local logs are vulnerable (disk full, instance terminated, attacker with root) and hard to search across a fleet. Ship them: - CloudWatch agent (AWS): tails files and/or the journal (via the collectd / journald input in recent versions, or rsyslog → file → agent) to CloudWatch Logs groups with retention; also collects memory and disk metrics (chapter 10). Configuration from SSM Parameter Store for fleets. - Vector, Fluent Bit, Promtail/Alloy, Filebeat : lightweight shippers to any backend (OpenSearch, Loki, Elastic, S3, Datadog). Vector and Fluent Bit parse JSON, add host metadata, redact fields and buffer to disk when the backend is down. - rsyslog over TLS to a central syslog server: traditional, still fine. @file: /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json (excerpt) { "logs": { "logs_collected": { "files": { "collect_list": [ { "file_path": "/var/log/nginx/api.access.log", "log_group_name": "/client/prod/nginx/access", "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}", "retention_in_days": 30 }, { "file_path": "/var/log/app/app.log", "log_group_name": "/client/prod/app", "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}", "retention_in_days": 90, "timestamp_format": "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" } ] } } } } Set retention on every group (CloudWatch Logs defaults to never expire, which is both a cost and a privacy problem); longer retention belongs in S3 with lifecycle policies. For audit logs, the tamper-evidence rules of Part IV chapter 22 apply: a separate group or account, restricted acce

- To stdout/stderr , one JSON object per line, with timestamp (UTC ISO 8601), level , message , logger , request id , user id / tenant id where relevant, route , status , duration ms , error.type , error.stack for errors. Part XI chapter 1 defines the schema; keep it consistent across services. - Bounded : no request/response bodies by default; truncate long fields; sample noisy debug logs. - No secrets or PII : redaction at the logger (Part IV chapters 22–23); never log Authorization , Cookie , passwords, tokens, card numbers. - Levels used honestly : ERROR means someone should look; WARNING means degraded but handled; INFO for lifecycle and request summaries; DEBUG off in production. - Request ID in every line and in the proxy's access log, so one ID joins proxy, app and worker records.

A method for "the API is returning errors": # 1. Proxy: which requests fail, since when, how many sudo tail -n 5000 /var/log/nginx/api.access.log | jq -r 'select(.status >= 500) | [.time, .status, .uri, .request_id, .urt] | @tsv' | tail -20 sudo tail -n 20000 /var/log/nginx/api.access.log | jq -r 'select(.status >= 500) | .time[0:16]' | sort | uniq -c # per-minute histogram # 2. Proxy error log: upstream refused? timed out? sudo tail -n 100 /var/log/nginx/api.error.log # 3. Application: follow the request ID journalctl -u app -o cat --since "-30min" | grep 7f3a9c2e | jq . # 4. System: anything killed or failing? journalctl -k --since "-30min" | grep -iE 'oom|killed|error'; systemctl --failed # 5. Dependencies: database and cache logs journalctl -u postgresql --since "-30min" -p warning Correlation by time and by request ID is the whole skill. Clocks must be synchronised and in UTC, or the time correlation lies.

- Journal volatile (lost on reboot) and unbounded, or file logs filling the root volume. - Logs only on the host; gone with the instance, or with the intruder. - CloudWatch groups with infinite retention. - Logging request bodies with PII and tokens. - Different timestamp formats and time zones across services. - Rotation without reopening; deleted-but-open files. - DEBUG in production flooding the journal and hitting rate limits silently. - No request ID in the access log; proxy and app logs cannot be joined. questions Why make the journal persistent on a server? options Faster queries So logs survive reboots, including the evidence of why the server went down It is required by systemd To enable rotation answer explain Volatile journals vanish exactly when you need them: after a crash and reboot. A log file is rotated by renaming it, but the application keeps writing to the old inode. What is the consequence? options Nothing The disk fills with a file not visible via du; the app must reopen logs on rotation (SIGHUP/copytruncate) Logs are duplicated The app crashes answer explain Deleted-but-open files are a classic disk-full cause. What makes it possible to follow one user request through the proxy, the API and a worker? options Timestamps alone A request/correlation ID generated at the edge and logged by every component Process IDs The user agent answer explain Timestamps narrow; IDs join. Why set retention on every CloudWatch Logs group? options Performance Default retenti

1. Make the journal persistent and bounded; reboot; confirm the previous boot's logs are available with journalctl -b -1 . 2. Configure the CloudWatch agent (or Vector) to ship Nginx and application logs with 30-day retention; find a request by ID in the central store. 3. Produce a per-minute error histogram from your access logs with jq ; then find the first failing request's ID and trace it through the application log.

- Read CPU, memory, disk, network and process metrics on a live server and tell saturation from noise. - Use the standard tools (top/htop, vmstat, iostat, free, df, ss, sar) and the USE method to find the bottleneck. - Export host metrics to a central system (CloudWatch agent, node exporter) and set the alarms that matter. - Avoid the misreadings that send engineers chasing the wrong resource. ::: Part I chapters 3 and 7; chapter 6 of this part. :::

"The server is slow" has four or five possible meanings, and the fix for each is different: more CPU, more memory, faster disk, a network limit, or a misbehaving process. Resource monitoring is how you decide in minutes rather than by trial. It also feeds capacity planning: knowing that a server runs at 70% CPU at peak tells you when to scale before users tell you.

For every resource, check three things: Utilisation (how busy), Saturation (how much work is queued), Errors . Saturation is the one people skip and the one that explains latency: a CPU at 80% utilisation with a run queue of 1 is fine; at 80% with a run queue of 12 it is saturated. Resource Utilisation Saturation Errors --- --- --- --- CPU top %us/%sy; vmstat us/sy run queue r in vmstat cores; load average vs cores; %steal dmesg MCE (rare) Memory free available; RSS per process swapping ( si / so ), page reclaim, OOM kills ( dmesg ) OOM kills Disk iostat -x %util await latency, queue depth ( aqu-sz ); CloudWatch VolumeQueueLength I/O errors in dmesg , SMART Network bandwidth vs instance allowance; sar -n DEV drops, retransmits ( nstat ), bw in/out allowance exceeded ENA metrics interface errors ( ip -s link ) File descriptors / sockets count vs limit accept queue overflow EMFILE in app logs

h: The tools, in the order to use them
x: uptime # load averages: compare with core count (nproc) top -bn1 | head -20 # or htop: who uses CPU/memory right now; press 1 (per core), M (sort by mem), P (by CPU) vmstat 1 5 # r (runnable), b (blocked), si/so (swap), us/sy/id/wa/st free -h # available is the number that matters iostat -xz 1 3 # per-disk r/s w/s, await, %util df -h; df -i # space and inodes ss -s; ss -ltnp # socket summary; listeners ip -s link # interface errors/drops sar -u 1 5; sar -r; sar -n DEV 1 5; sar -q # sysstat history (enable the collector for retrospective views) pidstat -u -r -d 1 5 # per-process CPU, memory, disk ps -eo pid,ppid,user,%cpu,%mem,rss,nlwp,stat,etime,cmd --sort=-%mem | head sudo nstat -az | grep -E 'TcpRetransSegs|TcpExtListenOverflows|TcpExtTCPTimeouts' cat /proc/pressure/cpu /proc/pressure/memory /proc/pressure/io # PSI: % of time tasks stalled on each resource (kernel ≥ 4.20) Pressure Stall Information (PSI) deserves a mention: /proc/pressure/ reports the fraction of time some or all tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O. It is the cleanest single saturation signal and is exposed by node exporter and the CloudWatch agent.

Load average counts runnable plus (on Linux) uninterruptible-I/O-waiting tasks. Load 8 on 2 cores with CPU idle 60% means I/O wait, not CPU. Load 8 on 2 cores with idle 0% means CPU saturation. Load 1 on 2 cores is calm. CPU breakdown : us (your code), sy (kernel: networking, I/O, context switches), wa (waiting on I/O), st (stolen by the hypervisor: burstable throttling or noisy neighbour), si/hi (interrupts: heavy network). High sy with moderate us often means too many small syscalls or too many connections; high st means move instance type. Memory : used includes cache; available is what processes can get. Swap in/out non-zero means the box is memory-constrained now . A process whose RSS climbs steadily is leaking (Part I chapter 7). OOM kills appear in dmesg with the victim's name. Disk : await is the latency per I/O in ms; on SSD/EBS, more than a few ms under load means saturation or throttling. %util near 100 on a device that can serve many parallel I/Os is less alarming than high await . Check EBS CloudWatch BurstBalance (gp2), VolumeQueueLength , and whether you are hitting the volume's or the instance's throughput cap. Network : EC2 instances have bandwidth allowances; exceeding them shows as ENA bw out allowance exceeded , pps allowance exceeded , conntrack allowance exceeded counters (visible via ethtool -S ). Retransmits indicate loss; ListenOverflows indicate the app is not accepting fast enough.

Host-level dashboards and alarms need metrics in a central system: - CloudWatch agent : collects memory, disk, swap, process and custom metrics (EC2 default metrics have no memory or disk usage) to CloudWatch; configuration in SSM Parameter Store for fleets; alarms via CloudWatch (chapter: Part VII chapter 13). - node exporter (Prometheus): exposes hundreds of host metrics on :9100 for a Prometheus server or Grafana Agent/Alloy to scrape; the standard outside AWS-native stacks (Part XI chapter 3). - Collect per-service metrics too: Nginx stub status /exporter, PostgreSQL exporter, application metrics. Alarms that earn their keep on a host: disk used 80% (per volume), memory available 85% for 15 minutes (or PSI cpu some 20%), load average 2× cores for 10 minutes, CPU credit balance low (burstable), status check failed (EC2), and systemctl --failed non-empty (a simple timer that publishes a metric). Everything else is a dashboard, not a page.

- "CPU is at 30%, so the server is not the problem": the server can be I/O- or memory-bound with idle CPUs. - "Memory is 95% used": cache; look at available . - "Load average is 4": meaningless without the core count and the CPU/wa breakdown. - "The disk is 100% utilised": SSDs serve parallel I/O; await is the latency signal. - "Network is fine, bandwidth is low": packets-per-second and connection-tracking limits bite before bandwidth. - Looking at a 5-minute CloudWatch average and missing 30-second spikes; use 1-minute (or high-resolution) metrics and percentiles for latency.

- Monitoring CPU only; no memory or disk metrics (EC2 defaults do not include them). - No alarms on disk space until it is full. - Alarms on averages for latency. - No historical data ( sar not enabled; no central metrics) to compare "now" with "normal". - Burstable instances without credit alarms. - Treating top as the only tool. questions Load average is 6 on a 2-core server; CPU idle is 60% and `wa` is 35%. What does PSI (/proc/pressure) report? options Power usage The fraction of time tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O Process count Temperature answer explain A direct saturation signal per resource. Which metrics are NOT collected by default for EC2 without an agent? options CPUUtilization NetworkIn/Out Memory and disk usage StatusCheckFailed answer explain Install the CloudWatch agent or node_exporter for memory and disk.

- Design a backup strategy from recovery objectives (RPO, RTO) rather than from tooling. - Back up databases, volumes, object storage and configuration correctly, with encryption, off-site copies and retention. - Prove recoverability with regular, timed restore tests. - Write a disaster recovery plan proportionate to the client's needs. ::: Chapter 6; Part VIII chapter 9 covers database-specific mechanics in depth. :::

Everyone has backups until they need them. Then the dump was of the wrong database, the snapshot was never automated, the encryption key is gone, the restore takes nineteen hours, or the backups were on the same volume that failed. A backup is not a thing you have; it is a restore you have rehearsed . Everything in this chapter follows from that sentence.

- RPO (recovery point objective): how much data loss is acceptable, as time. "We can lose at most 15 minutes of orders." Determines backup frequency and whether you need continuous (WAL/PITR) protection. - RTO (recovery time objective): how long the system may be down. "Back within 4 hours." Determines automation, warm standbys, and how many people must be reachable. - Retention : how far back you must be able to go (a corruption discovered after three weeks needs a three-week-old copy; regulations may require years). - Scope : what must be recoverable: databases, uploaded files, configuration and secrets, infrastructure definitions, DNS, certificates, code and build artifacts, encryption keys, documentation. Agree these with the client in writing. They drive cost: RPO of 5 minutes with RTO of 1 hour costs far more than nightly backups with a next-day restore. value (The calculator above shows how much downtime an availability target allows; RTO must fit inside it with room for the incidents you did not plan.)

Three copies of the data, on two different media or systems, one off-site (different region or account), plus: one offline or immutable (ransomware deletes online backups it can reach) and zero errors on restore test . In AWS terms: the live database; automated snapshots in the same region; copies replicated to another region in a separate backup account with Object Lock or AWS Backup Vault Lock so even a compromised primary account cannot delete them.

Untested backups are hope, not strategy. Schedule and automate: - Monthly (at least): restore the latest database snapshot to a fresh instance, run integrity checks (row counts, checksums, application smoke tests), record the elapsed time against RTO, destroy the instance. Automate with a pipeline or Lambda so it actually happens. - Quarterly : a full environment rebuild in a separate account or region from IaC plus backups: infrastructure, secrets, data, DNS cutover to a test name. Time it. This is the DR drill. - After any change to backup configuration, encryption keys or infrastructure code. - Measure : last successful restore test date, duration, data verified. Alert if a test is overdue or fails. Report to the client. # Example: automated RDS restore test (shell, run by a scheduled job) SNAP=$(aws rds describe-db-snapshots --db-instance-identifier prod-db --snapshot-type automated \ --query 'reverse(sort_by(DBSnapshots,&SnapshotCreateTime))[0].DBSnapshotIdentifier' --output text) aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier restore-test-$(date +%Y%m%d) \ --db-snapshot-identifier "$SNAP" --db-instance-class db.t4g.medium --db-subnet-group-name private-db \ --vpc-security-group-ids sg-restoretest --no-publicly-accessible --tags Key=purpose,Value=restore-test aws rds wait db-instance-available --db-instance-identifier restore-test-$(date +%Y%m%d) # run verification queries against the restored endpoint, record timings and counts, then: aws rds dele

title DR strategies, from cheapest to most resilient columns Strategy Relative cost Backup and restore Backups copied to another region/account; rebuild from IaC on demand Hours (or minutes with PITR replication) Hours to a day Lowest Most small client systems; non-critical workloads Pilot light Core data replicated continuously (RDS cross-region read replica, S3 replication); compute defined but off Minutes Tens of minutes to a couple of hours Low–moderate Business-important systems with a tolerance for an hour of downtime Warm standby Scaled-down full copy running in the second region; scale up and cut over Seconds to minutes Minutes Moderate–high Revenue-critical systems Multi-site active-active Both regions serve traffic; data replicated bidirectionally or partitioned Near zero Near zero Highest; significant complexity (Part IX chapter 10) Global, highly available systems with teams to run them Choose by objectives and budget; write the choice into the DR plan with its RPO/RTO and the drills that prove it. Most client systems are honestly served by backup-and-restore with PITR and a quarterly rebuild drill, upgraded to pilot light where the business case exists.

One page the on-call engineer can follow at 4 a.m.: 1. Scenarios covered : AZ failure, region failure, data corruption or deletion (including malicious), account compromise, loss of a key person. 2. Decision authority : who declares a disaster and authorises failover (and the cost it incurs). 3. Contacts : client, provider support, DNS registrar, on-call rota. 4. Procedures per scenario : numbered steps with commands, expected durations, verification checks and rollback. 5. Dependencies : what must exist beforehand (backup account access, break-glass credentials in a sealed location, IaC pipeline that can target the DR region). 6. Communication templates : internal, client, end users. 7. Drill log : dates, outcomes, time to recover, action items.

Assume an attacker with your production credentials will try to destroy backups. Defences: backups in a separate account with no cross-account delete permission from production; Object Lock / Vault Lock (immutable for the retention period); MFA delete on critical buckets; retention long enough to recover from a slow-burn compromise (30–90 days); alerts on backup deletion attempts and on backup job failures; and the restore drill that confirms the immutable copies are actually restorable.

- Backups never restored; discovered unusable during the incident. - Backups in the same account/region as production, deletable by the same credentials. - Database backups as volume snapshots only, without consistency or PITR. - Encryption key deleted or inaccessible; backups unreadable. - RPO and RTO never agreed; expectations discovered during the outage. - Runbook stored on the system that failed. - Backup jobs failing silently for weeks (no alert on failure or on age of last success). - Retention too short to cover late-discovered corruption. questions What is the only way to know that a backup works? options Checking that the backup job succeeded Restoring it and verifying the data, on a schedule Checking the file size Encrypting it answer explain A backup is a rehearsed restore. A business says it can lose at most 10 minutes of data and must be back within 2 hours. These are: options RTO 10 min, RPO 2 h RPO 10 min, RTO 2 h SLA and SLO MTTR and MTBF answer explain RPO is data loss in time; RTO is downtime. Why keep backup copies in a separate AWS account with Object Lock? options Cheaper storage So that compromised production credentials or ransomware cannot delete or encrypt the backups Faster restores Compliance only answer explain Backups reachable by production credentials are not safe from production compromise. Which DR strategy fits most small client systems with a few hours of tolerable downtime? options Active-active multi-region Warm standby Backup and restore

1. Write down RPO, RTO and retention for a system you operate; compare with what the current backups actually provide. Fix the biggest gap. 2. Automate a monthly restore test of your database with verification queries and timing; run it now and record the result. 3. Draft the one-page DR plan and run a tabletop drill: walk through the region-loss scenario step by step with a colleague and note every missing prerequisite.

- Establish a patching cadence for operating systems, runtimes and services that balances security against stability. - Apply updates with zero or minimal downtime using load balancers, rolling restarts and immutable images. - Run the recurring maintenance that keeps servers healthy: cleanup, rotation, certificate checks, capacity reviews. - Track and report compliance so clients can see the system is maintained. ::: Chapters 2, 4 and 5. :::

Unpatched systems are the most common root cause in breach reports after credentials and misconfiguration, because patching is nobody's favourite task: it risks breaking things, requires reboots, and produces no visible feature. Yet a server that is not maintained decays into a liability within months. The solution is to make maintenance routine, automated and boring, with a clear owner, and to design deployments so that patching does not require downtime.

- Kernel and OS packages : security updates daily (automated), full updates on a schedule; kernel updates need a reboot (or kernel live patching: Canonical Livepatch, kpatch, which defer reboots for critical fixes). - Runtimes (Python, Node, JVM, Go toolchain): follow their security releases; pinned in images (Part I chapter 9). - Application dependencies : Part IV chapter 20. - Infrastructure software : Nginx, Caddy, PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker, agents (CloudWatch, SSM, node exporter). - Base container images : rebuild on upstream updates. - Managed services : RDS minor versions (enable auto minor upgrade in a maintenance window), EKS versions (quarterly cadence imposed by Kubernetes releases), Lambda runtimes (deprecation schedule). - Firmware/hypervisor : the cloud provider's job (shared responsibility).

Severity Timeline Mechanism --- --- --- Critical, actively exploited (CISA KEV, vendor emergency) 24–72 hours, including reboot Emergency change; coordinate with client High security Within 7 days Automated daily security updates; scheduled reboot Other security Within 30 days Monthly maintenance window / image rebuild Non-security updates Monthly or quarterly Image rebuild and roll Major versions (OS LTS, PostgreSQL major, Kubernetes) Planned, 1–2 per year Project with testing in staging Choose a monthly maintenance window agreed with the client (e.g., second Tuesday 02:00–04:00 local, or whenever traffic is lowest), publish it, and use it for anything requiring a restart. Security-only updates apply automatically outside the window with reboots deferred to the window unless critical.

Behind a load balancer with N ≥ 2 instances : for each instance, deregister (or let the health check fail deliberately), wait for connection draining, patch and reboot, verify (health check passes, smoke test), re-register, proceed to the next. Capacity during the roll is N−1; schedule off-peak or add a temporary instance. Automate: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager with maintenance windows, or a script driving the target group API, or let the Auto Scaling Group do an instance refresh with a new AMI. Immutable infrastructure : never patch in place. Build a new AMI (Packer: base image + hardening + agents + runtime), test it in staging, then roll it through the Auto Scaling Group ( start-instance-refresh with a minimum healthy percentage). Old instances are terminated; drift is impossible; rollback is pointing the launch template at the previous AMI. This is the recommended model for fleets, and container platforms (Fargate, EKS managed node groups with Bottlerocket) give it to you for free. Single instance : downtime is unavoidable for kernel reboots; use the maintenance window, a maintenance page from the proxy (chapter 8), and keep it short by pre-downloading updates. Consider whether the single instance is acceptable at all for this client (Part IX chapter 2). Databases : RDS applies minor versions with a brief failover (Multi-AZ) in the maintenance window; self-managed PostgreSQL minor versions are a restart; major versions are a migration project with pg upgrade or logic

Chapter 4 configured unattended-upgrades . Check it works: sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug 2>&1 | tail -20 cat /var/log/unattended-upgrades/unattended-upgrades.log | tail cat /var/run/reboot-required 2>/dev/null && cat /var/run/reboot-required.pkgs # Debian/Ubuntu: pending reboot sudo needs-restarting -r # RHEL: reboot needed? sudo needs-restarting # services using updated libraries (restart them) A reboot-required flag that persists for weeks is a finding. Publish it as a metric (a small timer writing to CloudWatch) and alert when it exceeds your SLA.

AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager scans instances against a patch baseline (which severities, approval delays), reports compliance per instance, and installs patches during maintenance windows with reboot options; it works for Linux and Windows on EC2 and on-premises servers registered as managed instances. Combine with State Manager to enforce agent versions and configuration, and Inventory to know what is installed. Compliance reports become client-facing evidence. Part VII chapter 13.

# Monthly server maintenance - Apply pending updates; reboot if required; verify services and health checks after. - Review disk usage and growth trend; prune old releases, images, logs; confirm log rotation works. - Verify backups ran and the last restore test passed (chapter 11). - Check certificate expiry dates and renewal logs (chapter 8). - Review `systemctl --failed`, failed timers, and `journalctl -p err` for recurring errors. - Review user accounts and SSH keys against current staff; remove leavers (chapters 3–4). - Review security group and firewall rules for drift from infrastructure code. - Check monitoring agents are running and reporting; alarms not in INSUFFICIENT_DATA. - Review resource utilisation trends for capacity planning (chapter 10); right-size or plan scaling. - Rebuild the base image with current packages; roll it through the fleet. - Record what was done, by whom, and anomalies found; update runbooks. Automate what can be automated (cleanup timers, agent health metrics, compliance scans) and keep the human review short and scheduled.

Even routine maintenance is a production change: announce the window, have a rollback (previous AMI, snapshot before patching single instances), verify afterwards (smoke tests, error rates for 30 minutes), and record it (Part XII chapter 8). Emergency patches follow an expedited path with the same verification and recording.

Clients and auditors want evidence: patch compliance percentage over time, mean time from vendor release to deployment for critical fixes, list of pending updates and why (exceptions with owners and dates), reboot-required age, and the maintenance log. A monthly one-page report with these numbers builds trust and catches decay.

- Automatic updates never verified; the service silently broke months ago. - Reboots deferred indefinitely; a two-year-old kernel with a patched userland. - Patching in place on a fleet until every server is different. - No maintenance window agreed; every reboot is an argument. - Major upgrades attempted without staging rehearsal or rollback. - Agents (monitoring, SSM) never updated; eventually unsupported and silent. - Nobody owns maintenance after handover (Part XIII chapter 12). questions What is the most reliable way to keep a fleet of servers patched and consistent? options SSH into each and run apt upgrade Rebuild a hardened image regularly and roll it through the Auto Scaling Group Patch one server and clone it manually Rely on the cloud provider answer explain Immutable images eliminate drift and make rollback trivial. A server shows /var/run/reboot-required for six weeks. What does this indicate? options Nothing; the flag is informational Security updates (likely kernel) are installed but not active; the system remains vulnerable until rebooted The server needs more memory A failed update answer explain Track reboot-required age as a metric and act within the agreed window. Which timeline fits a critical, actively exploited vulnerability in a public-facing component? options Next quarterly window Next monthly window 24–72 hours via an emergency change, with verification and a record When convenient answer explain Exploited vulnerabilities need emergency handling wit

- Apply a repeatable diagnostic method to any server problem, from symptom to root cause, without guessing. - Recognise the incidents every operator eventually meets and resolve them from a mental catalogue. - Preserve evidence and communicate while troubleshooting. - Turn each incident into a prevention measure. ::: All previous chapters in this part; Part II chapter 19. :::

Under pressure, engineers reach for the first plausible action: restart the service, reboot the server, scale up. Sometimes it works and the cause is never learned, so it returns. A method replaces guessing with a sequence that finds the cause quickly and leaves evidence. The common incidents below are the ones that method keeps finding; knowing them in advance halves the time to recognise them.
