Each entry: how it presents, how to confirm, how to fix, how to prevent. Several appeared as full scenarios in earlier chapters; they are listed here so the catalogue is complete.

Presents as: writes failing everywhere at once (database errors, log errors, "no space left on device", services failing to start), often preceded by nothing. Confirm: df -h , df -i . Fix: find the consumer ( du , docker system df , journalctl --disk-usage , lsof +L1 for deleted-open files), remove or move; for databases, free space before anything else or risk corruption. Prevent: separate volumes, 80% alerts, rotation, pruning timers (chapters 6, 9; Part I chapter 4 scenario).

Presents as: processes disappearing, exit code 137, Killed process in dmesg , swap thrashing with everything slow. Confirm: dmesg -T grep -i oom , free , per-process RSS. Fix: restart the offender to recover; cap it (systemd MemoryMax , container limits); add memory if legitimately needed. Prevent: memory alarms, limits, leak detection (Part I chapter 7).

h: CPU saturation and burst credit exhaustion
x: Presents as: everything slow, load average high, %st high on burstable instances. Confirm: top , vmstat , CloudWatch CPUCreditBalance . Fix: find the hot process ( top , pidstat ), kill runaway jobs, scale up or out, change instance family. Prevent: credit alarms, non-burstable types for sustained load, autoscaling (chapters 1, 10).

Presents as: 502/503 at the proxy, systemctl status showing failed or activating (auto-restart) . Confirm: journalctl -u svc -n 100 . Causes: bad config (validation failure), missing dependency (database not reachable), port in use, permission denied, missing file after deploy, out of file descriptors. Fix per cause; reset-failed after start-limit. Prevent: preflight checks, config validation, alerts on --failed (chapter 5 scenario).

Presents as: all HTTPS clients failing at once, often at a round hour; browsers show certificate errors; API clients fail TLS. Confirm: openssl s client ... openssl x509 -noout -dates . Fix: renew now (Caddy restart, certbot renew --force-renewal or DNS-01 fallback) and reload the proxy. Prevent: automated renewal with hooks, external expiry monitoring (chapter 8; Part II chapter 10 scenario).

Presents as: "cannot reach" from some users or all, with servers healthy; NXDOMAIN or stale IPs. Confirm: dig +trace , compare resolvers. Fix: correct the record; wait out TTL; in emergencies, communicate the IP directly only as a stopgap. Prevent: dig +trace after every change; low TTLs around migrations; delegation checks (Part II chapter 7 scenario).

Presents as: timeouts to a specific destination; works from one host, not another. Confirm: nc -vz -w3 , tcpdump on the target, Reachability Analyzer, flow logs. Fix: the offending rule or route. Prevent: infrastructure as code for network rules, change review (Part II chapters 15, 19).

Presents as: FATAL: too many connections / remaining connection slots are reserved , or pool timeouts in the application; often after scaling out the app tier. Confirm: SELECT count( ) FROM pg stat activity; , per-application pool settings × instances. Fix: reduce pool sizes, terminate idle connections ( pg terminate backend for idle-in-transaction), add PgBouncer/RDS Proxy. Prevent: compute total connections before scaling; pooler; idle in transaction session timeout (Part VIII chapter 6).

Presents as: TLS errors on some hosts, AWS API SignatureDoesNotMatch / RequestTimeTooSkewed , JWTs rejected, log timelines that do not line up. Confirm: timedatectl , chronyc tracking . Fix: restart chrony, step the clock ( chronyc makestep ). Prevent: chrony everywhere, alarm on offset (Part I chapter 3).

Presents as: errors starting exactly at deploy time. Confirm: deploy log, version endpoint, compare with the previous release. Fix: roll back (previous image/release symlink/AMI), then investigate. Prevent: staging, canaries, automated rollback triggers (Part X).

Presents as: disk, CPU or database load climbing steadily; a timer or cron job that began failing and retrying, or logging in a loop. Confirm: systemctl list-timers , journalctl -u job , per-process I/O. Fix: stop the job; clean up. Prevent: job alerting on failure and on duration, rate limits on logging.

Presents as: authentication failures to a dependency after a rotation or a redeploy; 401 / 403 from a provider, database password rejected. Confirm: when was the secret rotated; which version does the service hold (started before rotation?). Fix: restart to pick up the new value, or fix the reference. Prevent: rotation procedures that include restarts or runtime refresh; alerts on auth failures to dependencies (Part IV chapter 17).

Presents as: intermittent slowness with no change in your metrics; EBS or network throttling counters rising. Confirm: ENA allowance exceeded , EBS BurstBalance , %st . Fix: larger instance or volume class. Prevent: size to allowances; alarms on throttling metrics (chapter 10).

h: Reboot that did not come back
x: Presents as: instance unreachable after a reboot or kernel update. Confirm: serial console / system log screenshot. Causes: fstab , broken bootloader, service blocking boot, sshd config. Fix: rescue volume procedure (chapter 2). Prevent: nofail , sshd -t , test reboots in staging.

- Before changing anything: copy the relevant logs ( journalctl -u svc --since ... /tmp/incident-svc.log ), snapshot the volume if data may be corrupted, record ps , ss , df , free output, note the time. - During: post each action and its result in the incident channel with timestamps. Say what you are about to do before you do it; someone may know why not. - Status updates to the client on a fixed cadence (every 30 minutes for a Sev1), even if the update is "still investigating, next update at HH:MM" (Part XI chapter 6). - After: the timeline is the postmortem's skeleton; good notes make it a 30-minute job.

- Know your normal: baseline dashboards for every resource so abnormal is visible at a glance. - Keep the toolkit installed on images ( htop , iotop , sysstat , tcpdump , jq , strace , lsof , mtr , nmap ); installing packages during an outage wastes minutes and may be impossible on a full disk. - Runbooks for the catalogue entries above, linked from alerts. - Practise: break staging on purpose monthly and time the diagnosis (Part XI chapter 9; Part XIV project 6).

- Rebooting first, losing the evidence and often the cause. - Fixing the symptom (freeing disk) without the cause (why it filled). - Checking the application before the host. - Not asking "what changed?" - Working in silence; nobody else can help or learn. - Declaring resolution without re-measuring the original symptom. questions What is the single most valuable fact to establish at the start of an incident? options Which engineer is on call The exact time of onset, to correlate with changes The CPU percentage The number of users answer explain Most incidents follow a change; the onset time finds it. Why avoid rebooting as the first action? options Reboots are slow It destroys evidence (process state, memory, open files) and often only resets the clock on the problem It costs money It requires approval answer explain Capture state first; reboot when needed to restore service with the evidence in hand. `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved` appears after scaling the API from 3 to 8 instances. The cause is most likely: options Disk full Total connections (pool size × instances) now exceed the database's limit A certificate answer explain Compute connection totals before scaling; add a pooler. What should happen immediately after the symptom is gone? options Close the incident Verify with the same measurement that defined the symptom, record the timeline, and schedule the prevention work Reboot to be safe Delete the logs answer explain Resolution is measured, not assu

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
x: - Explain the problems containers solve (dependency isolation, reproducible deployment, density) and the ones they do not (they are not VMs). - Describe the kernel features a container is built from: namespaces, cgroups, union filesystems, capabilities, seccomp. - Reason about container security boundaries honestly. - Inspect a running container from the host and see the kernel primitives directly. ::: Part I chapters 2, 3, 6 and 7. :::

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
x: Before containers, deploying an application meant making a server match the developer's machine: the right Python, the right system libraries, the right configuration files, in the right places, for every application sharing the server, without conflicts. Virtual machines solved isolation at the cost of a full operating system per application (gigabytes, minutes to boot). Containers deliver most of the isolation with none of the overhead by using features the Linux kernel already had: a process can be given a private view of the filesystem, network, process tree and hostname, and a hard limit on resources, while sharing the kernel with everything else on the host. The outcome that mattered for the industry: the image became the unit of deployment. Build once, run the identical bytes everywhere (Part I chapters 1 and 9). "Works on my machine" became "ships in my container".

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
x: There is no container object in the Linux kernel. A container is an ordinary process (tree) started with a particular combination of kernel features: title What makes a process a container layers Namespaces isolation of view summary Each namespace type gives the process its own instance of a global resource. examples pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time **pid**: its own process tree (PID 1 inside is some PID on the host). **net**: its own interfaces, IPs, routing table, ports (hence binding 0.0.0.0:8000 in many containers without conflict). **mnt**: its own mount table and root filesystem. **uts**: its own hostname. **ipc**: its own shared memory. **user**: UID 0 inside maps to an unprivileged UID outside (when enabled). **cgroup**: its own view of the cgroup tree. Control groups (cgroups v2) limits and accounting summary Limit and measure CPU, memory, I/O, PIDs for the process tree. examples memory.max, cpu.max, pids.max, io.max This is where `--memory=512m` and `--cpus=1.5` live, and where exit code 137 originates when memory.max is exceeded (Part I chapter 7). Kubernetes requests/limits map here too. Union / overlay filesystem the image summary Read-only image layers stacked with a writable layer on top, presented as one root filesystem via overlayfs. examples /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/merged Layers are shared between containers from the same image; the writable layer is discarded when the container is removed (hence volumes for persistence). t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
x: docker run -d --name demo --memory=256m --cpus=1 -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27 PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' demo) # namespaces: the container's processes live in different namespaces from your shell sudo ls -l /proc/$PID/ns/ # net, pid, mnt, uts... each a distinct inode vs. /proc/self/ns/ sudo nsenter -t $PID -n ip addr # enter its network namespace: its own eth0 with 172.17.0.x sudo nsenter -t $PID -p -m ps aux # its process tree: nginx is PID 1 there ps -o pid,user,cmd -p $PID # from the host it is just a process (often running as root!) # cgroups: the limits are files cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' demo).scope/memory.max # 268435456 cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-*/cpu.max # 100000 100000 (1 CPU) cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-*/memory.current # overlay filesystem: layers merged into one root docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data.MergedDir}}' demo sudo ls $(docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data.UpperDir}}' demo) # the writable layer: what the container changed # capabilities and seccomp docker inspect -f '{{.HostConfig.CapAdd}} {{.HostConfig.CapDrop}}' demo grep -E 'Cap(Eff|Bnd)|Seccomp' /proc/$PID/status The last ps line is the one to remember: by default the process inside runs as root, and that is root on the host kernel, constrained only by namespaces, capabilities and seccomp. Chapter 7 is about closing that gap.

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
x: - Reproducible artifacts : the image contains the runtime, libraries and code; the host needs only a container runtime. - Isolation of dependencies : two applications with conflicting library versions coexist. - Density and speed : start in milliseconds; dozens per host; share the kernel and image layers. - Portability : the same image runs on a laptop, CI, ECS, Kubernetes. - Declarative resource limits : memory and CPU bounds per process tree. - An ecosystem : registries, orchestrators, scanners, a common vocabulary with clients.

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
h: What containers do not give you
x: - A security boundary equal to a VM. Treat a container as a process with extra isolation. Multi-tenant workloads running untrusted code need microVMs or sandboxed runtimes. - Persistence. The writable layer vanishes with the container; data belongs in volumes or external stores (chapter 5). - Freedom from operations. Images must be rebuilt for patches (chapter 7), hosts must still be maintained (unless Fargate), orchestration adds its own complexity (chapters 8–14). - Performance isolation by default. Without limits, one container can starve the host; with limits, you must size them (Part I chapter 7).

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
x: The Open Container Initiative (OCI) standardises the image format and the runtime specification . runc is the reference low-level runtime that creates the namespaces and cgroups; containerd (used by Docker and Kubernetes) and CRI-O manage images and containers above it; Docker adds the build tooling, CLI and daemon; Podman offers a daemonless, rootless alternative with a Docker-compatible CLI. Images built with any OCI tool run on any OCI runtime, which is why "Docker image" and "container image" are used interchangeably. Rootless containers (Podman default, Docker rootless mode) run the daemon and containers as an unprivileged user with user namespaces, closing the "root in the container is root on the host" gap at some cost in features and performance.

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
h: Where you will meet these primitives again
x: Memory limits and OOM kills (Part I chapter 7); PID 1 and signals (Part I chapter 6); bind addresses and network namespaces (Part II chapter 5); non-root users and capabilities (chapter 7); Kubernetes requests and limits (chapter 9); and pod security standards (chapter 13). The primitives are the same everywhere; the orchestrators are policy layers on top.

t: Why Containers Exist: Namespaces and cgroups
x: - "Containers are lightweight VMs." They share the kernel; the isolation model is different and weaker. - "Root inside the container is harmless." It is root on the host kernel with fewer capabilities; escapes have happened via kernel bugs and misconfiguration (mounted Docker socket, --privileged ). - "The container has its own OS." It has its own userland files; the kernel is the host's. An Alpine image on an Ubuntu host runs on Ubuntu's kernel. - "Data written inside the container is saved." Only until the container is removed. questions What does a Linux container share with its host that a virtual machine does not? options The filesystem The kernel The network interface Nothing answer explain One kernel serves the host and all containers; this is the source of both efficiency and the weaker security boundary. Which kernel feature enforces a container's memory limit? options Namespaces cgroups overlayfs seccomp answer explain cgroups limit and account resources; exceeding memory.max triggers the OOM killer. A process inside a default Docker container shows as UID 0 on the host. What constrains it? options Nothing; it is full root Namespaces, a reduced capability set, seccomp and LSM profiles, but it is still root on the shared kernel The hypervisor Docker's user database answer explain Run as a non-root user and drop capabilities to shrink the blast radius (chapter 7). Why do Fargate and Lambda run each task in a microVM rather than a plain container? options Performance T

- Explain how images are built from layers, addressed by content digests, and distributed through registries. - Use tags and digests correctly for reproducible deployments. - Operate a registry (Amazon ECR) with lifecycle policies, scanning and access control. - Keep images small and layer caches effective. ::: Chapter 1; Part I chapter 9. :::

An image is the deployable artifact of the container era: the thing CI builds, the registry stores, and the orchestrator runs. Understanding its structure explains why builds are fast or slow, why "the same tag" can run different code, why images bloat, and how to get the reproducibility that Part I promised.

An image is an ordered list of read-only layers (each a tarball of filesystem changes) plus a config (environment, entrypoint, user, exposed ports) and a manifest that lists them. Every layer and the manifest are identified by the SHA-256 digest of their content. Two images sharing base layers share them on disk and in the registry; a one-line code change produces one new layer and reuses the rest. docker image inspect python:3.12-slim --format '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}' | jq # layer digests docker history --no-trunc myapp:2.4.0 # which Dockerfile instruction created each layer and its size docker manifest inspect myapp:2.4.0 # the manifest (and multi-arch index) The digest sha256:… of the manifest identifies the exact image. It never changes. A tag ( myapp:2.4.0 , python:3.12-slim , latest ) is a mutable pointer to a manifest: the registry owner can move it at any time. This is the key fact for reproducibility (Part I chapter 9): deploy by digest, or by a tag you control and never move (an immutable tag such as the Git SHA). docker pull python:3.12-slim docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' python:3.12-slim # python@sha256:2b5d... # Dockerfile: pin by digest for a reproducible base FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:2b5d3a1b... Multi-architecture images : a tag can point at an index listing manifests per platform ( linux/amd64 , linux/arm64 ); the client picks its own. Build with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 so the same tag runs on x86 hosts a

A registry is an HTTP service storing manifests and blobs (layers), addressed as host/namespace/repository:tag or @digest . Docker Hub ( docker.io/library/python ), GitHub Container Registry ( ghcr.io ), Amazon ECR ( 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/app ), Google Artifact Registry, and self-hosted options (Harbor, the OCI distribution reference). Clients authenticate ( docker login , ECR tokens from aws ecr get-login-password ), pull manifests, then fetch only the layers they do not have.

aws ecr create-repository --repository-name client/app --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true \ --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE --encryption-configuration encryptionType=KMS aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com docker tag app:local 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/client/app:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/client/app:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) aws ecr describe-images --repository-name client/app --query 'sort_by(imageDetails,&imagePushedAt)[-3:].[imageTags,imageDigest,imageScanStatus.status]' Settings that matter: immutable tags (a pushed tag cannot be overwritten; latest becomes impossible, which is the point); scan on push (basic scanning free; enhanced scanning via Inspector adds continuous rescanning and language packages); encryption with KMS; a lifecycle policy expiring untagged images after a day and keeping the last N tagged releases (registries fill up quietly and cost per GB); repository policies granting pull to the ECS task execution role or EKS nodes and push only to CI; replication to other regions for DR or multi-region deployments; pull-through cache rules so your hosts pull public images (Docker Hub, ECR Public, Quay) through ECR, avoiding rate limits and keeping copies under your control. { "rules": [ { "rulePriority": 1, "description": "expire untagged after 1 day", "selection": { "tagStatus": "unta

ECS task definitions and Kubernetes manifests reference images. Reference by immutable tag and record the digest, or by digest outright ( image: …/app@sha256:… ). Kubernetes imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent with a mutable tag is a classic source of "nodes running different code"; use unique tags or digests and Always is then unnecessary. For ECS, each deployment should create a new task definition revision pointing at the new tag; the revision history is your rollback list.

Why size matters: pull time on every scale-out and deploy (a 1.5 GB image takes a minute to pull cold; 80 MB takes seconds), attack surface (fewer packages, fewer CVEs), storage and transfer cost. - Start from minimal bases: python:3.12-slim (~120 MB) rather than python:3.12 (~1 GB); node:22-alpine or -slim ; distroless ( gcr.io/distroless/ , no shell, no package manager) for compiled languages and for runtimes with care; scratch for static Go/Rust binaries. - Multi-stage builds (chapter 3) so build tools never reach the final image. - One RUN for package installs with cleanup in the same layer ( apt-get install … && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/ ); a later RUN rm does not shrink earlier layers. - .dockerignore excluding .git , node modules , test data, local env files (also a security control: .env files must never be copied in). - Inspect with docker history and tools like dive to find the fat layers. Alpine note: musl libc instead of glibc; some Python wheels and native modules misbehave or compile slowly. -slim Debian images are often the better trade for Python; Alpine shines for Go and Node.

Docker reuses a layer if the instruction and all inputs are unchanged and every previous layer was reused. Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changing: base image, system packages, dependency manifests and install, then application code. Copying the whole source before installing dependencies invalidates the dependency layer on every code change. BuildKit's cache mounts ( RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip ) keep package caches between builds without baking them into layers; registry-backed cache ( --cache-to type=registry ) shares cache across CI runners. Chapter 3 shows the patterns.

OCI labels record provenance: org.opencontainers.image.source (repo URL), .revision (commit), .version , .created . Set them in CI. Together with SBOMs and signatures (Part IV chapter 20), they make "what is this image?" answerable from the registry alone.

- Deploying latest or any mutable tag; different nodes run different code; rollback target unknown. - No lifecycle policy; the registry quietly costs hundreds a month. - Full base images with build tools in production; 1 GB pulls and hundreds of CVEs. - Secrets or .env copied into images (they are in a layer forever, even if deleted later). - COPY . . before dependency installation, destroying the cache. - Mixing apt-get update and install in separate layers, producing stale package indexes. - Pulling public images directly in production without a cache; Docker Hub rate limits break deploys. - Forgetting multi-arch when moving to Graviton; exec format error at runtime. questions What is the difference between a tag and a digest? options No difference A digest is the immutable content hash of the exact image; a tag is a mutable pointer that the publisher can move Tags are for private registries Digests are only for base images answer explain Deploy by digest or by an immutable tag you control. Why does a later `RUN rm -rf /build-tools` not reduce image size? options rm is slow in containers Each instruction creates a layer; earlier layers still contain the files, and the deletion only adds a whiteout in a new layer Docker ignores rm It does reduce size answer explain Clean up in the same RUN, or use multi-stage builds. Which ECR setting makes `latest` deployments impossible by design? options Scan on push Immutable tags KMS encryption Replication answer explain Immutable tags

Write an ECR lifecycle policy and a pull-through cache rule; pull a public image through the cache and confirm it appears in your registry.

- Write Dockerfiles for Python and Node applications that are small, cache-friendly, reproducible and secure. - Use multi-stage builds to separate build-time tooling from the runtime image. - Handle dependencies, build secrets, non-root users, signals and health checks correctly. - Recognise the Dockerfile anti-patterns that cause slow builds, huge images and production bugs. ::: Chapters 1 and 2; Part I chapters 6 and 9. :::

A Dockerfile is a build script whose output ships to production. Most of them are written once, copied between projects, and never reviewed; they run as root, include compilers and test dependencies, rebuild everything on every change, and bake in secrets. The patterns below fix all of that and are reusable across projects.

@file: Dockerfile (FastAPI + uv, multi-stage) # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7 ARG PYTHON_VERSION=3.12.7 FROM python:${PYTHON_VERSION}-slim-bookworm AS base ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 # ---------- build stage: compilers, dependency resolution ---------- FROM base AS build RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential libpq-dev \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.4.18 /uv /usr/local/bin/uv WORKDIR /app COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \ uv sync --locked --no-dev --no-install-project # deps first: cached until lockfile changes COPY . . RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv uv sync --locked --no-dev # install the project itself # ---------- runtime stage: minimal ---------- FROM base AS runtime RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 curl tini \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \ && groupadd --system --gid 10001 app && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --home /app --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app WORKDIR /app COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/.venv /app/.venv COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app /app ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" PORT=8000 USER app EXPOSE 8000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready || exit 1 ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--"] CMD ["gunicorn", "app.main:app", "-c", "gunicorn.conf.py",

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7 FROM node:22.11.0-bookworm-slim AS base ENV NODE_ENV=production FROM base AS deps WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --ignore-scripts # exact lockfile install, no install scripts FROM base AS build WORKDIR /app COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules COPY . . RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev # compile TS, drop devDependencies FROM base AS runtime RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /app COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/node_modules ./node_modules COPY --chown=node:node package.json ./ USER node # the node image ships a non-root 'node' user (uid 1000) EXPOSE 3000 HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3000/health/ready || exit 1 ENTRYPOINT ["tini", "--"] CMD ["node", "--max-old-space-size=384", "dist/server.js"] # heap cap below the container limit (Part I ch.7)

Private package registries and private Git dependencies need credentials at build time. Never use ARG / ENV for them (they persist in image history). Use BuildKit secret mounts, which expose a file during one RUN and leave no trace: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci --ignore-scripts RUN --mount=type=ssh pip install git+ssh://git@github.com/client/private-lib.git docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc --ssh default -t app .

h: Configuration at runtime, not build time
x: Images are environment-agnostic: no environment-specific URLs, no ENV DATABASE URL , no copied .env . Configuration arrives from the orchestrator (ECS task definition, Kubernetes env/ConfigMap/Secrets) or a secrets manager at start (Part I chapter 8; chapter 6). The only ENV in a Dockerfile are runtime behaviour flags ( PYTHONUNBUFFERED , NODE ENV , PATH ).

.git .github node_modules .venv __pycache__ *.pyc .env* !.env.example tests/fixtures/large coverage *.md It shrinks the build context (faster uploads to the daemon), keeps secrets and junk out of layers, and avoids cache invalidation from irrelevant files. Treat it like .gitignore : review it.

A test stage ( FROM build AS test; RUN pytest ) that CI targets with docker build --target test ensures tests run against the exact dependencies in the image. Keep the runtime stage free of test code and test dependencies.

Sometimes start-up needs logic (wait for a dependency, render a config template, run migrations in a job). Keep entrypoint scripts tiny, set -euo pipefail , and end with exec "$@" so the application replaces the shell and receives signals. Do not run migrations from the API container's entrypoint in multi-replica deployments (races; failures take down every replica); run them as a separate one-shot task before the rollout (Part X chapter 8). #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # optional: wait for DB to accept connections (bounded) for i in $(seq 1 30); do pg_isready -h "$DATABASE__HOST" -q && break; sleep 1; done exec "$@"

- FROM python:latest / FROM node with no tag. - Single stage with build-essential shipped to production. - COPY . . before installing dependencies. - RUN apt-get update in its own layer (stale indexes on rebuild) or without cleaning lists. - Running as root; chmod -R 777 to fix permission issues. - Shell-form CMD ( CMD gunicorn … ), so PID 1 is sh and signals are lost. - Secrets via ARG / ENV / COPY .env . - EXPOSE as if it opened ports (it is documentation; publishing is a runtime decision). - Health check hitting / (heavy) or omitted entirely. - Pinning nothing, or pinning the base but not dependencies. - Huge contexts without .dockerignore . questions Why copy only the dependency manifest and lockfile before installing dependencies? options Smaller image So the dependency layer is cached and reused until the lockfile changes, instead of reinstalling on every code change Security Docker requires it answer explain Layer caching depends on inputs; code changes should invalidate only the final layers. What does a multi-stage build achieve? options Parallel builds Build tooling and intermediate files stay in earlier stages; the final image contains only the runtime and application Multiple architectures Faster pulls only answer explain Smaller, less vulnerable images that cannot compile attacker code. How should a private registry token be provided during `npm ci` in a build? options ARG NPM_TOKEN ENV NPM_TOKEN A BuildKit secret mount for the single RUN that needs it Copy .npmr

1. Convert a single-stage Dockerfile from a project into the multi-stage pattern; compare image size, CVE count and rebuild time after a one-line code change. 2. Add a test stage and run it in CI; make the build fail when a test fails. 3. Replace a shell-form CMD with tini plus exec-form; time docker stop before and after and observe the exit code.

- Define a complete local development environment (application, database, cache, proxy, workers) in one Compose file. - Use networks, volumes, healthchecks, dependency ordering, profiles and overrides correctly. - Keep development close to production without using Compose as a production orchestrator. - Troubleshoot Compose stacks quickly. ::: Chapters 2 and 3; Part I chapter 11. :::

A new engineer should be able to clone a repository and run the whole system locally in minutes, with the same database engine, cache and message broker as production (Part I chapter 11). Doing that by hand (install PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, set up users, configure ports) takes a day and produces machine-specific drift. Docker Compose describes the set of containers, their networks and volumes in one file, and starts them with one command. It is the standard tool for local development and integration tests, and a reasonable choice for single-host deployments of small systems; it is not an orchestrator for production fleets.

@file: docker-compose.yml name: clientapp services: db: image: postgres:16.4 environment: POSTGRES_USER: app POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app # development only; never real credentials in this file POSTGRES_DB: app ports: ["127.0.0.1:5432:5432"] # bind to localhost so the dev DB is not exposed on the LAN volumes: - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data - ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro # extensions, roles on first start healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d app"] interval: 5s timeout: 3s retries: 10 command: ["postgres", "-c", "log_statement=all", "-c", "log_min_duration_statement=200"] # see slow queries in dev redis: image: redis:7.4-alpine command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "128mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"] ports: ["127.0.0.1:6379:6379"] healthcheck: { test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"], interval: 5s, retries: 10 } localstack: # S3/SQS/Secrets Manager emulation for local AWS integration image: localstack/localstack:3.8 environment: { SERVICES: "s3,sqs,secretsmanager", DEFAULT_REGION: eu-west-1 } ports: ["127.0.0.1:4566:4566"] volumes: ["./localstack/init:/etc/localstack/init/ready.d:ro"] # create buckets/queues on start profiles: ["aws"] # only started with --profile aws api: build: context: . target: build # dev uses the build stage (has dev deps); prod uses runtime command: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload env_file: .env # developer's local config (gitignored); .env.example documents keys environment: DATABASE__HOST: db

- Networks : Compose creates a project network; services reach each other by service name ( db , redis ) via embedded DNS. Published ports are only for reaching services from the host. Add a second network to isolate groups when needed. - Volumes : named volumes ( pgdata ) persist data across container recreation and are managed by Docker; bind mounts ( .:/app ) share host directories for live code. The anonymous volume trick ( /app/.venv ) preserves a directory from the image that would otherwise be hidden by the bind mount. - Healthchecks and depends on conditions : service healthy waits for the dependency to be ready , not just started, removing the "connection refused on first start" race. Applications should still retry on start-up; real environments do not have Compose ordering. - Profiles : optional services (LocalStack, proxy, observability stack) started on demand. - Overrides : docker-compose.override.yml is merged automatically (developer-local tweaks); -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.ci.yml for CI variants (no bind mounts, no ports, target: runtime , test command). - Env substitution : ${VAR:-default} in the file, values from the shell or a .env next to the file (distinct from env file: for a service). - Resource limits : deploy.resources.limits is honoured by docker compose for local parity with production limits (useful to catch memory issues early).

CI can bring up the stack and run tests against real services: @file: docker-compose.ci.yml services: api: build: { context: ., target: test } command: pytest -q --junitxml=/reports/junit.xml volumes: ["./reports:/reports"] environment: { DATABASE__HOST: db, REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/0 } ports: [] docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.ci.yml run --rm --build api docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.ci.yml down -v Testcontainers (per-test ephemeral containers from code) is the alternative when tests need isolated databases per test class.

For a single-host deployment (Part V chapter 14 variation), docker compose up -d with a production file (images from the registry by immutable tag, no bind mounts, restart: unless-stopped , resource limits, logging driver configured, secrets from files or an external store, Caddy as the proxy) is legitimate and widely used for small systems. What it lacks: multi-host scheduling, rolling deploys with health gating (recreating a service drops connections briefly), autoscaling, secret management beyond files, and self-healing across hosts. When you need those, you need an orchestrator (chapters 8–14) or a managed container service (Part VII chapter 8). Do not stretch Compose into a fleet manager with scripts.

Symptom Likely cause Check --- --- --- connection refused to db on first start Dependency not ready depends on with service healthy ; app retry logic Code changes not reflected Bind mount path wrong, or --reload missing, or Compose Watch not running docker compose exec api ls /app ; docker compose watch ModuleNotFoundError after bind mount Host dir shadowed the image's venv/node modules Anonymous volume for /app/.venv or /app/node modules Port already allocated Another process/stack on the port ss -ltnp ; change host port Permission denied on volume UID mismatch between container user and host files Match UIDs, or user: "${UID}:${GID}" , or fix ownership Data vanished down -v , or a volume name changed with the project name docker volume ls ; set name: Slow on macOS/Windows Bind mount filesystem overhead Compose Watch sync, fewer mounted paths, named volumes for deps Service exits immediately Wrong command, missing env, crash docker compose logs svc ; docker compose run --rm svc sh

- Real credentials in the Compose file committed to Git. - Database ports published on 0.0.0.0 on a laptop on a shared network (Part V chapter 7 showed Docker bypasses ufw). - depends on without health conditions; flaky first starts. - down -v in a habit; development data lost repeatedly (or worse, run against a production host). - Compose stacks diverging from the production Dockerfile targets and environment variables. - Using Compose to manage multi-host production. questions How does the `api` service reach the database in a Compose stack? options Via localhost:5432 By the service name `db` through Compose's embedded DNS on the project network Through the published host port It cannot without a link answer explain Published ports are for host access; services talk by name internally. What does `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` provide? options Automatic restarts Waiting until the dependency's healthcheck passes before starting the dependent service Shared volumes Network isolation answer explain Plain depends_on only orders start, not readiness. Why add an anonymous volume for `/app/.venv` when bind-mounting the source directory? options For persistence So the host directory does not hide the virtual environment built into the image To share it with other services Compose requires it answer explain A bind mount replaces the whole directory; the nested volume preserves the image's contents there. When is Compose an inappropriate production tool? options Always

Two things confuse everyone who starts running containers: the container has its own network, so "localhost" means something different inside and outside; and the container's filesystem is disposable, so data written inside vanishes when it is replaced. Both are consequences of the isolation from chapter 1, and both have standard solutions once the model is clear.

By default Docker creates a virtual bridge ( docker0 , 172.17.0.0/16) and gives each container a network namespace with a virtual Ethernet pair: one end in the container ( eth0 , an IP on the bridge), one end on the host attached to the bridge. Containers on the same bridge talk directly by IP; the host NATs outbound traffic to its own IP (masquerade); inbound traffic reaches a container only through published ports (DNAT rules from a host port to the container's port). docker network ls; docker network inspect bridge # default bridge: no DNS between containers by name docker network create appnet # user-defined bridge: containers resolve each other by name docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:16 docker run -it --rm --network appnet postgres:16 psql -h db -U postgres # 'db' resolves via Docker's embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) docker run -d --name api --network appnet -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 app:2.4.0 # publish to the host's loopback only Rules of thumb: always use a user-defined network (name resolution, isolation from unrelated containers); publish ports only for what the host or the outside must reach, and bind them to 127.0.0.1 unless the service is meant to be public; remember that publishing bypasses host firewalls like ufw (Part V chapter 7); inside a container, localhost is the container itself, and reaching the host requires host.docker.internal (Docker Desktop) or the bridge gateway IP (Linux, or --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway ).

- host : the container shares the host's network namespace; no isolation, no port mapping, best performance. Used for monitoring agents and some network tools. Not available on Docker Desktop in the same way. - none : no network at all; for build steps and sandboxed processing. - macvlan/ipvlan : containers get addresses on the physical network; rare in cloud. - overlay : multi-host networks (Swarm); superseded in practice by orchestrator networking.

ECS awsvpc mode gives every task its own elastic network interface and VPC IP; containers in a task share that namespace (talk via localhost ); security groups attach per task; no port mapping, the task IP:port is the endpoint; the ALB targets task IPs. ECS bridge mode (EC2 only) is the Docker model with dynamic host ports. Service discovery via Cloud Map DNS or ECS Service Connect. Kubernetes gives each pod an IP (containers in a pod share it and talk via localhost ), every pod can reach every pod without NAT (the CNI plugin's job: VPC CNI on EKS assigns real VPC IPs), Services provide stable virtual IPs and DNS names ( orders.default.svc.cluster.local ) load-balancing to pods, and NetworkPolicies restrict traffic (chapter 13). Chapters 9–10.

The container's writable layer is deleted with the container. Anything that must outlive it goes elsewhere: title Where container data can live columns Option What it is Caveats Writable layer Copy-on-write layer on top of the image Temp files, caches that may vanish Gone on container removal; slow for heavy writes; grows the container tmpfs mount In-memory filesystem Secrets files, scratch, PID files Lost on stop; counts against memory Bind mount A host directory mapped into the container Development source code; host config files; host sockets Couples the container to a host path; permission/UID mismatches; not portable across hosts Named volume Docker-managed directory (or a volume plugin: EBS, EFS, NFS) Databases and stateful services on a single host; persistent data in Compose Lives on one host unless a plugin provides shared storage; back it up explicitly External service RDS, S3, ElastiCache, EFS Production data of every kind The right answer for production: containers stay stateless (Part III chapter 1) docker volume create pgdata docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16 # named volume docker run -d -v $(pwd)/config:/etc/app:ro app # bind mount, read-only docker run -d --mount type=tmpfs,destination=/run/secrets,tmpfs-size=1m app # tmpfs docker volume inspect pgdata # host path under /var/lib/docker/volumes docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-$(date +%F).tgz -C /data . # backup a volume Design

Files on a volume carry UIDs from whoever wrote them. A container running as UID 10001 cannot write to a bind-mounted host directory owned by UID 1000 ( Permission denied ), and files it creates appear as an unknown UID on the host. Options: run the container with the host user's UID ( --user $(id -u):$(id -g) in development), chown the mount point at image build time or in an entrypoint, Kubernetes fsGroup (which makes the volume group-writable by the pod's group), or named volumes initialised from the image (Docker copies the image's directory contents and ownership into an empty named volume on first use, which bind mounts do not do).

Overlay writable layers are slow for databases; volumes bypass the overlay. On macOS and Windows, bind mounts cross a VM boundary and are slow for large trees ( node modules ); use named volumes for dependencies and Compose Watch for code. EBS-backed volumes via CSI drivers in Kubernetes behave like EBS (chapter 10).

docker exec -it api sh -c 'ss -ltnp' # what is the app bound to? 127.0.0.1 = unreachable from outside docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}} {{end}}' api docker exec -it api getent hosts db # does the name resolve? docker exec -it api sh -c 'timeout 3 sh -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/db/5432" && echo open' # port reachable? docker run --rm -it --network container:api nicolaka/netshoot # full toolkit in the app's network namespace docker port api # published ports sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n # the DNAT rules behind publishing Checklist: bind address inside (0.0.0.0), same network as the peer, name resolution, port published if host access is needed, host firewall/security group for external access.

"My data disappeared": the container was recreated (new writable layer) without a volume; the volume name changed (Compose project name); down -v ; a bind mount path was wrong so writes went to the layer. "Permission denied": UID mismatch. "Database refuses to start": the data directory is not empty or has wrong ownership (PostgreSQL requires the directory owned by its user with mode 700).

- Using the default bridge and trying to resolve containers by name. - Publishing database ports on 0.0.0.0 on a shared network. - Stateful data in the writable layer; lost on deploy. - Bind-mounting host paths in production, tying images to hosts. - Ignoring UID mismatches and "fixing" with chmod 777 . - Expecting Docker named volumes to be backed up by anything other than your own job. - localhost confusion between host, container and pod. questions A service inside a container binds to 127.0.0.1:8000. The port is published with -p 8000:8000. Is it reachable from the host? options No; traffic arrives on the container's eth0, not its loopback. Bind to 0.0.0.0 Only over IPv6 Only with host networking answer explain Inside a container, localhost is the container's own loopback. Where should a production PostgreSQL's data live when the application runs in containers? options The container's writable layer A bind mount on the application host A managed service (RDS) or a dedicated stateful deployment with its own persistent storage and backups tmpfs answer explain Application containers stay stateless; state belongs in purpose-built, backed-up systems. Why can a container running as UID 10001 fail to write to a bind-mounted directory? options Bind mounts are read-only The host directory is owned by a different UID; Unix permissions apply across the mount Docker blocks writes SELinux always denies answer explain Align UIDs, chown the path, or use fsGroup/named volumes. 1. Create two containers on a user-defined network; show name resolution works and that a third container on another network cannot reach them. 2. Run PostgreSQL with and without a named volume; recreate the container each time and observe which keeps its data. Back up and restore the volume with tar. 3. Reproduce a UID mismatch with a bind mount, then fix it three ways (user flag, chown in entrypoint, named volume initialised from the image).

x: - Inject configuration and secrets into containers without baking them into images or exposing them more than necessary. - Set CPU and memory requests and limits that keep services stable, and tune runtimes to respect them. - Distinguish development images and settings from production ones. - Configure logging, health checks, restart policies and graceful shutdown for production containers. ::: Chapters 3 and 5; Part I chapters 6, 7 and 8; Part IV chapter 17. :::

t: Secrets, Configuration, Resource Limits and Production Containers
x: The same image must run in development, staging and production, so everything that differs must come from outside the image at runtime. Containers also share hosts, so an unbounded container can take the host down. And a container that does not stop cleanly, log properly or report health will fail in ways orchestrators cannot handle. This chapter is the production checklist for a container's runtime configuration.

t: Secrets, Configuration, Resource Limits and Production Containers
x: Three mechanisms, in order of preference for secrets: 1. Environment variables from the orchestrator (ECS task definition environment , Kubernetes env and envFrom ConfigMaps). Fine for non-secret configuration. For secrets they are acceptable but visible to every process in the container, to docker inspect , to the ECS/Kubernetes API readers, and to crash dumps. 2. Files mounted at runtime : Docker Compose secrets: (files under /run/secrets ), Kubernetes Secrets mounted as volumes (tmpfs), the Secrets Store CSI driver syncing from AWS Secrets Manager. Not in the environment; readable only by processes with file access; rotatable in place (mounted files update). 3. Fetched by the application at start from Secrets Manager/Parameter Store using the task role (Part IV chapter 17). Nothing stored by the orchestrator; audited per read; rotation handled by re-fetching. ECS supports a hybrid that is the practical default: the task definition's secrets field references a Secrets Manager or Parameter Store ARN; the ECS agent fetches it with the task execution role and injects it as an environment variable at start. Simple, no SDK code, auditable. Rotation requires a new deployment or task restart. t: Secrets, Configuration, Resource Limits and Production Containers
x: A container with no memory limit can consume the host; one with too low a limit is killed under normal load. Set both and size them (Part I chapter 7): - Memory limit = measured peak RSS × 1.3 (headroom), rounded up. Exceeding it is an OOM kill (exit 137). In Kubernetes set requests.memory equal to limits.memory for predictable scheduling (memory is incompressible). - CPU : Kubernetes requests.cpu guarantees a share; limits.cpu throttles above it (CFS quota), which can add latency even when the node is idle. Many teams set CPU requests and omit CPU limits for latency-sensitive services, relying on requests for fair scheduling. ECS Fargate requires choosing a task CPU/memory combination; containers within share it. - Runtime tuning : JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 , Node --max-old-space-size at ~75% of the limit, Python worker counts sized to memory, Go GOMEMLIMIT . Runtimes that ignore the cgroup limit are the number one cause of container OOM kills. - PIDs : a pids limit prevents fork bombs ( --pids-limit , Kubernetes podPidsLimit ). - Ephemeral storage : bound it (Kubernetes ephemeral-storage requests/limits) so a log-writing bug cannot fill the node; prefer read-only root filesystems with explicit writable mounts. docker run -d --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g --cpus=1.0 --pids-limit=512 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m app:3f9a1c4 docker stats # live CPU/memory per container

- Build images that minimise attack surface: minimal bases, non-root users, no secrets, pinned and scanned dependencies. - Harden the runtime: dropped capabilities, read-only filesystems, seccomp and AppArmor profiles, no privileged mode. - Scan, sign and verify images, and keep them patched through rebuilds. - Recognise the container-specific misconfigurations that lead to host compromise. ::: Chapters 1, 2, 3 and 6; Part IV chapter 20. :::

Containers made it easy to ship an entire userland with the application, and therefore easy to ship a userland full of unpatched packages, running as root, with the Docker socket mounted "for convenience". Image security is the discipline of shipping as little as possible, as an unprivileged user, verified and current, and of running it with the fewest privileges the kernel can grant.

1. Minimal base : -slim , distroless or scratch . Fewer packages, fewer CVEs, no shell for an attacker to use (distroless), smaller pulls. 2. Pin base images by digest and dependencies by lockfile (chapter 2; Part I chapter 9). 3. Non-root user with a fixed UID ( USER 10001 ); files owned appropriately; no sudo in the image. 4. No secrets in layers: BuildKit secret mounts for build-time credentials; .dockerignore for .env , keys, .git . 5. Multi-stage so compilers, package managers and dev dependencies never reach the runtime image (chapter 3). 6. No unnecessary tools : curl / wget only if health checks need them (or use a tiny static health binary), no ssh , no package manager in the final stage where possible. 7. Labels and SBOM : provenance metadata and a generated SBOM attached to the image (Part IV chapter 20). 8. Scan in CI and fail on critical/high with fixes available; rescan continuously in the registry (ECR enhanced scanning) because CVEs are published after you built. # Distroless runtime for a Python app (no shell, no package manager) FROM python:3.12-slim AS build # ... install deps into /app/.venv as in chapter 3 ... FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12:nonroot COPY --from=build --chown=nonroot:nonroot /app /app WORKDIR /app ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" USER nonroot ENTRYPOINT ["/app/.venv/bin/python", "-m", "gunicorn", "app.main:app", "-c", "gunicorn.conf.py"] Trade-offs: distroless has no shell, so docker exec … sh does not work (use kubectl debug epheme

The kernel primitives from chapter 1 become flags: docker run -d \ --user 10001:10001 \ --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \ --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \ # only if binding <1024; otherwise drop everything --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \ # setuid binaries cannot escalate --security-opt seccomp=default.json \ # Docker's default profile is applied automatically; a custom one tightens further --security-opt apparmor=docker-default \ --pids-limit 256 --memory 512m --cpus 1 \ --network appnet -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \ app:3f9a1c4 Kubernetes expresses the same in the pod securityContext (chapter 13): runAsNonRoot , runAsUser , readOnlyRootFilesystem , allowPrivilegeEscalation: false , capabilities.drop: [ALL] , seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault . ECS: user , readonlyRootFilesystem , linuxParameters.capabilities.drop , and Fargate's platform applies restrictions by default (no privileged, no host mounts).

- --privileged : disables nearly all isolation; the container can load kernel modules, access all devices, and trivially escape. Only for a few infrastructure agents, never for applications. - Mounting the Docker socket ( /var/run/docker.sock ) into a container: equivalent to root on the host. CI runners and "Docker-in-Docker" setups do this casually; use rootless builders (BuildKit, Kaniko) or dedicated build hosts. - Host network/PID/IPC namespaces for applications. - Host path mounts of sensitive directories ( / , /etc , /var/lib/docker ). - Adding SYS ADMIN or other powerful capabilities to "make something work". - Running as root because a port is below 1024 (use a higher port behind the load balancer, or NET BIND SERVICE ).

h: Patching: rebuild, do not patch in place
x: Containers are immutable; you do not apt upgrade inside a running container. Patching means rebuilding the image with updated base layers and dependencies, scanning, and redeploying. Automate a scheduled rebuild (weekly, plus on base-image security advisories) even when the application code has not changed; otherwise a service that has not deployed in three months runs three months of unpatched libraries. Dependabot/Renovate for base image tags and dependencies; a nightly CI job that rebuilds main and alerts on new findings.

Chapter 6 covered injection. Security specifics: secrets as files (tmpfs) rather than environment where feasible; never docker inspect -visible in CI logs; no secrets in image labels or ENV ; scan images for accidentally included secrets ( trivy image --scanners secret ).

Base images from official or verified publishers only (Docker Official Images, Chainguard, distroless, the language's official images); pull through a cache you control (ECR pull-through cache); verify base image signatures where published; pin by digest. A compromised or typosquatted base image is total compromise of everything built on it.

- Explain what an orchestrator does and why running containers across many hosts needs one. - Describe Kubernetes' architecture: control plane components, nodes, the API server, etcd, controllers and the reconciliation loop. - Understand the declarative model: desired state, actual state, controllers converging them. - Know what a managed Kubernetes service (EKS) runs for you and what remains yours. ::: Chapters 1 to 7; Part I chapter 14. :::

One host runs containers fine with Docker. Ten hosts raise questions Docker cannot answer: which host runs which container, what happens when a host dies, how traffic finds containers that move, how to roll out a new version without downtime, how to scale from 3 to 30 replicas and back, how to inject configuration and secrets uniformly, and how to isolate teams and workloads. An orchestrator answers them by taking a declaration of what you want running and continuously making it so across a cluster of machines. ECS, Nomad and Kubernetes are orchestrators. Kubernetes won the general-purpose space; ECS remains the simpler, AWS-native choice (Part VII chapter 8). This chapter explains Kubernetes because its model (desired state, controllers, reconciliation) is the vocabulary of modern infrastructure, even if a given client never runs it.

You do not tell Kubernetes "start three containers"; you submit an object saying "there should be three replicas of this pod spec". Controllers watch the API, compare desired state with actual state, and take actions to converge: start a pod, kill a pod, update a load balancer. If a node dies, the controller notices fewer replicas than desired and schedules replacements elsewhere. If you change the image tag, the deployment controller performs a rolling update. The same mechanism handles crashes, scaling, upgrades and drift. Infrastructure as code (Part X) applies the identical idea to cloud resources.

With EKS, AWS runs the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) across AZs, patches it, backs up etcd, and exposes an endpoint; you pay an hourly fee per cluster (around $0.10/hour, roughly $73/month, before any nodes) and manage the rest: nodes (managed node groups of EC2 instances, Fargate profiles for serverless pods, or Karpenter for just-in-time provisioning), the add-ons (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI driver: versioned, upgraded by you), cluster version upgrades (Kubernetes releases three times a year; EKS supports each for about 14 months with extended support at extra cost; upgrades are your recurring chore), IAM integration (IAM principals mapped to Kubernetes RBAC via access entries; pods get AWS permissions via IAM Roles for Service Accounts or Pod Identity), networking (VPC IPs per pod, which eats subnet space; plan /20s or prefix delegation), observability (Container Insights, Prometheus), and everything you deploy into it (ingress controller, cert-manager, external-dns, autoscalers, policy engines, logging agents). The control plane is the easy part; the platform you build on it is the work.

A platform for teams to deploy many services consistently with self-healing, scaling, rollouts, service discovery, configuration and policy, on any cloud or on-premises, with a vast ecosystem. The cost is operational: a platform team's worth of components to install, upgrade and secure, a steep learning curve, and quarterly version upgrades. Chapter 14 weighs when it is worth it; for many client projects it is not, and ECS Fargate or a PaaS delivers the same application outcomes with a fraction of the surface.

A pod is one or more containers sharing a network namespace and storage; it is the scheduling unit. - "kubectl apply is a deploy." It records desired state; the rollout is what controllers then do, and you must watch it ( kubectl rollout status ). questions Which component is the only one that reads and writes etcd? options kubelet Scheduler API server kube-proxy answer explain All other components interact through the API server, which enforces authentication, authorisation and admission. Three objects carry most of the daily work in Kubernetes: the Pod (what runs), the Deployment (how many and how to update), and the Service (how traffic finds them). Getting their specs right is the difference between a service that self-heals and rolls out cleanly and one that flaps, drops requests on deploy, or cannot be reached.

A pod is one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP, localhost between them), optionally share volumes, and are scheduled together on one node. Most pods have one application container; sidecars (log shippers, proxies) share the pod. apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod # you rarely create bare pods; this shows the spec a Deployment templates metadata: name: api-example labels: { app: api, version: "3f9a1c4" } spec: serviceAccountName: api # identity for RBAC and IAM (IRSA/Pod Identity) automountServiceAccountToken: false # unless the app calls the Kubernetes API securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true runAsUser: 10001 runAsGroup: 10001 fsGroup: 10001 seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault } containers: - name: api image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/client/app@sha256:9f3a… # by digest, or immutable tag ports: [{ name: http, containerPort: 8000 }] env: - { name: ENV, value: prod } - { name: DATABASE_URL, valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: api-db, key: url } } } envFrom: - configMapRef: { name: api-config } resources: requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" } limits: { memory: "512Mi" } # memory limit = request; CPU limit omitted (chapter 6) readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: http } periodSeconds: 5 failureThreshold: 3 livenessProbe: httpGet: { path: /health/live, port: http } periodSeconds: 10 failureThreshold: 3 startupProbe: httpGet: { path: /health/ready, port: http } periodSeconds: 5 failureThreshold: 30 # up to 150 s to start before

A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which manage pods from a template. Changing the template (new image) creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts replicas over according to the strategy. apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: { name: api, namespace: prod } spec: replicas: 3 revisionHistoryLimit: 10 # old ReplicaSets kept for rollback selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } } strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 } # add one new pod, wait until Ready, then remove one old: zero capacity loss minReadySeconds: 10 # a pod must stay Ready this long before counting as available progressDeadlineSeconds: 600 # rollout stalls → marked failed (alert on this) template: metadata: { labels: { app: api } } spec: { ... the pod spec above ... } kubectl apply -f api.yaml kubectl rollout status deployment/api -n prod # blocks until complete or failed; use in CI kubectl rollout history deployment/api -n prod kubectl rollout undo deployment/api -n prod # back to previous ReplicaSet kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=4 -n prod kubectl set image deployment/api api=…/app:NEWTAG -n prod # imperative; prefer applying manifests from Git kubectl scale deployment/api --replicas=5 -n prod # or let the HPA do it (chapter 11) How a rolling update avoids dropped requests: a new pod starts; its readiness probe passes; it is added to the Service endpoints; an old pod is selected for termination; it is removed from endpoints and sent SIGTERM at roughly the s

Pods have ephemeral IPs. A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances to the pods matching its selector, tracked via EndpointSlices. apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: { name: api, namespace: prod } spec: type: ClusterIP # internal only (default) selector: { app: api } ports: [{ name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http }] - ClusterIP : reachable inside the cluster at api.prod.svc.cluster.local:80 . The default for service-to-service traffic; an Ingress or Gateway routes external traffic to ClusterIP services (chapter 10). - NodePort : also opens a port (30000–32767) on every node. Rarely used directly in cloud; a building block. - LoadBalancer : asks the cloud controller to provision a load balancer (on EKS with the AWS Load Balancer Controller: an NLB, or an ALB via Ingress) pointing at the pods. One per service, so costly if used for every service; prefer one Ingress/Gateway fronting many services. - Headless ( clusterIP: None ): DNS returns pod IPs directly; used by StatefulSets and client-side load balancing (gRPC). - ExternalName : a CNAME alias to an external hostname (e.g., an RDS endpoint), useful for indirection. Traffic path: client resolves api.prod.svc via CoreDNS → ClusterIP → kube-proxy rules on the client's node DNAT to a ready pod IP → CNI routes to the pod. Only Ready pods are in the endpoints, which is why readiness probes are the key to zero-downtime deploys. Long-lived connections (HTTP/2, gRPC, WebSockets) pin to one pod; use a

Labels ( app , version , tier , team ) connect objects: Services select pods by label; Deployments own pods by label; policies and monitoring filter by label. Keep a consistent scheme (the app.kubernetes.io/ recommended labels). Namespaces separate environments or teams within a cluster with their own RBAC, quotas and network policies; prod and staging in one cluster is common for small teams, separate clusters for stricter isolation.

t: Health Probes, Autoscaling and Rolling Deployments
x: Kubernetes' self-healing and scaling only work as well as the signals you give it. Wrong probes restart healthy pods or send traffic to unready ones; wrong autoscaling thrashes or never scales; missing disruption budgets let a node drain take out every replica at once; a rollout strategy chosen by default drops requests. This chapter is the tuning guide.

t: Health Probes, Autoscaling and Rolling Deployments
x: title The three probes columns Probe Question On failure Should check Should not check startup Has the app finished starting? Keeps liveness/readiness disabled until it passes; container killed if it never passes within failureThreshold × period The same endpoint as readiness, with a generous threshold readiness Can this pod serve traffic right now? Pod removed from Service endpoints (no restart) Config loaded; warmed up; not draining; critical dependency reachable with a short timeout (judgement call) Slow or flaky things; anything that would mark all pods unready at once during a dependency blip (consider) liveness Is the process wedged beyond recovery? Container restarted (with backoff) A trivial in-process check: the event loop responds Dependencies (database, cache); anything that fails during load spikes The classic failure: a liveness probe that calls the database. The database has a 30-second hiccup; every pod fails liveness; Kubernetes restarts them all; cold starts amplify the outage. Liveness should fail only when a restart would help. Readiness including dependencies is a trade: it stops sending traffic to pods that would fail anyway (good) but if the dependency is down for everyone, all pods go unready and the load balancer returns 503 instead of the app's own error (sometimes fine, sometimes worse). Many teams make readiness check only local state plus a cached dependency status, and surface dependency health via metrics (Part XI chapter 5). Timing: periodSecond

x: The HPA adjusts a Deployment's replica count to hold a metric at a target: CPU utilisation (relative to requests , so requests must be set honestly), memory, or custom/external metrics (requests per second from the ingress, queue depth from SQS via KEDA or the external metrics API). apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: { name: api, namespace: prod } spec: scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api } minReplicas: 3 # ≥ number of AZs for availability maxReplicas: 30 metrics: - type: Resource resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60 } } - type: Pods pods: { metric: { name: http_requests_per_second }, target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "200" } } behavior: scaleUp: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0, policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 60 }] } # double fast scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300, policies: [{ type: Pods, value: 2, periodSeconds: 120 }] } # shrink slowly Rules: target 50–70% CPU to leave headroom for the scale-up delay (pods take time to start and warm); scale up fast and down slow; set minReplicas for availability, not cost; do not set the Deployment's replicas field when an HPA manages it (every apply would reset it); for workers, scale on queue depth (KEDA makes this straightforward: ScaledObject on SQS queue length, scaling to zero when idle). Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommends (or sets) requests from observed usage; use it in recommendation mo

t: Health Probes, Autoscaling and Rolling Deployments
x: The HPA adds pods; something must add nodes when pods go Pending. Cluster Autoscaler grows and shrinks node groups (ASGs) based on pending pods and utilisation. Karpenter (AWS-originated, now CNCF) provisions right-sized nodes directly from pending pod requirements in seconds, consolidates underused nodes, and mixes instance types and Spot; it is the better default on EKS for most teams. Both need pods with accurate requests , PodDisruptionBudgets so consolidation does not break availability, and limits on how far they may scale (cost guardrails). Fargate profiles avoid node management entirely for pods matching a selector, at a higher per-pod price and with some limitations (no DaemonSets, no privileged, slower start).

t: Health Probes, Autoscaling and Rolling Deployments
x: Nodes get drained for upgrades, Spot reclaims, autoscaler consolidation. Protect services: - PodDisruptionBudget : minAvailable: 2 (or maxUnavailable: 1 ) stops voluntary evictions from taking too many replicas at once. Without a PDB, a node drain can evict all replicas of a 2-replica service together. - Topology spread across zones and nodes (chapter 9's topologySpreadConstraints ), or pod anti-affinity, so one AZ or node failure leaves capacity. - Replicas ≥ 2 , ideally 3 across 3 AZs, for anything user-facing. - Graceful shutdown handling (chapter 9) so evictions do not drop requests. apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget metadata: { name: api, namespace: prod } spec: minAvailable: 2 selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }

t: Health Probes, Autoscaling and Rolling Deployments
x: Rolling update (Deployment default): maxSurge / maxUnavailable control the pace. maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 keeps full capacity; maxUnavailable: 25% saves resources at the cost of capacity. Combined with clean probes and shutdown, this is zero-downtime for most services. Monitor rollout status in CI and alert on progressDeadlineExceeded . Blue-green : run the new version as a separate Deployment (green) alongside the old (blue); switch the Service selector (or the Ingress backend) when green is verified; keep blue for instant rollback. Costs double capacity briefly; gives atomic switch and trivial rollback. Argo Rollouts and Flagger automate it. Canary : route a small percentage of traffic (via Gateway API weights, a service mesh, or Argo Rollouts/Flagger with an ingress that supports weighting) to the new version; watch error rate and latency metrics; promote in steps or abort automatically. The strongest protection against bad releases; requires good metrics and an L7 router that supports weights. Part X chapter 7 compares strategies platform-independently. Recreate : stop all old pods, then start new ones. Downtime; only for singletons that cannot run two versions.

x: kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous ReplicaSet in seconds; with GitOps (Argo CD, Flux) you revert the Git commit and the controller reconciles, which keeps the audit trail. Rollback is only safe if the previous version is compatible with the current database schema (expand/contract migrations, Part X chapter 8) and with any config changes shipped alongside. Test rollback in staging as part of every release.
