- Explain what Helm adds over raw manifests: packaging, templating, values, releases and upgrades. - Write a chart for your own application and consume third-party charts safely. - Operate releases: install, upgrade, rollback, diff, and integrate with CI/GitOps. - Know Helm's limits and the alternatives (Kustomize, GitOps tools). ::: Chapters 9 and 10. :::

A production service needs a Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret references, ServiceAccount, HPA, PDB and maybe NetworkPolicy: ten YAML files that differ slightly per environment (replicas, hostnames, resource sizes) and must be applied and upgraded as a unit. Copy-pasting manifests per environment drifts; sed scripts rot. helm packages manifests as a chart with templates and a values file, installs them as a named release tracked in the cluster, and upgrades or rolls back the whole set atomically.

- Chart : a directory ( Chart.yaml , values.yaml , templates/ ) or a packaged .tgz , versioned (chart version) and declaring the app version. - Values : parameters with defaults in values.yaml , overridden per environment ( -f values-prod.yaml , --set key=value ). - Templates : Go templates rendering Kubernetes manifests from values and built-in objects ( .Release.Name , .Chart.Version ). - Release : an installed instance of a chart in a namespace, with revision history stored as Secrets in the cluster. - Repository / OCI registry : where charts are published (ECR supports OCI charts).

charts/app/ Chart.yaml values.yaml values-staging.yaml values-prod.yaml templates/ _helpers.tpl deployment.yaml service.yaml ingress.yaml serviceaccount.yaml hpa.yaml pdb.yaml configmap.yaml externalsecret.yaml NOTES.txt @file: Chart.yaml apiVersion: v2 name: app description: Client App API type: application version: 1.8.0 # chart version: bump on any template/default change appVersion: "2.4.0" # the application version (informational; the image tag comes from values) @file: values.yaml (defaults; environment files override) image: repository: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/client/app tag: "" # REQUIRED at deploy time: set to the immutable build tag/digest replicaCount: 3 resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi } limits: { memory: 512Mi } autoscaling: { enabled: true, minReplicas: 3, maxReplicas: 30, targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 60 } pdb: { enabled: true, minAvailable: 2 } ingress: enabled: true className: alb host: "" # per environment certificateArn: "" group: prod-shared serviceAccount: create: true annotations: {} # eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn for IRSA, per environment config: LOG_LEVEL: info ENV: prod externalSecrets: enabled: true store: aws-secretsmanager secretKey: prod/app/db probes: { readinessPath: /health/ready, livenessPath: /health/live } @file: templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt) apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: {{ include "app.fullname" . }} labels: {{- include "app.labels" . | nindent 4 }} spec: {{- if not .Values.a

Most platform components ship as charts: ingress controllers, cert-manager, external-dns, Prometheus stack, External Secrets Operator, Argo CD. Rules: - Pin chart versions in your deployment repository ( helm upgrade … --version 4.11.2 , or in an umbrella chart's Chart.yaml dependencies with exact versions); never float. - Read the values before installing; defaults are often permissive (cluster-wide RBAC, public LoadBalancers) or undersized. - Keep your overrides in Git ; treat chart upgrades like dependency upgrades (changelog, staging first). - Prefer OCI registries or well-known repositories; verify provenance where charts are signed; mirror charts you depend on into your own registry for air-gapped or reliability reasons. - Render and review : helm template to see exactly what will be applied; scan rendered manifests with policy tools (kube-score, Polaris, Checkov) in CI.

Helm is imperative by itself ( helm upgrade from a CI job). With Argo CD or Flux , you declare "this chart, this version, these values" in Git and the controller reconciles the cluster continuously, with drift detection, a UI showing sync status, and rollback by Git revert. The pattern most mature teams use: application charts in the application repository, environment values and platform charts in a deployment repository, Argo CD or Flux applying them. CI builds images and updates the image tag in the deployment repository (a commit, often automated); the GitOps controller deploys. The audit trail is Git.

- Kustomize (built into kubectl): overlays patching base manifests per environment; no templating language, no release tracking; simpler for teams that dislike templates. Often used with Helm (render a chart, then patch with Kustomize). - Plain manifests with GitOps : viable for small numbers of services. - CDK8s, Pulumi, Jsonnet : generate manifests from real programming languages. - Operators : for complex stateful software, prefer an operator (CloudNativePG, Strimzi) over a chart that merely installs it.

- Floating chart versions and image tags. - Secrets in values.yaml committed to Git (use External Secrets or SOPS-encrypted values files). - Installing without reading defaults; a public LoadBalancer or cluster-admin RBAC appears. - Templating logic so complex the chart is unreadable; keep charts boring and push complexity to values validation ( values.schema.json ). - Forgetting the config checksum; config changes without pod restarts. - helm upgrade without --atomic / --wait ; CI passes, pods crash. - Manual kubectl edit on Helm-managed resources; the next upgrade reverts it (or fails on conflict). questions What does Helm track in the cluster that raw kubectl apply does not? options Pod logs Releases with revision history, enabling atomic upgrades and rollbacks of the whole set of manifests Node health Image digests answer explain Release metadata is stored as Secrets in the release namespace. Why add a checksum of the ConfigMap as a pod template annotation? options Security So a config change alters the pod template and triggers a rolling update; otherwise env-based config is not picked up Faster rendering Helm requires it answer explain Pods read env at start; the annotation forces replacement. What do `--atomic --wait` do on `helm upgrade`? options Speed up the upgrade Wait for resources to become ready and automatically roll back the release if they do not within the timeout Skip hooks Delete old pods immediately answer explain The production-safe invocation. How shoul

1. Write a chart for an application with the structure above, including values.schema.json to make image.tag and ingress.host required. Lint, template and validate it offline. 2. Install it with --atomic --wait , then deploy a broken image tag and watch Helm roll back automatically. 3. Set up Argo CD (or Flux) on a local cluster pointing at a Git repository containing the chart and values; change a value in Git and watch it reconcile; revert the commit to roll back.

- Apply a defence-in-depth baseline to a cluster: authentication and RBAC, pod security standards, network policies, secrets handling, supply chain controls, node and control-plane hardening. - Map Kubernetes identities to cloud IAM safely (IRSA / Pod Identity) and avoid over-privileged service accounts. - Use admission policy to make the secure configuration the only configuration. - Audit a cluster against the common misconfigurations. ::: Chapters 7 to 12; Part IV chapters 1, 7, 17 and 18. :::

A Kubernetes cluster concentrates every workload, secret and credential of a platform behind one API. Its defaults favour getting things running: pods run as root, every pod can talk to every pod, service accounts are auto-mounted, and anyone with kubectl access to a namespace can read its Secrets. A cluster secured only by its defaults is a single compromised container away from a full platform breach. The controls below are layered so that each failure is contained.

title Kubernetes security layers layers Cloud and cluster perimeter summary Private API endpoint (or restricted CIDRs), control plane logging, node security groups, IMDSv2 on nodes, encrypted etcd. EKS: enable control plane audit logs to CloudWatch; private endpoint access with a bastion/VPN or restricted public CIDRs; KMS envelope encryption for Secrets; nodes in private subnets. Authentication and RBAC summary Who may call the API and what they may do. EKS access entries map IAM principals to Kubernetes groups; SSO for humans. RBAC Roles per namespace with least privilege; ClusterRoles only for platform operators. No long-lived kubeconfig tokens. Workload identity summary Pods get AWS permissions via IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, scoped per service account. Never grant AWS permissions to the node role for workloads; a compromised pod would inherit them. Block pod access to the node's instance metadata. Pod security summary Non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, read-only root, seccomp; enforced by Pod Security Admission or policy engines. The Pod Security Standards 'restricted' profile is the target for application namespaces. Network policy summary Default deny within namespaces; explicit allows between services; egress restrictions. Requires a CNI that enforces policies (VPC CNI with network policy enabled, Calico, Cilium). Secrets summary External store as source of truth; etcd encryption; tight RBAC on Secrets; no secrets in manifests. Chapter 10. Supply c

Humans authenticate via the identity provider (EKS: IAM principals through SSO mapped by access entries with access policies, or OIDC directly). Map groups, not individuals; keep cluster-admin for a break-glass group with alerts on use. Developers get namespace-scoped roles: read pods/logs, maybe exec in staging, no Secrets read in production. apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: { name: developer, namespace: prod } rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: [pods, pods/log, services, configmaps, events] verbs: [get, list, watch] - apiGroups: [apps] resources: [deployments, replicasets] verbs: [get, list, watch] # no secrets; no pods/exec in prod; no create/delete --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: { name: developers, namespace: prod } subjects: [{ kind: Group, name: "eng-developers", apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }] roleRef: { kind: Role, name: developer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io } Audit RBAC: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:api ; tools like rbac-lookup , kubectl-who-can . Watch for wildcards ( verbs: [" "] ), cluster-admin bindings, and permission to create pods or pods/exec (which is effectively root in the namespace and, with host mounts, on the node).

Each service account that needs AWS access gets its own IAM role via IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts: the cluster's OIDC provider issues projected tokens the SDK exchanges with STS) or EKS Pod Identity (an agent on the node brokers role credentials per pod; simpler setup, fewer IAM trust policy edits). Either way: one role per workload, resource-scoped policies (Part IV chapter 18), and no workload permissions on the node instance role . Block pods from the node's IMDS (set hop limit to 1 on nodes, or use the VPC CNI's network policy, or Pod Identity's IMDS restrictions) so a pod cannot steal node credentials. apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: api namespace: prod annotations: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/prod-api # IRSA automountServiceAccountToken: false # pods that do not call the Kubernetes API should not have a token at all

The Pod Security Standards define three profiles: privileged, baseline, restricted. Pod Security Admission (built-in) enforces them per namespace via labels: apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: prod labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted restricted requires: non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped (NET BIND SERVICE allowed), seccomp RuntimeDefault or Localhost, no host namespaces or host paths, restricted volume types. The pod spec in chapter 9 complies. Platform namespaces (CNI, logging agents) legitimately need privileged or baseline ; keep them separate. For richer policy (require labels, restrict registries, verify signatures, forbid latest , require resource limits, mutate defaults), use Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper : apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1 kind: ClusterPolicy metadata: { name: restrict-registries } spec: validationFailureAction: Enforce rules: - name: only-our-ecr match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] } validate: message: "images must come from our ECR and not use :latest" pattern: spec: containers: - image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/* & !*:latest" Admission policy turns "we recommend non-root" into "non-root or it does not run".

Default Kubernetes networking is flat: a compromised frontend pod can connect to the database pod or the internal admin service directly. NetworkPolicy restricts pod-to-pod and egress traffic, enforced by a capable CNI (enable the VPC CNI's network policy feature on EKS, or run Calico/Cilium). # Default deny all ingress and egress in the namespace apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: prod } spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] --- # Allow DNS egress for everything (needed once default deny is on) apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: { name: allow-dns, namespace: prod } spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: [Egress] egress: - to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } } }] ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }] --- # api: ingress from the ingress controller / ALB; egress to RDS and the Internet on 443 apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: { name: api, namespace: prod } spec: podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } } policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] ingress: - from: [{ ipBlock: { cidr: 10.20.0.0/18 } }] # ALB nodes in public subnets (target-type ip) ports: [{ port: 8000 }] egress: - to: [{ ipBlock: { cidr: 10.20.128.0/22 } }] # data subnets (RDS, ElastiCache) ports: [{ port: 5432 }, { port: 6379 }] - to: [{ ipBlock: { cidr: 0.0.0.0/0, except: [10.0.0.0/8, 169.254.169.254/32] } }] # Interne

Chapter 10: external store as source of truth; etcd encryption with KMS; RBAC denying get secrets to developers in production; automountServiceAccountToken: false ; no secrets in Git or Helm values; scan manifests for leaked secrets.

Only images from your registry (policy above); signatures verified at admission (Kyverno verifyImages with cosign; or Sigstore policy-controller); scanned in CI and continuously (chapter 7); SBOMs attached; base images pinned. Platform charts pinned and reviewed (chapter 12).

Nodes: private subnets, no SSH (SSM if needed), minimal AMIs (EKS-optimised, Bottlerocket), regular rotation via managed node group updates or Karpenter drift, IMDSv2 required with hop limit 1, encrypted root volumes, security groups allowing only cluster traffic. Control plane: audit logging enabled and shipped; API endpoint private or CIDR-restricted; cluster version within support; add-ons current.

Enable Kubernetes audit logs (EKS control plane logging: audit , authenticator ) and alert on: exec / attach into production pods, Secret reads by humans, RBAC changes, creation of privileged pods, access denied spikes. Falco or GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring detects shells in containers, unexpected outbound connections, writes to sensitive paths, and privilege escalation attempts.

# Kubernetes cluster security review - API endpoint private or CIDR-restricted; control plane audit logs on and shipped. - Humans authenticate via SSO; RBAC by group; no cluster-admin for daily use; no wildcard verbs in application roles. - Secrets encrypted in etcd with KMS; developers cannot read production Secrets; external store is the source of truth. - Each workload has its own ServiceAccount and IAM role (IRSA/Pod Identity); node role grants nothing to workloads; pod access to IMDS blocked. - Application namespaces enforce Pod Security 'restricted'; platform namespaces separated. - Admission policy: approved registries only, no :latest, resource requests/limits required, signatures verified. - Default-deny NetworkPolicies with explicit allows; egress to metadata endpoint blocked. - Images scanned in CI and continuously; critical findings block; base images pinned by digest. - Nodes private, no SSH, IMDSv2 hop limit 1, encrypted disks, rotated on a schedule; cluster version in support; add-ons current. - Runtime detection (Falco/GuardDuty) and alerts on exec, Secret reads, RBAC changes. - automountServiceAccountToken false where the API is not used. - PDBs and topology spread for availability (not security, but reviewed together).

- Workload AWS permissions on the node role. - Pod Security not enforced; most pods root with all capabilities. - Flat network; no NetworkPolicy; metadata endpoint reachable from pods. - cluster-admin bound to a group everyone is in. - Secrets readable by developers; secrets in Helm values in Git. - Public API endpoint with 0.0.0.0/0 . - Audit logs off; no idea who ran kubectl exec in prod. - Clusters left on unsupported versions because upgrades are scary. questions Why should workloads never rely on the node's IAM role for AWS access? options It is slower Every pod on the node would share those permissions; a compromised pod inherits them. Use IRSA or Pod Identity per service account Nodes have no roles It costs more answer explain Per-workload identity is least privilege at the pod level. What does the Pod Security 'restricted' profile require? options Privileged containers Non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, seccomp, no host namespaces or host paths Only resource limits Signed images answer explain Enforce it per namespace with Pod Security Admission labels. What is the first NetworkPolicy to apply in a namespace, and what must accompany it? options Allow all Default deny ingress and egress, accompanied by an allow for DNS egress Deny DNS Allow egress to 0.0.0.0/0 answer explain Default deny without DNS breaks name resolution for every pod. Which control turns 'pods should not run as root' from a recommendation into a guarantee? options Documentation

1. On a local cluster, label a namespace restricted and try to deploy a root container; fix the spec until it is admitted. 2. Apply default-deny network policies and allow only what your app needs; verify with a debug pod that the database port is unreachable from an unrelated pod. 3. Run a cluster audit tool (kube-bench for CIS, Polaris or Kubescape for workloads) and triage the findings against the checklist.

Kubernetes Failure Scenarios and When Not to Use Kubernetes
x: The container exits repeatedly; Kubernetes restarts with exponential backoff (10 s → 5 min). Almost always application-level: bad config or missing env/secret (fail-fast validation prints the reason), cannot reach a dependency at start, wrong command or entrypoint, missing file, permission denied under non-root, port already in use within the pod. logs --previous holds the answer; if the container dies before logging (exec format error, missing binary), describe shows the exit code and reason.

Causes: requests far below actual usage (set memory requests equal to limits), logs filling the node disk (ephemeral-storage limits, log rotation), too many pods per node. Budget several engineer-days per upgrade, several times a year, forever. - Platform components : a dozen controllers to install, configure, secure, monitor and upgrade before the first application runs well. - Expertise : debugging requires understanding the material in chapters 8–13; a team without it will be stuck during incidents. - Baseline cost : the control plane fee plus minimum nodes plus the platform pods' resources before any application load; small clusters are proportionally expensive. - Security surface : chapter 13's checklist is the minimum. - Multi-tenancy pitfalls : quotas, network policies and RBAC for every team. x: - Explain what cloud computing actually provides and the economic model behind it. - Describe AWS's global structure (Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations) and use it to design for availability and data residency. - State precisely who is responsible for what under the shared responsibility model, per service type. - Choose a Region for a client and understand the consequences of that choice. ::: Part I chapter 1; Part V chapter 1. :::

t: Cloud Fundamentals, Regions, Availability Zones and Shared Responsibility
x: Cloud computing is renting computing resources (compute, storage, networking, databases, and hundreds of higher-level services) by the hour or request, provisioned by API in minutes, from a provider that operates the physical infrastructure at a scale no single client could. The economic shift is from capital expenditure (buy servers, amortise over years, over-provision for peaks) to operating expenditure (pay for what runs, scale with demand, release what you do not need). The engineering shift is that infrastructure becomes software: everything is an API call, therefore everything can be versioned, reviewed, tested and automated (Part X). Service models: IaaS (virtual machines, networks, disks: EC2, VPC, EBS; you manage the OS and up), PaaS/managed services (RDS, ECS Fargate, App Runner; you manage the application and data), serverless/FaaS (Lambda, DynamoDB, S3; you manage code and configuration), SaaS (finished applications). Part V chapter 1's spectrum mapped onto AWS.

t: Cloud Fundamentals, Regions, Availability Zones and Shared Responsibility
x: title AWS physical and logical structure layers Region e.g. eu-west-1 (Ireland), us-east-1 (N. Virginia) summary A geographic area with multiple isolated data-centre clusters. Most services are regional: resources exist in one Region and do not replicate elsewhere unless you arrange it. Regions are the unit of data residency (your data stays in the Region unless you move it), of service availability (new services launch in some Regions first), of pricing (prices differ), and of large-scale failure isolation (Regions are independent). Over 30 Regions exist; a client typically picks one primary Region. Availability Zone e.g. eu-west-1a, 1b, 1c summary One or more data centres within a Region with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to the other AZs by low-latency (1–2 ms) private links. The unit of high availability. Designing across at least two AZs (ALB, ASG, RDS Multi-AZ, subnets per AZ) means an AZ-level failure (which does happen) degrades rather than destroys your service. AZ names are mapped per account (your 1a may be another account's 1c); AZ IDs (euw1-az1) are consistent. Local Zones, Wavelength, Outposts summary Extensions placing compute closer to users or on-premises. Niche for most client work: low-latency requirements in specific metros, or regulatory requirements to run on the client's premises. Edge locations 400+ points of presence summary CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator, WAF and Shield run here, close to users. Not a place you deploy

t: Cloud Fundamentals, Regions, Availability Zones and Shared Responsibility
x: - Choose the Region by: data residency and client policy (EU data in an EU Region), proximity to users (latency, Part II chapter 18), service availability (check that every service you need exists there), price (varies 10–30% between Regions), and the client's existing footprint. us-east-1 is the oldest, cheapest and most feature-complete, and also the most frequently involved in large incidents; it is also where CloudFront certificates and some global service control planes live. - Use multiple AZs by default for anything production: subnets in at least two (ideally three) AZs; ALB across them; application instances spread by the ASG or ECS; RDS Multi-AZ; ElastiCache with replicas in different AZs. The cost is modest (some cross-AZ data transfer charges, standby database instances) and it is the single biggest availability improvement available. - Multi-Region is a different order of complexity and cost (Part IX chapter 10). For most clients: single Region, multi-AZ, with backups copied to a second Region for disaster recovery (Part V chapter 11).

t: Cloud Fundamentals, Regions, Availability Zones and Shared Responsibility
x: An AWS account is the top-level container for resources and billing, identified by a 12-digit ID. The root user (email and password) owns the account and should be used only for the handful of tasks that require it, with hardware MFA, no access keys, and credentials locked away. Everything else happens through IAM identities (chapter 2) and, for humans, through IAM Identity Center SSO (chapter 3). Multiple accounts under AWS Organizations separate environments and clients (chapter 2). The console is for exploring and emergencies; the CLI and SDKs are for work; infrastructure as code is for anything that persists (Part X). Console-created resources are undocumented and unreproducible; treat them as technical debt from the moment they exist.

t: Cloud Fundamentals, Regions, Availability Zones and Shared Responsibility

Chapter 4 covers monitoring and the usual surprises. The free tier (12 months of small instances and permanent allowances on some services) is useful for learning and dangerous for assumptions: a "free" t2.micro behind a NAT gateway costs $35/month.

Services, prices and compliance differ; data residency is a legal matter. - "The free tier means free." - Structure accounts with AWS Organizations so environments and clients are isolated, billed separately and governed centrally. - Write and reason about IAM policies: identities, resources, actions, conditions, and the evaluation logic that combines them. - Apply least privilege with roles, permission boundaries and service control policies. - Audit IAM for the dangerous patterns. ::: Chapter 1; Part IV chapters 1, 7 and 18. :::

Every AWS resource is protected by exactly one mechanism: IAM. A wrong policy is a public bucket, a deleted database, a stolen credential with admin rights. IAM is also where most teams accumulate the largest invisible debt: policies copied from Stack Overflow with "Resource": " " , users with access keys from 2019, a single account where staging can delete production. Account structure and IAM discipline are the foundation everything in Part VII sits on.

An account is the strongest isolation boundary AWS offers: separate IAM, separate billing line, separate service quotas, a blast radius wall. AWS Organizations groups accounts under a management account with consolidated billing, Organizational Units (OUs) for structure, and Service Control Policies (SCPs) that cap what any identity in a member account can do, root included. title A reference organisation for a consultancy delivering client systems legend nodes label Management account billing, Organizations, SCPs Runs nothing. Holds the organisation, consolidated billing, SCPs and Identity Center. Access tightly restricted; root with hardware MFA. label Security OU log-archive, security-tooling log-archive: CloudTrail and Config logs from every account, immutable (Object Lock). security-tooling: GuardDuty/Security Hub delegated administrator, read-only cross-account roles for auditors. infra label Infrastructure OU shared-services, network Shared CI/CD runners, artifact registry, DNS for internal domains, Transit Gateway if used. label Workloads OU One OU per client or product, containing separate accounts per environment. label client-a-prod Production for client A. SCPs forbid leaving the Region allow-list, disabling CloudTrail, or creating IAM users. label client-a-staging Staging. Same shape, smaller sizes. Cannot reach prod resources. label sandbox-* Per-engineer sandboxes with budgets and automatic cleanup (AWS Nuke or scheduled teardown). Learning happens here, not in

- Principals : IAM users (avoid for humans; chapter 3), roles (assumed temporarily by services, federated users and other accounts), and AWS services. - Policies : JSON documents granting (Allow) or denying (Deny) actions on resources under conditions . Identity-based policies attach to users/roles; resource-based policies attach to resources (S3 bucket policies, KMS key policies, SQS queue policies, role trust policies) and can grant access to principals in other accounts. - Managed policies (AWS-managed like AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess , or customer-managed) are reusable; inline policies are embedded in one identity. Prefer customer-managed policies in IaC; avoid AWS-managed policies broader than needed ( AdministratorAccess , PowerUserAccess are not least privilege). - Permission boundaries : a policy that caps the maximum permissions an identity can have, regardless of what is attached. Lets teams create roles for their workloads without being able to grant more than the boundary allows. - Trust policies : on roles, defining who may assume the role (a service, an account, an OIDC provider, with conditions). - Session policies and STS : temporary credentials with optional further restrictions (chapter 3). // A least-privilege policy for an application role: specific actions, specific resources, conditions { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadWriteOwnPrefix", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws

When a request arrives, IAM evaluates every applicable policy. The logic, simplified for the same-account case: 1. Default deny : nothing is allowed unless something allows it. 2. Explicit Deny anywhere wins : SCP, permission boundary, identity policy, resource policy or session policy with a matching Deny ends the evaluation. 3. SCPs must allow the action (they do not grant; they filter). 4. Permission boundary (if present) must allow. 5. Identity policy or resource policy must allow (within one account, either suffices; across accounts, both the identity's policy and the resource's policy must allow). 6. Session policy (if present) must allow. Consequences: a resource policy can grant access without any identity policy within the account (how S3 bucket policies make buckets public even when no user has s3:GetObject ); an SCP can block an administrator; a Deny statement is the only way to carve exceptions out of a broad Allow. The IAM Policy Simulator and IAM Access Analyzer (policy validation, unused access findings, external access findings) are the tools to test and audit.

The pattern that makes IAM safe: no long-lived credentials; identity flows through roles . - Workloads: instance profiles, ECS task roles, Lambda execution roles, EKS pod identities (Part IV chapter 18). - Humans: SSO via Identity Center into permission sets (roles) with session durations (chapter 3). - CI: OIDC federation from GitHub Actions/GitLab into a deploy role (Part X chapter 2). - Cross-account: roles with trust policies naming the other account and an external ID; assume with STS (Part XIII chapter 9). - Services acting on your behalf: service-linked roles and service roles (RDS enhanced monitoring, Config, Backup). Audit: aws iam list-users should be empty or nearly so; aws iam generate-credential-report shows every user's key age and MFA status; Access Analyzer's unused-access findings list roles and permissions never exercised, which you remove.

aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent (require MFA for sensitive actions), aws:SourceIp / aws:SourceVpce (restrict where calls may come from; careful with services that call on your behalf), aws:PrincipalOrgID (allow only principals from your organisation in resource policies: the standard guard against cross-account exposure), aws:RequestedRegion (in SCPs), aws:ResourceTag / aws:PrincipalTag (attribute-based access control: a role tagged team=payments may touch resources tagged team=payments ), s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption , kms:ViaService , iam:PassedToService (which services a role may be passed to, a frequent privilege-escalation path when unrestricted), ec2:ResourceTag for instance-scoped operations.

IAM has dozens of ways a limited identity can become an administrator if certain permissions are granted carelessly: iam:PassRole plus the ability to launch compute (attach an admin role to an instance you control), iam:CreatePolicyVersion , iam:AttachUserPolicy , iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy on a privileged role, lambda:UpdateFunctionCode on a function with a powerful role, sts:AssumeRole on . Tools (Prowler, PMapper, Cloudsplaining) find these; the defence is scoping iam: actions to specific resources, using permission boundaries for any role that creates roles, and never granting PassRole on .

- One account for everything; staging credentials can destroy production. - AdministratorAccess on application roles "temporarily". - IAM users with access keys for humans and CI. - "Resource": " " on data-plane actions; iam:PassRole on . - Resource policies with "Principal": " " and no condition. - No SCPs; CloudTrail disabled by a compromised admin. - Root user with access keys or without hardware MFA. - Never reviewing unused permissions; roles accrete power forever. questions An identity policy allows s3:GetObject on a bucket, but an SCP on the account denies all S3 actions outside eu-west-1 and the bucket is in us-east-1. Result? options Allowed; identity policies win Denied; an SCP deny (or non-allow) overrides identity permissions Allowed only via the console Depends on the bucket policy answer explain SCPs cap what any identity in the account can do; an explicit Deny anywhere ends evaluation. What is a permission boundary for? options Encrypting policies Capping the maximum permissions an identity can ever have, so delegated role creation cannot exceed it Granting cross-account access Logging IAM changes answer explain Boundaries enable safe delegation of IAM administration. Why is iam:PassRole on \"*\" dangerous? options It is slow It lets the identity attach any role, including administrative ones, to compute it controls, escalating privileges It disables MFA It is not dangerous answer explain Scope PassRole to the specific roles a workload or deployer legitimately

x: - Work from a laptop and from code without long-lived access keys: STS, role assumption, SSO sessions, the credential chain. - Configure the AWS CLI and SDKs with named profiles for multiple accounts and roles. - Set up IAM Identity Center for a team with permission sets and MFA. - Handle credentials safely in scripts, CI and shared environments. ::: Chapter 2. :::

t: Temporary Credentials, the AWS CLI and IAM Identity Center
x: The access key pair ( AKIA… /secret) was the original way to call AWS APIs, and it remains the most common thing attackers find in repositories, laptops and CI logs. A leaked key is valid until someone notices and rotates it, which averages weeks. Temporary credentials expire on their own (15 minutes to 12 hours), are issued per session with an audit trail, and can be scoped further at issue time. Every AWS workflow in 2026 can run without a single long-lived key; this chapter shows how.

t: Temporary Credentials, the AWS CLI and IAM Identity Center
x: The Security Token Service issues short-lived credential triplets (access key, secret, session token ) through: - AssumeRole : an authenticated principal assumes a role, receiving credentials with the role's permissions for a session (default 1 hour, up to 12 as configured on the role). Used for cross-account access, privilege separation, and by SSO and CI. - AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity : exchange an OIDC token (from GitHub Actions, EKS, Cognito, Google) for role credentials. No AWS secret involved anywhere. - AssumeRoleWithSAML : federation from enterprise IdPs. - GetSessionToken : for IAM users to obtain MFA-protected session credentials (legacy). - Automatic : EC2 instance profiles, ECS task roles and Lambda execution roles deliver rotating credentials to the workload via metadata endpoints; the SDKs fetch and refresh them transparently. Every STS call appears in CloudTrail with the assumed role session name, so "who did this?" is answerable even through role chains, provided you set meaningful session names ( --role-session-name ana.lopez ).

t: Temporary Credentials, the AWS CLI and IAM Identity Center
x: IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) is the way humans should access AWS: a single sign-on portal, backed by its own directory or your IdP (Entra ID, Okta, Google Workspace via SAML/SCIM), granting permission sets (role templates) on specific accounts to users and groups, with MFA enforced and sessions of configurable length. Setup outline: enable Identity Center in the management account (or delegate administration to a security account); connect the IdP or create users; create permission sets ( ReadOnly , Developer , PowerUser , Administrator , each a managed or custom policy plus optional boundary); assign groups to accounts with permission sets; enforce MFA (prefer phishing-resistant: passkeys/security keys) and a session duration (1–8 hours; shorter for admin sets). Offboarding happens at the IdP; provisioning via SCIM keeps groups in sync. aws configure sso # one-time: start URL, Region, then pick account and role; creates a profile # ~/.aws/config # [sso-session company] # sso_start_url = https://company.awsapps.com/start # sso_region = eu-west-1 # sso_registration_scopes = sso:account:access # [profile client-a-prod] # sso_session = company # sso_account_id = 123456789012 # sso_role_name = Developer # region = eu-west-1 # output = json aws sso login --sso-session company # browser auth + MFA; caches a short-lived token aws sts get-caller-identity --profile client-a-prod export AWS_PROFILE=client-a-prod # tools and SDKs pick it up No access keys are created; the CLI

t: Temporary Credentials, the AWS CLI and IAM Identity Center
x: SDKs and the CLI look for credentials in order: explicit parameters in code (avoid), environment variables ( AWS ACCESS KEY ID / AWS SECRET ACCESS KEY / AWS SESSION TOKEN , or AWS PROFILE ), the shared config/credentials files ( ~/.aws/config , ~/.aws/credentials ) including SSO and role arn profiles, the container credential endpoint (ECS task roles), and finally the EC2 instance metadata (instance profile). Understanding the order explains the classic mistakes: a stale AWS ACCESS KEY ID in a shell overriding your SSO profile; a developer's ~/.aws/credentials baked into a Docker image; code that "worked locally" because the laptop had keys and fails on ECS because the task role lacks a permission. Rules: code never contains or loads credentials explicitly; local development uses SSO profiles; containers and servers use their attached roles; CI uses OIDC. If something needs an environment variable, it is AWS PROFILE or AWS REGION , never a secret.

t: Billing, Tagging, Budgets and Cost Monitoring
x: - Read an AWS bill and attribute cost to services, environments and clients. - Implement cost allocation tags, budgets and anomaly alerts so surprises are caught in hours, not at month end. - Recognise the recurring surprise charges and design to avoid them. - Estimate and present costs to clients honestly, including the cost of operating. ::: Chapters 1 and 2; Part V chapter 1. :::

t: Billing, Tagging, Budgets and Cost Monitoring
x: Cloud bills are itemised to the second across hundreds of line items, and nobody reads them until one is shocking. The two classic failures: a client receives a bill several times the estimate because of charges the estimate omitted (data transfer, NAT, load balancers, logs), or nobody notices a runaway resource (a forgotten instance, an infinite Lambda loop, a misconfigured log group) until it has cost thousands. Cost is an engineering property like latency: measured, attributed, alerted on and designed for.

t: Billing, Tagging, Budgets and Cost Monitoring
x: Charges accrue per account , per service , per usage type (e.g. EUW1-BoxUsage:t3.medium , EUW1-DataTransfer-Out-Bytes , EUW1-NatGateway-Hours ), per Region , and are visible in Cost Explorer (interactive, by day/month, filterable and groupable by service, account, tag, usage type), the Cost and Usage Report (hourly detail to S3 for Athena/QuickSight analysis), and Billing (invoices, credits, free tier usage). With Organizations, the management account sees everything consolidated; member accounts see their own. Monthly rhythm: on the first working day, review last month by service and account against the estimate; investigate anything over 10% off; note trends. Weekly: glance at the daily cost graph for steps.

t: Billing, Tagging, Budgets and Cost Monitoring
x: A tag is a key-value label on a resource. Cost allocation tags (activated in Billing) make tags available as dimensions in Cost Explorer and reports. Without them, you know that "EC2 cost $2,400" but not which client or environment. A minimal tagging standard, applied by IaC to every taggable resource: Tag Values Purpose --- --- --- Environment prod , staging , dev , sandbox Separate environment costs; policy conditions Project / Client client-a , internal-platform Attribution and chargeback Service api , worker , frontend , shared Which component Owner team or email Who to ask CostCenter client's code Their finance mapping ManagedBy terraform , console Find console-created drift Enforce with: default tags in the Terraform provider ( default tags ), AWS Config rule required-tags , SCPs that deny creating certain resources without tags ( aws:RequestTag conditions), and Tag Policies in Organizations. Some costs cannot be tagged (data transfer, some support fees); use account separation to attribute those.

t: Billing, Tagging, Budgets and Cost Monitoring
x: AWS Budgets : monthly cost budgets per account and per tag with alerts at thresholds (50/80/100% actual, and forecasted 100%), delivered to SNS/email/Slack. Also usage budgets (hours of a resource type) and RI/Savings Plan coverage budgets. Set one per environment and per client at minimum. Cost Anomaly Detection : machine-learned baselines per service/account/tag with alerts on deviations; catches the runaway resource in a day rather than a month. Enable it with a monitor per account and an alert threshold (e.g., anomalies over $50). CloudWatch billing alarms (us-east-1 only, on EstimatedCharges ): the oldest mechanism; still worth one alarm per account as a backstop. Free tier alerts : enable so learners and sandboxes get warned.

t: VPC Architecture: Subnets, Route Tables, Internet and NAT Gateways
x: The VPC is the network your whole AWS system lives in, and it is almost impossible to change later without downtime: CIDRs are fixed at creation (secondary CIDRs can be added, with constraints), subnets cannot be resized, and everything references them. Getting it right the first time (address plan, tiering, routing, egress) is one of the few infrastructure decisions that deserves slow, careful work before anything else is built.

t: VPC Architecture: Subnets, Route Tables, Internet and NAT Gateways
x: Inbound to the ALB : Internet → IGW (maps the ALB node's public IP to its private IP) → public subnet → ALB node (security group check) → ALB opens a new connection to a target IP in a private subnet → local route → target ENI (its security group check). The target never has a public IP and never sees the Internet directly. Outbound from an app task : task in private subnet connects to api.stripe.com → route table: 0.0.0.0/0 → nat- → NAT gateway rewrites source to its EIP → IGW → Internet. Replies traverse back through the NAT's connection table. If the destination is S3 and a gateway endpoint exists, the more specific prefix-list route wins and traffic never touches the NAT. App to database : task → 10.20.128.10:5432 → local route → RDS ENI; the database's security group must allow 5432 from the task's security group; the data subnet's route table is irrelevant for this (local). Nothing in the data subnet can initiate outbound to the Internet because no route exists. Lambda in a VPC : Lambda attaches ENIs (Hyperplane) in your private subnets; functions then follow the same routes (and need NAT or endpoints to reach AWS services; Lambda functions outside a VPC have Internet access by default but cannot reach your private resources).

t: VPC Architecture: Subnets, Route Tables, Internet and NAT Gateways
x: Dual-stack VPCs assign a /56 and each subnet a /64; instances get globally routable IPv6 addresses (no NAT needed). An egress-only Internet Gateway gives private subnets outbound IPv6 without inbound. Benefits: no NAT costs for IPv6 traffic, no IPv4 address charges, future-proofing. Costs: every security group and NACL needs IPv6 rules too; some AWS services and many third parties remain IPv4-only, so NAT stays for them. Enable dual-stack on new VPCs and ALBs; it is much harder to add later.

t: Security Groups, Network ACLs, Elastic IPs and VPC Endpoints
x: The VPC's routing decides where packets can go; security groups and NACLs decide whether they are allowed . Most AWS exposure incidents are a security group rule with 0.0.0.0/0 on the wrong port, and most "it cannot connect" tickets are a missing security group reference. The mechanics are simple; the discipline is in the design.

t: Security Groups, Network ACLs, Elastic IPs and VPC Endpoints
x: A security group is a stateful virtual firewall attached to elastic network interfaces (instances, tasks, RDS, load balancers, Lambda ENIs, endpoints). Rules are allow-only; traffic not matched by any rule on any attached group is denied; return traffic for allowed connections is permitted automatically. Inbound rules specify protocol, port range and a source (CIDR, prefix list, or another security group ); outbound rules likewise with a destination. Default: no inbound, all outbound.

x: Stateless, subnet-level, ordered allow/deny rules evaluated lowest number first; the default NACL allows everything. Because they are stateless, allowing inbound 443 requires allowing outbound ephemeral ports (1024–65535) for replies, and vice versa for outbound connections. Use them for: a hard deny of known-bad CIDRs; subnet-tier isolation that must hold even if a security group is misconfigured (data subnets accept 5432/6379 only from app subnet CIDRs); compliance requirements for subnet-level controls. Keep them few and documented; a forgotten NACL rule produces baffling one-directional timeouts (Part II chapter 15). Data-subnet NACL (example) Inbound: 100 allow TCP 5432 from 10.20.64.0/18 (app tier) | 110 allow TCP 6379 from 10.20.64.0/18 | 120 allow TCP 1024-65535 from 10.20.0.0/16 (replies to any outbound the tier makes, e.g. to endpoints) | * deny all Outbound: 100 allow TCP 1024-65535 to 10.20.64.0/18 (replies) | 110 allow TCP 443 to 10.20.0.0/16 (to interface endpoints for backups/monitoring) | * deny all

x: Instances in public subnets may receive a dynamic public IPv4 at launch (changes on stop/start). An Elastic IP is a static public IPv4 you allocate and attach (to an instance ENI or a NAT gateway), remappable on failure. Since 2024, every public IPv4 address costs ~$0.005/hour (~$3.60/month) , attached or not, which changes the calculus: minimise public IPs (private subnets plus a load balancer), use IPv6 where possible, and release unused EIPs. The ALB's own public IPs are managed by AWS and change; NLBs can hold EIPs when partners need static addresses (Part II chapter 13). Bring Your Own IP exists for enterprises with owned ranges. Elastic IPs are also the egress identity of your NAT gateways; record them in the runbook and in partner allow-list documentation, and manage them in IaC so a rebuild does not silently change them (Part II chapter 19 scenario).

Endpoints provide private paths: - Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB): a route-table entry via a prefix list; free; regional. Always create them. - Interface endpoints (PrivateLink, most other services): an ENI with a private IP per subnet/AZ and private DNS so the service's normal hostname resolves to it; ~$0.01/hour per AZ per endpoint (~$7.30/month/AZ) plus $0.01/GB. Create them for high-volume or sensitive services (ECR api + dkr, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, SSM trio for Session Manager, STS, KMS); for low-volume services the NAT may be cheaper. Attach sg-vpce allowing 443 from the tiers that need them. - Endpoint policies restrict which resources are reachable through the endpoint (e.g., only your buckets via the S3 endpoint, preventing exfiltration to an attacker's bucket). t: Compute: EC2, AMIs, Instance Types and Auto Scaling Groups
x: An AMI is the template an instance boots from. Three strategies: 1. Vendor AMI + user data : Ubuntu/Amazon Linux official image; everything installed at boot. Simple; slow boots (minutes of apt installs); fragile (repository outages break launches); drift between instances launched at different times. 2. Golden AMI : a pre-built image (Packer) with OS hardening, agents, runtime and sometimes the application; user data only sets environment-specific configuration. Fast, consistent boots; the image is scanned and versioned; rollback is "previous AMI". The right approach for fleets. 3. Containers on EC2 : the AMI is just the ECS/EKS-optimised image; applications are images (Part VI). The AMI still needs updating on a schedule. @file: packer/app.pkr.hcl (excerpt) source "amazon-ebs" "app" { region = "eu-west-1" instance_type = "m7g.large" source_ami_filter { filters = { name = "ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd-gp3/ubuntu-noble-24.04-arm64-server-*", virtualization-type = "hvm" } owners = ["099720109477"] # Canonical most_recent = true } ssh_username = "ubuntu" ami_name = "client-a-app-{{timestamp}}" encrypt_boot = true tags = { Project = "client-a", Role = "app", BuiltAt = "{{timestamp}}", GitSha = var.git_sha } } build { sources = ["source.amazon-ebs.app"] provisioner "ansible" { playbook_file = "ansible/harden-and-install.yml" } # Part V chapters 4, 5, 9, 10 provisioner "shell" { inline = ["sudo apt-get clean", "sudo rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*", "sudo cloud-init clean"] } } Lifecycle: bu

t: Compute: Lambda, ECS and Fargate, EKS and App Runner

Volume types: gp3 (default: 3,000 IOPS/125 MB/s baseline, independently provisionable up to 16,000/1,000), io2 Block Express (consistent high IOPS, sub-ms, for demanding databases), st1/sc1 (throughput-optimised/cold HDD for sequential big data), gp2 (legacy; migrate to gp3 for lower cost and consistent performance). Volumes are AZ-bound; attach to one instance (io2 multi-attach exists for clustered filesystems). Encryption via KMS: enable EBS encryption by default at the account/Region level so every volume and snapshot is encrypted without thinking. Snapshots are incremental, stored in S3 (durable, multi-AZ), crash-consistent (Part V chapter 6), and the basis of AMIs. Automate with Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup (schedules, retention, cross-Region/account copies, Vault Lock). Restore by creating a volume from the snapshot in the target AZ. Fast Snapshot Restore pre-warms for immediate full performance at a cost. Delete orphaned volumes (unattached, from terminated instances with delete on termination = false ) and snapshot sprawl; both are classic silent costs (chapter 4). Operations: resize online (volume modify, then grow the filesystem, Part V chapter 6); monitor VolumeQueueLength , BurstBalance (gp2), throughput versus the instance's EBS bandwidth cap (small instances cap EBS throughput regardless of volume type); use EBS-optimised instances (default on current generations).

A managed NFSv4 filesystem spanning AZs, mounted by many EC2 instances, ECS tasks (including Fargate via volume configuration) and EKS pods (EFS CSI). Use when an application genuinely needs a shared POSIX filesystem (legacy CMS uploads directories, shared build caches, certain ML pipelines, home directories); otherwise S3 is cheaper and more scalable. Modes: Standard (multi-AZ) or One Zone; throughput Elastic (pay for what you use; the modern default), Bursting, or Provisioned; Infrequent Access lifecycle to cut cost for cold files. Security: mount targets in private subnets with a security group allowing 2049 from clients, encryption at rest and in transit (TLS via the EFS mount helper), access points per application with enforced POSIX user and root directory, IAM authorisation for mounts. Backups via AWS Backup. Performance: per-operation latency is higher than EBS; metadata-heavy workloads (millions of small files, ls on huge directories) suffer; measure before committing.

t: Databases: RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB and ElastiCache
x: Aurora (PostgreSQL- and MySQL-compatible) separates compute from a distributed, self-healing storage layer replicated six ways across three AZs. Consequences: storage grows automatically to 128 TiB; up to 15 low-lag read replicas sharing the storage (failover in ~30 s to a replica, with a reader endpoint load-balancing reads); Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute in fractions of an ACU within seconds (excellent for spiky or low-average loads, and for dev/staging); Global Database replicates to other Regions with sub-second lag for DR and read locality; backtrack (MySQL) rewinds without restore; faster recovery; Aurora I/O-Optimized pricing for I/O-heavy workloads. The premium over RDS is roughly 20% on compute plus storage/I/O charges; it pays off when you need the replica scaling, the failover speed, the serverless elasticity, or global replication. For a small, steady client database, RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ is simpler and cheaper; Aurora is the upgrade path, not the default.

x: A fully managed key-value/document store with single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale, no servers, no connections, pay-per-request or provisioned capacity. The design discipline is inverted from relational: you model access patterns first , then design a partition key (and optional sort key ) so that every query is a lookup or a range on a key. There are no joins and no ad-hoc queries without a scan. # Single-table design sketch: tenant-scoped orders and their items # PK = "TENANT#t_7" SK = "ORDER#2026-03-14T10:21:07Z#ord_01HZX" → order header # PK = "ORDER#ord_01HZX" SK = "ITEM#1" / "ITEM#2" → line items # GSI1: PK = "CUSTOMER#cus_42" SK = "ORDER#2026-03-14..." → orders by customer table.put_item(Item={"PK": "TENANT#t_7", "SK": f"ORDER#{created}#{order_id}", "status": "pending", "total": "49.90", "GSI1PK": "CUSTOMER#cus_42", "GSI1SK": f"ORDER#{created}", "ttl": expires_epoch}) table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("PK").eq("TENANT#t_7") & Key("SK").begins_with("ORDER#2026-03")) Essentials: hot partitions come from low-cardinality keys (a tenant with 90% of traffic, a date as the whole key); GSIs add alternative access patterns (eventually consistent, own capacity); LSIs must be defined at creation; TTL expires items for free (sessions, idempotency keys, tokens); Streams feed Lambda for change events; transactions ( TransactWriteItems ) give atomic multi-item writes; conditional writes implement optimistic concurrency and create-once; on-demand capacity for unpredictab

Production configuration: cluster mode disabled with a primary and one or two replicas across AZs and automatic failover for sessions/caches up to a node's memory; cluster mode enabled (sharded) for larger datasets or throughput; encryption at rest and in transit; AUTH token or RBAC users (Redis 6+); private subnets with a security group from the app tier; maxmemory-policy chosen for the use ( allkeys-lru for pure caches, volatile-lru when some keys must persist); snapshots if the data matters (usually not for caches); Multi-AZ. ElastiCache Serverless removes node sizing for variable loads at a per-GB-hour and per-request price. Treat Redis as losable from the application's perspective (Part III chapter 8) and as a hard dependency only for sessions where you have made it highly available. Cost: cache.t4g.micro ≈ $12/month; a replicated cache.m7g.large pair ≈ $200+/month.

x: Chapter-length treatment in Part IV chapters 16–17; the AWS specifics: AWS managed keys ( aws/s3 , aws/rds ) are free and automatic but shared across your account's use of that service with no policy control; customer managed keys (~$1/month each plus requests) give you the key policy (who may administer and use), aliases , rotation (automatic yearly for symmetric keys; old material retained for decryption), grants for services, multi-Region keys for DR, and CloudTrail logging of every use. Use customer managed keys for anything regulated or client-sensitive: database, S3 data buckets, Secrets Manager, backups. Key policy must allow the account root (so IAM policies can grant use) and should deny deletion without a scheduled window; never make a key policy that locks out everyone (AWS can help recover, slowly). Deleting a key is scheduled 7–30 days out and is irreversible: data encrypted under it is gone. Alarm on ScheduleKeyDeletion and DisableKey .

Add data events selectively (S3 object-level for sensitive buckets, Lambda invocations, DynamoDB) because they are voluminous and billed. Integrate with CloudWatch Logs for metric filters and alarms on: root login, console login without MFA, IAM policy changes, security group changes, CloudTrail/Config/GuardDuty disabled, KMS key deletion scheduled, unauthorised API calls. CloudTrail Lake or Athena over the S3 bucket for investigations ("every action by this role in the last 30 days"). Retain 1 year hot, longer in S3 per policy (Part IV chapter 22).

Remediation actions (SSM Automation documents) can auto-fix some findings (close a public bucket, enable encryption). Aggregate to the security account for a single compliance view. Config is also your drift detector: "who changed this security group and when" is answered from its timeline when CloudTrail is too noisy. Cost: per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation; noisy resources (frequent ECS task changes) can make it expensive; exclude high-churn resource types if needed.

Findings include: credential exfiltration (instance credentials used from outside AWS), crypto-mining, communication with known command-and-control, port scanning, unusual API patterns (new Region, disabled logging), S3 anomalous access, brute-force logins to RDS, malware in EBS (Malware Protection). Enable in every Region of every account with a delegated administrator; route findings (severity ≥ medium) to a channel a human reads and high severity to paging; integrate with Security Hub; suppress known-benign patterns with suppression rules rather than ignoring the feed. It is inexpensive relative to what it catches and is often the first signal of a compromised key.

Inspector scans EC2 instances (via SSM agent), ECR images and Lambda functions for CVEs and network exposure, continuously. Macie discovers sensitive data (PII, credentials) in S3 buckets, useful for data-classification audits (Part IV chapter 23). Detective builds investigation graphs from GuardDuty findings. Audit Manager maps evidence to frameworks for compliance programmes.

t: Security Services: KMS, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, WAF and Shield
x: AWS WAF attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync and Cognito. A web ACL contains rules: managed rule groups (AWS Core Rule Set for OWASP-style patterns, Known Bad Inputs, SQL injection, Linux/PHP/WordPress-specific, Amazon IP reputation, Anonymous IP, Bot Control with its own pricing), rate-based rules (e.g. 2,000 requests per 5 minutes per IP, with scope-down to login paths for tighter limits), geo-match, IP sets, and custom rules on headers, URIs, bodies and labels. Start every rule group in count mode, review sampled requests and CloudWatch metrics for a week, then switch to block; keep an allow rule for health checks and known partners; log to S3/CloudWatch/Kinesis for investigation; expect to tune false positives (a legitimate JSON body containing SQL keywords). Cost: per web ACL, per rule, per million requests; Bot Control and Fraud Control cost more. WAF is a shield against commodity attacks and floods, not a substitute for secure code (Part II chapter 15, Part IV). Shield Standard is automatic and free: network/transport-layer DDoS protection for CloudFront, Route 53, ALB/NLB. Shield Advanced ($3,000/month per organisation plus data fees) adds enhanced detection, response team access, cost protection for scaling during attacks, and application-layer protections; justified for high-profile targets or contractual requirements, not for typical client systems. Architecturally, putting everything behind CloudFront and Route 53 gives you most practical DDoS resilie

t: Observability and Operations: CloudWatch, Logs, Alarms, X-Ray, Systems Manager and AWS Backup
x: Every AWS service publishes metrics to CloudWatch namespaces ( AWS/ApplicationELB , AWS/ECS , AWS/RDS , AWS/Lambda , AWS/SQS …) at 1- or 5-minute resolution (enable detailed monitoring for 1-minute EC2 metrics). You add custom metrics via the CloudWatch agent (memory, disk, processes), the Embedded Metric Format (structured log lines that CloudWatch turns into metrics with no API calls: ideal for Lambda and containers), PutMetricData from SDKs, or OpenTelemetry exporters. Custom metrics are billed per metric per month; high-cardinality dimensions (one metric per user) get expensive fast. Metric math combines series (error rate = 5xx / requests); anomaly detection bands learn seasonality; Metrics Insights queries across dimensions with SQL-like syntax. Container Insights (ECS/EKS) and Lambda Insights add per-task/function resource metrics. The metrics that matter per component (Part XI chapter 4's golden signals): ALB request count, 4xx/5xx (ELB and target), target response time percentiles, healthy host count; ECS service CPU/memory utilisation and running task count; RDS CPU, connections, free storage, read/write latency, replica lag; SQS visible messages and age of oldest message; Lambda errors, throttles, duration p99, concurrent executions; application-level request rate, error rate and latency per route via EMF.

t: Observability and Operations: CloudWatch, Logs, Alarms, X-Ray, Systems Manager and AWS Backup
x: Log groups per application and environment ( /client-a/prod/api ), streams per task or instance; retention set on every group (defaults to never expire); encryption with KMS for sensitive logs; subscription filters to stream to OpenSearch, Kinesis or Lambda; Logs Insights for ad-hoc queries; metric filters turning log patterns into metrics (count of "level":"error" , or a specific exception); data protection policies to detect and mask PII (Part IV chapter 23). Structured JSON logs (Part XI chapter 1) make Insights queries trivial: fields @timestamp, request_id, route, status, duration_ms | filter status >= 500 | stats count() as errors, pct(duration_ms, 99) as p99 by route | sort errors desc Shipping: ECS awslogs driver or FireLens; Lambda automatic; EC2 via the CloudWatch agent (Part V chapter 9); EKS via Fluent Bit. Costs: ingestion is the dominant line ($0.50/GB in us-east-1 standard class; the Infrequent Access class is cheaper for logs you rarely query); storage per GB-month; Insights per GB scanned. Control volume with log levels and sampling, not by dropping errors.

t: Observability and Operations: CloudWatch, Logs, Alarms, X-Ray, Systems Manager and AWS Backup
x: X-Ray collects traces: segments and subsegments per request across services (ALB → ECS → RDS/SQS → Lambda), showing where time goes and where errors originate, with a service map. Instrument with the X-Ray SDK or, preferably, OpenTelemetry via the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), exporting to X-Ray (and optionally elsewhere); the trace header propagates through ALB ( X-Amzn-Trace-Id ), SQS message attributes and HTTP calls. Sample (1 request/second plus 5% by default) to control cost; always capture errors. Application Signals builds SLO dashboards and service-level views on top of these traces and metrics with minimal configuration. Part XI chapter 2 covers tracing design.

x: A fleet management toolbox for EC2 (and on-premises servers registered as managed nodes) via the SSM agent and an instance role: - Session Manager : shell and port forwarding without SSH, logged (Part II chapter 16). - Run Command : execute scripts across instances by tag (restart a service everywhere; collect diagnostics) with output in S3/CloudWatch. - Patch Manager : baselines, maintenance windows, compliance reports (Part V chapter 12). - State Manager and Automation : enforce configuration and run runbooks (AMI building, instance recovery, remediation of Config findings). - Parameter Store : configuration and secrets (chapter 12). - Inventory and Fleet Manager : what is installed where; a console view of nodes. - Incident Manager : on-call schedules, escalation, response plans integrated with alarms (an alternative to PagerDuty for AWS-centric teams). - OpsCenter : operational work items aggregating alarms and findings. For Fargate-based systems SSM matters less (no hosts), apart from Parameter Store and ECS Exec (which uses Session Manager under the hood).

t: Observability and Operations: CloudWatch, Logs, Alarms, X-Ray, Systems Manager and AWS Backup
x: A central policy-based backup service across RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EBS, EFS, S3, FSx, EC2 and more. Backup plans define schedules, retention, lifecycle to cold storage, and copy actions to other Regions/accounts; resource selections by tag ( Backup = daily ) so new resources are covered automatically; backup vaults with KMS encryption and Vault Lock (immutability: even administrators cannot delete backups before retention ends); restore testing plans that automatically restore backups on a schedule and run validation (the automated version of Part V chapter 11's drill); cross-account management via the organisation. Audit Manager/Backup Audit Manager reports compliance with backup policies. Use it as the single backup system for client accounts, with a locked vault in the backup account, and treat its restore-testing reports as evidence. resource "aws_backup_plan" "prod" { name = "client-a-prod-daily" rule { rule_name = "daily" target_vault_name = aws_backup_vault.prod.name schedule = "cron(0 2 * * ? *)" start_window = 60 completion_window = 240 lifecycle { cold_storage_after = 30, delete_after = 365 } copy_action { destination_vault_arn = aws_backup_vault.dr_other_region.arn, lifecycle { delete_after = 365 } } } } resource "aws_backup_selection" "by_tag" { name = "tagged" plan_id = aws_backup_plan.prod.id iam_role_arn = aws_iam_role.backup.arn selection_tag { type = "STRINGEQUALS", key = "Backup", value = "daily" } }

x: - Application code baked into the AMI, so every release needs an AMI build and staging/prod diverge. - Migrations in user data, running N times. - Grace period too short; refresh loops. - Hand changes on instances that the next refresh erases. - Secrets in user data or in the AMI. - Single AZ, single instance, outside an ASG. - No /version endpoint; nobody can confirm what rolled out. - Forgetting deregistration delay and lifecycle hooks; dropped requests on every deploy. questions Why is application code fetched at boot rather than baked into the AMI in this design? options AMIs cannot contain code So one hardened AMI serves every environment and version; releases do not require image builds, and rollback is a user-data change To make boot slower Packer forbids it answer explain The AMI is the platform layer; the artifact is the application layer. Where do database migrations run in an ASG-based deploy? options In each instance's user data As a separate one-off step before the fleet rolls, applying backward-compatible changes After all instances are replaced Never; schemas are fixed answer explain Running per instance causes races and repeated execution. How is rollback performed? options SSH into instances and restore files Apply the previous app_version to the launch template and let instance refresh replace the fleet Restore the database Reboot the instances answer explain Immutable infrastructure: rollback is a forward deploy of the old version. x: - Explain the relational model (tables, keys, constraints, relationships) and why it remains the default for business data. - Follow a query through the database: parsing, planning, execution, storage, WAL, buffer cache. - Know the practical differences between PostgreSQL and MySQL and choose between them for a client. - Use the SQL that production engineers actually need, including the features ORMs hide. ::: Part III chapter 1; Part I chapter 3. :::

t: Relational Database Fundamentals with PostgreSQL and MySQL
x: Business data is relationships: customers have orders, orders have items, items reference products, payments reference orders. The relational model stores each kind of thing once, in a table with a declared schema, and expresses relationships with keys; constraints make invalid states unrepresentable (an order cannot reference a customer that does not exist; a quantity cannot be negative); transactions make multi-table changes atomic; SQL answers questions nobody anticipated when the schema was designed. Fifty years on, it is still the best default for the system of record. NoSQL stores (chapter 2) trade some of these properties for specific gains; choose them deliberately, not by default.

t: Relational Database Fundamentals with PostgreSQL and MySQL
x: - Table (relation): a set of rows with declared columns and types. - Primary key : uniquely identifies a row. Prefer generated identifiers: bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY or UUIDv7 (time-ordered, avoids index fragmentation of random UUIDv4). Natural keys (email, national ID) change; use them as unique constraints, not as the primary key. - Foreign key : a column referencing another table's primary key, with declared behaviour on delete/update ( RESTRICT , CASCADE , SET NULL ). Enforced by the database, every time, regardless of which application writes. - Constraints : NOT NULL , UNIQUE , CHECK (qty 0) , exclusion constraints; the cheapest, most reliable validation you will ever write because it cannot be bypassed. - Indexes : separate structures for fast lookup (chapter 4). - Views : saved queries; materialised views : precomputed and refreshed. - Schemas (PostgreSQL namespaces): group tables ( app , audit , analytics ) for organisation and permissions. CREATE TABLE customers ( id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id), email citext NOT NULL, name text NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), UNIQUE (tenant_id, email) ); CREATE TABLE orders ( id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(), -- PostgreSQL 18 has uuidv7(); earlier: use an extension or app-generated tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id), customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT, status text NOT NULL CHECK

Connections are expensive (memory, startup), hence pooling (chapter 6). label parse, rewrite, plan title Planning detail The parser checks syntax and resolves names; the rewriter applies views and rules; the planner estimates costs for alternative plans (sequential scan vs index scan, join orders and algorithms) using table **statistics** gathered by ANALYZE, and picks the cheapest. Prepared statements cache plans. label chosen plan title Execution detail The executor runs the plan tree: scans, joins (nested loop, hash, merge), sorts, aggregates, returning rows to the client incrementally. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the plan with actual timings (chapter 4). label read pages title Buffer cache detail Data is read in 8 KB pages through shared_buffers and the OS page cache. A working set that fits in memory makes reads fast; one that does not makes every query a disk read (Part V chapter 10 scenario). label on miss: read from heap/index files title Storage detail Tables (heaps) and indexes are files; TOAST stores large values out of line. t: NoSQL Fundamentals with MongoDB and DynamoDB
x: "NoSQL" groups stores that relax parts of the relational model for specific gains: flexible or absent schema, horizontal partitioning built in, simpler data models that map to application objects, and in some cases extreme scale or latency. The gains come with losses: joins (do them in the application or denormalise), multi-record transactions (limited or absent), ad-hoc queries (only along designed access paths), and constraints (your code is the only guard). The decision is architectural, not fashionable: what does this data need? title Data models columns Model Examples Shape Strengths Costs Relational PostgreSQL, MySQL Tables, rows, declared schema, joins Integrity, flexibility of queries, transactions Scaling writes beyond one node is hard Document MongoDB, DocumentDB, Firestore, Couchbase JSON-like documents in collections; nested structures Maps to objects; flexible schema; horizontal sharding Joins are manual or expensive; duplication; weaker integrity Key-value / wide-column DynamoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Bigtable Items by partition key (+ sort key); columns per row Predictable latency at any scale; managed partitioning Access patterns fixed at design time; no ad-hoc queries Graph Neo4j, Neptune Nodes and edges Deep relationship traversal Niche; operationally specialised Search OpenSearch, Elasticsearch Inverted indexes over documents Full-text, faceting, aggregations Not a system of record; eventual consistency Time series Timestream, InfluxDB, TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL)

t: NoSQL Fundamentals with MongoDB and DynamoDB
x: Part VII chapter 11 covered DynamoDB's AWS mechanics. The design discipline: 1. List every access pattern ("get order by ID", "list a tenant's orders by date", "list a customer's orders", "find pending orders older than an hour"). 2. Choose a partition key with high cardinality and even traffic (tenant alone is dangerous: one big tenant becomes a hot partition; tenant + something, or order ID, spreads it). 3. Use the sort key for ranges and hierarchy ( ORDER , ITEM ), enabling begins with and between queries. 4. Add GSIs for alternative patterns (by customer, by status + date), accepting eventual consistency and extra write cost. 5. Single-table design co-locates related entities under shared keys to fetch them in one query; it is powerful and makes the data model hard to read for newcomers; document it in a table of entities → key patterns. 6. No scans in the request path; scans are for migrations and analytics exports. Consistency: eventually consistent reads by default (cheaper), strongly consistent on request for the base table (not GSIs); transactions across up to 100 items; conditional expressions for optimistic concurrency and uniqueness ( attribute not exists(PK) ); item size 400 KB. Capacity: on-demand for unknown or spiky load, provisioned with autoscaling for steady high volume (significantly cheaper at scale). TTL, Streams, PITR, Global Tables as covered. DynamoDB fits: serverless architectures, session/idempotency/rate-limit stores, event logs, high-scale key-bas

x: Distributed stores choose, during a network partition, between answering with possibly stale data (availability) and refusing to answer (consistency) (Part IX chapter 5). Document and key-value stores expose this through read/write concerns and consistency flags; the defaults are often the weaker, faster choice.
