- Design normalised schemas that model the business correctly, and denormalise deliberately for read paths. - Model one-to-many and many-to-many relationships, hierarchies, history and soft deletes. - Choose types for identifiers, time, money, text, enums and flexible attributes. - Evolve schemas safely over years without rewrites. ::: Chapter 1; Part III chapter 2. :::

Schema mistakes outlive code. A column that should have been a table, a missing tenant key, a float for money, a status string with twelve spellings, a soft-delete flag nobody filters on: each becomes a migration project once data exists. Good schema design is boring: a few principles applied consistently, documented, and reviewed before the first row is written.

Normalisation removes duplication so a fact lives in one place. In practice: each table represents one kind of thing; each column depends on the whole key; repeating groups become child tables; attributes of other things live in those things' tables. Third normal form is the working target for transactional schemas. The payoff is integrity (one update changes the fact everywhere) and flexibility (new queries do not require new copies). Denormalise deliberately for specific reads: a customers.order count maintained by trigger or application for a dashboard; a snapshot of product name and price copied into order items because an order must show what was sold then ; a materialised view for reporting. Each denormalisation is a documented decision with a maintenance mechanism and a reconciliation check.

- One-to-many : foreign key on the many side ( orders.customer id ). Index the foreign key (PostgreSQL does not do this automatically; MySQL does). - Many-to-many : a junction table with a composite primary key and both foreign keys ( order tags(order id, tag id) ), plus any attributes of the relationship ( added at ). Index both directions as needed. - One-to-one : usually the same table; a separate table for optional or sensitive data ( customer payment profiles ) or very wide rarely-used columns. - Hierarchies (categories, org charts): adjacency list ( parent id ) with recursive CTEs for most cases; closure tables or ltree for heavy traversal. - Polymorphic associations (a comment on an order or a product): avoid (target type, target id) without foreign keys; prefer separate junction tables per target or a supertype table. CREATE TABLE order_items ( order_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, line_no smallint NOT NULL, product_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id), sku text NOT NULL, -- snapshot: what was sold name text NOT NULL, -- snapshot qty integer NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0), unit_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (unit_cents >= 0), PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no) ); CREATE INDEX order_items_product_idx ON order_items (product_id); CREATE TABLE order_tags ( order_id uuid REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, tag_id bigint REFERENCES tags(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, added_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (order_id, tag_id) ); CREATE IND

Concern Use Avoid --- --- --- Primary keys bigint identity , or UUIDv7 when IDs are generated by clients or must be unguessable UUIDv4 on hot tables (random inserts fragment indexes); natural keys Public identifiers Prefixed random IDs ( ord 01HZX… ) or UUIDs; map to internal keys if needed Sequential integers exposed in URLs Time timestamptz (stored UTC); date for dates; interval for durations timestamp without zone; strings; epoch ints unless required Money bigint minor units with a currency char(3) , or numeric(19,4) float , double Text text with CHECK (length(x) <= n) where limits matter; citext for case-insensitive varchar(255) by reflex; char(n) padding Enumerations text with a CHECK constraint, or a lookup table (when values carry attributes or change often); PostgreSQL enum only if the set is truly static Magic integers; free text Booleans boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false Nullable booleans (three states) Flexible attributes jsonb with a GIN index, validated by application schema Entity-attribute-value tables; one column per possible attribute Large blobs S3 with a key column bytea in hot tables Arrays PostgreSQL arrays for small, owned lists Arrays as a substitute for junction tables

Every tenant-scoped table carries tenant id NOT NULL with it first in composite indexes and unique constraints ( UNIQUE (tenant id, email) ), foreign keys include it where child and parent must share a tenant (composite foreign keys), and row-level security enforces it (Part III chapter 15).

Soft delete ( deleted at timestamptz ): keeps data for recovery and references; every query must filter it (views or RLS help; forgotten filters are the classic bug); unique constraints need partial indexes ( UNIQUE (tenant id, email) WHERE deleted at IS NULL ); hard-delete on a schedule for privacy (Part IV chapter 23). Use when undo or referential integrity matters; otherwise hard delete. History : for "what did this look like on March 3rd?", either an audit/history table written by trigger or application on every change (row snapshots with valid from / valid to ), or event sourcing for domains that need it. Audit of who changed what belongs in a separate append-only table (Part IV chapter 22). Temporal tables (system-versioned) exist in MariaDB and via extensions in PostgreSQL. created at and updated at on every table, maintained by defaults and a trigger (or the application), are cheap and endlessly useful.

A schema with NOT NULL , CHECK , UNIQUE and foreign keys documents the business rules in the one place every writer must pass. Add COMMENT ON TABLE/COLUMN for meaning and ownership; generate schema docs from the catalogue. Name constraints explicitly ( orders status check ) so error messages and migrations are readable.

Schemas change for years. Habits that keep changes cheap: additive changes first (new nullable column, new table) and removal later (expand/contract, Part X chapter 8); no SELECT in application code; views for stable interfaces over changing tables when external consumers read the database (better: no external consumers of the database at all; use the API); avoid wide "god tables" (split by access pattern); keep lookup data in tables so adding a value is data, not a deploy; version JSONB document shapes with a schema version key.

# Schema review - Every table: primary key, tenant_id (if multi-tenant), created_at/updated_at, meaningful constraint names, comments. - Types per the table above: timestamptz, integer money, text with checks, booleans NOT NULL. - Foreign keys on every relationship with explicit ON DELETE behaviour; indexes on foreign keys. - Unique constraints express business uniqueness (scoped by tenant); partial where soft deletes exist. - Indexes match the known queries (tenant first; chapter 4), no speculative indexes. - Denormalisations documented with their maintenance mechanism. - No polymorphic (type, id) pairs without integrity; no EAV tables. - Soft-delete filtering strategy decided (view/RLS) and privacy hard-delete scheduled. - Public identifiers unguessable; internal keys stable. - Migration plan is additive; rollback considered.

- Missing foreign keys and indexes on them. - Enum-like strings with inconsistent casing and no check. - timestamp without time zone; servers in different zones; off-by-hours bugs. - Money in floats; totals that do not add up. - Soft-delete flag without a filtering mechanism; deleted users still receive emails. - One giant users table with sixty columns from every feature. - EAV or JSONB for everything; no constraints; every query a parsing exercise. - Schema designed around the first UI screen rather than the domain. questions Why copy the product name and price into order_items rather than joining to products? options Joins are slow An order must show what was sold at the time; products change later. This is deliberate denormalisation of a snapshot Products may be deleted To avoid foreign keys answer explain Historical facts are snapshots; current facts are references. The root cause is: options Soft deletes are impossible Queries forgot to filter deleted_at; the strategy (views or RLS) was never established The index is missing CASCADE deleted related rows answer explain Soft delete requires a mechanism that applies the filter everywhere, not developer memory. - Explain how B-tree indexes work and why they make equality and range lookups fast, and what they cost on writes. - Design composite, partial, covering and expression indexes that match real queries; know when GIN, BRIN and hash indexes apply. - Read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output and recognise the common bad plans. - Find slow queries in production and fix them methodically. ::: Chapters 1 and 3. :::

A query without a usable index reads every row (a sequential scan). On a thousand rows nobody notices; on ten million, a two-millisecond lookup becomes a two-second table scan that holds a connection, burns I/O, and under load takes the service down (Part V chapter 10's scenario). Conversely, an index on every column makes writes slow and wastes memory. Indexing is the art of matching structures to the queries the application actually runs.

A b-tree index stores the indexed column values in sorted order in a balanced tree whose leaves point at table rows. Finding a value is a few page reads from root to leaf (logarithmic in table size: a billion rows is roughly four levels), then following pointers to the heap for any columns not in the index. Because leaves are ordered, range queries ( BETWEEN , , prefix LIKE 'abc%' ) and ORDER BY on the indexed columns are also fast. Equality on a non-leading column, LIKE '%abc' , or a function applied to the column ( lower(email) = … ) cannot use a plain B-tree on that column. Every index costs: disk, memory (indexes compete with data for the buffer cache), and write amplification (every insert/update/delete touches every index on the table). An index that is never used is pure cost; pg stat user indexes shows usage.

An index on (tenant id, created at) serves WHERE tenant id = ? , WHERE tenant id = ? AND created at ? , and WHERE tenant id = ? ORDER BY created at , but not WHERE created at ? alone (the leading column is missing). Rule: equality columns first, then the range or sort column . For multi-tenant systems the tenant key leads almost every index. One well-chosen composite index usually beats several single-column indexes, because the planner can only combine single-column indexes with bitmap scans at extra cost.

Index only the rows a query cares about: CREATE INDEX ON jobs (created at) WHERE status = 'queued' is tiny and perfect for the worker's SELECT … WHERE status='queued' ORDER BY created at . Also the mechanism for unique constraints with soft deletes (chapter 3).

CREATE INDEX ON orders (tenant id, created at) INCLUDE (status, total cents) lets a query that reads only those columns be answered entirely from the index (an index-only scan ), never touching the heap, provided the visibility map says the pages are all-visible (so VACUUM matters here too).

CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email)) serves WHERE lower(email) = lower($1) ; CREATE INDEX ON events ((payload- 'type')) serves JSON attribute equality. The query must use the identical expression.

- GIN : inverted index for JSONB containment ( @ ), arrays, full-text search; larger and slower to update. - GiST / SP-GiST : geometric, range types, exclusion constraints, nearest-neighbour. - BRIN : block-range summaries for huge, naturally ordered tables (append-only time series); tiny indexes, good for range scans over time. - Hash : equality only; rarely better than B-tree. - pgvector (HNSW/IVFFlat) : vector similarity for embeddings.

EXPLAIN shows the planner's intent with cost estimates; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) runs the query and shows actual rows, times and I/O. Always use the second for diagnosis (on a copy of production data or in production with care; it executes writes too, so wrap in a rolled-back transaction). EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT o.id, o.total_cents FROM orders o WHERE o.tenant_id = 't_7' AND o.created_at > now() - interval '30 days' AND o.status = 'paid' ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 50; Limit (cost=0.56..95.12 rows=50 width=24) (actual time=0.041..0.412 rows=50 loops=1) Buffers: shared hit=58 -> Index Scan Backward using orders_tenant_created_idx on orders o (cost=0.56..2345.11 rows=1240 width=24) (actual time=0.040..0.405 rows=50 loops=1) Index Cond: ((tenant_id = 't_7') AND (created_at > (now() - '30 days'::interval))) Filter: (status = 'paid') Rows Removed by Filter: 12 Buffers: shared hit=58 Planning Time: 0.210 ms Execution Time: 0.450 ms Reading it: the index satisfied tenant and date (Index Cond) and the sort order (Backward scan, no Sort node); status was filtered after fetching (Rows Removed by Filter: 12, cheap here; if it removed 50,000 rows, add status to the index or a partial index); 58 buffer hits, zero reads: everything in cache; 0.45 ms. The estimate (1240 rows) versus actual (50, because of LIMIT) is fine. Patterns that signal trouble: Plan feature Meaning Fix --- --- --- Seq Scan on a large table with a selective filter No usable index, or stale statistics,

1. pg stat statements ordered by total exec time (what costs the most overall) and by mean exec time (what is slow per call); log min duration statement for the long tail; RDS Performance Insights for wait events and top SQL (Part VII chapter 11). 2. Reproduce with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) using realistic parameters (plans depend on values; a query fast for a small tenant may scan for a big one). 3. Fix in order: make the predicate sargable (no functions on the column unless expression-indexed; no implicit casts: WHERE id = '123' on a bigint column is fine, but WHERE text col = 123 is not); add or extend the right index; rewrite the query (avoid SELECT , OFFSET , NOT IN on nullable columns, correlated subqueries); batch N+1 patterns in the application; consider a materialised view for heavy aggregates. 4. Verify in staging with production-shaped data, deploy, and watch pg stat statements again. Creating an index on a live table: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids locking writes (takes longer, cannot run in a transaction; migration tools support it, chapter 7). Dropping unused indexes recovers write performance; confirm zero scans over a representative period first.

Autovacuum keeps statistics fresh and dead tuples cleaned; monitor n dead tup , last autovacuum times, and bloat ( pgstattuple , bloat queries); tune autovacuum to be more aggressive on hot tables ( autovacuum vacuum scale factor per table). REINDEX CONCURRENTLY fixes bloated indexes. Long-running transactions block vacuum (Part III chapter 13). Statistics targets can be raised for skewed columns.

InnoDB clusters the table on the primary key (secondary indexes point to the primary key, so a small primary key keeps secondaries small); EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON and EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) show plans; the optimizer trace helps; covering indexes behave similarly; prefix indexes exist for long strings; the slow query log and Performance Schema replace pg stat statements .

- No index on foreign keys (PostgreSQL); joins and cascading deletes scan. - Single-column indexes everywhere instead of the composite that matches the query. - Wrong column order (range first, equality second). - Functions on indexed columns in WHERE clauses. - OFFSET 100000 pagination (chapter: Part III chapter 2). - Speculative indexes "just in case"; write amplification and cache pressure. - Never looking at pg stat statements ; discovering slow queries from users. - CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a production table; writes blocked for minutes. - Testing plans on an empty development database where everything is a cheap sequential scan. questions Which query can use an index on (tenant_id, created_at)? options WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day' WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC WHERE lower(tenant_id) = $1 WHERE created_at::date = current_date answer explain The leading column must be constrained by equality; functions on columns defeat plain indexes. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 'Rows Removed by Filter: 480000' and 50 rows returned. What does it suggest? options The query is optimal The index is not selective enough; add the filtered column to the index or create a partial index The table needs VACUUM Use OFFSET answer explain Fetching and discarding hundreds of thousands of rows is the cost to eliminate. Why create indexes CONCURRENTLY on production tables? options It is faster It avoids taking a lock that blocks writes for the duration of the build I

t: Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks
x: - Atomicity : all statements in a transaction commit or none do; implemented by WAL and rollback of uncommitted changes on failure. - Consistency : a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another; constraints are checked (immediately or at commit for deferred constraints). Note: this is "constraints hold", not the distributed-systems meaning (Part IX chapter 5). - Isolation : concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states, to a degree chosen by the isolation level. - Durability : once committed, changes survive crashes; WAL fsync before commit acknowledgement ( synchronous commit , and synchronous replication for durability across nodes, chapter 8).

t: Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks
x: Both PostgreSQL and InnoDB implement multi-version concurrency control : readers see a snapshot of committed data as of their statement or transaction start, without blocking writers, and writers do not block readers. Updates create new row versions; old versions remain for transactions that might still need them (PostgreSQL in the heap, cleaned by VACUUM; InnoDB in undo logs, purged). Writers block writers on the same row (row-level locks) until the first transaction ends.

t: Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks
x: Row locks are taken by UPDATE / DELETE and by SELECT … FOR UPDATE (exclusive) / FOR SHARE / FOR NO KEY UPDATE / FOR KEY SHARE ; they last until commit. Table-level locks protect against conflicting DDL ( ALTER TABLE needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for many operations: everything waits behind it, and it waits behind any running query, which is how a "quick" migration freezes production; chapter 7). Advisory locks ( pg advisory xact lock(key) ) implement application-level mutual exclusion (one job runner per key) without a lock table. Patterns: - Atomic update instead of read-modify-write : UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = $1 AND balance = 100 RETURNING balance (Part III chapter 13). - Pessimistic lock for a workflow : SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the parent row, do work, commit; keep it short. - Queue consumption : FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many workers take different rows without blocking. - Optimistic concurrency : a version column; UPDATE … WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 ; zero rows means someone else changed it; the API returns 409 (Part III chapter 2). - Consistent lock ordering : when a transaction must lock several rows, lock them in a fixed order (sorted IDs) to avoid deadlocks.

t: Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks
x: Transaction A holds row 1 and wants row 2; B holds 2 and wants 1. The database detects the cycle after deadlock timeout (1 s) and aborts one with error 40P01 . Causes: inconsistent lock ordering, long transactions touching many rows, foreign key checks acquiring locks on parent rows, batch updates in different orders. Fixes: order locks consistently; shorten transactions; batch by sorted key; retry on deadlock (the aborted transaction is the victim, not a corruption). Diagnose from the PostgreSQL log ( log lock waits = on shows waits over a second with both queries) and pg locks joined to pg stat activity : SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocked.query AS blocked_query, blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, blocking.query AS blocking_query, now() - blocked.query_start AS waiting FROM pg_stat_activity blocked JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) > 0;

t: Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks
x: statement timeout (per role or session; e.g. 30 s for the API, longer for reports), lock timeout (fail fast instead of queueing behind a lock; essential in migrations), idle in transaction session timeout (kill connections that opened a transaction and went idle: the top cause of bloat and lock pile-ups, usually a bug or an interactive session left open). Set them on the application role, not globally, so administrative sessions can override.

t: Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks
x: synchronous commit = on (default) waits for WAL fsync; off risks losing the last few hundred milliseconds of commits on a crash in exchange for throughput, acceptable for some logging workloads, never for money. With replicas, synchronous standby names makes commits wait for a replica to confirm (zero data loss on failover at a latency cost; RDS Multi-AZ does this for you). fsync = off is never acceptable in production.

What can happen? options Nothing; transactions prevent it A lost update: both read 500, both write 400, one debit vanishes A deadlock A dirty read answer explain Make the write atomic (balance = balance - 100 WHERE balance >= 100) or use explicit locking/Serializable. Which anomaly does Repeatable Read NOT prevent in PostgreSQL? options Dirty read Non-repeatable read Write skew Phantom read answer explain Write skew involves disjoint rows; only Serializable detects it. What must application code do when using Serializable isolation? options Nothing special Retry transactions that fail with serialisation errors, with backoff Lock every table

- Explain why database connections are expensive and why unbounded connections take databases down. - Size application pools correctly across many instances and workers, and configure them for failover and idle timeouts. - Deploy an external pooler (PgBouncer or RDS Proxy) and understand transaction versus session pooling. - Diagnose and resolve connection exhaustion incidents. ::: Chapters 1 and 5; Part II chapter 6; Part VII chapter 11. :::

A PostgreSQL connection is a server process with its own memory (several MB), authenticated and configured at startup (tens of milliseconds, more with TLS). Opening one per request is slow and wasteful; keeping thousands open consumes memory and CPU on the database and degrades every query (PostgreSQL's performance falls as active backends exceed a few times the core count). max connections exists to protect the server, and when it is hit the error is immediate and total: FATAL: too many connections , for every new client. Connection exhaustion is one of the top three database incidents, and it is almost always caused by arithmetic nobody did.

A connection pool keeps a bounded set of open connections per process and lends them to requests: # SQLAlchemy / asyncpg pool settings worth setting explicitly engine = create_async_engine( url, pool_size=5, # steady connections per process max_overflow=5, # temporary extra under burst (total 10 per process) pool_timeout=5, # wait at most 5 s for a connection, then fail (503) rather than queue forever pool_recycle=600, # recycle connections every 10 min (below any idle timeout on the path: NAT 350 s, proxies, DB idle timeouts) pool_pre_ping=True, # validate before use: detect connections killed by failover or timeouts connect_args={"server_settings": {"application_name": "api", "statement_timeout": "30000"}}, ) The arithmetic: total connections = processes × (pool size + max overflow) × instances , plus workers, plus migrations, plus admin sessions, plus replicas' own needs. Example: 4 Gunicorn workers × 10 × 6 ECS tasks = 240 connections from the API alone, before workers. A db.t4g.medium RDS instance defaults to roughly 400 max connections (RDS derives it from memory). Scale the API to 12 tasks and the database rejects connections. Rule: compute the total for max autoscaling, keep it under ~70% of max connections , and remember that PostgreSQL performs best with far fewer active connections than that (often 2–4× cores); more connections than that means queueing inside the database rather than in your pool. Pool size per process should be small: an API worker handling I/O-bo

When many processes (dozens of tasks, hundreds of Lambda invocations) each need a pool, the total still exceeds what the database should hold. An external pooler multiplexes: thousands of client connections map onto a few dozen server connections. title Pooling modes columns Server connection assigned Supports Breaks Session For the client connection's lifetime Everything (prepared statements, SET, temp tables, advisory locks, LISTEN) Nothing, but gives little multiplexing Legacy apps that rely on session state Transaction For each transaction, returned at COMMIT/ROLLBACK Normal queries and transactions Session-level state: SET without LOCAL, session prepared statements (PgBouncer ≥1.21 supports protocol-level prepared statements), advisory session locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, temp tables across transactions The default for web applications Statement Per statement Autocommit single statements only Multi-statement transactions Rare; sharding middleware PgBouncer : lightweight, single-threaded (run several or use so reuseport ), configure pool mode = transaction , default pool size per database/user (20–50 is typical), max client conn high (thousands), server idle timeout , query wait timeout ; run it as a sidecar per host/task, or as a central service in the data tier with its own HA (two instances behind an NLB). Authenticate clients to PgBouncer ( auth type = scram-sha-256 , auth query ) and PgBouncer to PostgreSQL with TLS. RDS Proxy : managed, Multi-AZ, with IAM authentication, S

Multi-AZ failover changes the endpoint's address; existing connections die. Clients need: short DNS caching, pool pre ping or retry-on-connection-error with backoff, and a connect timeout so a dead address fails fast. Idle connections through NAT or firewalls die silently (Part II chapter 4); pool recycle below the shortest idle timeout plus TCP keepalives ( keepalives idle=60 in libpq) keep pools healthy. The database's own idle in transaction session timeout kills leaked transactions (chapter 5).

Each concurrent Lambda execution environment is a process with its own pool; 500 concurrent invocations means 500+ connections. Options: RDS Proxy (the standard fix), reserved concurrency to cap invocations, Data API for Aurora (HTTP, no connections), or DynamoDB for Lambda-heavy designs. Never let Lambda connect directly to a small RDS instance without a cap.

SHOW max_connections; SELECT count(*), state, application_name, usename, client_addr FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 2,3,4,5 ORDER BY 1 DESC; SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle in transaction') AS idle_in_txn, count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle') AS idle, count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'active') AS active FROM pg_stat_activity; SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS txn_age, application_name, left(query,80) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' ORDER BY txn_age DESC LIMIT 10; Interpretation: many idle connections from one application: pools oversized relative to need (lower pool sizes or add a pooler); many idle in transaction : application bug (transaction opened, I/O performed, never committed) or interactive sessions (set the timeout, fix the code); many active with long durations: slow queries or locks (chapter 4, 5), not a pooling problem per se; connections from unknown client addr : something else (a BI tool, a developer laptop) is consuming slots. Immediate relief: pg terminate backend the idle-in-transaction offenders; raise max connections only as a stopgap (it needs a restart on RDS via parameter group and costs memory). Structural fix: pool arithmetic, pooler, timeouts. title Autoscaling the API took down the database situation During a traffic spike, ECS scaled the API from 4 to 16 tasks. Within a minute the API began returning 503s with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections`. symptoms RDS

- Pools sized without multiplying by processes and instances. - No pool timeout ; requests hang when the pool is empty. - No pool pre ping /recycle; the first requests after failover or idle fail. - Lambda directly to RDS at scale. - Session-level SET behind a transaction-mode pooler; mysterious state leakage. - Raising max connections to 2,000 as the fix; the database slows for everyone. - Developers' and BI tools' connections uncounted. - No alarm on connection count. questions An API runs 4 worker processes per task with pool_size 10 and max_overflow 10 and scales to 10 tasks. What is the potential connection count? options answer explain 4 × 20 × 10 = 800, likely exceeding the database's max_connections. Compute before scaling. What does transaction-mode pooling break? options Normal SELECT/UPDATE statements Session-level state such as SET without LOCAL, session advisory locks and LISTEN/NOTIFY Transactions answer explain Server connections are reassigned per transaction; anything assuming a persistent session misbehaves. Why keep pool_timeout short? options To save memory So pool exhaustion produces a fast, visible failure and metric instead of requests hanging indefinitely Databases require it To reduce connections answer explain Fail fast, alert, and fix the budget; hanging requests cascade into worker exhaustion. Which is the standard fix for many Lambda functions connecting to RDS? options Bigger RDS instance RDS Proxy (multiplexing and IAM auth) plus concurrency lim

- Manage schema changes as versioned, reviewed, repeatable migrations applied identically across environments. - Apply zero-downtime patterns: expand/contract, backfills in batches, concurrent indexes, lock timeouts, and compatibility with running code. - Handle data migrations and rollbacks realistically. - Integrate migrations into the deployment pipeline safely. ::: Chapters 3, 4 and 5; Part I chapter 13; Part X chapter 8 covers the pipeline side. :::

Schemas change constantly: new columns, new tables, renamed fields, indexes, constraints. Applying changes by hand is unrepeatable and undocumented; applying them carelessly locks tables, breaks the running version of the application, or takes a production database offline for an hour while a column is rewritten. Migrations as code solve the first problem; the patterns in this chapter solve the second.

A migration tool (Alembic for SQLAlchemy, Django migrations, Flyway or Liquibase for JVM and SQL-first teams, Prisma Migrate, golang-migrate, Rails migrations, sqitch) keeps an ordered set of migration files in the repository and a table in the database recording which have been applied. migrate up applies pending ones in order, inside transactions where the database supports transactional DDL (PostgreSQL does; MySQL does not). Rules: migrations are immutable once merged (fix forward with a new migration); every migration is reviewed like code, with the generated SQL inspected ( alembic upgrade --sql ); migrations are tested against a production-shaped database in staging; the application version N must run against schema N−1 and N (the deploy applies the migration, then rolls the code; Part VII chapter 15); and no migration is run by hand in production, ever: the pipeline runs it. # Alembic migration: additive, safe def upgrade(): op.add_column("orders", sa.Column("fulfilment_channel", sa.Text(), nullable=True)) # nullable: no table rewrite, no lock on reads op.execute("ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_fulfilment_channel_check CHECK (fulfilment_channel IN ('web','store','partner')) NOT VALID") # add constraint without scanning # validated in a later migration after backfill: ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock) def downgrade(): op.drop_constraint("orders_fulfilment_channel_check", "orders") op.drop_column("orders", "fulfilmen

PostgreSQL DDL takes locks; the dangerous ones are ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (blocks everything, including reads) and long rewrites. Know the categories: Operation Lock / cost (PostgreSQL ≥ 12) Safe approach --- --- --- Add nullable column, no default Brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, metadata only Fine Add column with constant default Brief; stored as metadata (fast since PG 11) Fine Add column NOT NULL on a populated table Needs a default or a backfill; SET NOT NULL scans the table Add nullable → backfill in batches → add CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID → VALIDATE → SET NOT NULL (PG 12+ uses the validated check to skip the scan) Change column type Full table rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE Add new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, drop old (expand/contract) Rename column/table Brief lock, but breaks running code immediately Avoid; add new, migrate, drop old; or ensure code handles both via a view Add index Blocks writes for the build CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (outside a transaction; handle failure leaving an INVALID index) Add foreign key Scans the referenced table under lock ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID , then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT Add unique constraint Index build blocks writes Create unique index CONCURRENTLY, then add constraint USING INDEX Drop column Brief lock; space reclaimed later Fine, after code stops using it Large UPDATE/DELETE Long transaction, locks, WAL flood, replication lag Batch (chapter 1's pattern), sleep between batches, monitor lag Even "brief" ACCESS EXCLUSIVE l

The pattern for any change that is not purely additive: title Renaming orders.channel to orders.fulfilment_channel without downtime actors label Migration 1 (expand) label App vN+1 label Backfill job label App vN+2 label Migration 2 (contract) steps label add fulfilment_channel (nullable) title Expand the schema detail Additive change; old code ignores the new column; new code can start using it. Deployed before any code that depends on it. label write both columns; read old title Dual write detail The application writes channel and fulfilment_channel on every insert/update and still reads channel. Both old (vN) and new (vN+1) code work against this schema during the rolling deploy. label UPDATE … SET fulfilment_channel = channel WHERE fulfilment_channel IS NULL LIMIT batches title Backfill in batches detail A job copies existing rows in batches of a few thousand with pauses, watching replication lag and lock waits. Idempotent and resumable. May take hours on big tables; that is fine. label read new; write both (or new only) title Switch reads detail Once the backfill completes and a verification query shows no mismatches, deploy code that reads fulfilment_channel. Keep writing both until you are confident; then write only the new column. label add NOT NULL/constraints; drop channel title Contract detail A later migration (days or weeks later, after any rollback window has passed) validates constraints on the new column and drops the old one. Rollback of the application to vN

Separate schema migrations (fast, in the deploy) from data migrations (slow, idempotent, run as jobs). A backfill: processes in bounded batches by primary key range; commits each batch; sleeps briefly; records progress so it can resume; verifies at the end; is safe to re-run; and runs off-peak with replication lag monitored. Never a single UPDATE over millions of rows in a migration file: it holds locks, bloats, lags replicas, and if it fails at 99% it rolls back everything.

Down migrations exist in theory; in practice, data-destroying downgrades (dropping a column with data) are rarely safe, and most teams roll forward : a new migration that fixes the problem. The expand/contract discipline makes application rollback safe without touching the schema at all, which is the real goal (Part X chapter 8). Write down migrations for the additive steps (cheap), test them, and treat the contract step as a point of no return that you schedule deliberately. For catastrophic data mistakes, PITR (chapter 9), not downgrade scripts.

Order: build artifact → run migration task (new image, migration command, lock timeout set, one instance only, exit code checked) → deploy application → verify. Staging first, always, against a database restored from a recent production snapshot (anonymised), so the migration's duration and lock behaviour are known before production. Record the migration's start and end in the deploy log. Give the migration role DDL privileges and the application role none (chapter 10). Alert on migrations that take longer than expected (a statement timeout for DDL that is generous but finite).

- Running migrations by hand in production psql. - ALTER TABLE … TYPE on a large table during business hours; hour-long outage. - CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a live table. - Renames that break the running version mid-deploy. - Giant single-transaction backfills. - No lock timeout ; a quick migration queues behind a report and freezes everything. - Migrations in the application's startup path, racing across replicas (Part VI chapter 3). - Contract step run immediately, destroying the rollback path. - Never testing migration duration on production-sized data. questions Why add a column as nullable first rather than NOT NULL with a backfill in the same migration? options Nullable columns are faster to query Adding NOT NULL on a populated table requires scanning or rewriting under a lock; the safe sequence is nullable → batched backfill → NOT VALID check → VALIDATE → SET NOT NULL NOT NULL is deprecated ORMs cannot handle it answer explain Decompose into steps that each take brief locks. What does `SET lock_timeout = '3s'` before DDL protect against? options Slow queries The migration queueing behind a long-running query while blocking every other query on the table; it fails fast instead so you can retry Deadlocks Replication lag answer explain A waiting ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock blocks everyone behind it. t: Replication, Read Replicas, Partitioning and Sharding
x: Three reasons: availability (a standby to fail over to), durability (a copy on another machine or AZ), and read scaling (serve reads from replicas). A single database node is a single point of failure and a ceiling on read throughput; replication addresses both at the cost of consistency subtleties and operational complexity.

t: Replication, Read Replicas, Partitioning and Sharding
x: The primary ships its WAL to replicas, which replay it, producing byte-identical copies (same major version, whole cluster). Asynchronous : the primary commits without waiting; replicas lag by milliseconds to seconds (or minutes under heavy write load or long replica queries). Synchronous : the primary waits for at least one replica to confirm receipt (or apply) before acknowledging commit: zero data loss on failover at the cost of latency and a dependency on the replica's availability (configure a quorum or a fallback). RDS Multi-AZ is synchronous replication to a standby that does not serve reads; RDS read replicas are asynchronous and do. Failover : promote a replica to primary; repoint applications (DNS endpoint change, or a proxy that follows the primary). With async replication, transactions not yet shipped are lost (RPO 0); clients must handle the connection break (Part VIII chapter 6). Automated failover needs a fencing mechanism so the old primary cannot accept writes after promotion (split brain); managed services handle this; self-managed setups use Patroni, repmgr or Stolon.

t: Replication, Read Replicas, Partitioning and Sharding
x: Replicates row changes (not WAL bytes) for selected tables via publications and subscriptions; works across major versions and to different schemas; the subscriber is writable. Uses: zero-downtime major version upgrades (replicate to a new version, switch over), selective replication to reporting systems, change data capture (Debezium → Kafka) for event-driven integration, migrating between providers. Costs: DDL is not replicated (coordinate schema changes), sequences are not replicated, conflicts possible if the subscriber is also written, and initial sync of large tables takes time.

t: Replication, Read Replicas, Partitioning and Sharding
x: Routing reads to replicas offloads the primary, but asynchronous lag introduces the classic bug: a user updates their profile (write to primary), the next request reads the profile from a replica that has not caught up, and the change "vanishes". Strategies: - Read your own writes : after a write, pin the session to the primary for a short window (a cookie or a timestamp in the session), or route reads that follow writes to the primary. - Replica for non-critical, lag-tolerant reads only : reports, analytics, dashboards, search indexing, background jobs; keep the request path on the primary unless load demands otherwise. - Lag-aware routing : check pg last wal replay lsn() /lag metric and fall back to the primary when lag exceeds a threshold; some proxies (pgpool, ProxySQL for MySQL) do this. - Monitor lag ( ReplicaLag in CloudWatch; pg stat replication on the primary) and alert; long replica queries can delay replay ( max standby streaming delay ), and cancelled replica queries ( hot standby feedback ) are the trade-off. # Simple routing: explicit choice per query; default to primary class DB: def __init__(self, primary, replica): self.primary, self.replica = primary, replica def reader(self, *, tolerate_lag: bool): return self.replica if tolerate_lag and self.replica_healthy() else self.primary # usage: db.reader(tolerate_lag=True).fetch("SELECT ... FROM reports ...") # report # db.primary.fetch("SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE id = $1") # balance check: never stale Aurora's

t: Replication, Read Replicas, Partitioning and Sharding
x: Partitioning splits one logical table into physical pieces by a key (range on created at , list on tenant id or region, hash on an ID) within a single database. Queries that include the partition key touch only relevant partitions (partition pruning); old partitions can be dropped instantly instead of deleted row by row (retention for events, logs, audit); indexes and vacuum work per partition; very large tables become manageable. CREATE TABLE events ( id uuid NOT NULL, tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL, type text NOT NULL, payload jsonb, PRIMARY KEY (occurred_at, id) -- partition key must be part of unique constraints ) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at); CREATE TABLE events_2026_03 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-03-01') TO ('2026-04-01'); CREATE TABLE events_2026_04 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-04-01') TO ('2026-05-01'); CREATE INDEX ON events (tenant_id, occurred_at DESC); -- created on each partition -- retention: DROP TABLE events_2025_03; (instant, no bloat) Operational notes: create future partitions ahead of time (pg partman automates it); queries without the partition key scan all partitions; too many partitions (thousands) slow planning; foreign keys referencing partitioned tables have constraints; unique constraints must include the partition key. Partition when a table is tens of millions of rows with time- or tenant-based access and retention needs, not before.

t: Replication, Read Replicas, Partitioning and Sharding
x: Sharding splits data across multiple databases by a shard key (tenant ID, user ID range, hash). It is the only way to scale writes beyond one primary, and it costs: every query must know its shard (no cross-shard joins or transactions without application-level coordination), rebalancing when shards fill is complex, schema changes multiply, backups and monitoring multiply, and uniqueness and reporting become distributed problems. Before sharding: vertical scaling (bigger instance; modern instances are enormous), read replicas, caching, partitioning, archiving cold data, and moving high-volume non-relational data (events, logs) to purpose-built stores. If sharding is still needed, shard by tenant where possible (tenant-per-database or groups of tenants per shard, Part III chapter 15), use a routing layer (Citus distributes PostgreSQL tables transparently; Vitess for MySQL; application-level directories), and plan for rebalancing from day one. Most client systems never need it; saying so, with the evidence, is part of the job.

t: Replication, Read Replicas, Partitioning and Sharding
x: Replicas protect against hardware and AZ failure; they faithfully replicate a DROP TABLE within milliseconds. Backups and PITR (chapter 9) protect against mistakes and corruption. You need both.

- Distinguish logical and physical backups and choose the right combination for a database. - Implement point-in-time recovery with WAL archiving (self-managed) or managed PITR (RDS/Aurora). - Run and automate restore drills that prove recoverability and measure RTO. - Protect backups from the failures that destroy them: same-account storage, missing keys, silent job failure. ::: Chapter 8; Part V chapter 11. :::

Logical backups ( pg dump , mysqldump ) export schema and data as SQL or a custom archive. Portable across major versions and architectures; selective (one table, one schema); human-readable; slow to restore at scale (hours for hundreds of GB, because it replays inserts and rebuilds indexes); a snapshot as of the dump's start (consistent within a single transaction). Essential for migrations between providers or versions and as an independent copy; insufficient alone for low RPO. Physical backups copy the data files plus the WAL needed to make them consistent: pg basebackup , filesystem/volume snapshots, RDS automated snapshots. Fast to restore (copy files, replay WAL); same version and architecture only; whole cluster. Combined with continuous WAL archiving , physical backups give point-in-time recovery : restore the base backup and replay WAL up to any chosen moment before the mistake. title Backup methods columns Method Restore speed Granularity pg_dump nightly Up to 24 h Slow (replay) Table/schema Portability, secondary copy, small databases pg_basebackup + WAL archive (pgBackRest, WAL-G) Seconds (WAL shipped continuously) Fast (file copy + WAL replay) Whole cluster Self-managed production: PITR Volume snapshots (EBS) Snapshot interval Whole volume Crash-consistent; pair with WAL or freeze for databases RDS automated backups + PITR 5 minutes (transaction logs uploaded continuously) Minutes to tens of minutes (new instance) Whole instance The default for RDS; retention ≤ 3

# pgBackRest: full backup weekly, differential daily, WAL archived continuously to S3 (encrypted) # postgresql.conf # archive_mode = on # archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=prod archive-push %p' # wal_level = replica # /etc/pgbackrest.conf # [global] repo1-type=s3 repo1-s3-bucket=client-a-db-backups repo1-s3-region=eu-west-1 repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc repo1-retention-full=4 process-max=4 # [prod] pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/16/main pgbackrest --stanza=prod --type=full backup pgbackrest --stanza=prod --type=diff backup pgbackrest --stanza=prod info # last backups, WAL archive range # Restore to a point in time on a fresh server pgbackrest --stanza=prod --delta --type=time --target="2026-03-14 10:15:00+00" --target-action=promote restore systemctl start postgresql # recovers to the target, promotes Monitor: WAL archive failures ( pg stat archiver.failed count , and the archive command's exit status: a failing archive command fills the disk with unshipped WAL and eventually stops the database), backup job success and age, and repository size. Test restores monthly on a separate instance and time them.

RDS: enable automated backups (retention 7–35 days), which combines daily snapshots with continuous transaction log upload for PITR to any second within the window; copy snapshots (automated via AWS Backup) to another Region and account for DR; manual snapshots for pre-migration safety points (kept until deleted); restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time creates a new instance (plan the endpoint switch, security groups, parameter group, which are not all carried over). Aurora adds continuous backup to its storage layer and fast database cloning (copy-on-write clones in minutes for testing restores, migrations and analytics on production data without touching production). Encryption follows the source; a snapshot encrypted with a customer managed key needs that key accessible in the destination account/Region (multi-Region keys or re-encryption on copy).

A restore you have not performed is a hypothesis. The drill (automated monthly, Part V chapter 11): 1. Restore the latest backup/PITR to a fresh instance in an isolated network. 2. Run verification: row counts for key tables versus production at the restore point, checksums of recent rows, application smoke tests against the restored copy, pg dump of the restored copy to confirm it is readable end to end. 3. Record elapsed time (provisioning + recovery + verification) against the RTO; record the RPO achieved (time between the restore point and the newest data available). 4. Destroy the instance; file the results where the client can see them. Also drill the operator-error scenario : "a migration at 14:02 dropped a column; recover the data." Steps: identify the exact time; PITR to 14:01 on a new instance; extract the lost data; reconcile into production (or fail over to the restored instance if the whole database must revert, accepting loss of post-14:02 writes). Knowing the procedure cold is what turns a disaster into a bad afternoon.

- Different account and Region , immutable (Object Lock / Vault Lock), so production credentials or ransomware cannot destroy them (Part V chapter 11). - Keys : backups encrypted under a key that will exist when you need it; multi-Region keys; key deletion alarmed. - Job monitoring : alert on absence of a successful backup within the expected window, not only on failures (a cron job that never runs produces no failure). - Retention matching the slowest discovery of problems (corruption found after three weeks needs a four-week-old copy) and legal requirements; logical dumps retained longer in cold storage. - Access : a backup role for the jobs; humans via break-glass; restore permissions separate from delete permissions. - Consistency : database-aware methods (PITR, dumps) rather than raw volume snapshots of a live database unless frozen (Part V chapter 6).

mysqldump --single-transaction (InnoDB) for consistent logical dumps; Percona XtraBackup for hot physical backups; binary log archiving for PITR ( mysqlbinlog replay to a point); RDS MySQL has the same automated backup and PITR model.

- Harden a database: network isolation, authentication, least-privilege roles, encryption, auditing and patching. - Protect sensitive columns with field-level encryption, masking and access separation. - Implement data retention and deletion as database mechanisms, not intentions. - Audit a database's security posture quickly. ::: Part IV chapters 11, 16, 17, 22, 23; Part III chapter 15; chapters 1 and 5 of this part. :::

Everything else exists to protect what is in the database. Application vulnerabilities become data breaches here; a leaked database credential is the breach itself. Database security is layers: nobody can reach it (network), only the right identities can connect (authentication), each identity can do only its job (authorisation), data is unreadable where it rests and travels (encryption), everything is recorded (audit), and the software is current (patching). Plus the part teams skip: data that no longer needs to exist is deleted.

Private subnets with no Internet route (Part VII chapter 5); security group allowing the port only from application and worker security groups and from a controlled administrative path (SSM port forward, bastion, VPN); no public endpoint, ever ( publicly accessible = false ); rds.force ssl / ssl = on with verify-full on clients; VPC Flow Logs capturing connection attempts.

No shared superuser used by applications. Options in order of preference: IAM database authentication (short-lived tokens, no passwords, per-role audit); managed, rotated secrets (Secrets Manager rotation for RDS; apps re-read on failure); long-lived passwords only where unavoidable, strong and rotated. PostgreSQL pg hba.conf (self-managed) restricts which users may connect from which networks with which methods ( scram-sha-256 , never md5 or trust ). The master user is for administration and emergencies, stored in a secrets manager, used rarely and audited.

At rest : storage encryption with a customer managed KMS key (RDS at creation; cannot be added later without snapshot-restore); covers data files, backups, snapshots, replicas, logs. Protects against media and snapshot exposure, not against anyone with credentials. In transit : TLS enforced and verified (chapter: Part VII chapter 16). Field-level : for the most sensitive columns (government IDs, bank details, health data, third-party tokens) encrypt in the application with envelope encryption (Part IV chapter 16) so that database credentials alone cannot read them; store ciphertext; search via blind indexes (HMAC of the value) when equality lookups are required. pgcrypto can encrypt in the database, but then the database (and anyone with its credentials and the key) can decrypt; application-level encryption with keys in KMS keeps the key away from the database. Masking and views : give support and analytics roles views that mask or omit sensitive columns ( SELECT id, left(email, 2) ' ' AS email … ); dynamic data masking features exist in some engines; column-level grants (above) are the simplest tool.

What happened in the database and who did it: pgAudit (session and object audit logging of DDL, role changes, reads/writes on sensitive tables) on self-managed and RDS PostgreSQL; log connections / log disconnections ; MySQL audit plugins; RDS activity streams (Aurora, near-real-time to Kinesis, tamper-proof) for regulated workloads; CloudTrail for control-plane actions (snapshots, parameter changes, deletions). Ship logs off-box with retention (Part IV chapter 22). Alert on: new roles or grants, failed logins spike, DDL outside deploy windows, access to sensitive tables by unexpected roles, snapshot sharing or export ( ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute , a known exfiltration path).

Minor versions automatically in the maintenance window (RDS auto minor version upgrade ); majors as planned projects with Blue/Green deployments or logical replication (chapter 8); extensions kept current; self-managed hosts per Part V chapter 12. Database engines publish CVEs; a database two years behind is exposed to known authentication and privilege bugs.

Data retention is a security control (what you do not hold cannot leak) and a legal obligation (Part IV chapter 23). Make it mechanical: - Define retention per table or data class in the schema documentation ( events: 90 days; audit: 7 years; sessions: 30 days; deleted customers: hard-delete 30 days after soft delete ). - Implement with partitions dropped on schedule (chapter 8), scheduled batched deletes ( pg cron or an application job), TTLs where the store supports them (DynamoDB, Redis), and S3 lifecycle for exports and backups. - Propagate deletion to replicas (automatic), caches, search indexes, analytics copies, backups (expire on rotation; document the window), and processors (Part IV chapter 23). - Verify with a periodic query that nothing older than the policy exists, and record the proof. - Anonymise where records must persist for integrity (orders of a deleted customer: replace PII with tokens, keep the financial facts). -- pg_cron (available on RDS): nightly retention job in batches SELECT cron.schedule('retention-events', '15 3 * * *', $$ DELETE FROM app.events WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM app.events WHERE occurred_at < now() - interval '90 days' LIMIT 20000) $$); SELECT cron.schedule('hard-delete-customers', '45 3 * * *', $$ SELECT app.hard_delete_customers(now() - interval '30 days') -- function anonymises orders, deletes PII rows, logs counts $$);

Backups contain everything; a leaked backup is a full breach. Encrypted, access-restricted, in a separate account (chapter 9). Exports for analysts, migrations and support tickets are the most common uncontrolled copies: provide masked exports by default, require approval and logging for raw exports, and expire them (presigned URLs, short-lived buckets).

# Database security review - No public endpoint; private subnets; SG only from app/worker/admin paths; flow logs on. - TLS enforced and verified; IAM auth or rotated secrets; master credential in a secrets manager and unused by applications. - Roles per function; application role DML-only on its schema; no superuser or owner privileges for runtime roles; RLS where multi-tenant; column grants for support. - statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout on application roles. - Encryption at rest with a customer managed key; field-level encryption for the most sensitive columns; masked views for analysts. - pgAudit/activity streams on for DDL, role changes and sensitive tables; logs shipped and retained; alerts on grants, DDL off-window, snapshot sharing. - Minor versions current; major version in support; extensions current. - Retention defined per table and implemented mechanically; verification query passes; deletion propagated to caches/indexes/exports. - Backups encrypted, cross-account, immutable, restore-tested; exports masked by default and expiring. - Access review done this quarter: roles, grants, people, integrations.

- Application connecting as the master user; injection becomes total compromise. - Public endpoint "for the dashboard tool". - Unencrypted at creation; discovered at audit time. - Retention "policy" in a document with no job behind it; a decade of PII. - Snapshots shared publicly or to the wrong account (a real exfiltration vector; AWS Config rule rds-snapshots-public-prohibited ). - Raw production dumps given to analysts and contractors. - No audit logging; "who read this record" unanswerable. - Roles and grants never reviewed; former contractors' logins still valid. questions Why should the application connect with a DML-only role rather than the owner or master user? options Performance A SQL injection or leaked credential is bounded to reading and writing application data, not dropping tables, altering schema or reading other schemas Required by RDS Owners cannot use pools answer explain Least privilege at the database bounds the blast radius of the most common application vulnerability. Can they read sensitive columns? options No, the data is encrypted Yes; at-rest encryption is transparent to authenticated clients. Field-level encryption with KMS-held keys is needed to protect against credential compromise Only backups Only with the KMS key answer explain Different controls address different threats. - Use Redis's data structures for the jobs they fit: caching, sessions, counters, rate limits, locks, queues, pub/sub, leaderboards. - Configure Redis for production: persistence, eviction, replication, cluster mode, security, memory. - Apply cache invalidation strategies and understand why it is hard. - Operate Redis: monitoring, slow commands, big keys, failover behaviour. ::: Part III chapter 8; Part VII chapter 11. :::

An in-memory data structure server: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLogs, geospatial indexes, plus pub/sub, Lua scripting, transactions ( MULTI / EXEC ), and optional persistence. Single-threaded command execution (I/O threads aside) means every command is atomic and ordering is total, which is why Redis is the natural home for counters, locks and rate limiters. Latency is sub-millisecond; throughput hundreds of thousands of operations per second per node. Valkey is the open-source fork (Linux Foundation) that AWS and others now ship alongside Redis OSS; the API is the same.

- Memory : maxmemory set below the instance's RAM (leave headroom for replication buffers and fork overhead); maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru for pure caches, volatile-lru / volatile-ttl when some keys must never be evicted (sessions with TTL evicted before config without TTL), noeviction only for queues/locks where losing data is worse than errors. Monitor used memory , evicted keys , fragmentation ratio. - Persistence : none for pure caches (fast restart, repopulate); AOF ( appendonly yes , everysec ) for sessions, queues and anything you would rather not lose; RDB snapshots for backups. On ElastiCache, enable backups where data matters. - Replication and HA : primary plus replicas across AZs with automatic failover (Sentinel self-managed; ElastiCache Multi-AZ). Replication is asynchronous: a failover can lose the last writes; clients must reconnect (use a client with topology refresh or the ElastiCache primary endpoint). - Cluster mode : shards data across nodes by key hash slot for datasets beyond one node or very high throughput; multi-key operations must target the same slot ( {hashtag} in key names); clients must be cluster-aware. Start without cluster mode; move when memory or throughput requires. - Security : never on a public IP (exposed Redis instances are compromised within minutes); TLS in transit; requirepass /ACL users (Redis 6+) with least-privilege command sets per application ( +@read +@write -@dangerous ); disable or rename FLUSHALL , CONFIG , KEYS , DEBUG for

Phil Karlton's joke is true because invalidation requires knowing every place a changed fact was copied to. Strategies, roughly in order of preference: 1. TTL only : accept staleness up to the TTL; simplest; right for data whose staleness is harmless (catalogue listing, rates refreshed hourly). 2. TTL + delete on write : the writer deletes the entity's cache key after committing (Part III chapter 8); the TTL catches missed deletes. Works when keys map one-to-one to entities. 3. Versioned keys : include a version in the key ( user:42:v17:profile ); the writer increments the version stored in a small hot key; readers look up the version then the data; old versions expire by TTL. No deletes needed; two lookups per read (or embed the version in a frequently cached parent). 4. Tag-based invalidation : track dependencies in sets ( tag:product:9 → {key1, key2…} ); on change, delete all members. Powerful for derived views (a product change invalidates every listing containing it); the sets themselves need bounding and TTLs. 5. Event-driven : publish change events (outbox, Part IX chapter 6); cache maintainers subscribe and invalidate or update. Decoupled; eventually consistent; more moving parts. 6. Write-through / refresh-ahead : the cache is updated on write or proactively refreshed; coherence by construction for the paths that go through it, at the cost of making the cache part of the write path. Rules that save you: keys scoped by tenant and user; never cache data whose staleness

SET lock NX PX 30000 gives a lock on a single Redis node. It fails if the node fails over before replication (two holders), if the holder pauses (GC, network) longer than the TTL (expired lock, two holders), or if release is not token-checked (deleting someone else's lock). Use Redis locks for efficiency (avoid duplicate work) with idempotent operations, not for correctness of invariants; for correctness use the database (row locks, unique constraints, conditional updates) or a consensus store. Redlock over multiple independent nodes is debated; the database is usually the better answer. -- release only if we hold it if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end

Metrics: used memory vs maxmemory , evicted keys , keyspace hits/misses (hit ratio per workload, not globally), connected clients , instantaneous ops per sec , rejected connections , replication lag ( master repl offset vs replica), latency percentiles from the client side, CPU (single-threaded: 100% of one core is saturation). ElastiCache exposes these in CloudWatch ( EngineCPUUtilization , DatabaseMemoryUsagePercentage , Evictions , CurrConnections , ReplicationLag ). Alarm on memory 80%, evictions when they should not happen, CPU 80%, replication lag, and connection count near maxclients . Failover tests: force a failover in staging and verify clients recover.

- Diagnose database performance problems from symptoms to causes using metrics, wait events and query statistics. - Fix the common application-side causes: N+1 queries, missing indexes, over-fetching, chatty transactions, connection churn. - Tune the server sensibly: memory, autovacuum, checkpoints, and the handful of parameters that matter on managed services. - Follow a scaling ladder from a single instance to replicas, caching, partitioning and beyond, with the cost and complexity of each rung. ::: Chapters 4, 5, 6, 8 and 11; Part V chapter 10. :::

Database slowness has a small number of causes: the query reads too much (missing index, bad plan), too many queries (N+1, chatty code), waiting (locks, I/O, CPU saturation), too many connections, or the working set no longer fits in memory. The method: measure which, then fix that, then measure again. Guesswork (bigger instance first) is expensive and often wrong. title Database performance triage actors label Symptom label Host / instance metrics label Wait events stmts label pg_stat_statements label EXPLAIN ANALYZE label steps label latency up / timeouts title Is the instance saturated? detail CPU, memory (freeable, cache hit ratio), disk IOPS/throughput vs provisioned, queue depth, connections vs max, replication lag (Part V chapter 10; RDS metrics). Saturated CPU with low I/O: expensive queries or too many connections. High I/O wait: working set exceeds memory or an unindexed scan. Nothing saturated: locks or application-side latency. label what are sessions waiting on? title Wait events detail Performance Insights or `pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type`: CPU (running), IO (DataFileRead: reading tables), Lock (blocked by another transaction), LWLock (buffer contention), Client (idle in transaction, waiting on the app). The dominant wait names the problem class. stmts label which statements? title Top queries detail `pg_stat_statements` by total_exec_time (overall cost), mean_exec_time (slow per call), calls (chatty), rows (over-fetching), shared_blks_read (I/O heavy). N+1 queries : load 100 orders, then one query per order for its customer: 101 round trips. Symptom: thousands of fast identical queries per request in pg stat statements ; trace shows a staircase of tiny spans. Fix: eager loading ( selectinload / joinedload in SQLAlchemy, select related / prefetch related in Django, include in Prisma), or an explicit WHERE id = ANY($1) batch, or a join. Detect with query counters in tests (assert a request issues fewer than N queries). Over-fetching : SELECT on wide rows, loading entire tables to filter in Python, fetching 10,000 rows to show 20. Fix: select needed columns, filter and paginate in SQL (keyset), aggregate in the database. Chatty transactions : many small statements in one transaction with network round trips between them; a transaction held across an external call (Part III chapter 13). Fix: fewer, set-based statements; shorter transactions. Connection churn : opening a connection per request or per Lambda invocation (chapter 6). Lock contention : hot rows updated by every request (a counters table), long transactions, lock-order deadlocks (chapter 5). Fix: shard counters, use Redis for high-frequency counts, shorten transactions. Missing indexes and bad plans : chapter 4. Unbounded growth : tables that only grow (events, logs) slowing every query and vacuum; retention and partitioning (chapters 8 and 10).

On managed services most parameters are set sensibly by instance class; the handful worth reviewing: - Memory : shared buffers (RDS default ~25% of RAM is reasonable), work mem (per sort/hash per query: raise for reporting roles via ALTER ROLE … SET work mem , not globally, to avoid memory blow-ups under concurrency), effective cache size (tells the planner how much cache exists; RDS sets it), maintenance work mem (faster index builds and vacuum). - Autovacuum : more aggressive on hot tables ( autovacuum vacuum scale factor = 0.02 , autovacuum vacuum cost limit higher) so bloat and stale statistics do not accumulate; monitor n dead tup and last autovacuum times; watch for transaction ID wraparound warnings (a database that stops accepting writes is the end state of neglected vacuum). - Checkpoints : checkpoint timeout 15 min and max wal size large enough that checkpoints are time-based, not size-based (frequent checkpoints cause I/O spikes); checkpoint completion target 0.9 . - Planner : random page cost 1.1 on SSD (RDS sets it); statistics targets for skewed columns; CREATE STATISTICS for correlated columns. - Logging : log min duration statement , log lock waits , pg stat statements (chapters 1 and 4). - Connections : max connections is not a performance knob; poolers are (chapter 6). MySQL equivalents: innodb buffer pool size (~70% of RAM on a dedicated host), innodb log file size , innodb flush log at trx commit (1 for durability), the slow query log, performance schema .

The cheapest read scaling is not reading: Part III chapter 8 and chapter 11. Cache hot entities and expensive aggregates with short TTLs and delete-on-write; keep the database for the source of truth and for writes. Measure the database QPS saved, not the hit ratio.

t: Choosing a Database for a Client Project
x: The database choice is the hardest to reverse: migrations between models take months and risk data. It is also where fashion does the most damage: a document store chosen because the demo was quick, a NoSQL store chosen "for scale" at 50 requests per second, or a relational database chosen by habit for a workload that is genuinely a key-value stream. The framework below forces the questions in the right order and produces a document the client can understand.

t: Requirements, Capacity Estimation and Latency Budgets
x: Order-of-magnitude arithmetic, done early, prevents both panic and complacency. bytes write Method: 1. Users and actions : daily active users × actions per user per day = requests per day. 50,000 DAU × 40 = 2,000,000 requests/day. 2. Average and peak rate : ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23 rps average; peak factor 3–5× for business apps (more for events, launches, media): ~100 rps peak. Design and load test for 2–3× peak. 3. Read/write mix : typically 80–95% reads. Writes drive database sizing and replication; reads drive caching. 4. Payload and bandwidth : average response 3 KB × 100 rps × 8 bits ≈ 2.4 Mbps egress at peak; trivial for a load balancer, a cost line for data transfer (Part VII chapter 4). 5. Storage : writes per day × bytes per record × retention; plus indexes (×1.5–2), plus blobs separately. 300,000 writes/day × 600 B ≈ 180 MB/day ≈ 65 GB/year before indexes: a small RDS instance for years. 6. Growth : apply the client's expected growth (and a stretch case) to see when the next scaling rung arrives (Part VIII chapter 12). 7. Connections and concurrency : concurrent requests ≈ rps × average latency (Little's law): 100 rps × 0.2 s = 20 in flight; pool sizes and worker counts follow (Part VIII chapter 6). The point is the tier : this example is "one modest application fleet and a small managed database", and anything more elaborate needs a justification other than scale.

- Define availability, reliability and scalability precisely and measure them. - Identify single points of failure and the standard remedies at each layer. - Understand redundancy, failover, degradation and the cost curve of each additional nine. - Design a system to an availability target proportionate to the client's needs. ::: Chapter 1; Part II chapter 13; Part VII chapters 1 and 11. :::

- Availability : the fraction of time (or of requests) the system is usable. Measured as an SLI against an SLO (Part XI chapter 4): successful requests / total requests over a window, or uptime of a synthetic check. - Reliability : the probability the system performs correctly for a period; includes correctness, not just being up. A system that answers quickly with wrong data is available and unreliable. - Scalability : the ability to handle growth in load or data by adding resources, ideally proportionally and without redesign. - Resilience : the ability to absorb failures and recover; the engineering that produces availability. - Durability : the probability that stored data survives (Part VII chapter 10).

Draw the architecture and ask of each component: if this dies, what happens? Anything whose death takes the system down is a single point of failure (SPOF). Typical SPOFs and remedies: SPOF Remedy Cost --- --- --- One application instance Several instances across AZs behind a load balancer; autoscaling with min ≥ 2 Instances ×2–3; stateless design required One database instance Multi-AZ standby with automatic failover; read replicas; backups and PITR Roughly 2× database cost One Availability Zone Everything across ≥ 2 (ideally 3) AZs: subnets, ASG/ECS placement, RDS Multi-AZ, ElastiCache replicas, NAT per AZ Cross-AZ transfer; NAT per AZ One Region Multi-Region DR (chapter 10) Large; complexity One NAT gateway One per AZ Hourly cost each The load balancer Managed ALB/NLB is multi-AZ by design Included DNS Managed (Route 53 is 100% SLA); health-checked failover Included A cache node Replication with automatic failover; application tolerates cache loss Replica cost A queue Managed SQS is multi-AZ; self-managed brokers need clusters Included / cluster cost An external API Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, fallbacks, queues; contractual SLAs Engineering A certificate Automated renewal and monitoring (Part II chapter 10) Nearly free A person Runbooks, shared on-call, documentation, handover (Part XIII) Discipline A deploy pipeline Not an availability SPOF, but a recovery one: can you deploy a fix when CI is down? Keep a documented manual path Documentation Hidden SPOFs: a singl

Redundancy means more than one of something; failover means the system switches to the redundant one when the primary fails. Three qualities matter: detection time (health checks every 10 s with 2 failures: ~20 s), switch time (ALB target removal: seconds; RDS Multi-AZ failover: 60–120 s; DNS failover: TTL-bound), and state (stateless components fail over trivially; databases need replication; sessions need a shared store). Active-active (all replicas serve) beats active-passive (standby idle) for utilisation and tested readiness, where the data model allows. Test failover regularly: terminate an instance, force an RDS failover, kill a cache node, block an AZ's subnets in staging (Part XI chapter 9). An untested failover is a hypothesis with the same credibility as an untested backup.

Full availability of every feature is not the only option. Design so that when a dependency fails, the system sheds the affected feature rather than everything: recommendations disappear but checkout works; search falls back to the database; reports queue for later; the cache is bypassed with higher latency. Requires: timeouts and circuit breakers (chapter 8), feature flags as kill switches (Part X chapter 7), a clear priority of features, and UI that handles absence. Partial availability is often what the SLO actually needs.

title What each level of availability typically requires columns Target Monthly downtime Architecture Operations ~99% (two nines) Single instance, single AZ, nightly backups Manual recovery; business-hours on-call 99.5% ~3.6 h Load-balanced instances, Multi-AZ database, automated restarts Runbooks; alerts; occasional out-of-hours response 99.9% (three nines) ~43 min Multi-AZ everything, autoscaling, health-gated deploys, tested failover, graceful degradation, no SPOFs within the Region 24×7 on-call, SLO monitoring, game days, change management 99.95% ~22 min As above plus faster failover (Aurora/proxy), canary deploys, strict dependency timeouts, regional DR tested Mature incident response; error budgets enforced 99.99% (four nines) ~4 min Multi-Region active-active or hot standby with automated failover; redundant everything including DNS strategy Platform team; chaos engineering; sub-minute detection 99.999% ~26 s Telecom-grade; cell-based architecture; no shared fate anywhere Dedicated organisation Most client systems belong at 99.5–99.9%. Promising 99.99% to a client with a two-person team is a promise you will break; the honest conversation is "here is what each level costs in infrastructure and in people, and here is what your business actually loses per hour of downtime."

Vertical (bigger machine) and horizontal (more machines) scaling (Part I chapter 14, Part VIII chapter 12). Horizontal scaling requires statelessness (chapter 3), load distribution (Part II chapter 13), and data tier strategies (Part VIII chapters 8, 11, 12). Scalability has dimensions: request throughput, data volume, number of tenants, geographic spread, team size; a system scalable in one is not automatically scalable in another. Measure the scaling factor : adding a second instance should roughly double capacity; if it adds 20%, a shared bottleneck (database, lock, cache node) is the real limit. Autoscaling (Part VII chapters 7–8) handles variation; capacity planning (Part XI chapter 8) handles growth.

Components that fail together share fate: everything in one AZ, every service on one database, every tenant in one deployment. Reducing blast radius: AZ isolation, bulkheads per tenant or workload (chapter 8), cell-based architectures (independent stacks each serving a subset of tenants, with a thin routing layer), separate accounts per environment (Part VII chapter 2), and staged rollouts (Part X chapter 7). The question for every design review: what is the largest thing one failure can take out?

Correctness under concurrency (Part VIII chapter 5), idempotency under retries (Part III chapter 3), data integrity (constraints, Part VIII chapter 3), and recoverability (backups, Part V chapter 11) are reliability. A system can meet its uptime SLO while silently corrupting data; include correctness SLIs (reconciliation checks, data validation jobs) in the definition of reliable.

t: Stateless versus Stateful Services and Load Distribution
x: - Make services stateless so any instance can serve any request, and know where each kind of state must live instead. - Handle the unavoidable stateful components (databases, caches, brokers, connection-heavy services) with the patterns that keep them available. - Distribute load fairly across heterogeneous instances and long-lived connections. - Recognise hidden state that breaks horizontal scaling and deployments. ::: Part III chapter 1; Part II chapters 11, 13 and 14. :::

t: Stateless versus Stateful Services and Load Distribution
x: A stateless service keeps nothing between requests that another instance would need. Consequences: any instance handles any request (load balancing is trivial); instances can be added, removed or replaced at will (autoscaling, rolling deploys, self-healing); a crashed instance loses nothing; and tests are simpler. Almost every architectural property in this part (availability, scalability, easy deployment) depends on it. State does not disappear; it moves to components designed to hold it.
