t: Stateless versus Stateful Services and Load Distribution
x: The instance that "works fine until we added a second one": - Local disk : uploads written to /var/app/uploads , PDFs generated to /tmp and served later, SQLite files. Second instance cannot see them. Move to S3 or a shared store. - In-memory sessions or caches used as truth : logins "lost" when the load balancer sends the next request elsewhere; stale permission caches per instance. Shared store, or accept per-instance caches only for harmless data. - In-process schedulers ( setInterval , APScheduler) running on every instance: jobs run N times. Externalise scheduling or elect a leader. - Sticky sessions as a design: uneven load, lost sessions on deploy (Part II chapter 13). - Instance-specific configuration edited by hand; drift. - Sequence generation in memory (counters, IDs): duplicates across instances. Use database sequences or UUIDs. - Long-lived connections pinned to instances (WebSockets, HTTP/2 from a few heavy clients): load concentrates; deploys disconnect everyone. - Local queues ( asyncio.create task fire-and-forget, in-memory job lists): lost on restart. Detect by asking of every write: where does this go, and can the next request from the same user land on a different instance?

t: Stateless versus Stateful Services and Load Distribution
x: Some components must hold state; the patterns: - Databases : replication and failover (Part VIII chapter 8); connections pooled and bounded (Part VIII chapter 6); the application treats the endpoint as potentially changing. - Caches : replicated with failover; the application survives cache loss (Part III chapter 8). - Brokers : managed (SQS) or clustered; consumers idempotent (Part III chapter 7). - Connection servers : a dedicated tier scaled on connection count with a backplane; graceful drain on deploy (Part III chapter 11). - Leader-based singletons (a scheduler, a reconciliation loop): leader election via a lease ( SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a leases row, Redis SET NX PX with renewal, or Kubernetes Lease objects); the leader renews; others wait; failover on lease expiry (chapter 6). - StatefulSets / stateful instances : stable identities and storage where the software requires it (self-managed brokers, search clusters); prefer managed services.

- Choose among cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind and refresh-ahead for a given read/write profile. - Design a cache hierarchy (browser, CDN, edge, application, database) and reason about coherence across layers. - Decide what to cache, for how long, and how invalidation propagates, with staleness as an explicit requirement. - Measure cache effectiveness and avoid the failure modes caches introduce. ::: Part II chapters 8 and 17; Part III chapter 8; Part VIII chapter 11. :::

Part III chapter 8 covered the mechanics of an application cache; this chapter is about strategy : which pattern, at which layer, with what staleness contract. Every cache trades freshness and complexity for latency and load. The design question is never "should we cache?" but "which data, where, how stale may it be, and how do we know it is working?"

Write-behind only for data whose loss is acceptable.

Requests can be answered at several layers, each closer to the user and cheaper, each with its own invalidation story: 1. Browser cache : Cache-Control , ETag ; zero network cost. For assets and conditional API GETs. 2. CDN / edge : shared across users; for public, cacheable responses; keyed carefully (Part II chapter 17). 3. Reverse proxy / API gateway cache : for public API responses with s-maxage . 4. Application cache (Redis) : per-entity or per-query results scoped by tenant/user. 5. In-process cache : tiny, hot, harmless-if-stale data (config, flags). 6. Database caches : buffer pool, materialised views, query result caches. Effective staleness is the sum along the path: a 60 s CDN TTL over a 300 s Redis TTL can serve data six minutes old. Design TTLs per layer with the end-to-end contract in mind, and make the shortest-TTL layer the one you can invalidate.

Good candidates: read-heavy, expensive to compute or fetch, tolerant of staleness, with a bounded key space: catalogue entities, configuration, computed aggregates, permission sets with short TTL, external API responses (rates, geocoding), rendered fragments. Poor candidates: data read once, data with strict freshness (balances at transaction time, inventory at checkout, authorization decisions beyond seconds), data whose key space is unbounded with low reuse (per-request computed results), very large objects (cache a pointer instead), and anything personal in a shared layer. Decide and document per data class: TTL , invalidation trigger , tolerated staleness , fallback when the cache is unavailable .

Strategies from Part III chapter 8 and Part VIII chapter 11 apply per layer; across layers, propagate in order from origin outward: database commit → application cache delete (synchronous) → CDN purge or short TTL (asynchronous) → browser via ETag revalidation. Event-driven invalidation (outbox events consumed by cache maintainers and CDN purgers) scales to many consumers; versioned URLs (fingerprinted assets, versioned API resources) avoid invalidation entirely for immutable content; and for everything else, a TTL is the backstop that bounds how wrong you can be.

Caches that fail together create thundering herds: a cache cluster restart, a deploy that changes key prefixes, synchronised TTL expiry, or a popular key expiring under load. Mitigations: jittered TTLs; single-flight/request coalescing per key; stale-while-revalidate; cache warming after deploys (replay hot keys); gradual key migration (dual-read old and new prefixes); origin rate limiting and load shedding so a cache failure degrades rather than destroys (chapter 9); and treating cache availability as part of the capacity plan (if the cache dies, can the origin serve the load for the minutes it takes to recover? If not, the cache is a hard dependency and must be highly available).

Cache "not found" briefly to stop repeated misses for missing items (and to blunt enumeration); cache partial results (a list of IDs, then entities) so the expensive part is reused while entities stay fresh; cache per-field (hash) when fields change at different rates.

Per key family: hit ratio, origin requests saved, latency with and without, memory consumed, eviction rate, staleness observed (sample and compare with the source). A cache is justified when it removes origin load or latency that matters; review quarterly and remove caches that do neither (every cache is also a correctness risk).

Shared layers must never hold personal responses; keys must include every dimension the data depends on (tenant, user, locale, role); encrypt sensitive values if the cache store is less protected than the database; respect data retention (cached PII is still PII, Part IV chapter 23); and never trust cache contents as authoritative for authorization decisions beyond a short TTL with invalidation on permission change.

- Define the consistency models engineers actually meet (linearizable, sequential, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual) and recognise them in real systems. - State what the CAP theorem says and does not say, and use PACELC to reason about trade-offs under normal operation. - Choose consistency per data class and implement the application patterns that deliver it over asynchronous replication. - Recognise consistency bugs from their symptoms. ::: Part VIII chapters 5 and 8; chapter 3 of this part. :::

Once data lives in more than one place (replicas, caches, services, regions), "what is the current value?" has no single answer at any instant. Systems choose how much disagreement to allow and for how long; applications must be written for the choice. Most consistency bugs come from engineers assuming a stronger model than their infrastructure provides: reading from a replica after a write, caching across a change, or coordinating two services as if they shared a transaction.

From strongest to weakest, as application-visible guarantees: - Linearizable (strong): every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its start and end; all clients see the same order. A single-leader database with reads from the leader behaves this way for committed data. Costly across distance (coordination round trips). - Sequential : all clients see the same order of operations, but not necessarily in real time. - Causal : operations that are causally related (a reply after the post it answers) are seen in order by everyone; unrelated operations may be seen in different orders. - Read-your-writes : a client sees its own writes; others may lag. The minimum users expect. - Monotonic reads : a client never sees time go backwards (no reading a newer value, then an older one from a lagging replica). - Eventual : given no new writes, replicas converge. No guarantee about when , and reads may return any recent value meanwhile. Real systems: a Multi-AZ RDS primary gives linearizable reads from the primary; asynchronous read replicas give eventual consistency with monotonic reads only if you keep reading from the same replica; DynamoDB offers eventually consistent reads by default and strongly consistent reads on request (base table only); S3 is strongly consistent for object operations; CDNs are eventually consistent up to their TTL; a cache in front of a database is eventually consistent up to its invalidation delay; microservices sharing data via e

The cap theorem: in the presence of a network partition (nodes cannot communicate), a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write, or errors) and availability (every request receives a non-error response). You cannot have both during a partition . Partitions happen (cross-AZ links fail, regions disconnect, a node is isolated), so the choice is real but applies only in those moments. What CAP does not say: that you choose two of three at design time forever (partition tolerance is not optional in a networked system); that "AP" systems are always available (they may still fail for other reasons); that "CP" systems are always consistent (they refuse requests during partitions to stay consistent); or anything about latency and consistency during normal operation, which is most of the time. PACELC fills the gap: if there is a Partition, trade Availability against Consistency; Else, trade Latency against Consistency. Synchronous replication across regions is consistent but slow (every write waits for the far side); asynchronous replication is fast but eventually consistent. Most systems that call themselves "AP" are really "EL": they chose low latency over consistency even when nothing is broken.

- Read-your-writes : after a write, route the user's reads to the primary for N seconds (a wrote at timestamp in the session) or compare the replica's replay position with the write's LSN before trusting it. - Monotonic reads : stick a user to one replica (consistent hashing on user ID) or carry a version/LSN in the client and reject older values. - Causal ordering across services : include a version or sequence per entity in events; consumers apply only newer versions (last-writer-wins by version, not by arrival time). - Bounded staleness : measure replication lag; route to the primary when lag exceeds the bound; alert. - Compensation : when eventual consistency produces a conflict (two regions accept the same username), detect and resolve with a defined rule (first by timestamp with a tie-breaker, or manual review), and design the domain so conflicts are rare (reserve usernames in one region; partition by tenant).

- Single-leader (primary/replica): all writes to one node; simple reasoning; replicas for reads and failover; the common choice (Part VIII chapter 8). - Multi-leader : several nodes accept writes (multi-region active-active); conflicts must be resolved (last-writer-wins loses data; CRDTs or application rules); only for data designed for it (chapter 10). - Leaderless (Dynamo-style quorums: write to W of N, read from R of N, W + R N for overlap): tunable consistency; used inside Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak; the application rarely sees it directly on managed services.

t: Leader Election, Distributed Transactions and Eventual Consistency
x: Agreeing on one value across machines that can fail and lose messages is the hard problem of distributed systems. consensus algorithms (Paxos, Raft) solve it correctly at the cost of round trips and operational care; they run inside etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Kubernetes, DynamoDB, Aurora's storage layer, Kafka's controller and every managed database's failover. You almost never implement consensus; you use systems that have it and design your application so that most operations need no cross-node agreement at all.

t: Leader Election, Distributed Transactions and Eventual Consistency
x: A singleton (a scheduler, a batch coordinator, a reconciler) must run exactly once across N instances, and keep running when the current runner dies. The practical mechanism is a lease : a record with an owner and an expiry that the leader renews; others try to acquire when it expires. -- leases table: (name text primary key, owner text, expires_at timestamptz) -- acquire or renew, atomically; returns the row only if we now hold it INSERT INTO leases (name, owner, expires_at) VALUES ('scheduler', $1, now() + interval '30 seconds') ON CONFLICT (name) DO UPDATE SET owner = EXCLUDED.owner, expires_at = EXCLUDED.expires_at WHERE leases.owner = EXCLUDED.owner OR leases.expires_at < now() RETURNING owner; The leader loop: acquire; while held, do leader work and renew every 10 s; if a renewal fails (someone else holds it), stop leader work immediately. Correctness caveats: the leader may be paused (GC, network) past expiry while believing it leads, so leader work must be idempotent or guarded with a fencing token (the lease's version number passed with every write and checked by the target). Kubernetes Lease objects, Redis SET NX PX with renewal, and DynamoDB conditional writes implement the same pattern; a database you already run is the simplest, most reliable choice. For scheduled work specifically, consider not electing at all: an external scheduler (EventBridge → SQS/Lambda/ECS task) runs the job once; idempotency handles the rare double fire (Part III chapter 6).

t: Leader Election, Distributed Transactions and Eventual Consistency
x: A business process spanning services (reserve inventory → charge payment → create shipment) cannot be one transaction. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event that triggers the next, with compensating actions to undo earlier steps when a later one fails (release inventory if payment fails; refund if shipment cannot be created). Two styles: choreography (each service reacts to events; simple for short chains, hard to follow as they grow) and orchestration (a coordinator, often a workflow engine, drives the steps and compensations; explicit, observable, easier to change). Design rules: every step idempotent; every compensation idempotent and able to run after partial failure; the saga's state persisted (orchestrator) or derivable from events (choreography); timeouts for steps that never respond; and semantic locks or status fields ( order.status = 'payment pending' ) so other operations know a saga is in flight. title Order saga with compensation (orchestrated) actors label Orchestrator label Inventory label Payments label Shipping steps label ReserveStock(order, items) [idempotency key] title Step 1 detail Inventory reserves and records the reservation; replies Reserved or Insufficient. label Charge(order, amount) [idempotency key] title Step 2 detail Payments charges via the provider with an idempotency key; replies Charged or Declined. x: 2PC makes several resources commit atomically via a coordinator (prepare, then commit). It exists (XA transactions, some databases' distributed transactions) and is rarely appropriate for services: it blocks all participants while waiting, the coordinator is a single point of failure that can leave participants locked, it couples availability of every participant, and most message brokers and HTTP APIs do not participate. Use it only within a single database cluster that supports it natively, and even then prefer designs that avoid it.

Step Functions integrates with AWS services natively and is the pragmatic choice on AWS for order processing, document pipelines and provisioning flows; Temporal when you need code-first workflows across clouds. The trade is another system and a learning curve; for two-step processes, an outbox and idempotent consumers suffice.

h: Kafka concepts, since you will meet them
x: A topic is split into partitions ; each partition is an ordered, append-only log; messages with the same key go to the same partition (ordering per key); a consumer group divides partitions among its members (each partition to exactly one member), so parallelism is bounded by partition count; consumers track offsets and commit them; retention keeps messages for a time or size regardless of consumption, enabling replay and multiple independent consumer groups; compacted topics keep the latest value per key (a changelog). Producers batch and can be idempotent; transactions make produce-and-commit-offsets atomic for exactly-once stream processing. Operational concerns: partition count (hard to change without re-keying; over-provision moderately), consumer lag monitoring, rebalances (consumers joining/leaving pause processing), broker storage, under-replicated partitions, and version upgrades. Schema Registry (Avro/Protobuf/JSON Schema) enforces compatibility of message shapes. Kafka is superb for streams: event sourcing, change data capture, analytics ingestion, feeding many downstream systems from one firehose. It is a poor job queue: no per-message acks (offsets are positional, so a slow message blocks its partition's progress or must be parked), no delayed delivery, no native dead-letter semantics, and a lot to operate.

AMQP broker: producers publish to exchanges ; bindings route to queues by routing key or headers; consumers ack messages individually; unacked messages are redelivered; dead-letter exchanges capture rejected or expired messages; priorities, TTLs and delayed delivery (plugin); quorum queues replicate for HA; streams add Kafka-like replay. Excellent routing flexibility and per-message semantics; moderate operational load (Amazon MQ manages the broker but you size and configure it). Natural for on-premises or multi-cloud clients and for complex routing topologies.

Part III chapters 6–7 covered the patterns. Reminders: standard queues are at-least-once and unordered; FIFO queues order within a message group and deduplicate by ID for five minutes (and have throughput limits per group); visibility timeout must exceed processing time; long polling; batching for cost; DLQ with maxReceiveCount ; redrive to source. SNS fans out to SQS queues, Lambda, HTTP endpoints with message filtering per subscriber; EventBridge adds content-based rules , schema discovery, archive and replay, scheduler, and integrations with SaaS and AWS service events (the right home for "something happened in AWS" automation). Both are serverless with no operations.

Regardless of broker: - Envelope : event ID, type, version, occurred-at, producer, trace context, and the payload (Part III chapter 7). The event ID is the dedup key. - Idempotent consumers (Part III chapter 3): dedup by event ID with a bounded store; version checks for out-of-order. - Keys for ordering : choose the entity whose order matters (order ID, tenant ID); never expect global order. - Bounded retries : exponential backoff; dead-letter after N; alert on DLQ depth; a replay tool. - Backpressure : consumers pull at their pace (SQS, Kafka); producers may need to slow when queues or lag grow; alert on age of oldest message or consumer lag. - Poison messages : a message that always fails must not block the queue (SQS: DLQ; Kafka: park it in a retry/DLQ topic and commit past it). - Schema evolution : additive changes; version field; consumers tolerant of unknown fields (Part III chapter 7). - Security : encryption at rest and in transit; IAM/ACLs per producer and consumer; validate message content as untrusted input. - Observability : trace propagation through message attributes; per-queue/topic metrics; end-to-end latency.

- Work queue on AWS → SQS (standard; FIFO only if ordering per key is required and throughput fits). - Fan-out of domain events to several AWS consumers → SNS → SQS or EventBridge (when routing rules, schema registry or SaaS sources matter). - Replayable event stream, CDC, analytics feeds, many consumer teams, very high volume → Kafka (MSK Serverless or Confluent to limit operations), with a team that will own it. - Complex routing, AMQP clients, on-premises → RabbitMQ . - Lightweight in-app queue where Redis already exists and loss is tolerable → Redis Streams (Part VIII chapter 11). Default to the simplest broker that meets the semantics; Kafka clusters for a three-service system are a common and expensive regret.

- Assuming ordering across partitions or standard queues. - Kafka as a job queue; slow messages block partitions. - Partition count chosen tiny; cannot scale consumers. - Retries without backoff or limit; a poison message consumed forever. - Visibility timeouts shorter than processing (duplicate processing) or far longer (slow recovery). - No DLQ or nobody watching it. - Breaking schema changes stranding old messages. - No idempotency; duplicates become double emails and double charges. - Choosing by hype; operating a cluster nobody owns. questions What bounds consumer parallelism in Kafka? options Broker count The number of partitions in the topic (one consumer per partition per group) Message size Retention answer explain Choose partition counts with future parallelism in mind; re-partitioning is disruptive. Which broker is the most appropriate default for an AWS work queue? options Kafka RabbitMQ Redis Pub/Sub answer explain Serverless, at-least-once, DLQ built in, no operations. Why is Kafka a poor fit for a classic job queue? options It is slow Offsets are positional: a slow or failing message blocks its partition unless parked; no per-message ack, delay or native DLQ It cannot persist It has no consumer groups answer explain Use SQS or RabbitMQ for jobs; Kafka for streams. What must every consumer implement regardless of broker? options Exactly-once delivery Idempotent processing with deduplication by event ID and tolerance for out-of-order delivery Global ordering Sync

- Implement timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads and idempotency so that dependency failures stay contained. - Understand retry storms, cascading failures and metastable states, and how these patterns prevent them. - Use distributed locks and leases safely for efficiency, not correctness. - Configure these patterns consistently via libraries, meshes and gateways. ::: Part II chapters 6 and 18; Part III chapters 3 and 5; chapter 6 of this part. :::

Every outbound call (database, cache, another service, a third-party API) can fail, hang or slow down. Without discipline, one slow dependency consumes all your threads or connections, your service slows, its callers retry, the dependency receives more load, and a small fault becomes a full outage: a cascading failure . The patterns here are the engineering of containment, and they are mostly configuration once you know what to set.

A call without a timeout is a promise to wait forever. Every call gets: a connect timeout (short, 1–3 s: a dropped SYN should fail fast), a read/response timeout (per call, based on the dependency's p99 plus margin), and ideally a total deadline propagated across hops (the caller's remaining budget, so a downstream service does not keep working on a request the user has already given up on). Set them lower than the caller's own timeout so failures surface where they can be handled. Timeouts are errors (Part III chapter 12): log them, count them, and treat them as retryable only if the operation is idempotent. import httpx client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(connect=2.0, read=5.0, write=5.0, pool=1.0), limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=50, max_keepalive_connections=20))

Retries hide transient failures (a dropped packet, a restarting instance) and amplify sustained ones (a saturated dependency receives N× the load). Rules: - Retry only idempotent operations or those protected by idempotency keys (Part III chapter 3). - Retry only retryable errors : timeouts, connection errors, 429, 502/503/504; never 400/401/403/404/422. - Bound attempts (2–3 for interactive paths; more for background jobs) and total time. - Exponential backoff with full jitter : sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)) . Jitter prevents synchronised retry waves from many clients. - Honour Retry-After . - Make retries visible : a metric per dependency; a spike in retries is an early warning. - Avoid retry amplification across layers: if the client, the gateway and the service each retry 3 times, the dependency sees 27 attempts. Retry at one layer (usually the outermost that can judge idempotency), or budget retries as a fraction of traffic (e.g., at most 10% extra load). import random, asyncio async def with_retries(fn, attempts=3, base=0.2, cap=3.0, retry_on=(TimeoutError, ConnectionError, RetryableHTTP)): for i in range(attempts): try: return await fn() except retry_on as e: if i == attempts - 1: raise delay = random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * (2 ** i))) metrics.increment("retry", tags={"dep": fn.__name__}) await asyncio.sleep(delay)

When a dependency is failing, continuing to call it wastes resources (threads blocked on timeouts) and makes its recovery harder. A circuit breaker tracks failures per dependency; after a threshold (e.g., 50% failures over 20 calls) it opens : calls fail immediately without touching the dependency for a cooling period (30 s); then half-open : a few trial calls go through; success closes it, failure re-opens. Combine with a fallback : cached data, a default, a degraded response, or a queued deferral (chapter 9). Breakers belong around every external dependency and non-critical internal one; they are the mechanism behind graceful degradation (chapter 2). Libraries: pybreaker / aiobreaker , Resilience4j (JVM), Polly (.NET), opossum (Node); service meshes and Envoy implement outlier detection and circuit breaking per upstream; API gateways can too.

Named after ship compartments: isolate resources so one failing dependency or one noisy tenant cannot exhaust everything. Separate connection pools and thread pools per dependency (a slow payment API cannot consume the connections needed for the database); per-tenant concurrency limits (semaphores) on expensive operations; separate worker pools or queues per job type (Part III chapter 6); separate instances or cells for critical versus bulk traffic. The cost is some idle capacity in each compartment; the benefit is that the blast radius of any single failure is one compartment. # Per-dependency bulkheads: bounded concurrency payment_sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10) async def charge(order): async with asyncio.timeout(5): async with payment_sem: # at most 10 in-flight payment calls per instance return await breaker_payment.call(lambda: payments_client.charge(order))

Retries, redeliveries and failovers all produce duplicates. Idempotent operations make all of them safe (Part III chapter 3). Every pattern above assumes it; without it, retries are dangerous and circuit breakers' fallbacks may double-apply effects.

For efficiency (avoid two workers doing the same expensive work) a lock in Redis or a database lease is fine, provided the work is idempotent and the lock has a TTL and token-checked release (Part VIII chapter 11; chapter 6). For correctness (ensure at most one of something), rely on the database (unique constraints, conditional updates, row locks) or on fencing tokens, because distributed locks can be held by two parties after pauses and failovers. State explicitly which kind each lock is.

When overloaded, serving everyone badly is worse than serving most well. Shed early: reject (503 with Retry-After ) when queue depth or in-flight count exceeds capacity, prioritise critical endpoints and paying tenants, drop low-value work first (analytics events before orders), and apply backpressure to upstream producers. Adaptive concurrency limits (based on observed latency, as in Netflix's concurrency-limits ) adjust automatically. Chapter 9 covers this with rate limiting.

h: Metastable failures and the role of these patterns
x: A system can enter a state where load from retries and recovery work keeps it saturated even after the original trigger disappears (a metastable failure ): caches empty, everything misses, database overloaded, timeouts, retries, more load. Breaking the loop requires shedding load, pausing retries, warming caches, or scaling. Prevent it by: bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers that stop hammering, load shedding at the entry, cache warming on restart, and capacity headroom. Recognise it in incident reviews: "the trigger ended at 14:05 but we stayed down until 14:40 because retries kept the database pinned."

Resilience settings scattered across code drift. Centralise: a client factory per dependency that sets timeouts, retries, breaker and bulkhead from configuration; a service mesh or gateway enforcing timeouts, retries and outlier detection at the network layer for service-to-service calls; documented values per dependency (its p99, your timeout, retry policy, breaker thresholds, fallback). Review them when dependencies change.

Fault injection in staging: add latency and errors to a dependency (toxiproxy, AWS Fault Injection Service, mesh fault injection) and verify timeouts fire, breakers open, fallbacks serve, and the service stays within its SLO. Unit tests for retry classification (never retry 400). Game days that pull a dependency entirely (Part XI chapter 9).

- No timeouts; threads consumed by a dead dependency. - Retrying everything, including non-idempotent POSTs and 4xx errors. - Retries without jitter; synchronised storms. - Retry at every layer; 27× amplification. - Circuit breakers without fallbacks; or breakers on the database (where a tripped breaker is the outage; use timeouts, pools and shedding instead). - One shared pool for every dependency; one slow API starves the database connections. - Redis locks guarding money. - Resilience "handled by the mesh" that nobody configured. questions Why add jitter to exponential backoff? options To make retries faster To desynchronise retries from many clients so they do not arrive in waves that re-overload the dependency It is required by HTTP To reduce logging answer explain Full jitter spreads retry load across the window. What does an open circuit breaker do? options Blocks all traffic to the service Fails calls to a failing dependency immediately for a cooling period, then tests recovery with a few trial calls Retries faster Restarts the dependency answer explain It protects both your resources and the dependency's recovery. Which errors should never be retried? options Timeouts 503 Service Unavailable 400/401/403/404/422 client errors Connection resets answer explain Client errors will fail identically on retry; retrying wastes capacity and may mask bugs. What is a bulkhead in software? options A firewall Isolated resource pools per dependency or tenant so one failure cannot e

t: Service Discovery, Fault Tolerance, Graceful Degradation and Rate Limiting
x: When demand exceeds capacity, choose who to disappoint. Shedding is designed and tested in advance; improvised shedding during an incident means random failures.

t: Disaster Recovery, Multi-Region Architecture and Cost versus Complexity
x: The complexity lives in data. Options: - Partition by tenant or geography : each tenant's data has a home Region; the other Region serves only on failover (for that tenant). Avoids write conflicts; routing must send tenants to their home; cross-tenant features become cross-Region. - Globally replicated data stores with conflict resolution : DynamoDB Global Tables (last-writer-wins by timestamp: design keys and writes to avoid conflicts), Aurora Global Database with write forwarding (writes go to the primary Region; reads local), CRDT-based stores for mergeable data. - Read-local, write-global : reads served from the nearest Region's replica; writes routed to a single primary Region (latency for writes; strong consistency preserved). Often the pragmatic compromise. Everything else multiplies: deployments to multiple Regions (pipelines, staged rollouts per Region), observability aggregated globally, secrets and keys per Region, compliance (data residency may forbid replication to some Regions), cost of cross-Region data transfer, and testing of failure modes between Regions (partial partitions). A single-Region multi-AZ design plus pilot light achieves 99.9%+ for most purposes; active-active is for 99.99% and beyond with an organisation to match (chapter 2).

Code generation : options are a counter encoded in base62 (short, sequential: enumerable, reveals volume), a random base62 string of 7+ characters (62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion: collisions negligible, check on insert and retry), or a hash of the URL (same URL → same code; privacy and custom-alias conflicts). Choose random 7-character codes with a unique constraint and retry on collision; custom aliases are validated (allowed characters, reserved words, length) and must be unique per domain. Codes are case-sensitive; document it. Redirect status : 301 is cached permanently by browsers (fewer hits, but analytics lose repeat clicks and you cannot change the target); 302/307 re-request each time (accurate analytics, changeable targets, more load). Default 302; offer 301 for permanent links. Hot path : CloudFront in front caches responses per code briefly, so a viral code is served from the edge; the service uses Redis cache-aside with a TTL and negative caching; the database is read only on misses. Analytics never block the redirect: publish-and-forget to a queue with a tiny timeout; if the queue is unavailable, drop the event and count the drop (redirect availability beats analytics completeness). Data model : links(code PK, target text, owner id, tenant id, created at, expires at, kind {temporary, permanent}, status {active, disabled, flagged}, custom bool) with indexes on (tenant id, created at) and (owner id) ; click counts(code, day, count) maintained by the consumer; raw clicks in S3

- Hot code : one code receives 5,000 rps. Edge caching absorbs almost all; Redis handles the remainder; without CloudFront, a single Redis key could become hot (fine at this scale; replicate into process memory with a 1 s TTL if needed). - Redis down : every redirect hits the database; at 500 rps PostgreSQL copes, so the cache is a soft dependency; short timeouts and fallthrough. - Database down : redirects fail except edge-cached ones; management down. Multi-AZ RDS; consider a read replica and a last-known-good local cache for the hottest codes. - Queue down : drop events, count drops, alert; redirects unaffected. - Enumeration : attackers probe random codes to find private links; 7-character random space makes this impractical; negative caching and rate limiting blunt it; private links can additionally require a token. - Cache invalidation : changing a target or disabling a link must evict Redis and (short) CloudFront TTL keeps edge staleness under a minute; for take-downs of malicious links, issue a CloudFront invalidation.

Open redirects are the product, so: validate target URLs (http/https only; no javascript: ; resolve and block private IP ranges to avoid the shortener being used for SSRF against internal endpoints, Part IV chapter 12); interstitials for flagged links; authentication and per-tenant authorisation on management; audit logs; rate limits; secrets in a secrets manager; TLS everywhere; HSTS; CSP on management UI; the redirect domain separate from the management domain (cookies not sent to redirect domain).

Metrics: redirect p99, cache hit ratio (edge and Redis), 404/410 rates, creation rate, flagged link count, queue age, drop count. Alarms: redirect 5xx rate, p99 50 ms at origin, Redis unavailable, queue age 5 min, Safe Browsing API failures. Cost: dominated by CloudFront requests and Fargate tasks; tiny database; S3 storage for clicks. Runbooks: take down a link, rotate the salt, restore from PITR, scale for a viral event.

Edge-serving of redirects from a KV store at the edge (CloudFront KeyValueStore or Cloudflare Workers KV), DynamoDB for the link table (key-based, global tables for multi-Region), Kinesis for clicks, pre-aggregation in stream processing. The design above already has the seams for each. questions Why generate codes randomly rather than from a counter? options Random codes are shorter Sequential codes reveal volume and make every link enumerable; random 7-character codes make guessing impractical Counters cannot be unique Random codes compress better answer explain Check uniqueness on insert and retry on the rare collision. Why must the click-analytics write never be synchronous on the redirect path? options Analytics are illegal Redirect latency and availability are the product; analytics is secondary and must not add latency or fail the redirect Databases cannot handle it Queues require it answer explain Publish asynchronously with a tiny timeout; drop and count on failure. What is the shortener-specific security control on target URLs? options Shortening only HTTPS Validating scheme and resolving/blocking private and link-local addresses so the service cannot be used for SSRF, plus malware/phishing checks and interstitials Encrypting targets answer explain A redirector is an open redirect by design; constrain what it will redirect to. What makes the Redis cache a soft dependency here? options It is replicated The database can serve the redirect load directly if the cache fai

1. Implement the redirect service with Redis cache-aside, negative caching and asynchronous click publishing; load test a single hot code and measure origin hits with and without an edge cache. 2. Add target validation against private IP ranges and a Safe Browsing check with an interstitial for flagged links. 3. Write the one-page design document (requirements, estimates, decisions, failure modes, costs) and have someone review it against chapters 1–10.

- Design an identity platform serving several applications: registration, login, sessions and tokens, MFA, SSO federation, account recovery, administration. - Reason about the availability, security and privacy constraints that make authentication different from ordinary services. - Decide when to build versus buy (Cognito, Auth0, Keycloak) and what remains yours either way. ::: Part IV chapters 3–8; chapters 1–10 of this part. :::

Functional : email/password and passkey registration and login; TOTP and WebAuthn MFA; social login (Google, Microsoft) and enterprise SSO (OIDC/SAML per tenant); issue sessions for first-party web apps and OAuth 2.0 tokens for APIs and mobile; refresh and revocation; password reset and MFA recovery; admin console (users, roles, tenants, audit); SCIM provisioning for enterprise tenants; audit log of all authentication events. Non-functional : availability 99.99% for token validation and login (every application depends on it); login p95 < 500 ms; token validation local (no network call) at p99 < 2 ms; 1 million users, 200,000 daily logins, peak 100 logins/s; strong security (this is the system whose compromise is total); privacy (minimal personal data, regional residency); auditability for compliance.

title Authentication platform nodes label Client apps web, mobile, APIs client Relying parties. Web apps use OIDC code flow with PKCE and get a session; mobile gets refresh+access tokens; APIs validate access tokens locally with the JWKS. label CloudFront + WAF Rate rules on /login, /token, /reset; bot control; geo rules per tenant policy. label Auth service stateless ×N, 3 AZs OIDC provider endpoints (authorize, token, userinfo, jwks, logout), credential verification (Argon2id), MFA, passkeys (WebAuthn), federation brokering, session management. admin label Admin + SCIM API Separate service and deployment: tenant config (IdP settings, policies), user management, SCIM endpoints, audit queries. SSO with MFA for operators; strict RBAC. label KMS / HSM signing keys Token signing (ES256) via KMS asymmetric keys: private key never leaves the HSM; rotation with kid; JWKS publishes public keys. label PostgreSQL (Aurora or RDS Multi-AZ) users, credentials, tenants, audit Users keyed by stable ID; credentials (Argon2 hashes, encrypted TOTP secrets, passkey public keys); tenant IdP configs (secrets in Secrets Manager); append-only audit table; RLS per tenant. redis label Redis (HA) sessions, rate limits, codes Server-side sessions with rotation; login rate limits; one-time codes; refresh-token family tracking; hard dependency: Multi-AZ with failover. label External IdPs Google, Entra, client SAML Federation targets; per-tenant configuration; token validation per Part IV chapter 6. labe

Build or buy : managed IdPs (Cognito, Auth0/Okta CIC, Entra External ID) or self-hosted Keycloak/Ory provide the protocols, MFA, federation and much of the hardening; building from scratch is justified only with strong reasons (unusual requirements, cost at very large scale, residency constraints a vendor cannot meet). Even when buying, you own: user data model and tenancy, role mapping, session handling in your apps, recovery policy, audit integration, and the vendor's configuration. This case study assumes building the core to teach the trade-offs; in practice recommend buying unless the client has a reason not to. Tokens and sessions : first-party web apps get a server-side session cookie from the auth service's domain via OIDC (the apps are relying parties); APIs receive short-lived (10 min) ES256 access tokens signed via KMS with kid , validated locally against cached JWKS (so token validation has no runtime dependency on the auth service, which is what makes 99.99% for validation achievable); refresh tokens are opaque, stored hashed, rotated on use with family revocation on reuse (Part IV chapter 5); revocation is immediate for sessions and refresh tokens and bounded by 10 minutes for access tokens (plus an optional short-TTL denylist check for high-risk apps). Credentials : Argon2id with tuned parameters; breached-password check at set time; passkeys as the preferred factor; TOTP with replay protection; WebAuthn security keys for admins; recovery codes hashed; recovery

- Argon2 CPU : 100 logins/s × 100 ms CPU = 10 CPU-seconds per second: 12+ vCPUs just for hashing at peak. Size for it; put hashing on a dedicated worker pool so a credential-stuffing burst cannot starve token endpoints; rate-limit per account and IP before hashing (reject early); use a dummy hash for unknown users to equalise timing. - Credential stuffing : the dominant traffic during attacks. WAF rate rules, per-account and per-IP limits, progressive delays, device fingerprint reputation, breached-password checks, and MFA. Monitor failure rates as the attack signal. - Redis unavailable : sessions and rate limits fail; fail closed (503) for session validation; HA Redis is therefore mandatory, not optional. - KMS latency and quotas : signing via KMS adds ~5–10 ms and has request quotas; cache nothing about private keys (they never leave KMS) but batch and keep token issuance rate within quota; request quota increases; alternatively hold signing keys in memory loaded from KMS-wrapped storage for very high rates, accepting a weaker boundary. - Key rotation : publish the new public key in JWKS, wait longer than the longest client cache, start signing with it, retire the old key after all tokens signed with it expire. A client that caches JWKS forever will break; document cache TTLs and kid handling for integrators. - Email deliverability : reset links in spam; SPF/DKIM/DMARC configured; a provider with reputation management; status visible to support.

Everything in Part IV chapters 3–9 applies, plus: the auth service's own admin access via hardware-key MFA and SSO; separate deployment and network path for admin/SCIM; secrets (IdP client secrets, signing configuration) in Secrets Manager with per-tenant scoping; strict CSP and no third-party scripts on login pages; signed and pinned dependencies; regular penetration tests focused on the protocol flows; incident runbooks for "signing key compromised" (rotate immediately, revoke all sessions, force re-authentication) and "tenant IdP compromised" (disable federation for the tenant, notify).

SLIs: login success rate and latency, token issuance latency, JWKS availability, MFA success rate, reset completion rate; alarms on failure-rate spikes (attack), on error budget burn, on KMS throttling, on Redis failover; dashboards per tenant for enterprise customers; audit queries for support; drills for key rotation and regional failover. questions How does the design achieve 99.99% availability for token validation even if the auth service is down? options Multi-Region active-active Access tokens are validated locally by relying parties against cached JWKS, so validation has no runtime dependency on the auth service for the token's lifetime Redis caching of tokens KMS replication answer explain Short-lived signed tokens plus cached public keys decouple validation from availability. Why run password hashing on a dedicated worker pool with pre-hash rate limiting? options Argon2 requires it Hashing is CPU-expensive by design; a credential-stuffing burst could otherwise starve token endpoints; rejecting early and isolating the pool is a bulkhead To reduce memory For audit answer explain Capacity planning for an authentication service is capacity planning for attacks. What should happen to sessions if Redis is unavailable? options Treat users as anonymous Fail closed with 503 for authenticated routes; make Redis highly available so this is rare Fall back to JWTs Allow all requests answer explain Security controls that cannot decide must deny. When should a client build its own

1. Write the token and session design (lifetimes, rotation, revocation, JWKS cache guidance) as the integration guide you would give relying-party developers. 2. Size the hashing capacity for 100 logins/s with Argon2id at 100 ms and design the pre-hash rate limiting; load test with a credential-stuffing simulation in a sandbox. 3. Rehearse the "signing key compromised" runbook on a test deployment: rotate the key, revoke sessions, verify clients recover.
- JWTs: Limitations and Safe Usage - OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and SSO - Password Storage, MFA and Passkeys

- Design the backend for an online store: catalogue, cart, checkout, orders, payments, inventory and fulfilment. - Handle the hard parts: inventory consistency under concurrent purchases, payment idempotency, flash-sale traffic and exactly-once-looking order creation. - Apply the consistency, messaging and resilience patterns from this part to a domain where mistakes cost money. ::: Chapters 1–10 of this part; Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks; Message Brokers. :::

Functional : browse and search a catalogue (500,000 SKUs); product pages with price, stock, images, reviews; cart (anonymous and logged-in, merged on login); checkout with address, shipping options, promotions and tax; payment via a provider (card, wallets); order lifecycle (placed, paid, packed, shipped, delivered, cancelled, refunded); inventory across warehouses; notifications; back office for merchandising and customer service. Non-functional : 99.95% for browse and checkout (a 10-minute checkout outage at peak is lost revenue and public complaints); product page p95 < 300 ms; checkout p95 < 1.5 s excluding the payment provider; 2 million daily visitors, 50,000 daily orders, peak 20× average during sales (flash sales reach 5,000 requests/s on a few hot SKUs); never oversell beyond a defined tolerance; never charge twice; PCI scope minimised (card data never touches your servers); auditability of every price, stock and money change.

Quantity Estimate Implication --- --- --- Page views 2M visitors × 8 pages = 16M/day ≈ 185/s avg, ~2,000/s peak Browse must be served mostly from caches and a CDN Orders 50,000/day ≈ 0.6/s avg, ~15/s peak, 200/s in a flash sale Order writes are small; the contention is on hot SKUs, not volume Catalogue 500k SKUs × ~5 KB = 2.5 GB Fits in a search index and a cache comfortably Images 500k × 6 × 300 KB ≈ 900 GB S3 + CDN, resized variants generated once Orders stored 50k/day × 5 KB × 7 years ≈ 640 GB Partition by month; archive cold months

title E-commerce backend nodes label Storefront web + mobile client Server-rendered or SPA; talks to a BFF/API. Carries a cart token (anonymous) or session. label CDN + WAF Caches product pages/fragments and images; bot management (scalpers in flash sales); rate rules on checkout and login. label Catalogue service read-heavy Product data from a read model: cache (Redis) in front of PostgreSQL replicas; search via OpenSearch fed by change events. Prices and stock are embedded with short TTLs and invalidated on change. label Cart service Carts in Redis (TTL 30 days) keyed by cart ID; logged-in carts also persisted to PostgreSQL; merge on login. label Checkout + Orders transactional Price recalculation, promotions, tax, shipping; creates the order in a transaction; reserves inventory; initiates payment; publishes OrderPlaced. Idempotency keys everywhere. label Inventory service Owns stock per SKU per warehouse; reservations with expiry; atomic decrement with constraint check; hot-SKU protection (per-SKU serialisation or token buckets for flash sales). label Payment service Wraps the provider: creates payment intents, handles webhooks with signature verification, reconciles. Stores provider IDs and statuses only; never card data. label PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ) orders, inventory, customers Source of truth for money and stock; strict constraints (stock >= 0); outbox table for events; read replicas for reporting. redis label Redis cache, carts, locks Product cache, carts, rate limits,

title Place order and pay participants Storefront Checkout Inventory Payment Provider Event bus steps Storefront Checkout label POST /orders (Idempotency-Key, cart, address) detail The client generates a UUID idempotency key when the user first clicks Pay and reuses it on retries. The server stores the key with the request hash and the response. Networks fail at the worst moment: without the key a retry creates a second order. Checkout Checkout label Recalculate prices, promotions, tax detail Never trust prices from the client. Recompute from the catalogue and promotion rules; compare to the cart total the user saw and ask for confirmation if changed. Checkout Inventory label Reserve items (order ID, lines) detail UPDATE stock SET reserved = reserved + n WHERE sku = ? AND available - reserved >= n. Zero rows affected means out of stock. Reservation expires in 15 minutes if payment never completes. The constraint check and the update are one atomic statement; this is what prevents overselling. Checkout Checkout label INSERT order (status=pending_payment) + outbox event detail Order, lines, snapshot of prices and addresses, and the OrderPlaced outbox row in the same transaction. Checkout Payment label Create payment intent (amount, order ID as idempotency key) detail The provider's idempotency key is derived from the order ID so a retry returns the same intent instead of a second charge. Payment Provider label POST /payment_intents detail Card details were collected by the prov

Inventory consistency : the stock row is the serialisation point. Use a single atomic conditional update rather than read-then-write; use reservations with expiry so abandoned checkouts release stock; tolerate a small, configured oversell for marketplace-style catalogues where suppliers can backfill, but never for limited editions. For flash sales on a few SKUs, the row becomes a hotspot: pre-allocate a fixed number of "purchase tokens" into Redis at sale start and admit only token holders to checkout, turning a thundering herd at the database into a cheap Redis decrement and a polite "sold out" for everyone else. Money : integers in minor units; every change to an order's financial state is an append-only ledger entry, not an update; payment state machine with explicit allowed transitions; reconciliation job comparing the provider's settlement report to the ledger daily; refunds through the same idempotent path. Idempotency : client-generated keys on order creation; order-derived keys to the provider; event IDs for consumers; webhook deduplication by provider event ID. Store processed keys with TTLs matching retry windows (24 h for orders, forever for payments). Read path : product pages assembled from a cached read model; stock shown as "in stock / low / out" rather than exact counts so the cache can be a little stale; price and stock fragments carry short TTLs and are invalidated by StockChanged and PriceChanged events; search index updated from events within seconds. Prom

- Hot SKU at sale start : thousands of transactions contend on one row; lock waits balloon; the whole database slows. Mitigation: Redis admission tokens, per-SKU queueing, or sharding stock into buckets that are summed lazily. - Payment provider slow or down : checkout waits. Set timeouts (10 s), create the order as pending, and let the webhook complete it; show "we are confirming your payment" rather than failing; circuit-break and show a maintenance message if the provider is down for minutes; never retry a charge without the idempotency key. - Webhook ordering : succeeded may arrive before created , or twice. Make handlers transition-aware and idempotent; fetch the current state from the provider when in doubt. - Cache stampede on a popular product : use request coalescing and stale-while-revalidate (chapter 4). - Reservation leaks : a crash between reservation and order insert leaves stock reserved. Reservations expire; a sweeper releases expired ones; the order insert and reservation can also live in the same transaction if both are in the same database. - Search index lag : a new product appears in the catalogue before it is searchable; acceptable and documented, with a reindex job for drift. - Reporting queries on the primary during peak: route to a replica or warehouse; forbid ad hoc queries on the primary.

Price and quantity manipulation (recompute server-side; validate quantities and SKUs); coupon abuse (rate limit, single-use enforcement, bind to account); account takeover for stored payment methods (MFA, re-authentication before using a saved method or changing address); PCI scope kept to SAQ A/A-EP by using hosted fields; webhook signature verification and replay windows; IDOR on orders ( /orders/{id} must check ownership, Part IV chapter 7); scraping and scalper bots (WAF bot control, proof-of-work or CAPTCHA at sale time); admin back office behind SSO with audit; PII minimisation and retention for addresses and emails; fraud screening hooks before capture.

SLIs: checkout conversion funnel per step, order creation success rate, payment success rate by provider and method, p95 latencies, oversell count (should be zero), reservation leak count, webhook lag, search index lag. Alarms on payment failure spikes (provider incident or fraud wave), on oversells, on queue backlogs in fulfilment. Runbooks: provider outage, flash-sale preparation (pre-scale, token allocation, cache warm), stuck orders reconciliation. Load test the hot-SKU path before every big sale. questions Why is a single conditional UPDATE (available - reserved >= n) preferred over reading stock and then writing? options It is faster to type It makes the check and the decrement atomic, so two concurrent buyers cannot both pass the check for the last unit Reads are expensive It avoids using transactions answer explain Read-then-write is a race; the conditional update serialises on the row. What role does the client-generated Idempotency-Key play on POST /orders? options It authenticates the user A network retry of the same request returns the same order instead of creating a duplicate It encrypts the cart It selects the warehouse answer explain Idempotency keys turn at-least-once retries into exactly-once effects. How should a flash sale on one SKU avoid melting the database? options Add more read replicas Admit buyers through a fixed pool of Redis tokens so only as many checkouts proceed as there is stock Disable constraints temporarily Increase the connection pool answ

1. Implement the reservation and confirmation SQL and test it with 200 concurrent buyers for 10 units; verify exactly 10 succeed. 2. Write the payment state machine (states, allowed transitions, which webhook events drive them) and the idempotent webhook handler. 3. Design the flash-sale admission mechanism and run a load test showing the database stays healthy under 5,000 requests/s to one SKU.
- Transactions, ACID, Isolation Levels and Locks - Message Brokers - Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access

t: Case Study: File Upload and Processing Service
x: Functional : authenticated users upload files up to 5 GB (video) and 50 MB (documents, images); files belong to a workspace and have permissions; processing per type: image resize and format conversion, thumbnail generation, document text extraction and preview, video transcoding to streaming formats; virus and malware scanning; download and inline viewing with permission checks; resumable uploads; retention and deletion (including legal deletion within 30 days); audit of access. Nothing is served from this bucket. t: Case Study: File Upload and Processing Service
x: Direct-to-storage uploads : the API never proxies bytes. It authorises and issues a presigned URL (or multipart upload ID) bound to a specific key, maximum size and content type, valid for minutes. This keeps the API stateless and small, lets S3 absorb the bandwidth, and makes resumable multipart uploads straightforward. The trade-off: the API cannot inspect the content before it lands, hence the quarantine bucket. Quarantine and promotion : raw uploads are untrusted and unreadable by anyone until the scanner promotes them. Promotion copies the object to the content bucket under a content-addressed key (SHA-256), which deduplicates identical files and makes the stored path independent of the user-supplied filename (which is stored only as metadata and sanitised on download via Content-Disposition ). Processing isolation : parsers for images, PDFs and video are historically the richest source of remote code execution bugs. Run them in minimal containers with no outbound network, read-only filesystems, memory and CPU limits, seccomp profiles, a hard timeout, and the least IAM privilege (read quarantine key, write content key). A compromised processor should be able to do nothing but corrupt its own output. Treat decompression bombs and pathological inputs (giant dimensions, deep PDF object nesting) as expected and fail them fast. Serving : a separate domain (never the app's origin) so stored HTML or SVG cannot run with the app's cookies; Content-Type from your validated metadat

t: Case Study: File Upload and Processing Service
x: - Lost events : S3 event notifications are at-least-once but a misconfiguration can drop them. Belt and braces: the client calls complete on the API, which enqueues the job too; a sweeper finds rows stuck in uploading for over an hour and checks S3 directly. - Poison files : a file that crashes the processor every time will be retried forever. Max receive count with a dead-letter queue; the record is marked failed with a reason; alerts on DLQ depth. - Thundering transcodes : one customer uploads 10,000 videos. Per-workspace concurrency limits and fair queueing so one tenant does not starve others; priority lanes for interactive uploads. - Scanner signature freshness : ClamAV definitions must update; a scanner with stale definitions should fail health checks. Supplement with commercial scanning APIs for high-risk workspaces. - Large multipart uploads abandoned : incomplete multipart parts cost money silently; lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after 1 day. - Signed URL leakage : a shared link works for anyone until it expires. Keep expiry to minutes for private files, bind to the requester where possible, and offer explicit shareable links as a distinct, audited feature.

t: Case Study: File Upload and Processing Service
x: Everything in File Uploads and Object Storage applies: validate type by content, not extension; limit size at the presigned URL ( content-length-range ) and again in the scanner; strip metadata (EXIF location) from images on re-encode; re-encode images rather than passing bytes through; never execute, include or render stored files server-side; separate serving domain; permission check on every download; audit log of uploads, downloads and shares; SSRF prevention in any "import from URL" feature (Part IV chapter 12); IAM policies that let the API only generate URLs for keys under the caller's workspace prefix; bucket policies denying public access and unencrypted puts; KMS encryption with per-environment keys and optional per-tenant keys for enterprise.

t: Case Study: File Upload and Processing Service
x: SLIs: upload success rate, time-to-ready per type, scanner rejection rate, DLQ depth, processing cost per GB, storage by tier and tenant. Alarms on time-to-ready SLO breaches, on DLQ growth, on scanner definition age, on orphaned objects after reconciliation. Cost review monthly: storage growth, egress through the CDN, transcoding minutes. questions Why do uploads go directly to object storage with a presigned URL instead of through the API? options Presigned URLs are more secure than TLS The API stays stateless and off the data path; S3 absorbs bandwidth and supports resumable multipart uploads It avoids authentication S3 scans files automatically answer explain The API authorises; S3 moves bytes. The price is needing a quarantine step for content inspection. Why serve files from a separate domain with Content-Type set from stored metadata? options For better caching So user-controlled content (HTML, SVG) cannot execute with the application's cookies, and browsers cannot be tricked by a user-supplied type Separate domains are cheaper To bypass CORS answer explain Stored XSS via uploaded files is neutralised by origin separation and strict types. A file crashes the image processor on every attempt. What prevents an infinite retry loop? options Nothing; restart the workers A maximum receive count moves the message to a dead-letter queue and the record is marked failed with an alert Increase the timeout Delete the file answer explain Poison-pill handling is a required part of a

- Design a platform that delivers notifications to users across channels (in-app real time, push, email, SMS) with preferences, batching and delivery guarantees. - Handle fan-out, connection management at scale, ordering, deduplication and the long tail of unreachable devices. - Keep a system that touches every user's attention from becoming a spam engine or a privacy leak. ::: WebSockets, Server-Sent Events and gRPC; Real-Time Applications; Message Brokers. :::

Functional : producers (other services) emit events ("comment on your document", "deploy finished", "invoice due"); the platform resolves recipients, applies user and tenant preferences (channels, quiet hours, digests), renders templates per channel and locale, and delivers: in-app via a persistent connection, mobile push (APNs/FCM), email, SMS, and webhooks to integrations; an inbox API with read/unread state; delivery status and analytics; rate limiting and digesting to prevent floods; unsubscribe and compliance (CAN-SPAM, GDPR consent for marketing). Non-functional : 5 million users, 500,000 concurrently connected; 50 million notifications/day (~580/s average, 10,000/s peak during broadcast events); in-app delivery p95 < 1 s to connected users; push within 5 s; email within 1 minute; 99.9% availability for ingestion (producers must never block); at-least-once delivery with deduplication so users do not see duplicates; ordering within a user's inbox; a full month of inbox history retrievable.

title Notification platform nodes label Producer services client Emit domain events with an idempotency key, event type, actor, recipients (users, roles or topics) and payload. They never know about channels. ingest label Ingest API validate, dedupe, enqueue Authenticates producers (service credentials), validates against the event schema registry, dedupes by producer key (Redis SETNX 24 h), writes to the ingest stream. Returns 202 in milliseconds. stream label Kafka / Kinesis partitioned by user Durable, ordered per partition. Topic-based broadcasts are expanded by the fan-out stage into per-user records. label Fan-out + preferences Resolves recipients (role → users, topic → subscribers), loads preferences (cached), applies quiet hours, digest rules and rate limits, decides channels. Writes an inbox record and emits per-channel delivery tasks. inbox label Inbox store DynamoDB or Cassandra Partition key user ID, sort key time-ordered ID (ULID). Read/unread state, 30-day TTL for cheap retention; archive to S3 for history. label Connection gateway WebSocket/SSE, ×N Holds 500k connections across ~25 nodes (20k each). Subscribes to a pub/sub channel per node; a presence registry maps user → node(s). Delivers immediately to connected clients; clients reconcile via the inbox API on reconnect. pubsub label Redis pub/sub / cluster Presence (user → gateway nodes, with TTL heartbeats) and fast delivery channel to the right node. Loss here is tolerable: the inbox is the source of truth.

The inbox is the source of truth; real time is an optimisation : every notification is written to the inbox store first, then pushed to connected clients. A client that misses a push (network blip, node restart) reconciles on reconnect by fetching since its last seen ID. This turns the hardest problem (reliable delivery over flaky connections) into a simple one (durable write plus best-effort push plus catch-up read). Partition by user : events for one user land on the same partition, so processing order per user is preserved and the inbox sort key reflects creation order. Broadcasts to a topic with a million subscribers are expanded into per-user records by the fan-out stage in batches, with the expansion itself checkpointed so a restart does not double-send. Connection gateway design : stateless except for the in-memory connection table; each node registers the users it holds in the presence registry with heartbeats; delivery publishes to the specific node's channel. Nodes drain gracefully on deploy (stop accepting, tell clients to reconnect with jitter, close). Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter; a mass reconnect after a node failure is the platform's own thundering herd, so the load balancer uses connection-aware routing and new nodes warm slowly. Preferences and digests : resolved at fan-out time, cached with event-driven invalidation; quiet hours delay rather than drop; digest rules collapse many low-priority events into one email per hour or day via

- Broadcast fan-out : a tenant-wide announcement to a million users generates a million inbox writes and pushes. Rate the expansion (for example 20,000 users/s), prioritise interactive events in a separate lane, and write inbox records in batches. - Reconnect storms : a gateway deploy or network incident disconnects 100,000 clients who all reconnect at once. Jittered backoff on clients, connection rate limits at the load balancer, and never deploying all gateway nodes simultaneously. - Presence staleness : a node dies without cleaning the registry; deliveries publish to nobody. Heartbeat TTLs (30 s) expire entries; delivery is best-effort anyway because the inbox catches up. - Hot users : a user subscribed to everything gets 10,000 events per hour. Per-user rate limiting at fan-out collapses into a digest and protects their partition from dominating a consumer. - Provider throttling : APNs and FCM throttle bursts; email providers enforce sending rates per domain; SMS costs real money per message. Token buckets per provider, cost caps per tenant per day, alerts on anomalies (a bug that sends 50 SMS to each user is a budget incident within minutes). - Clock skew and ordering : ULIDs generated on different fan-out workers can interleave slightly out of order; acceptable for an inbox, and the per-partition order is preserved for causally related events from the same producer. - Inbox store hot partitions : a single user's partition receiving a flood; DynamoDB adaptive capacity ha

Notifications carry snippets of private data to devices and third-party providers. Minimise payloads sent to push providers (send a title and an ID; fetch content on open) so content never transits APNs/FCM in clear text where policy demands; strip PII from logs; authenticate producers and validate that a producer may notify the recipients it names (a service for tenant A must not notify tenant B's users); webhook URLs owned by customers are SSRF targets (allowlist schemes, resolve and block private ranges, Part IV chapter 12); unsubscribe links signed and single-purpose; consent and suppression respected before any marketing send; the WebSocket handshake authenticates with a short-lived token, not a long-lived cookie reused cross-origin (Part II chapter 14); per-tenant and per-user data deletion covers inbox records, archives and provider-side data where possible.

SLIs: ingest latency and success rate, end-to-end delivery latency per channel (p50/p95), connected clients, reconnect rate, delivery failure rate per provider, DLQ depths, cost per channel per day. Alarms on delivery latency SLO burn, on provider circuit breakers open, on reconnect storms, on daily SMS/email cost above budget. Dashboards per tenant for enterprise customers. Game days: kill a gateway node, pause a provider, replay a partition and verify no duplicates. questions Why write to the inbox store before pushing over WebSocket? options WebSockets are unreliable so the write is a backup The durable write is the source of truth; the push is a best-effort optimisation, and clients reconcile from the inbox on reconnect It is required by Kafka To calculate analytics answer explain Durable first, fast second: this is how at-least-once delivery over flaky connections becomes simple. What makes a replayed stream partition harmless to users? options Replays are forbidden Deterministic notification IDs (hash of event and user) make inbox writes idempotent Users do not notice duplicates Kafka deduplicates automatically answer explain Idempotent writes keyed by a stable identity absorb at-least-once delivery. How should a tenant-wide broadcast to a million users be handled? options One message to a 'broadcast' channel that every client subscribes to Expand to per-user records at a controlled rate in a separate lane, writing the inbox in batches, so interactive events are not del

- Design a B2B SaaS platform serving hundreds of organisations from shared infrastructure with strong isolation, per-tenant configuration and enterprise features (SSO, audit, data residency). - Choose a tenancy model deliberately and understand how it affects every layer: database, cache, queues, storage, observability and billing. - Build the controls that prevent the single worst SaaS incident: one tenant seeing another tenant's data. ::: Multi-Tenancy and Tenant Isolation; Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC and Resource-Level Access; chapters 1–10 of this part. :::

Functional : organisations (tenants) sign up self-serve or are provisioned by sales; each tenant has users, roles, projects and data; tenant admins manage members, SSO, API keys and billing; enterprise tiers require SSO/SAML, SCIM, audit log export, data residency (EU or US), custom retention, and optionally a dedicated database; public API with per-tenant keys and rate limits; integrations via webhooks; usage-based billing. Non-functional : 2,000 tenants from 5-seat startups to a 20,000-seat enterprise; 99.95% availability with per-tenant status visibility; zero cross-tenant data exposure (a hard requirement verified by tests, not a goal); noisy-neighbour protection so one tenant's load cannot degrade others beyond defined limits; tenant onboarding in under a minute for the shared tier; ability to move a tenant between tiers (shared → dedicated) and Regions; per-tenant cost attribution.

Tenant context is established once and enforced everywhere : the first middleware resolves the tenant from the host or token, verifies that the authenticated principal belongs to it, and places an immutable context on the request. Database access goes through a repository layer that opens the connection for the right pool and sets app.tenant id for RLS inside the transaction; cache, storage and queue clients take the context, not a raw ID, so forgetting the tenant is a compile-time or startup error rather than a data leak. Background jobs carry the tenant ID in the payload and re-establish the context before any I/O. Defence in depth against cross-tenant leaks : RLS as the floor (even a buggy query cannot return another tenant's rows); application-level scoping as the first line; tests that run the entire API as tenant A against data seeded for tenant B and assert zero results and zero 200s on B's object IDs; a canary tenant whose data is fingerprinted and alerted on if it ever appears in another tenant's responses or exports; database roles for the app that cannot bypass RLS and cannot access other tenants' dedicated databases. Provisioning as a workflow : creating a tenant is multi-step (registry row, database or RLS setup, migrations, default roles, billing customer, DNS for custom domains) and must be idempotent and resumable (Step Functions or a durable workflow library), with a "tenant status" that gates login until ready. Deprovisioning is the mirror image, with a grac

- One big tenant on the shared pool : a 20,000-seat tenant dwarfs others; indexes leading with tenant id become skewed; move such tenants to dedicated databases (tooling for live migration: dual-write or replicate, cut over with a short read-only window). - Connection explosion with database-per-tenant: 200 dedicated databases × pool of 10 × 20 app instances is 40,000 connections. Use a proxy (RDS Proxy or PgBouncer) per database, lazy pools that close idle tenant connections, and route tenants to app instance subsets. - Migration stragglers : a dedicated database fails a migration; the application must tolerate mixed versions during the window and the runner must surface the straggler loudly. - Cache key leaks : a developer forgets the tenant prefix; prevented by a cache client that derives keys from the context and fuzz tests that look for unprefixed keys. - Registry as a single point of failure : every request needs the tenant registry; cache it aggressively with a fallback to the last known good snapshot and a short TTL for changes. - Custom domains and certificates : hundreds of customer domains need validation and renewal; use ACM with DNS validation and automate CNAME instructions; monitor expiring validations.

Tenant isolation is the security property customers buy. Beyond the controls above: tenant-scoped admin roles (a tenant admin cannot see another tenant); support access to tenant data only through an audited, time-bound, consented "break glass" flow with tenant notification; per-tenant encryption keys for enterprise tiers so a tenant's departure can be enforced by key destruction; export and deletion APIs that are complete across every store; audit log export per tenant (SIEM integration); SSO enforcement options and session policy per tenant; API keys bound to tenant and scopes with rotation and last-used tracking; webhooks with per-tenant secrets; penetration tests specifically targeting cross-tenant access; threat model entries for "malicious tenant admin" and "compromised tenant user".

SLIs per tenant and global: availability, latency, error rate, job latency, API quota consumption; per-tenant status pages for enterprise; alerts when a single tenant's error rate deviates (their integration broke) separately from global alerts (we broke); cost per tenant monthly; migration fleet health; provisioning success rate and duration. Runbooks: throttle a tenant, move a tenant to dedicated, suspend for non-payment (read-only mode), rotate a tenant's keys, respond to a suspected cross-tenant leak (containment, evidence, notification obligations). questions Why use row-level security when the application already filters by tenant_id? options RLS is faster RLS is the floor: a query that forgets the filter still cannot return another tenant's rows, so one bug is not a breach RLS replaces indexes It is required by PostgreSQL answer explain Defence in depth: application scoping first, database enforcement as the backstop. A 20,000-seat tenant dominates the shared pool. What is the right move? options Add read replicas for everyone Migrate that tenant to a dedicated database using dual-write or replication with a short cutover, keeping the same application code Increase statement timeouts Shard by user ID answer explain The hybrid model exists exactly for this: shared by default, dedicated when size or requirements demand. How should support staff access a tenant's data? options With a shared admin password Through an audited, time-bound, consented break-glass flow with ten

Design the provisioning workflow as an idempotent state machine with compensation steps and failure handling for each stage. 3. Plan the live migration of a tenant from the shared pool to a dedicated database with a cutover window under 60 seconds; identify every store that holds tenant data.

t: Case Study: Production Application for a Small Client

t: Case Study: Production Application for a Small Client
h: Key decisions and the reasoning a client can follow
x: Containers on Fargate, not EC2 and not Kubernetes : no servers to patch, two tasks for resilience, rolling deploys with health checks. Kubernetes would add a control plane fee larger than the whole compute bill and an operational skill requirement the client does not have (Part VI chapter 14). A single EC2 instance would be cheaper but someone must patch it and it is a single point of failure; the Fargate premium buys away a class of operational work. Multi-AZ RDS even though it doubles the database cost : the client cannot perform a manual failover or restore at 02:00; Multi-AZ gives automatic failover and zero-downtime patching. The 35 USD per month is the cheapest insurance in the design. No microservices, one repository, one container : the application is small; a monolith with clear modules deploys in one step and is debuggable by one person. Background jobs (invoice sync, email digests) run as scheduled tasks from the same image with a different command. Identity : staff via the firm's existing Microsoft Entra tenant (OIDC), so joiners and leavers are handled by the IT generalist in a system they already use; clients via a managed identity provider (Cognito or similar) with passkeys and TOTP so that password storage, MFA and recovery are not your code to maintain. Clear role model: staff roles from Entra groups; clients scoped to their own organisation's records with resource-level checks and RLS. Document handling follows the file-upload case study in miniature: presig

The job's error handling retried indefinitely and inserted a staging row per attempt. t: Case Study: Highly Available Enterprise Application

x: - Split brain after a hasty failover : promoting Region B while Region A still accepts writes creates divergent data. The failover workflow fences the old writer first (revoke write access, stop the application's write path) and only then promotes; Aurora's managed failover handles the database side, the workflow handles the application side. - Replication lag spikes : a bulk job in Region A pushes lag to seconds, breaking read-your-writes for Region B users. Route a user's session to the writer Region for a short window after they write, or read from the writer for sensitive confirmations; throttle bulk jobs. - Direct Connect loss : both circuits share a provider segment nobody knew about. Diversity verified with the provider, VPN backup tested quarterly, and the façade's degradation mode exercised. - Correlated deploys : a bad release deployed to both Regions within minutes defeats the redundancy. Mandatory soak between Regions with automatic halt on SLO regression. - Control-plane dependencies : failover scripts that call APIs in the failing Region or depend on a global service in a degraded state. Keep failover tooling Region-independent and tested from both sides. - Certificate and DNS mistakes : the most mundane cause of enterprise outages. Automated renewal, expiry alarms at 30 and 7 days, DNS changes through the pipeline with review. - Month-end capacity : 3× traffic with batch jobs running; scheduled scaling ahead of time, batch windows separated from peak, and tests
